0.title: The God Who Redeems: The Book of Exodus
0.overview:
The message. Exodus tells how God rescues a people for himself and comes to live among them. Israel is enslaved in Egypt and can only cry out, and the LORD hears: “I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt … and I have come down to deliver them” (3:7–8). He breaks the power of Pharaoh and his gods, shelters his people under the blood of the Passover lamb and brings them through the sea. At Sinai he binds them to himself and gives them his law, not so that they might earn their freedom but because he has already given it. When they betray him almost at once, he forgives them and comes to live among them: “the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” (40:34). Salvation is the LORD’s from first to last, and its goal is God dwelling with his people.

Background: the writer. The book names no author, but it says that Moses wrote down events and laws (17:14; 24:4; 34:27), and Jesus calls it “the book of Moses” (Mark 12:26). Many modern scholars think the five books of Moses were compiled centuries later from several sources. Others answer that this remains a theory, with no surviving source behind it, and that the books’ own claims and the words of Christ point to Moses. This commentary holds that Moses wrote Exodus in substance, with possible later inspired touches such as updated place-names.

When and where. Exodus picks up where Genesis ends, with Jacob’s family of seventy settled in Goshen, in the eastern Nile delta (1:1–7). Israel lived in Egypt 430 years (12:40), long enough for a family to become a nation, and for a new king “who did not know Joseph” (1:8) to set them building his store cities (1:11). Egypt was one of the great powers of the ancient world, and its king, the Pharaoh, was held to be a god. The date is debated. The early date, about 1446 BC, comes from Scripture’s count of 480 years from the exodus to Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 6:1); the late date, about 1260 BC under Rameses II, rests on the city name Raamses (1:11) and the archaeology of Canaan. Faithful scholars hold both, and this commentary leaves the question open, since nothing in the book’s message hangs on it. Egypt left no record of the exodus, which is not surprising, since its monuments did not record defeats; but by about 1210 BC an Egyptian inscription, the Merneptah stele, names Israel as a people in Canaan.

The kind of writing. Exodus is history told to make God known: real events, chosen and shaped so that “the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD” (7:5), and Israel too. Into the story are set the Ten Commandments, the case laws of chapters 21–23, the Song of the Sea (chapter 15) and long instructions for the tabernacle. Read the laws as the terms of a covenant with a people already rescued, and the tabernacle chapters as a building that preaches how sinners may come near a holy God.

How the book makes its case. The book moves from building for Pharaoh to building for God, in three movements. First, redemption (chapters 1–18): God preserves a deliverer and calls him at the burning bush (chapters 1–4), revealing his name, “I AM WHO I AM” (3:14); the plagues (chapters 5–11) judge Pharaoh and “all the gods of Egypt” (12:12); Passover and the sea set Israel free (chapters 12–15); and in the wilderness God feeds a grumbling people (15:22–18:27). Second, covenant (chapters 19–24): God reminds them that he “bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself” (19:4), gives the commandments and seals the covenant with blood (24:8). Third, presence (chapters 25–40): God gives the pattern of the tabernacle (chapters 25–31); the golden calf nearly undoes everything, until Moses intercedes and God renews the covenant (chapters 32–34); then the tent is built “as the LORD had commanded Moses” (39:1), and the glory comes down (chapters 35–40). The order is the message: God saves first, then gives his law, and the goal of both is to dwell with his people.

Who hardened Pharaoh’s heart? Exodus says both that Pharaoh “hardened his heart” (8:15) and that “the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh” (9:12). Some read this as God confirming Pharaoh’s own choice; others see God’s purpose behind the whole, as Paul does when he quotes 9:16: “For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you” (Romans 9:17). This commentary’s view: God ordains all that comes to pass, Pharaoh’s hardening included, without being the author of sin. Pharaoh was no innocent forced against his will; he chose freely and was justly judged.

Did it happen as written? Some explain the plagues and the crossing as natural events, and read the “six hundred thousand men on foot” (12:37) as a far smaller company, since the Hebrew word for “thousand” can mean a clan. But the census silver of 38:25–26 matches 603,550 men at half a shekel each exactly, a sum that cannot be read as clans. This commentary takes the numbers as written, the fruit of the multiplying the book opens with (1:7), and the plagues, the crossing and the manna as real miracles. God used an east wind to drive back the sea (14:21), but the timing was his alone.

Where it leads: to Christ. The New Testament reads Exodus as the pattern of a greater rescue. At the transfiguration Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus “of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luke 9:31); the Greek word is exodos. He died at Passover: “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Israel’s firstborn lived because a lamb died in their place; we live because he died in ours. His cup is “the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20), echoing “the blood of the covenant” at Sinai (24:8). He is “the true bread from heaven” (John 6:32), and of the desert rock Paul says, “the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). Moses offered to be blotted out for the people’s sin (32:32) and could not be; Christ did die for his people, faithful “over God’s house as a son” where Moses was a servant (Hebrews 3:5–6). Above all, the God who came down to live in a tent came in person: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14), “full of grace and truth”, the glory proclaimed to Moses as “abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (34:6). These links are not forced; the New Testament draws them itself.

For us. Exodus shows what salvation is: not self-improvement but rescue, by a God who sees, comes down and pays the price. On Passover night the question was not whether a household was better than its neighbours, but whether the blood was on the door: “when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (12:13). We are safe for the same reason, under the blood of Christ. God did not give the law to slaves to set them free; he set them free and then gave them the law. We obey not to be saved but because we have been. And the goal is not only freedom but God himself: “If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here” (33:15). One day the redeemed will sing “the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb” (Revelation 15:3).

1.title: A People Multiplied in the Furnace
1.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob, each with his household:<sup>2</sup>Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah,<sup>3</sup>Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin,<sup>4</sup>Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher.<sup>5</sup>All the descendants of Jacob were seventy persons; Joseph was already in Egypt.<sup>6</sup>Then Joseph died, and all his brothers and all that generation.<sup>7</sup>But the people of Israel were fruitful and increased greatly; they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong, so that the land was filled with them.<sup>8</sup>Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.<sup>9</sup>And he said to his people, "Behold, the people of Israel are too many and too mighty for us.<sup>10</sup>Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, lest they multiply, and, if war breaks out, they join our enemies and fight against us and escape from the land."<sup>11</sup>Therefore they set taskmasters over them to afflict them with heavy burdens. They built for Pharaoh store cities, Pithom and Raamses.<sup>12</sup>But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and the more they spread abroad. And the Egyptians were in dread of the people of Israel.<sup>13</sup>So they ruthlessly made the people of Israel work as slaves<sup>14</sup>and made their lives bitter with hard service, in mortar and brick, and in all kinds of work in the field. In all their work they ruthlessly made them work as slaves.<sup>15</sup>Then the king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives, one of whom was named Shiphrah and the other Puah,<sup>16</sup>"When you serve as midwife to the Hebrew women and see them on the birthstool, if it is a son, you shall kill him, but if it is a daughter, she shall live."<sup>17</sup>But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them, but let the male children live.<sup>18</sup>So the king of Egypt called the midwives and said to them, "Why have you done this, and let the male children live?"<sup>19</sup>The midwives said to Pharaoh, "Because the Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they are vigorous and give birth before the midwife comes to them."<sup>20</sup>So God dealt well with the midwives. And the people multiplied and grew very strong.<sup>21</sup>And because the midwives feared God, he gave them families.<sup>22</sup>Then Pharaoh commanded all his people, "Every son that is born to the Hebrews you shall cast into the Nile, but you shall let every daughter live."
1.overview:
Where we are. Exodus opens where Genesis closed. Jacob’s family of seventy went down to Egypt to survive the famine, and Joseph, who saved them, is now dead with all his generation. Centuries have passed, and the family has become a people.

The message. God keeps his promise, and no power on earth can stop him. The blessing he spoke over the first man and repeated to Abraham, to be fruitful and multiply, is coming true in a foreign land, and when the greatest king on earth sets himself against it, every one of his schemes only feeds the growth he is trying to stop. And God’s quiet heroes are the people who fear him more than they fear the king.

Why it was said. Israel first heard this chapter as free people, tempted to forget what Egypt had been and to fear the nations around them (see the introduction). It told them where they came from: not from their own strength but from a God who made them grow under the whip.

How the chapter makes its case. First the promise is kept: the names of Jacob’s sons, the death of their generation, and a people “fruitful” and “multiplied” until the land is filled (vv. 1–7). Then the promise is opposed, and opposition fails three times. A king who will not acknowledge Joseph enslaves Israel, and the more he oppresses them, the more they multiply (vv. 8–14). He orders the midwives to kill the baby boys, but they fear God and let them live, and God gives them families (vv. 15–21). Finally he commands the whole nation to throw every Hebrew son into the Nile (v. 22), and the chapter ends in darkness, with the river where the deliverer will be found.

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern. The chapter shows God guarding the offspring through whom he will bless the world (Genesis 12:3), against a king who tries to kill the sons, just as Herod later tried to kill the child Jesus (Matthew 2:16). The ancient war of the serpent against the woman’s offspring (Genesis 3:15) runs through this chapter, and it reaches its end in Christ, the Son God called out of Egypt (Matthew 2:15) and the one in whom every promise is “Yes” (2 Corinthians 1:20).

For us. God’s purposes for his people do not depend on friendly governments or easy times; he can make them grow under pressure. The fear of God sets us free from the fear of people, and that fear grows best in those who know his forgiveness. No costly act of faithfulness, however hidden, is lost on him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God is keeping his promise: the family has become a nation. The book opens with the names of Jacob’s sons who went down to Egypt, a household of seventy, joining Exodus to the end of Genesis (vv. 1–5). Then one sentence records the death of Joseph and his whole generation (v. 6). The witnesses are gone, but the promise is not. In a foreign land God makes Israel “fruitful” so that they “multiplied” and “the land was filled with them” (v. 7), the very words of his first blessing on mankind (Genesis 1:28). What he said in Eden and swore to Abraham is coming true.
verseByVerse.theology:
From Family to Nation

The people multiply after Joseph and every other protector has died.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: God kept his promise to Abraham unseen, through generations when nothing seemed to happen.

Now: God knows his people by name, and his kingdom advances by ordinary generations more often than by dramatic intervention.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob, each with his household: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin, Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher. All the descendants of Jacob were seventy persons; Joseph was already in Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Exodus begins as the next chapter of Genesis: the God who promised Abraham a nation knows each of Jacob’s sons by name, and the whole family that went down to Egypt numbered seventy.

These are the names. The Hebrew opens with “and”, joining the book to the end of Genesis, and its Hebrew title is Shemot, “Names”. A list of names is not filler: God deals with people one by one, not as statistics (Isaiah 43:1). These are the twelve sons of Jacob, the fathers of Israel’s tribes.

Seventy persons. This was the whole family (Genesis 46:27). Seventy is also the number of the nations listed in Genesis 10: here is a small household that will carry blessing to the world (Genesis 12:3).

In everyday life. God knows your name and your family’s story. You are not lost in the crowd.

Textual note. Stephen says seventy-five (Acts 7:14), following the Greek Old Testament, which counts five more descendants of Joseph. The Hebrew counts seventy. These are different ways of counting, not a contradiction.
verseByVerse.note: Exodus means “going out.”

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joseph died, and all his brothers and all that generation. But the people of Israel were fruitful and increased greatly; they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong, so that the land was filled with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph and his whole generation die, but God’s promise does not: he makes Israel grow until they fill the land. The promise never depended on any one protector, and God goes on keeping it long after the witnesses are gone.

Then Joseph died. With Joseph dies every witness to God’s providence in Genesis. The new generation has only the promise.

Fruitful and increased greatly. The five verbs of verse 7 (fruitful, increased, multiplied, grew strong, filled) echo creation (Genesis 1:28) and the promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:2; 15:5). God is keeping his word in a foreign land, in Goshen in the eastern Nile delta, where Jacob’s family settled (Genesis 47:27).

What it does not mean. Not that numbers prove God’s blessing; Israel will soon be enslaved while still growing. Blessing and suffering run side by side.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-14 — The Pharaoh Who Did Not Know Joseph
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One sentence swings the chapter from blessing to bondage, and Pharaoh’s scheme fails on the spot. A new king who will not acknowledge Joseph looks at God’s blessing on Israel and sees only a security threat (vv. 8–10). He sets taskmasters over them and makes them build his store cities, but the more they are oppressed, the more they multiply, and it is Egypt that comes to dread its slaves (vv. 11–12). So he tightens the grip, and the text dwells on the ruthless labour and the bitterness of their lives (vv. 13–14). God sees it all, and will say so (3:7).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pharaoh Who Did Not Know Joseph

A new king refuses Egypt's debt to Joseph and calls God's blessing a security problem. Forced labour follows, and fails.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the bitter herbs of Passover would recall this labour every year (12:8). Now: pressure has never yet wiped out the people of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new king refuses to honour what Egypt owed Joseph, and blessing turns to bondage.

There arose a new king over Egypt. Perhaps a king from a new dynasty. The narrator never names him: the most powerful man on earth stays anonymous, while two slave midwives are named (v. 15).

Did not know Joseph. The Hebrew verb “know” means to acknowledge, to recognise a relationship, not merely to have heard of. Egypt had survived the famine through a Hebrew (Genesis 41), and this king refused to honour it.

In everyday life. Where gratitude is forgotten, hostility often follows. Remember what you owe to God, who has done far more for you than Joseph did for Egypt.

Where Christians differ: the date of the exodus. Some date it about 1446 BC, from 1 Kings 6:1 (480 years before Solomon’s temple). Others date it about 1260 BC, from the city name Raamses (v. 11) and archaeology. This commentary’s view: both views are held by faithful scholars. The exodus was a real event; its exact date is less certain than the fact.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to his people, "Behold, the people of Israel are too many and too mighty for us. Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, lest they multiply, and, if war breaks out, they join our enemies and fight against us and escape from the land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh looks at God’s blessing on Israel and sees only a threat to be managed, and he plots to keep them down. The fruitfulness that fulfils God’s promise looks, to unbelief, like a security problem.

Let us deal shrewdly with them. To “deal shrewdly” is to act with calculating, self-protecting cunning. It echoes the crafty serpent (Genesis 3:1), and “Come, let us” echoes the builders of Babel (Genesis 11:3–4): human schemes against God’s purposes.

They join our enemies. The fear made sense to him, for Goshen lay on Egypt’s eastern frontier, the route of any invader from Canaan. He wants their labour, not their absence; yet his fear that they will “escape from the land” foretells exactly what God will do.

Where the sin lies. Wise planning is not the sin here. The sin is planning against God and against the weak (Psalm 2:1–4).

In everyday life. When the world treats Christian growth as a threat, do not be surprised. Pray, and keep living faithfully.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore they set taskmasters over them to afflict them with heavy burdens. They built for Pharaoh store cities, Pithom and Raamses. But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and the more they spread abroad. And the Egyptians were in dread of the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh enslaves Israel to crush them, but the more they are oppressed, the more they multiply. He is fighting God’s word, and every measure backfires.

They set taskmasters over them to afflict them. Taskmasters were overseers of forced labour gangs. To “afflict” is to humble and crush, the very word God used when he foretold this to Abraham (Genesis 15:13). Even the suffering was within his word.

Store cities. Supply depots for grain and military stores.

The more they multiplied. God turns the whip into the means of growth. The Egyptians come to feel a sickened dread of Israel: the powerful empire is afraid of its powerless slaves.

What it does not mean. Not that suffering is good in itself, nor that God sends it without care. He uses it, as he will later use persecution to spread the church (Acts 8:1–4).
verseByVerse.note: Pithom and Raamses were store cities in the eastern Nile delta.

verseByVerse.quote: So they ruthlessly made the people of Israel work as slaves and made their lives bitter with hard service, in mortar and brick, and in all kinds of work in the field. In all their work they ruthlessly made them work as slaves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt makes Israel’s life bitter with crushing labour, and Scripture records the suffering in full rather than hurrying past it. God does not treat his people’s pain as unimportant; he sees it and records it (3:7).

Ruthlessly. The Hebrew word (perek) means harsh, crushing severity, work meant to break a person, and it opens and closes the description. The law later forbids Israel to rule anyone this way (Leviticus 25:43, 46).

In mortar and brick. Mud bricks mixed with straw were the basic building material of Egypt, and making them was the work of slaves and labour gangs.

Pharaoh’s economy never rests. Egypt’s system had one measure of a person: how many bricks he made. The Old Testament scholar Walter Brueggemann has argued that Pharaoh stands for every economy of anxious, endless production, in which there is never enough and no one may stop. We think we left Egypt long ago, yet many of us live by the same measure, only now we need no taskmaster: we check the numbers ourselves, feel worthless on unproductive days, and treat rest as something to be earned. The idol beneath it is the belief that my worth is my output, and it is a hard master, because the quota is never met.

A Master who reverses Pharaoh’s values. The God of Exodus sees the bricks and the bitterness, and the whole book tells how he brought a people out of that house of slavery to serve him instead. Pharaoh used people to build his name, but “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). He values us by his grace, not by our output.

In everyday life. If your work feels crushing, tell God honestly. He sees. And if you manage others, never rule them harshly; you too have a Master in heaven (Colossians 4:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15-22 — The Fear of God Versus the Fear of Pharaoh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When oppression fails, Pharaoh turns to murder, and two women who fear God defeat him. He secretly orders the Hebrew midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, to kill every newborn boy at the moment of birth (vv. 15–16). They fear God more than the king and let the boys live (v. 17). Called to account, they give Pharaoh an answer that protects the children (vv. 18–19), and God deals well with them, giving them families of their own while Israel keeps growing (vv. 20–21). Then the mask comes off: Pharaoh commands his whole nation to throw every Hebrew son into the Nile (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Fear of God Versus the Fear of Pharaoh

Two midwives who fear God undo the king's plan, and God deals well with them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: two women with no power undid the king's plan. Now: "We must obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29); the fear of God is where courage comes from.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives, one of whom was named Shiphrah and the other Puah, "When you serve as midwife to the Hebrew women and see them on the birthstool, if it is a son, you shall kill him, but if it is a daughter, she shall live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When forced labour fails, Pharaoh turns to murder, ordering the Hebrew midwives to kill every newborn boy at the moment of birth.

The Hebrew midwives. Midwives helped at childbirth, a respected profession, and the two named may have led a larger group. Their names, “Beauty” and perhaps “Splendour”, are Semitic.

On the birthstool. Pharaoh strikes when mother and child are most helpless.

If it is a daughter, she shall live. Boys would grow into fighters; girls could be absorbed into Egypt. Behind Pharaoh, as behind Herod (Matthew 2:16), stands the enemy who tries to destroy the promised offspring (Genesis 3:15; Revelation 12:4). He failed here, and he failed at Bethlehem, where the child he most wanted dead was carried to safety, in Egypt of all places (Matthew 2:13–15).

The worth of every life. The text treats the killing of infants as monstrous, and gives no support to the idea that unborn or newborn lives are less valuable.

Uncertain wording. “Birthstool” is literally “the two stones”, a rare word. It most likely means the stones or bricks on which a woman crouched to give birth, as known from Egypt, though some have taken it of the child’s body. And “Hebrew midwives” can mean midwives who were Hebrews or midwives to the Hebrews. Their Semitic names make the first more likely, and most take them as Hebrews.

verseByVerse.quote: But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them, but let the male children live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The midwives fear God more than the king, and they refuse to kill the boys. They fear the God they cannot see more than the king they can.

The midwives feared God. This fear is not terror but reverent awe that takes God more seriously than anyone else, the root of wisdom (Proverbs 1:7).

Did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them. The first recorded refusal in Scripture to obey a ruler’s wicked order, and God honours it.

What it does not mean. Not a licence to disobey authorities whenever we disagree. Christians are to be subject to rulers (Romans 13:1). But when a ruler commands sin, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

In everyday life. Is there a command at work or in your culture that would require you to do wrong? The fear of God sets you free from the fear of people, and it grows not from willpower but from knowing the God who forgives (Psalm 130:4).

verseByVerse.quote: So the king of Egypt called the midwives and said to them, "Why have you done this, and let the male children live?" The midwives said to Pharaoh, "Because the Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they are vigorous and give birth before the midwife comes to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Summoned before Pharaoh, the midwives give an answer that protects the children: Hebrew women give birth before they arrive.

Why have you done this? Two slave women answer to the king of Egypt, knowing that defying him could cost their lives.

They are vigorous. Literally “lively”, full of life. Their answer may have been partly true, but it was meant to mislead.

In everyday life. Courage under pressure matters. Pray for wisdom to protect the vulnerable without needing to deceive.

Where Christians differ: did they lie, and was it right? Some (Augustine, Calvin) hold it was a lie, a real sin that God forgave while rewarding their faith. Others argue that deceiving a murderer to save life is not the sin of lying, since he had no right to the truth. This commentary’s view: God rewards their fear of him and their protection of life (v. 20), and the second view is the more likely: deceiving those bent on murder is not the lie the ninth commandment forbids. Rahab stood in the same place, and is honoured for her faith (Hebrews 11:31). Ordinary lying is still sin (Colossians 3:9).

verseByVerse.quote: So God dealt well with the midwives. And the people multiplied and grew very strong. And because the midwives feared God, he gave them families.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God honours the midwives who feared him, giving them families of their own, and Israel keeps multiplying. He does not remove the danger, but he deals well with them in it.

He gave them families. Literally “made them houses”, households and descendants. Those who protected Israel’s families are given families of their own. Meanwhile Pharaoh’s second plan fails like the first.

What it does not mean. This is not a promise that obedience always brings children or material reward, which would wound many faithful people. It shows that God sees and honours those who fear him (Hebrews 6:10): no act of costly faithfulness goes unnoticed by him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh commanded all his people, "Every son that is born to the Hebrews you shall cast into the Nile, but you shall let every daughter live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh makes murder public policy, commanding his whole nation to throw every Hebrew baby boy into the Nile. The chapter ends in darkness, but not in defeat.

The Nile. Egypt’s source of water, food and life, worshipped as a god (Hapi). Pharaoh turns the river of life into a grave. Later the Nile will turn to blood (7:20), and Egypt’s army will drown (14:28).

You shall let every daughter live. Pharaoh underestimates women: it is women who will save Moses (2:1–10).

Looking ahead. In the next verses the same river will carry the deliverer in a basket (2:3). God is already at work.

In everyday life. When evil seems to have the last word, keep reading. Pray for children at risk today, and for those who protect them.

1.theology:
The faithfulness of God to his promises. Israel's growth is God keeping his covenant with Abraham (Gen. 12, 15). No empire can cancel what God has sworn. The whole book rests on this: God remembers.

The fear of God. Shiphrah and Puah show that reverence for God is the root of moral courage. To fear God is to be set free from the tyranny of the fear of man.

Suffering and providence. God's people are not promised ease but his presence. Their affliction is real, yet God so rules over it that it serves his purposes and cannot defeat them.
1.examples:
Then: A favoured immigrant people became despised slaves under a regime that feared their numbers and sought their destruction, and was met by the quiet defiance of God-fearing women.

Now: Christians under pressure should not be surprised; the church has often grown where it is persecuted. We are called, like the midwives, to a higher allegiance, and the Spirit who lives in believers is the one who frees us from fear of what the powerful threaten (2 Timothy 1:7).

keyVerse.quote: But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and the more they spread abroad.
keyVerse.note: This verse states the theme of the whole chapter. Pharaoh’s power is real and cruel, but it is fighting against the word of God, and every blow he strikes only spreads what he is trying to crush. The same pattern runs through the history of the church, and it rests on a God who keeps his promises.

1.reflection:
Verse 7 echoes God’s first blessing on mankind (Genesis 1:28) and his promise to Abraham. How does it help to see Israel’s growth in Egypt as God keeping his word, even while they are slaves? Where do you need to remember that his promises do not depend on easy circumstances?

Pharaoh looked at God’s blessing on Israel and saw a threat (vv. 9–10). Why does the world sometimes treat the growth of God’s people as dangerous, and how should Christians respond when they are viewed that way?

The midwives “feared God” more than they feared the king (v. 17). What does the fear of God mean, and how does it free us from the fear of people? Is there an area of your life where you are tempted to obey people rather than God?

The chapter ends with a decree to kill every Hebrew son (v. 22), yet God is already at work. How does the story of Jesus, who was also threatened as a baby by a king, help us trust God when evil seems to have the last word?

2.title: Drawn Out of the Water
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Now a man from the house of Levi went and took as his wife a Levite woman.<sup>2</sup>The woman conceived and bore a son, and when she saw that he was a fine child, she hid him three months.<sup>3</sup>When she could hide him no longer, she took for him a basket made of bulrushes and daubed it with bitumen and pitch. She put the child in it and placed it among the reeds by the river bank.<sup>4</sup>And his sister stood at a distance to know what would be done to him.<sup>5</sup>Now the daughter of Pharaoh came down to bathe at the river, while her young women walked beside the river. She saw the basket among the reeds and sent her servant woman, and she took it.<sup>6</sup>When she opened it, she saw the child, and behold, the baby was crying. She took pity on him and said, "This is one of the Hebrews' children."<sup>7</sup>Then his sister said to Pharaoh's daughter, "Shall I go and call you a nurse from the Hebrew women to nurse the child for you?"<sup>8</sup>And Pharaoh's daughter said to her, "Go." So the girl went and called the child's mother.<sup>9</sup>And Pharaoh's daughter said to her, "Take this child away and nurse him for me, and I will give you your wages." So the woman took the child and nursed him.<sup>10</sup>When the child grew older, she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, "Because," she said, "I drew him out of the water."<sup>11</sup>One day, when Moses had grown up, he went out to his people and looked on their burdens, and he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his people.<sup>12</sup>He looked this way and that, and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.<sup>13</sup>When he went out the next day, behold, two Hebrews were struggling together. And he said to the man in the wrong, "Why do you strike your companion?"<sup>14</sup>He answered, "Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you mean to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?" Then Moses was afraid, and thought, "Surely the thing is known."<sup>15</sup>When Pharaoh heard of it, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from Pharaoh and stayed in the land of Midian. And he sat down by a well.<sup>16</sup>Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters, and they came and drew water and filled the troughs to water their father's flock.<sup>17</sup>The shepherds came and drove them away, but Moses stood up and saved them, and watered their flock.<sup>18</sup>When they came home to their father Reuel, he said, "How is it that you have come home so soon today?"<sup>19</sup>They said, "An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds and even drew water for us and watered the flock."<sup>20</sup>He said to his daughters, "Then where is he? Why have you left the man? Call him, that he may eat bread."<sup>21</sup>And Moses was content to dwell with the man, and he gave Moses his daughter Zipporah.<sup>22</sup>She gave birth to a son, and he called his name Gershom, for he said, "I have been a sojourner in a foreign land."<sup>23</sup>During those many days the king of Egypt died, and the people of Israel groaned because of their slavery and cried out for help. Their cry for rescue from slavery came up to God.<sup>24</sup>And God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.<sup>25</sup>God saw the people of Israel—and God knew.
2.overview:
Where we are. Pharaoh has ordered every Hebrew baby boy thrown into the Nile (1:22). Forced labour and secret murder have failed to stop Israel’s growth, and now the whole nation of Egypt is enlisted in killing.

The message. God is at work long before anyone can see him, and the rescue is his, not ours. He saves the deliverer through a mother’s faith, a sister’s watch and the pity of Pharaoh’s own daughter, turning the tyrant’s decree and household against his plan. When the grown Moses tries to save Israel in his own strength, he fails and flees. Then the chapter ends with God himself stepping forward: he heard, remembered, saw and knew.

Why it was said. Israel needed to know that their deliverer was God’s gift, not a self-made hero, and that their rescue rested on God’s covenant with their fathers, not on their own goodness (see the introduction). Every generation that groaned under hardship could take heart from the last three verses.

How the chapter makes its case. A Levite mother hides her son, then places him in a basket among the reeds of the very river meant to drown him, and Pharaoh’s daughter draws him out, pays his mother to nurse him and names him Moses (vv. 1–10). Grown up, Moses goes out to his people, kills an Egyptian, is rejected by a Hebrew (“Who made you a prince and a judge over us?”) and flees to Midian (vv. 11–15). There, at a well, he rescues again, this time without violence, marries and settles as “a sojourner in a foreign land” (vv. 16–22). Meanwhile Israel’s cry goes up, and God hears and remembers his covenant (vv. 23–25).

Where it leads. By pattern and by covenant. Moses is a baby spared from a murderous king, a deliverer first rejected by his own people, an exile who will return to save them: each is a faint outline of Jesus, spared from Herod (Matthew 2:13–15) and rejected by his own (John 1:11), and Stephen draws the line himself (Acts 7:35). But Moses’ failure also shows the need: Israel’s rescue would never come by a man’s fist. It came by the God who remembers his covenant, the covenant he kept in full when he sent his Son, “to remember his holy covenant, the oath that he swore to our father Abraham” (Luke 1:72–73).

For us. God is often most at work when he seems most silent. He uses ordinary faithfulness, a parent’s care or a stranger’s meal, and he does not need our strength to save. If all you can bring him is a groan, bring it: he hears it, for the sake of his Son.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-10 — The Basket on the Nile
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Against a death decree, God begins his rescue with a baby, and turns the tyrant’s own plan upside down. A Levite couple have a son, and his mother, by faith, hides him (vv. 1–2). When she can hide him no longer, she places him in a waterproofed basket among the reeds of the Nile, the river meant to be his grave, while his sister watches (vv. 3–4). Pharaoh’s own daughter finds him and takes pity (vv. 5–6). His sister arranges for his mother to nurse him, paid by Pharaoh’s household (vv. 7–9), and the princess adopts him and names him Moses (v. 10). No miracle is reported, yet every turn is God’s.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Basket on the Nile

The deliverer is saved through the waters meant for his death, in an ark like Noah's, by the tyrant's own daughter.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Hebrews calls the parents' hiding faith (Heb. 11:23). Now: God's rescues are often built out of small, ordinary things: a basket, a sister, a crying baby, each of them needed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a man from the house of Levi went and took as his wife a Levite woman. The woman conceived and bore a son, and when she saw that he was a fine child, she hid him three months.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s answer to Pharaoh’s death decree begins quietly, with a Levite marriage, a baby, and parents who trust God enough to hide him.

A man from the house of Levi. The parents come from the tribe that will later carry the priesthood, but they are not yet named: at this point they are ordinary slaves.

A fine child. Literally “good” (tov), the word of Genesis 1 (“God saw that it was good”). Stephen calls him “beautiful in God’s sight” (Acts 7:20). His beauty moved his parents to act, but it is not what made him valuable: every child bears God’s image (Genesis 9:6).

She hid him. Hebrews 11:23 calls this faith: his parents were not afraid of the king’s edict. They trusted God and defied the order to kill.

In everyday life. God’s great works often begin in ordinary homes, with faithful parents protecting a child.
verseByVerse.note: Moses’ parents are named later as Amram and Jochebed.

verseByVerse.quote: When she could hide him no longer, she took for him a basket made of bulrushes and daubed it with bitumen and pitch. She put the child in it and placed it among the reeds by the river bank. And his sister stood at a distance to know what would be done to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When she can hide him no longer, his mother entrusts him to God in a little waterproofed ark among the reeds, and his sister watches.

A basket made of bulrushes. The word for the basket (tevah) is used elsewhere only of Noah’s ark. Both carried God’s chosen safely through waters meant for death. And the reeds (suph) look ahead: Israel will later cross the yam suph, the “Sea of Reeds” (13:18).

She put the child in it. The mother has not given up. She does put her son in the river, as Pharaoh ordered, but in an ark, trusting God with the outcome.

His sister stood at a distance. The sister is probably Miriam (15:20). Faith does what it can, then watches and waits.

In everyday life. When you have done what you can for someone you love, entrust them to God and keep watching in hope.
verseByVerse.note: The basket was made of papyrus reeds (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the daughter of Pharaoh came down to bathe at the river, while her young women walked beside the river. She saw the basket among the reeds and sent her servant woman, and she took it. When she opened it, she saw the child, and behold, the baby was crying. She took pity on him and said, "This is one of the Hebrews' children."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of all people in Egypt, it is the daughter of the man who ordered the killing who finds the crying baby and chooses mercy. This is providence: God’s quiet direction of ordinary events, and nothing in the account calls it coincidence.

The baby was crying. At this moment God’s weapon against Egypt is a crying baby (1 Corinthians 1:27).

She took pity on him. She knows the decree and recognises him as one of the Hebrews’ children, yet she takes pity on him. God can move any heart (Proverbs 21:1), and he was arranging events for his people’s good long before they knew it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then his sister said to Pharaoh's daughter, "Shall I go and call you a nurse from the Hebrew women to nurse the child for you?" And Pharaoh's daughter said to her, "Go." So the girl went and called the child's mother. And Pharaoh's daughter said to her, "Take this child away and nurse him for me, and I will give you your wages." So the woman took the child and nursed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Miriam brings the baby’s own mother as his nurse, and Pharaoh’s household pays her to raise her own son. God turns the death decree upside down (Psalm 2:4).

Shall I go and call you a nurse? Wet-nurses were common for royal children, and babies were nursed for two or three years.

I will give you your wages. In those early years his mother could teach him that he was a Hebrew and who Israel’s God was. Egypt would give him his education; his mother gave him his identity (Hebrews 11:24–25).

What it does not mean. Not that Miriam and Jochebed deceived the princess. The princess knew he was Hebrew (v. 6); Scripture does not say she knew who the nurse was.

In everyday life. Parents and grandparents: the early years matter. Teach children who God is, trusting him, not your skill, to give them faith.

verseByVerse.quote: When the child grew older, she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, "Because," she said, "I drew him out of the water."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The child is handed over a second time and adopted into Pharaoh’s household, and the one drawn out of the water will one day draw Israel out through water.

When the child grew older. After weaning, Jochebed keeps her word and brings him to the princess: a second, harder surrender. As a royal son he was “instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians” (Acts 7:22), yet privilege did not erase his identity.

She named him Moses. The name sounds like the Hebrew mashah, “draw out”.

Another child spared from a king. Jesus too was an infant spared from a king who killed baby boys, and was called out of Egypt (Matthew 2:13–15). Moses is the shadow, a faint outline in advance; Christ is the true deliverer.

Uncertain wording. “Moses” is most likely an Egyptian name meaning “son” or “born of” (as in Thutmose), which an Egyptian princess would naturally give, and which happens to sound like the Hebrew for “draw out”. Whether she spoke the Hebrew pun herself or the narrator brings it out is not certain. The Hebrew form Mosheh strictly means “one who draws out” rather than “one drawn out”, which may hint at his future task.
verseByVerse.note: “Moses” sounds like the Hebrew for “draw out” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11-22 — The Failed Deliverer in Exile
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses tries to deliver Israel in his own strength, fails and flees, and God begins to train him in the wilderness. Grown up, he goes out to his people, sees an Egyptian beating a Hebrew and kills him in secret (vv. 11–12). The next day his own people reject him (“Who made you a prince and a judge over us?”), and Moses is afraid (vv. 13–14). Pharaoh seeks his life, so he flees to Midian (v. 15). There, at a well, he rescues the priest’s daughters, this time without violence (vv. 16–17), is welcomed to a meal (vv. 18–20), marries Zipporah and names his son for his exile (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Failed Deliverer in Exile

Moses' own attempt at deliverance ends in rejection and exile, where God will make a shepherd of him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Stephen pointed out that the man Israel rejected was the one God had appointed (Acts 7:35). Now: seeing a wrong that God also sees does not give us the right to act in God's place, and long hidden years are where God shapes a man.

verseByVerse.quote: One day, when Moses had grown up, he went out to his people and looked on their burdens, and he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his people. He looked this way and that, and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses chooses his own people and their suffering, but tries to deliver them in his own way: he kills an Egyptian in secret.

He went out to his people. Grown up (Stephen says forty years old, Acts 7:23), Moses sees their burdens with sympathy, as God himself will “see” their affliction (3:7). Hebrews 11:24–26 calls it faith: he chose to suffer with God’s people rather than enjoy “the fleeting pleasures of sin”.

He looked this way and that. He checks for witnesses but not for God’s direction, and he hides the body.

In everyday life. Zeal for justice is not wrong, but good causes can tempt us to wrong methods. Ask not only “Is this right?” but “Is this God’s way?”

Where Christians differ: murder or justice? Some see a justified rescue: Stephen says Moses supposed his brothers would see that God was saving them by his hand (Acts 7:25). Others see a sinful killing. This commentary’s view: his compassion and his calling were real, but his method and timing were his own. The secrecy shows he knew it was not lawful. God would later deliver Israel by his power, not Moses’ fist.

verseByVerse.quote: When he went out the next day, behold, two Hebrews were struggling together. And he said to the man in the wrong, "Why do you strike your companion?" He answered, "Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you mean to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?" Then Moses was afraid, and thought, "Surely the thing is known."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses tries words instead of force, and his own people reject him, so the would-be deliverer becomes afraid.

Who made you a prince and a judge over us? The question mocks him, yet God will in fact make him Israel’s ruler and judge (18:13; Acts 7:35). Like Joseph before him and Christ after him, Moses is rejected first by his own people (John 1:11).

Then Moses was afraid. The child whose parents were not afraid of the king is now afraid for his life. The fear of man is a snare (Proverbs 29:25).

In everyday life. If you are rejected when you try to make peace, you walk the road of Moses and of Christ. Keep loving.

verseByVerse.quote: When Pharaoh heard of it, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from Pharaoh and stayed in the land of Midian. And he sat down by a well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In one day Moses loses position, home and plans, and flees to Midian, where he sits down by a well.

Moses fled from Pharaoh. Midian was a desert region east of the Gulf of Aqaba, beyond Egypt’s reach. (Hebrews 11:27 says he left Egypt “not being afraid of the anger of the king”, probably looking ahead to the exodus itself.)

He sat down by a well. In Genesis, wells are where God’s story turns, as with Rebekah (Genesis 24) and Rachel (Genesis 29): something new is about to begin.

In everyday life. When your plans collapse, God has not lost track of you. The wilderness can be his school.
verseByVerse.note: The Midianites descended from Abraham through Keturah (Genesis 25:1–2).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters, and they came and drew water and filled the troughs to water their father's flock. The shepherds came and drove them away, but Moses stood up and saved them, and watered their flock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses rescues the oppressed again, this time without violence, and then serves them. His instinct for justice is God-given; it is being trained.

The priest of Midian. He is Reuel, also called Jethro (3:1), who will later bless Israel’s God (18:10–11).

Moses stood up and saved them. The verb yasha is the root of the names Joshua and Jesus. He drives off the bullying shepherds and then waters their flock.

In everyday life. Who is being pushed aside near you? Stand up for them, and then help practically, as the God who saw Israel’s affliction came down for you.

verseByVerse.quote: When they came home to their father Reuel, he said, "How is it that you have come home so soon today?" They said, "An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds and even drew water for us and watered the flock." He said to his daughters, "Then where is he? Why have you left the man? Call him, that he may eat bread."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejected by his own people and taken for an Egyptian by strangers, Moses is welcomed to a meal, and God feeds his fugitive servant through an ordinary kindness.

An Egyptian delivered us. Moses belongs nowhere: too Hebrew for Egypt, too Egyptian for Midian.

Call him, that he may eat bread. Sharing a meal meant welcome and protection.

In everyday life. Invite someone to eat. You may be God’s provision for a lonely stranger (Hebrews 13:2).
verseByVerse.note: Moses’ father-in-law is called Reuel here and Jethro elsewhere; men often had more than one name or title.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses was content to dwell with the man, and he gave Moses his daughter Zipporah. She gave birth to a son, and he called his name Gershom, for he said, "I have been a sojourner in a foreign land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who left a palace settles contentedly as a shepherd and names his son for his homelessness.

Moses was content to dwell with the man. He lives quietly as a shepherd for about forty years (Acts 7:29–30). He marries Zipporah (“bird”), a Midianite, a detail that will matter later (Numbers 12:1).

I have been a sojourner in a foreign land. “Gershom” sounds like the Hebrew for “sojourner”: a resident foreigner without the rights of a citizen.

Not wasted years. God was preparing a shepherd to lead his flock through the wilderness (Psalm 77:20).

In everyday life. If you are in a long, quiet season, God is not idle. Believers are sojourners too, looking for a better country (Hebrews 11:13–16).
verseByVerse.note: “Gershom” sounds like the Hebrew for “sojourner” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23-25 — God Heard, Remembered, Saw, Knew
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king dies, but nothing improves, and God himself steps into the story. Israel’s groaning under slavery is not described as polished prayer, but their cry “came up to God” (v. 23). Then, for the first time in the book, God becomes the subject of the sentences. He heard their groaning, remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, saw the people of Israel and knew (vv. 24–25). These four verbs turn the whole book. The rescue that follows rests not on Israel’s merit or on the ruler of Egypt, but on God’s faithfulness to his promise.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Heard, Remembered, Saw, Knew

God answers groaning out of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the rescue rests on a promise to men long dead, not on Israel's worth. Now: God counts even wordless groaning as prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: During those many days the king of Egypt died, and the people of Israel groaned because of their slavery and cried out for help. Their cry for rescue from slavery came up to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king dies, but slavery goes on, and Israel’s groaning rises to God. Tyrants die and tyranny continues: hope does not lie in a change of ruler.

The king of Egypt died. His death also clears the way for Moses to return, for “all the men who were seeking your life are dead” (4:19).

Cried out for help. This is not polished prayer but the cry of pain. The text does not say they called on God by name, yet the cry “came up to God”. God does not answer only eloquent or theologically correct prayers; he hears wordless groans (Romans 8:26).

In everyday life. If all you can manage today is a groan, bring it to God. He hears.

verseByVerse.quote: And God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob. God saw the people of Israel—and God knew.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God hears, remembers his covenant, sees and knows: after two chapters of silence, he becomes the subject of every verb, and the book turns.

God remembered his covenant. For God to “remember” does not mean he had forgotten; in Scripture it means he acts on his promise (Genesis 8:1; Luke 1:72). His covenant is a binding relationship sealed by his oath: he had promised Abraham that his offspring would be enslaved four hundred years and then brought out with great possessions (Genesis 15:13–14). Rescue rests on God’s promise, not Israel’s merit.

And God knew. The verb has no object in the Hebrew: he knew everything about them, personally and with care.

What it does not mean. Not that God was absent before. He was at work in midwives, a basket and a princess. Now he acts openly.

Still true. Because of his covenant in Christ, he hears, remembers, sees and knows his people still.

2.theology:
Providence. An unseen hand governs every detail, bending Pharaoh's own household toward Israel's rescue.

The weakness of human effort. Moses' violent attempt at deliverance, made too soon and in his own strength, must fail so that the rescue is plainly God's. Salvation is the LORD's, not the deliverer's.

Covenant remembrance. God's saving acts flow from his faithfulness to his covenant, not from Israel's worthiness.
2.examples:
Then: Under a death decree, God preserved a deliverer through the very waters meant to kill him, raised him in the enemy’s house, then drove him into forty years of obscurity to prepare him.

Now: God still uses long, hidden seasons to empty us of self-confidence and fit us for his service. And he still hears the cry of his afflicted people; our groaning is never lost in the silence.

keyVerse.quote: And God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.
keyVerse.note: After two chapters in which God has worked out of sight, he becomes the subject of the story. The verse shows what moves him to save: not Israel’s goodness or eloquence but his own promise. Everything that follows in Exodus is God acting on this remembering.

2.reflection:
Moses’ mother, his sister and Pharaoh’s daughter each played a part in saving him (vv. 1–10). How do you see God working through ordinary people and events in this story? Where can you look back and see his hand in your own life, even when you did not notice it at the time?

Moses had real compassion for his people, but he tried to deliver them his own way (vv. 11–15). Why is it so tempting to pursue good goals by our own methods? How can we tell the difference between zeal for God and acting in our own strength?

Moses spent about forty years as a shepherd in Midian, calling himself “a sojourner in a foreign land” (v. 22). How might God use a long, quiet or disappointing season to prepare someone? What does it mean for Christians to live as sojourners?

Israel’s cry was a groan, not a polished prayer, yet God heard, remembered, saw and knew (vv. 23–25). What does this teach you about prayer in hard times, and how does Jesus, who was himself rejected and saved by God, give us confidence that God hears us?

3.title: I AM WHO I AM
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Moses was keeping the flock of his father-in-law, Jethro, the priest of Midian, and he led his flock to the west side of the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God.<sup>2</sup>And the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush. He looked, and behold, the bush was burning, yet it was not consumed.<sup>3</sup>And Moses said, "I will turn aside to see this great sight, why the bush is not burned."<sup>4</sup>When the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the bush, "Moses, Moses!" And he said, "Here I am."<sup>5</sup>Then he said, "Do not come near; take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground."<sup>6</sup>And he said, "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." And Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God.<sup>7</sup>Then the LORD said, "I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters. I know their sufferings,<sup>8</sup>and I have come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians and to bring them up out of that land to a good and broad land, a land flowing with milk and honey, to the place of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.<sup>9</sup>And now, behold, the cry of the people of Israel has come to me, and I have also seen the oppression with which the Egyptians oppress them.<sup>10</sup>Come, I will send you to Pharaoh that you may bring my people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt."<sup>11</sup>But Moses said to God, "Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?"<sup>12</sup>He said, "But I will be with you, and this shall be the sign for you, that I have sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain."<sup>13</sup>Then Moses said to God, "If I come to the people of Israel and say to them, 'The God of your fathers has sent me to you,' and they ask me, 'What is his name?' what shall I say to them?"<sup>14</sup>God said to Moses, "I AM WHO I AM." And he said, "Say this to the people of Israel: 'I AM has sent me to you.'"<sup>15</sup>God also said to Moses, "Say this to the people of Israel: 'The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.' This is my name forever, and thus I am to be remembered throughout all generations.<sup>16</sup>Go and gather the elders of Israel together and say to them, 'The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob, has appeared to me, saying, "I have observed you and what has been done to you in Egypt,<sup>17</sup>and I promise that I will bring you up out of the affliction of Egypt to the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, a land flowing with milk and honey."'<sup>18</sup>And they will listen to your voice, and you and the elders of Israel shall go to the king of Egypt and say to him, 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us; and now, please let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God.'<sup>19</sup>But I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go unless compelled by a mighty hand.<sup>20</sup>So I will stretch out my hand and strike Egypt with all the wonders that I will do in it; after that he will let you go.<sup>21</sup>And I will give this people favor in the sight of the Egyptians; and when you go, you shall not go empty,<sup>22</sup>but each woman shall ask of her neighbor, and any woman who lives in her house, for silver and gold jewelry, and for clothing. You shall put them on your sons and on your daughters. So you shall plunder the Egyptians."
3.overview:
Where we are. Forty years have passed since Moses fled Egypt. Israel’s cry has gone up and God has heard, remembered, seen and known (2:23–25). Now God speaks, to an eighty-year-old shepherd at the far side of the desert.

The message. The holy God has come down to save his people, and he will do it by his own presence. He blazes in holiness yet does not destroy, and he sees his people’s suffering and keeps his word. He sends a weak and reluctant man, and his answer to “Who am I?” is not “You are able” but “I will be with you”, and then his name: “I AM WHO I AM”, the eternal God who depends on nothing and will be everything he has promised.

Why it was said. After centuries among the gods of Egypt, Israel needed to know which God had rescued them (see the introduction). This chapter gave them his name and showed that their freedom began with his compassion and his covenant, not with Moses’ courage.

How the chapter makes its case. Moses, keeping another man’s sheep, turns aside to see a bush that burns without being consumed, and God calls him by name, warns him off holy ground and names himself the God of the fathers (vv. 1–6). God has seen, heard and come down to deliver, and he sends Moses; to Moses’ “Who am I?” he promises his presence (vv. 7–12). Asked his name, he gives it, “I AM WHO I AM”, the LORD, “my name forever” (vv. 13–15). Then he tells Moses the end before the beginning: the elders will listen, Pharaoh will refuse until compelled by God’s mighty hand, and Israel will leave laden with Egypt’s gifts (vv. 16–22).

Where it leads. By the character of God revealed in Christ, and by promise. The God who came down to deliver came down in person: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). The one who said “before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58) claimed the name of the bush, and this commentary holds that the angel in the flame was the Son himself before his incarnation. The promise “I will be with you” becomes his name, Immanuel, and his last word to his church: “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).

For us. Come to God both boldly and humbly, for he calls you by name and he is holy fire. When you feel unequal to what he asks, the answer is not more self-confidence but his presence. And he has given us his name so that we may call on it: the God who needs nothing from us has given us himself in Jesus.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The holy God comes to an obscure shepherd, and his first words are a call, a limit and a reminder of his promises. Forty years into exile, Moses leads another man’s flock to Horeb, the mountain of God (v. 1). The angel of the LORD appears in a flame in a bush that burns without being consumed, and Moses turns aside to look (vv. 2–3). God calls him by name, but tells him to come no nearer and to take off his sandals, for the ground is holy (vv. 4–5). Then he names himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and Moses hides his face in fear (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology:
Holy Ground

The God who calls Moses by name is holy, and he is the God of the fathers.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jesus proved the resurrection from verse 6, where God still calls himself the God of men long dead (Matt. 22:32). Now: God found Moses at ordinary work, and asked first not for competence but for reverence.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Moses was keeping the flock of his father-in-law, Jethro, the priest of Midian, and he led his flock to the west side of the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses’ great calling begins while he is minding his father-in-law’s sheep at the far edge of the desert: he is not seeking God, but God comes to him.

Keeping the flock of his father-in-law. The former prince is now a hired hand for a foreigner: forty years in Egypt, forty in Midian (Acts 7:23, 30). Jethro is another name or title for Reuel (2:18).

The west side of the wilderness. Literally “behind the wilderness”, the far side, where shepherds went when nearer grazing ran out.

Horeb, the mountain of God. Horeb is another name for Sinai, called “the mountain of God” because of what will happen there. The Midian years were not wasted: God was training a shepherd for his people (Psalm 77:20).

In everyday life. If you think your useful years are behind you, God meets people in the middle of ordinary work.
verseByVerse.note: Jethro’s name probably means “excellence.”

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush. He looked, and behold, the bush was burning, yet it was not consumed. And Moses said, "I will turn aside to see this great sight, why the bush is not burned."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God appears in a fire in a thornbush that burns without burning up: a picture of the holy God who needs nothing and blazes without destroying.

A flame of fire. In Scripture fire is a sign of God’s holy presence: the torch at Abraham’s covenant (Genesis 15:17), the pillar of fire (13:21), Sinai (19:18), Pentecost (Acts 2:3). Ordinary fire needs fuel; this fire needs nothing, like the God whose name will be given in v. 14. Some also see Israel in the bush, afflicted but not destroyed.

A bush. The bush (seneh) is a worthless thorny shrub: God chose the humblest of plants to speak from.

The angel of the LORD. “Angel” means “messenger”, but here the one in the bush speaks as God himself (vv. 4–6), and the text moves freely between “the angel of the LORD”, “the LORD” and “God”.

In everyday life. Turn aside when God catches your attention, in his word above all.

Where Christians differ: who is the angel? Some take him as a created angel speaking for God. Many, from the early church fathers to the Reformers, have seen the Son of God appearing before his incarnation. This commentary’s view: he is identified with God and speaks as God, so he is no ordinary angel, and he is best read as the Son appearing before his incarnation, though the text does not name him.
verseByVerse.note: Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai.

verseByVerse.quote: When the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the bush, "Moses, Moses!" And he said, "Here I am." Then he said, "Do not come near; take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God calls Moses by name and in the same breath holds him back: he comes near, but he is not to be approached casually.

Moses, Moses! The doubled name, as with Abraham (Genesis 22:11) and Samuel (1 Samuel 3:10), is personal and urgent. Moses answers hinneni, “Here I am”, which speaks not of location but of readiness to serve.

Holy ground. Holy means set apart, belonging to God, pure. The dirt is ordinary, but it is holy because God is present. Removing sandals showed reverence and humility (Joshua 5:15).

What it does not mean. Not that some places today are holier for worship. In Christ, God meets his people anywhere in Spirit and truth (John 4:21–24), yet reverence is still due (Hebrews 12:28–29). So we come to God both boldly and humbly: called by name, aware of his holiness.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." And Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God introduces himself as the God who made promises to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and keeps them, and Moses hides his face in awe. After four centuries, the promises have not lapsed.

Moses hid his face. Sinful people cannot see God’s face and live (33:20). This is not cringing terror of a cruel God but the right awe of a creature before the Holy One (Isaiah 6:5). Later Moses will ask to see God’s glory (33:18), and on another mountain he will stand with Jesus in glory (Luke 9:30–31).

Jesus’ use. Jesus quoted this verse to the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection (Matthew 22:31–32). His argument rests on the covenant: the faithful God binds himself to these men as their God, so death cannot be the end of them. He is not the God of the dead but of the living.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7-12 — I Have Come Down to Deliver
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Moses what he does whenever he saves: he comes down to deliver, and he sends someone. He has seen his people’s affliction, heard their cry and come down to bring them out of Egypt into a good land (vv. 7–8). Because their cry has reached him, he sends Moses to Pharaoh (vv. 9–10). Moses, whose last attempt at rescue ended in flight, asks, “Who am I?” (v. 11). God does not answer by building up Moses’ confidence but with the promise of his presence, “I will be with you”, and with a sign that Moses will see only after he has obeyed: Israel worshipping on this very mountain (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology:
I Have Come Down to Deliver

The God who has come down sends Moses, and answers his inadequacy with his presence.
verseByVerse.examples: Now: Christ sends his people as the Father sent him, and goes with them (Matt. 28:20; John 20:21).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said, "I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters. I know their sufferings, and I have come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians and to bring them up out of that land to a good and broad land, a land flowing with milk and honey, to the place of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has seen, heard, known and come down: he is not distant from suffering, and he has come to rescue his people and give them a good land. The four verbs answer 2:24–25.

I have come down. This is God’s pattern: he came down at Babel (Genesis 11:5), at Sinai (19:20), and finally in the incarnation (John 1:14), when he came down in Christ to deliver us.

A land flowing with milk and honey. Rich pasture for herds and wildflowers for bees: a fertile land of plenty. Its peoples, the Canaanites and the rest, are those whose land God will judge for their sin (Leviticus 18:24–25).

Why so long? God had foretold four hundred years of affliction (Genesis 15:13), partly to wait until “the iniquity of the Amorites” was full (Genesis 15:16). His timing joins patience with the Canaanites and faithfulness to Israel.

What it does not mean. Suffering does not mean God approves of it or has forgotten. He sees, and acts in his time.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, behold, the cry of the people of Israel has come to me, and I have also seen the oppression with which the Egyptians oppress them. Come, I will send you to Pharaoh that you may bring my people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s coming down and his sending of Moses belong together: God is the deliverer, and Moses is his instrument.

My people. Israel belongs to God, not to Pharaoh. The plagues will settle whose people they are.

In everyday life. When you pray for God to act in a situation, be ready for him to send you.

verseByVerse.quote: But Moses said to God, "Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses honestly asks, “Who am I?”, and God turns the question from Moses to himself. Forty years earlier Moses went in his own strength; now he has no confidence at all.

God’s answer. Not how capable Moses is, but “I will be with you” (v. 12).

Humility or excuse. Humility is not wrong, but self-doubt can become an excuse for disobedience (4:13–14). Gideon (Judges 6:15) and Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:6) raised the same objection.

In everyday life. When you feel inadequate for what God asks, do not try to talk yourself up. Look to his presence (2 Corinthians 3:5).

verseByVerse.quote: He said, "But I will be with you, and this shall be the sign for you, that I have sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises his presence, and gives a sign that Moses will see only after he obeys: Israel worshipping God on this mountain.

I will be with you. In Hebrew ehyeh immak, and “I will be” (ehyeh) is the verb God will use for his name in v. 14.

This shall be the sign for you. A sign confirms God’s word, but strangely this one comes after the mission. Faith must go first and see later. God does give Moses signs beforehand in chapter 4, but the deepest confirmation comes through obedience.

You shall serve God on this mountain. To “serve” God is to worship him. The goal of the exodus is not only freedom from Pharaoh but service to God (4:23), fulfilled at Sinai (19:1–2).

For the church. The same promise is given to the church by the risen Christ: “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives his name for ever and tells Moses the end of the story before it begins. Moses asks what to say when Israel asks God’s name (v. 13). God answers, “I AM WHO I AM” (v. 14), and gives his covenant name, the LORD, tied for ever to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (v. 15). Then he lays out what will happen: the elders will listen to the promise of rescue (vv. 16–17); Pharaoh will refuse even a request to worship until God compels him with his mighty hand and his wonders (vv. 18–20); and Israel will not leave empty-handed, for the Egyptians will give them silver, gold and clothing (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Name: I AM

God reveals his name, and tells Moses beforehand how the contest with Pharaoh will end.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the plunder was back wages for generations of unpaid work. Now: Jesus took the name on himself: "before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses said to God, "If I come to the people of Israel and say to them, 'The God of your fathers has sent me to you,' and they ask me, 'What is his name?' what shall I say to them?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses asks for God’s name, because Israel will want to know which God has sent him and what he is like. In Scripture a name expresses character, and Israel had lived for centuries among the many named gods of Egypt.

What is his name? Israel did know the God of their fathers; they needed to know him more fully as the one who acts to save (6:2–3).

A lever? In the ancient world, knowing a god’s name was thought to give power over him in ritual. God will reveal his name, but not as something to control.

verseByVerse.quote: God said to Moses, "I AM WHO I AM." And he said, "Say this to the people of Israel: 'I AM has sent me to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God names himself “I AM WHO I AM”: the eternal God who depends on nothing and will be all he has promised to his people.

He simply is. The Hebrew ehyeh asher ehyeh comes from the verb “to be”. Everything else depends on something else; God depends on nothing. He simply is, unchanging and eternal (Psalm 90:2; Malachi 3:6). This is the fire that needs no fuel. In context it also promises: I will be with you (v. 12). And it cannot be used to manipulate him.

He needs nothing. Everything you have you received. Worship the one who received nothing and gives everything (Acts 17:25).

Jesus. “Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58). His hearers took up stones, understanding the claim to be God. The voice from the bush and the voice in the temple courts are one.

Only one being can say “I am who I am”. Our culture has borrowed the sentence. It is sung in anthems and printed on T-shirts: I am who I am, take me or leave me. The modern self is meant to be self-defining, owing its identity to no one. It sounds like freedom, and it is exhausting, because a self that defines itself must keep defending the definition against critics, failure and the ageing body. Only one being can say those words without strain, because only one depends on nothing. For the rest of us identity is not a sculpture we carve but a gift we receive, and the question is whose word we receive it from. The great I AM, who needs nothing from us, came near in Jesus, and to people who could never hold themselves together he says what only the self-existent God can say with authority: “I have called you by name, you are mine” (Isaiah 43:1).

Uncertain wording. The words can be translated “I am who I am” or “I will be what I will be” (the Hebrew verb covers both present and future), and some suggest “I am the one who is”, as the ancient Greek translation took it. The likely sense holds both: not an abstract idea of “being” but the living God, who exists in himself and will show himself faithful to his people.
verseByVerse.note: “I AM WHO I AM” may also be rendered “I will be what I will be” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: God also said to Moses, "Say this to the people of Israel: 'The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.' This is my name forever, and thus I am to be remembered throughout all generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives his personal covenant name, the LORD, as his name for ever, and ties it to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

The LORD. Small capitals in English Bibles stand for the Hebrew YHWH, formed from the verb “to be” in v. 14. Out of reverence Jews later read it aloud as Adonai, “Lord”, and many still say HaShem, “the Name”.

The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. The eternal God ties his name to flawed men with real histories: he is the God of sinners he has chosen and kept.

This is my name forever. His name is to be “remembered”, called upon in worship; he wants to be known and named. It is not a magic word, and not a name to use lightly (20:7).

In everyday life. Call on the LORD by name today. He has given it so that you may.

Uncertain wording. Because the name was not spoken aloud for centuries, its original pronunciation is not certain. “Yahweh” is the most likely form, from ancient evidence; the older “Jehovah” came from combining the consonants of YHWH with the vowels of Adonai.
verseByVerse.note: Jews still often say “HaShem,” “the Name,” in place of the divine name.

verseByVerse.quote: Go and gather the elders of Israel together and say to them, 'The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob, has appeared to me, saying, "I have observed you and what has been done to you in Egypt, and I promise that I will bring you up out of the affliction of Egypt to the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, a land flowing with milk and honey."'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses is to tell Israel’s elders that God has visited them, and to repeat his promise to bring them out to the land.

Gather the elders of Israel. The elders were the heads of Israel’s families and tribes.

I have observed you. The verb paqad means to visit, to attend to with purpose. Joseph had promised, “God will visit you” (Genesis 50:24–25), using the same word, and it is now happening.

I promise that I will bring you up. God repeats the promise of v. 8, because discouraged people need to hear it twice. And he gives Moses the words; this is not a message Moses invents.
