verseByVerse.quote: And they will listen to your voice, and you and the elders of Israel shall go to the king of Egypt and say to him, 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us; and now, please let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God.' But I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go unless compelled by a mighty hand. So I will stretch out my hand and strike Egypt with all the wonders that I will do in it; after that he will let you go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before any plague falls, God tells Moses how it will go: the elders will listen, Pharaoh will refuse, and God’s mighty hand will compel him. The delays will not mean God is losing.

The God of the Hebrews. A name Pharaoh could understand. The wonders are the plagues of chapters 7–12.

Is the request for a three days’ journey deceptive, since God means to bring them out for good? An opening request is not a lie: it tests Pharaoh with a small, reasonable demand, and his refusal of even that exposes his heart (5:2).

What it does not mean. Not that Pharaoh is a puppet. He refuses freely, and God also hardens him (see 4:21).

In everyday life. When opposition seems strong, remember that God has already said how the story ends.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will give this people favor in the sight of the Egyptians; and when you go, you shall not go empty, but each woman shall ask of her neighbor, and any woman who lives in her house, for silver and gold jewelry, and for clothing. You shall put them on your sons and on your daughters. So you shall plunder the Egyptians."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel will not leave empty-handed: God will make the Egyptians willing to give, and the slaves will go out with back wages.

Each woman shall ask. Fulfilled in 12:36. The verb sha’al means to ask or request; the King James “borrow” misled readers into thinking it was a trick. It was a request, freely granted.

So you shall plunder the Egyptians. Like soldiers taking spoil, but without a battle: back wages for generations of unpaid slavery. The law later required freed slaves to be sent away generously (Deuteronomy 15:13–14), and God had promised this to Abraham (Genesis 15:14). It is not theft, nor licence to take others’ goods, but God’s justice for the oppressed.

A warning ahead. This gold will be used both for the golden calf (32:2–4) and for the tabernacle (35:22). Gifts can serve idols or God; use what he has given you for his worship.

3.theology:
The holiness of God. The fire, the holy ground and the hidden face all proclaim that God is set apart, approachable only on his own terms.

God depends on nothing. "I AM WHO I AM" reveals a God who simply is: self-existent, eternal, unchanging, the source of all being. (Theologians call this his aseity.)

The compassion of God. The holy I AM is also the God who has seen, heard and come down. Holiness and mercy meet in the bush as they will meet at the cross.
3.examples:
Then: A discarded fugitive met the eternal God in a desert and was commissioned to confront an empire, armed with nothing but a name and a promise: “I will be with you.”

Now: The same I AM meets us in Christ. When we feel inadequate to our calling, the answer is not our record but his presence, by the Spirit he has given (John 14:16–17). The God who is enough has promised to be with us.

keyVerse.quote: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM.” And he said, “Say this to the people of Israel: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”
keyVerse.note: Here God gives the name by which he will be known for ever (v. 15). It declares that he depends on nothing and no one, and in context it promises that he will be with his people and be all he has said. Jesus took this name on his own lips (John 8:58), and in him the great I AM came down to deliver.

3.reflection:
God met Moses in the middle of ordinary work, after forty quiet years (vv. 1–3). What does this suggest about where and when God meets people? How can we learn to “turn aside” when he is speaking, especially through his word?

God called Moses by name and in the same breath told him, “Do not come near” (vv. 4–6). How do we hold together God’s nearness and his holiness? Which do you tend to forget, and how does Jesus make it possible to come boldly to a holy God?

Moses asked, “Who am I?”, and God answered, “I will be with you” (vv. 11–12). Where do you feel inadequate for what God is asking of you? How does his promise of presence change the question?

God’s name, “I AM WHO I AM”, means he depends on nothing (v. 14). Our culture says, “I am who I am”, meaning we define ourselves. How does knowing the self-existent God, and receiving our identity from him in Christ, set us free?

4.title: The Sufficiency of God in Our Weakness
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Moses answered, "But behold, they will not believe me or listen to my voice, for they will say, 'The LORD did not appear to you.'"<sup>2</sup>The LORD said to him, "What is that in your hand?" He said, "A staff."<sup>3</sup>And he said, "Throw it on the ground." So he threw it on the ground, and it became a serpent, and Moses ran from it.<sup>4</sup>But the LORD said to Moses, "Put out your hand and catch it by the tail"—so he put out his hand and caught it, and it became a staff in his hand—<sup>5</sup>"that they may believe that the LORD, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you."<sup>6</sup>Again, the LORD said to him, "Put your hand inside your cloak." And he put his hand inside his cloak, and when he took it out, behold, his hand was leprous like snow.<sup>7</sup>Then God said, "Put your hand back inside your cloak." So he put his hand back inside his cloak, and when he took it out, behold, it was restored like the rest of his flesh.<sup>8</sup>"If they will not believe you," God said, "or listen to the first sign, they may believe the latter sign.<sup>9</sup>If they will not believe even these two signs or listen to your voice, you shall take some water from the Nile and pour it on the dry ground, and the water that you shall take from the Nile will become blood on the dry ground."<sup>10</sup>But Moses said to the LORD, "Oh, my Lord, I am not eloquent, either in the past or since you have spoken to your servant, but I am slow of speech and of tongue."<sup>11</sup>Then the LORD said to him, "Who has made man's mouth? Who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD?<sup>12</sup>Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak."<sup>13</sup>But he said, "Oh, my Lord, please send someone else."<sup>14</sup>Then the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses and he said, "Is there not Aaron, your brother, the Levite? I know that he can speak well. Behold, he is coming out to meet you, and when he sees you, he will be glad in his heart.<sup>15</sup>You shall speak to him and put the words in his mouth, and I will be with your mouth and with his mouth and will teach you both what to do.<sup>16</sup>He shall speak for you to the people, and he shall be your mouth, and you shall be as God to him.<sup>17</sup>And take in your hand this staff, with which you shall do the signs."<sup>18</sup>Moses went back to Jethro his father-in-law and said to him, "Please let me go back to my brothers in Egypt to see whether they are still alive." And Jethro said to Moses, "Go in peace."<sup>19</sup>And the LORD said to Moses in Midian, "Go back to Egypt, for all the men who were seeking your life are dead."<sup>20</sup>So Moses took his wife and his sons and had them ride on a donkey, and went back to the land of Egypt. And Moses took the staff of God in his hand.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "When you go back to Egypt, see that you do before Pharaoh all the miracles that I have put in your power. But I will harden his heart, so that he will not let the people go.<sup>22</sup>Then you shall say to Pharaoh, 'Thus says the LORD, Israel is my firstborn son,<sup>23</sup>and I say to you, "Let my son go that he may serve me." If you refuse to let him go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son.'"<sup>24</sup>At a lodging place on the way the LORD met him and sought to put him to death.<sup>25</sup>Then Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son's foreskin and touched Moses' feet with it and said, "Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me!"<sup>26</sup>So he let him alone. It was then that she said, "A bridegroom of blood," because of the circumcision.<sup>27</sup>The LORD said to Aaron, "Go into the wilderness to meet Moses." So he went and met him at the mountain of God and kissed him.<sup>28</sup>And Moses told Aaron all the words of the LORD with which he had sent him to speak, and all the signs that he had commanded him to do.<sup>29</sup>Then Moses and Aaron went and gathered together all the elders of the people of Israel.<sup>30</sup>Aaron spoke all the words that the LORD had spoken to Moses and did the signs in the sight of the people.<sup>31</sup>And the people believed; and when they heard that the LORD had visited the people of Israel and that he had seen their affliction, they bowed their heads and worshiped.
4.overview:
Where we are. At the burning bush God has revealed his name, promised his presence and told Moses how the rescue will unfold (chapter 3). But Moses is not yet willing to go.

The message. God’s rescue does not depend on the strength or eagerness of the one he sends. Moses meets God’s call with excuse after excuse, and God answers each one not by flattering Moses but by showing more of himself: his power over signs, his lordship over the human mouth, his promise to be present, and even, in his anger, a helper. At the heart of the chapter is a staggering claim: “Israel is my firstborn son”. The exodus is a Father reclaiming his child to worship him.

Why it was said. Israel needed to know that Moses, their great leader, was a reluctant and flawed man made great only by God’s call and help, and that they themselves were God’s son by his choice, not their merit (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. To Moses’ “they will not believe me”, God gives three signs: the staff that becomes a serpent, the hand made leprous and healed, and Nile water turned to blood (vv. 1–9). To “I am not eloquent”, he answers, “Who has made man’s mouth?” (vv. 10–12). When Moses simply asks him to send someone else, God’s anger burns, yet he gives Aaron to be his mouth (vv. 13–17). Moses sets out, and God tells him what to say to Pharaoh: let my firstborn son go, or I will kill your firstborn (vv. 18–23). On the way the LORD meets Moses to put him to death, until Zipporah circumcises their son (vv. 24–26). Aaron meets Moses, and the people believe and worship (vv. 27–31).

Where it leads. By pattern and promise. Israel, the firstborn son called out of Egypt, points to the true Son: “Out of Egypt I called my son” is fulfilled in Jesus (Matthew 2:15), and the Father who demanded Egypt’s firstborn “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). Moses needed a mouth and wanted someone else sent; Christ is the Son who came willingly and in whom God speaks to us himself (Hebrews 1:1–2). And at the lodging place, as at Passover, death turns away only where blood is shed.

For us. When you feel unable to do what God asks, he does not need you to be impressive, only willing; he supplies what he commands. But reluctance can harden into refusal, so do not hope he will give your task to someone else. And remember whose child you are: in Christ, God calls you his son or daughter.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-9 — Three Signs for a Doubting Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers Moses’ fear that no one will believe him with three signs of his power. Moses objects that the people will deny that the LORD has appeared to him (v. 1). God turns his shepherd’s staff into a serpent and back again, the emblem of Pharaoh’s power caught by the tail (vv. 2–5). He makes Moses’ hand leprous and then restores it, showing that he can wound and heal (vv. 6–7). And if they still do not believe, water from the Nile, Egypt’s lifeblood, will become blood on the ground (vv. 8–9). God meets unbelief with patience, and his signs point not to Moses but to the God who sent him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Three Signs for a Doubting Servant

Each sign is a credential, showing Israel that the LORD has truly appeared to Moses.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: each sign previews a place where God will strike Egypt: its royal power, its people’s bodies and its river. Now: God is not stingy with a servant who is struggling to believe.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses answered, "But behold, they will not believe me or listen to my voice, for they will say, 'The LORD did not appear to you.'" The LORD said to him, "What is that in your hand?" He said, "A staff."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses fears that no one will believe him, and God begins his answer with the ordinary stick already in his hand.

They will not believe me. This contradicts what God had already told him: that the elders would listen (3:18).

What is that in your hand? Only a shepherd’s staff, worn by forty years of use. By v. 20 it bears the name “the staff of God”. It will divide the sea (14:16), bring water from the rock (17:5–6) and be raised over Israel’s battle (17:9).

Where the power lies. The stick itself had no power. Power belongs to God, who chooses to work through ordinary means, and so your skills, your work and your home can become instruments in his service too.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Throw it on the ground." So he threw it on the ground, and it became a serpent, and Moses ran from it. But the LORD said to Moses, "Put out your hand and catch it by the tail"—so he put out his hand and caught it, and it became a staff in his hand— "that they may believe that the LORD, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God turns the staff into a serpent and back, and makes Moses take it by the tail: the emblem of Pharaoh’s power is in the LORD’s hand.

By the tail. Anyone who handles snakes knows this is the most dangerous grip. Moses has just run from the serpent; now he must reach for it in plain obedience.

Egypt’s serpent. The cobra on Pharaoh’s crown symbolised his royal power and divine protection. When Aaron’s staff swallows the magicians’ staffs (7:12) the point is made again.

What it does not mean. This is no model for handling snakes in worship. Signs served a particular moment of God’s revelation, and Mark 16:18 is no command to test God (Matthew 4:7).

verseByVerse.quote: Again, the LORD said to him, "Put your hand inside your cloak." And he put his hand inside his cloak, and when he took it out, behold, his hand was leprous like snow. Then God said, "Put your hand back inside your cloak." So he put his hand back inside his cloak, and when he took it out, behold, it was restored like the rest of his flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God makes Moses’ hand diseased and then heals it: he can wound and he can heal (Deuteronomy 32:39).

Leprous like snow. The skin turned white and flaky. Such diseases made a person unclean and cut off from the community (Leviticus 13).

Jesus touched a leper. Jesus touched a leper and made him clean (Mark 1:40–42): the same power that healed Moses’ hand, now present in person. Thank God, who cleanses what is unclean, including you (1 John 1:7).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word translated “leprous” (tsara’at) covers several skin diseases, (and in Leviticus even mould). It is not necessarily what is now called leprosy (Hansen’s disease).
verseByVerse.note: “Leprous” covers several skin diseases (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "If they will not believe you," God said, "or listen to the first sign, they may believe the latter sign. If they will not believe even these two signs or listen to your voice, you shall take some water from the Nile and pour it on the dry ground, and the water that you shall take from the Nile will become blood on the dry ground."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers unbelief with patience, offering a third sign rather than a rebuke: Nile water turned to blood.

The Nile. Egypt’s life, worshipped as a god (Hapi). Turning it to blood shows that the LORD rules what Egypt worships, and previews the first plague (7:17–21).

What signs are for. Not magic tricks to impress. Signs point beyond themselves to the God who sends Moses.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses runs out of reasons and finally simply refuses, yet God still provides. Moses pleads that he is not eloquent (v. 10). God answers that he made man’s mouth and every ability and disability, and promises, “I will be with your mouth” (vv. 11–12). When Moses asks God to send someone else, God’s anger burns, but he does not withdraw his call: Aaron, already on his way, will speak for Moses, and God will teach them both (vv. 13–16). Moses is to take the staff with which he will do the signs (v. 17). God’s patience is great, but reluctance has its cost.
verseByVerse.theology:
"Who Made Man's Mouth?"

God's answer to weakness is his presence, and even his anger at refusal comes with a gift.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the prophet is a mouth carrying a word he did not invent. Now: God speaks at last by his Son, who needs no Aaron (Heb. 1:1-2), and the Spirit teaches his people what to say (Luke 12:12).

verseByVerse.quote: But Moses said to the LORD, "Oh, my Lord, I am not eloquent, either in the past or since you have spoken to your servant, but I am slow of speech and of tongue."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses pleads that he has never been a speaker, and the confident young man of Egypt is gone.

I am not eloquent. Literally “not a man of words”. Stephen says that in Egypt Moses was “mighty in his words and deeds” (Acts 7:22).

In everyday life. God does not use only gifted speakers. Paul too came “in weakness” and not with lofty words (1 Corinthians 2:1–5). If you feel unable to speak for Christ, you are in good company: God supplies what he asks.

Uncertain wording. “Slow of speech and of tongue” is literally “heavy of mouth and heavy of tongue”. It may mean a speech difficulty, or simply a lack of fluency, perhaps rusty Egyptian after forty years in Midian; the text does not say.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to him, "Who has made man's mouth? Who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD? Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God made man’s mouth and rules every ability and disability, so he answers Moses’ weakness with his presence, not with Moses’ improvement.

Mute, deaf, seeing, blind. This is hard, but it is also comfort: disability is not a sign that God has looked away (John 9:1–3).

What it does not mean. Not that disability is a punishment for personal sin, nor that God is indifferent to suffering. Christ healed the blind and deaf as signs of the coming kingdom, where every body will be made whole (Isaiah 35:5–6).

I will be with your mouth. Jesus promised the same to disciples on trial (Matthew 10:19–20). Before a hard conversation, pray: “Lord, be with my mouth.”

verseByVerse.quote: But he said, "Oh, my Lord, please send someone else." Then the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses and he said, "Is there not Aaron, your brother, the Levite? I know that he can speak well. Behold, he is coming out to meet you, and when he sees you, he will be glad in his heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With no reason left, Moses simply asks God to send someone else: humility has become refusal, and God is angry, yet he does not withdraw his call.

The anger of the LORD. His holy displeasure at persistent unwillingness. His patience is great, but not endless; yet even in anger he remains merciful (Psalm 103:8–10).

Aaron, your brother, the Levite. Aaron was three years older than Moses (7:7), and he was already on his way: God’s provision came before Moses’ refusal.

In everyday life. Is there something God has made clear which you are hoping he will give to someone else? He met Moses’ reluctance with a brother at his side, and he still sends help with the task.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall speak to him and put the words in his mouth, and I will be with your mouth and with his mouth and will teach you both what to do. He shall speak for you to the people, and he shall be your mouth, and you shall be as God to him. And take in your hand this staff, with which you shall do the signs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aaron will speak God’s words for Moses, as a prophet speaks for God, and Moses will carry the staff of the signs.

Put the words in his mouth. The pattern of prophecy: God gives the word, the prophet passes it on unchanged (7:1; Deuteronomy 18:18; Jeremiah 1:9).

As God to him. Moses will stand to Aaron as God stands to a prophet, as the source of the message; it does not mean Moses is divine.

A second best. Moses refused God’s promise, “I will be with your mouth”, and was given a go-between instead. Aaron will later lead Israel into idolatry (32:1–6).

God himself speaks in person. In the last days God has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2): no go-between, but God himself.

Take in your hand this staff. The sign of God’s authority.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18-31 — Return to Egypt and the Firstborn Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses sets out for Egypt, and God shows what is at stake: his firstborn son, and his covenant. Moses takes leave of Jethro and, since those who sought his life are dead, returns with his family and the staff of God (vv. 18–20). God warns that Pharaoh will refuse, and gives the message that frames everything: Israel is my firstborn son; let him go, or I will kill your firstborn (vv. 21–23). At a lodging place the LORD seeks to kill Moses, until Zipporah circumcises their son (vv. 24–26). Aaron meets Moses at the mountain of God, the elders hear and see the signs, and the people believe and worship (vv. 27–31).
verseByVerse.theology:
Return to Egypt and the Firstborn Son

The Father claims his son, and his messenger must first give his own son the covenant sign, circumcision.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: blood on the household turns death away, a Passover in miniature. Now: God did not spare his own firstborn Son (Rom. 8:32), and the goal was always worship, not simply getting out of Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses went back to Jethro his father-in-law and said to him, "Please let me go back to my brothers in Egypt to see whether they are still alive." And Jethro said to Moses, "Go in peace." And the LORD said to Moses in Midian, "Go back to Egypt, for all the men who were seeking your life are dead." So Moses took his wife and his sons and had them ride on a donkey, and went back to the land of Egypt. And Moses took the staff of God in his hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses returns to Egypt with his family and the staff of God, and God removes the fear Moses did not voice.

To see whether they are still alive. Moses gives a modest reason and asks Jethro’s leave, honouring family even while following God’s call. Jethro blesses him with shalom, wholeness and well-being.

All the men who were seeking your life are dead. Matthew echoes this when the angel tells Joseph to return from Egypt because those who sought the child’s life are dead (Matthew 2:20).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "When you go back to Egypt, see that you do before Pharaoh all the miracles that I have put in your power. But I will harden his heart, so that he will not let the people go. Then you shall say to Pharaoh, 'Thus says the LORD, Israel is my firstborn son, and I say to you, "Let my son go that he may serve me." If you refuse to let him go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God warns that Pharaoh will refuse, and names what the contest is about: Israel is his firstborn son, and he will have his son back.

Harden his heart. The heart is the centre of will and thought; to harden it is to make it stubborn and unresponsive. Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his heart (8:15, 32) and that God hardened it (9:12; 10:20).

My firstborn son. The first time Israel is called God’s son. The firstborn is the heir, specially loved (see the firstborn), and God claims Israel as his own family.

I will kill your firstborn son. The judgment fits the crime, for Egypt drowned Israel’s sons (1:22).

A Father who gave his own firstborn. “Out of Egypt I called my son” (Hosea 11:1) is fulfilled in Jesus, the true Son (Matthew 2:15), whose Father gave his own Son to save others (Romans 8:32).

Where Christians differ. Some hold that God only confirmed what Pharaoh chose. Others hold that God actively hardened him for his own purposes, while Pharaoh remained guilty. This commentary’s view: both are taught. God hands Pharaoh over to the hardness he chooses, and in his sovereignty uses it to display his power (9:16; Romans 9:17–18). Pharaoh is never a puppet; he is fully responsible.
verseByVerse.note: Israel is God’s firstborn son — the background to the last plague.

verseByVerse.quote: At a lodging place on the way the LORD met him and sought to put him to death. Then Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son's foreskin and touched Moses' feet with it and said, "Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me!" So he let him alone. It was then that she said, "A bridegroom of blood," because of the circumcision.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses, sent to tell Pharaoh “Israel is my firstborn son”, had not given his own son the covenant sign, and the LORD meets him in deadly earnest until the blood of circumcision is shed.

Why? Circumcision was the sign God gave Abraham of belonging to his covenant people, and the uncircumcised male was to be cut off (Genesis 17:10–14).

A flint. A sharp stone knife, still used for circumcision in Joshua’s day (Joshua 5:2).

Passover in view. A household under sentence of death, blood applied, and the LORD lets him alone: the pattern of chapter 12.

For leaders. God is not capricious: he takes his covenant seriously, above all with his leaders (James 3:1). Leaders must keep at home what they preach in public, and where they have failed, the way back is still through blood: for us, the blood of Christ.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew pronouns are unclear: it may be Moses or his son whom the LORD seeks to kill, and whose “feet” Zipporah touches (Moses’ is most likely). “A bridegroom of blood” appears nowhere else; perhaps she means that by this blood she has her husband back from death. The main point is clear.
verseByVerse.note: A hard passage: Moses had apparently failed to circumcise his son, the sign of the covenant whose people he was about to lead.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Aaron, "Go into the wilderness to meet Moses." So he went and met him at the mountain of God and kissed him. And Moses told Aaron all the words of the LORD with which he had sent him to speak, and all the signs that he had commanded him to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends Aaron to meet Moses, and at the mountain of God Moses hands on to his brother all God’s words and signs.

The mountain of God. Horeb, where the bush burned and where the law will be given. The brothers greet each other warmly after forty years apart.

All the words. The first task of God’s messengers is to hear and hand on the whole message (Acts 20:27).

In everyday life. Thank God for the brothers and sisters he sends to share your work.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses and Aaron went and gathered together all the elders of the people of Israel. Aaron spoke all the words that the LORD had spoken to Moses and did the signs in the sight of the people. And the people believed; and when they heard that the LORD had visited the people of Israel and that he had seen their affliction, they bowed their heads and worshiped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people believe, exactly what Moses said would not happen, and they worship God for his promise while still slaves.

Visited. Hebrew paqad, as in 3:16: God has come to act for them, as Joseph promised (Genesis 50:24).

Bowed their heads and worshiped. Before deliverance, they trust God’s word and adore him. We too may worship God for what he has promised before we see it.

Faith still to be tested. Within a chapter they will turn on Moses when life gets harder (5:21); faith must be tested.

4.theology:
The sufficiency of God in human weakness. God’s call rests on his power, not on the servant’s gifts, and his question “Who has made man’s mouth?” silences every excuse.

Divine sovereignty. God claims authority over speech, disability, Pharaoh's heart and the outcome of history. Nothing lies outside his rule.

Redemption for worship. "Let my son go that he may serve me." Salvation's goal is not mere liberation but the worship of God.
4.examples:
Then: A reluctant shepherd, full of excuses, was sent to confront a superpower, assured only that the God who made his mouth would go with him.

Now: When God calls us beyond our competence, the question is never "Am I able?" but "Is God able?" Our weakness is the stage for his strength. And we are redeemed not for ourselves but to serve and worship our Redeemer.

keyVerse.quote: Then you shall say to Pharaoh, ‘Thus says the LORD, Israel is my firstborn son, and I say to you, “Let my son go that he may serve me.”
keyVerse.note: Here God names what the whole contest with Pharaoh is about: a Father claiming his son, so that the son may serve him in worship. It explains the last plague (12:29) and reaches forward to Jesus, the true Son called out of Egypt, whose Father gave his own firstborn to set his children free.

4.reflection:
God asked Moses, “What is that in your hand?” and used an ordinary shepherd’s staff (v. 2). What ordinary things has God put in your hands that he might use for his purposes?

Moses’ objections moved from honest fear to plain reluctance: “Please send someone else” (v. 13). How can we tell the difference between humility and refusal? Is there something God has made clear that you are hoping he will give to someone else?

God calls Israel “my firstborn son” (v. 22). What does it mean that God’s rescue is a Father reclaiming his child? How does this help us understand what Jesus did as the true Son, and what it means to be adopted into God’s family?

The people believed and worshipped while they were still slaves (v. 31). What would it look like for you to worship God for his promises before you see them fulfilled?

5.title: When Obedience Makes Things Worse
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Afterward Moses and Aaron went and said to Pharaoh, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Let my people go, that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness.'"<sup>2</sup>But Pharaoh said, "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and moreover, I will not let Israel go."<sup>3</sup>Then they said, "The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Please let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God, lest he fall upon us with pestilence or with the sword."<sup>4</sup>But the king of Egypt said to them, "Moses and Aaron, why do you take the people away from their work? Get back to your burdens."<sup>5</sup>And Pharaoh said, "Behold, the people of the land are now many, and you make them rest from their burdens!"<sup>6</sup>The same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters of the people and their foremen,<sup>7</sup>"You shall no longer give the people straw to make bricks, as in the past; let them go and gather straw for themselves.<sup>8</sup>But the number of bricks that they made in the past you shall impose on them, you shall by no means reduce it, for they are idle. Therefore they cry, 'Let us go and offer sacrifice to our God.'<sup>9</sup>Let heavier work be laid on the men that they may labor at it and pay no regard to lying words."<sup>10</sup>So the taskmasters and the foremen of the people went out and said to the people, "Thus says Pharaoh, 'I will not give you straw.<sup>11</sup>Go and get your straw yourselves wherever you can find it, but your work will not be reduced in the least.'"<sup>12</sup>So the people were scattered throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.<sup>13</sup>The taskmasters were urgent, saying, "Complete your work, your daily task each day, as when there was straw."<sup>14</sup>And the foremen of the people of Israel, whom Pharaoh's taskmasters had set over them, were beaten and were asked, "Why have you not done all your task of making bricks today and yesterday, as in the past?"<sup>15</sup>Then the foremen of the people of Israel came and cried to Pharaoh, "Why do you treat your servants like this?<sup>16</sup>No straw is given to your servants, yet they say to us, 'Make bricks!' And behold, your servants are beaten; but the fault is in your own people."<sup>17</sup>But he said, "You are idle, you are idle; that is why you say, 'Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.'<sup>18</sup>Go now and work. No straw will be given you, but you must still deliver the same number of bricks."<sup>19</sup>The foremen of the people of Israel saw that they were in trouble when they said, "You shall by no means reduce your number of bricks, your daily task each day."<sup>20</sup>They met Moses and Aaron, who were waiting for them, as they came out from Pharaoh;<sup>21</sup>and they said to them, "The LORD look on you and judge, because you have made us stink in the sight of Pharaoh and his servants, and have put a sword in their hand to kill us."<sup>22</sup>Then Moses turned to the LORD and said, "O Lord, why have you done evil to this people? Why did you ever send me?<sup>23</sup>For since I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has done evil to this people, and you have not delivered your people at all."
5.overview:
Where we are. At the burning bush God sent Moses back to Egypt, and the elders of Israel believed and worshipped (4:29–31). Now Moses and Aaron stand before Pharaoh for the first time with God’s word.

The message. Obeying God can make things worse before he makes them right, and that is not a sign that he has failed. Pharaoh does not know the LORD and will not obey him, so the battle that follows is about whose word rules: the king’s or God’s. God lets the darkness deepen so that when rescue comes, no one will doubt who brought it.

Why it was said. Israel in the wilderness, often tempted to remember Egypt fondly (16:3), needed to remember what Pharaoh’s rule had really been, and that their first hope had seemed to collapse (see the introduction). Their freedom did not come from Pharaoh’s kindness or their own strength.

How the chapter makes its case. God’s demand meets Pharaoh’s scorn: “Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice?” (vv. 1–2). Asked for three days to worship, Pharaoh calls rest idleness and orders bricks without straw (vv. 3–9). The order passes down the chain of command, the people scatter for stubble, and the Israelite foremen are beaten (vv. 10–14). Their appeal to Pharaoh is thrown back at them (vv. 15–19), and they curse Moses and Aaron (vv. 20–21). Moses takes it all to God: “Why did you ever send me?” (vv. 22–23).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by pattern. A people who cannot free themselves, whose appeals to the tyrant fail and who turn on their own deliverer, need a rescuer who is stronger than Pharaoh and who will not give up on them. Moses, rejected by his own, foreshadows the Saviour who “came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11), and whose obedience led, for a time, to apparent defeat on the cross before the great deliverance.

For us. When doing what God says brings trouble rather than relief, do not conclude that he has abandoned you; take your “why” to him, as Moses did. Our worth is not measured in bricks, for Christ has done the work that frees us, and he gives rest to the weary (Matthew 11:28).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pharaoh meets God’s word with open defiance, and answers a request for worship with heavier work. Moses and Aaron speak in the LORD’s name, “Let my people go” (vv. 1–2), and Pharaoh replies that he does not know the LORD and will not obey him. When they ask for a three days’ journey to sacrifice, the king sees only lost labour and resents the people’s rest (vv. 3–5). The same day he orders that straw no longer be supplied, though the quota of bricks stays the same, and calls God’s message “lying words” (vv. 6–9). The first meeting sets the terms of the contest: whose word will rule in Egypt?
verseByVerse.theology:
"Who Is the LORD?"

Pharaoh will not bow to the God of slaves, and treats worship as idleness and God's word as lies.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the question is answered over ten chapters, until his own army cries "the LORD fights for them" (14:25). Now: the world still thinks that people who give time to worship must have too little to do.

verseByVerse.quote: Afterward Moses and Aaron went and said to Pharaoh, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Let my people go, that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness.'" But Pharaoh said, "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and moreover, I will not let Israel go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God commands Pharaoh to let his people go, and Pharaoh refuses to acknowledge the LORD at all.

Thus says the LORD is the formula of a royal messenger, used hundreds of times by the prophets: the words carry the authority of the one who sent them.

Let my people go, because Israel belongs to God, not to Pharaoh. The feast is a pilgrimage festival, for the goal of freedom is worship (3:12).

Who is the LORD? Pharaoh, himself honoured as a god, will not recognise Israel’s God. “I do not know” uses the same verb as 1:8, where a new king “did not know Joseph”: it is not ignorance of facts but refusal to acknowledge. Yet his ignorance does not excuse him. By the end he will say, “The LORD is in the right” (9:27), and Egypt will know that he is the LORD (14:4).

In everyday life. People still ask, “Who is God, that I should obey him?” The best answer is not an argument but the story of what he has done.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they said, "The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Please let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God, lest he fall upon us with pestilence or with the sword." But the king of Egypt said to them, "Moses and Aaron, why do you take the people away from their work? Get back to your burdens." And Pharaoh said, "Behold, the people of the land are now many, and you make them rest from their burdens!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh sees worship as lost labour and resents the people’s rest.

The God of the Hebrews has met with us. They speak in terms Pharaoh can grasp. The fear of pestilence or sword shows that serving God is not optional; neglecting his worship is dangerous.

Why do you take the people away from their work? Pharaoh sees only lost labour. To him worship is wasted work time.

You make them rest. The verb is Hebrew shabat, the root of “Sabbath”. Pharaoh resents rest. God will later command Sabbath rest as a memorial of freedom from Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:15).

Pharaoh’s voice in a modern head. “You are idle, you are idle” (v. 17) is no longer shouted by a foreman, but many of us carry it inside. We feel guilty on a day off and answer “How are you?” with “Busy”, as if busyness proved we mattered. The German philosopher Josef Pieper warned of a world of “total work”, where rest is only recharging for more output and a person is worth what he produces. That is Pharaoh’s economy: bodies valued for bricks. Scripture’s answer is not a tip about balance but a different verdict on who you are. Israel was to rest because it had been redeemed, not because it had earned a break, and the one who redeems us still says, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Rest becomes an act of faith that your worth was settled by someone else’s work.

In everyday life. Work is good, but life is more than production. If your employer, or your own drive, treats rest and worship as waste, remember who you belong to.

verseByVerse.quote: The same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters of the people and their foremen, "You shall no longer give the people straw to make bricks, as in the past; let them go and gather straw for themselves. But the number of bricks that they made in the past you shall impose on them, you shall by no means reduce it, for they are idle. Therefore they cry, 'Let us go and offer sacrifice to our God.' Let heavier work be laid on the men that they may labor at it and pay no regard to lying words."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh answers the request with heavier work: find your own straw, make the same number of bricks.

You shall no longer give the people straw. Straw bound the bricks (see the note); now the workers must find their own.

They are idle, that is, lazy. Pharaoh treats a desire to worship as laziness, and heavier work as the cure. God’s message, confirmed by signs, he dismisses as lying words.

Why did God let this happen? Had Israel been released at once, they might have left thinking Pharaoh had been kind. Things get worse so that it will be clear who freed them (6:6–7).

In everyday life. Obedience does not always make things easier at first. Sometimes it makes them harder (John 16:33).
verseByVerse.note: Chopped straw mixed into the mud bound the bricks and helped them set.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pharaoh’s order falls hardest on the people it was meant to crush, and they turn against the men God sent. The command passes from taskmasters to Israelite foremen, and the people scatter across Egypt to gather stubble (vv. 10–12). The quotas are not met, and the foremen are beaten (vv. 13–14). They appeal to Pharaoh as his servants and are told only, “You are idle” (vv. 15–19). Coming out, they meet Moses and Aaron and call on the LORD to judge them for making Israel hateful to Pharaoh (vv. 20–21). Obedience has, for now, made everything worse.
verseByVerse.theology:
Bricks Without Straw

Oppression sets the oppressed against their deliverer.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the foremen cursed the men God sent to free them. Now: Christ too came to his own and was not received (John 1:11), and went on delivering those who shouted against him.

verseByVerse.quote: So the taskmasters and the foremen of the people went out and said to the people, "Thus says Pharaoh, 'I will not give you straw. Go and get your straw yourselves wherever you can find it, but your work will not be reduced in the least.'" So the people were scattered throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh’s order passes down the chain of command, and the people scatter to scrape up stubble.

The chain of command. Egyptian taskmasters stood above, with Israelite foremen beneath them, responsible for the quotas.

Thus says Pharaoh. The same formula as “Thus says the LORD” (v. 1). Two kings are now speaking in Egypt, and the question is whose word will stand.

Stubble, the stalks left in a field after harvest, was poorer than straw and harder to collect. God’s firstborn son (4:22) is kept scattered and worn out, too tired to resist.

In everyday life. When competing voices claim your obedience, ask whose word carries final authority.

verseByVerse.quote: The taskmasters were urgent, saying, "Complete your work, your daily task each day, as when there was straw." And the foremen of the people of Israel, whom Pharaoh's taskmasters had set over them, were beaten and were asked, "Why have you not done all your task of making bricks today and yesterday, as in the past?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The quotas cannot be met, and the Israelite foremen are beaten for it.

The foremen were beaten. Israelites set over Israelites take the blows. Oppression often works by making some of the oppressed answerable for the rest.

Scripture and harsh rule. Scripture does not approve such systems: the law will forbid ruling another “ruthlessly” (Leviticus 25:43), and masters are told they too have a Master in heaven (Colossians 4:1). If you are caught between demanding bosses and struggling colleagues, God sees the cost.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the foremen of the people of Israel came and cried to Pharaoh, "Why do you treat your servants like this? No straw is given to your servants, yet they say to us, 'Make bricks!' And behold, your servants are beaten; but the fault is in your own people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The foremen appeal to Pharaoh for fairness, but being right is useless before an unjust king.

Your servants. They call themselves Pharaoh’s servants three times, appealing to his sense of fairness.

Cried to Pharaoh. They take their cry to Pharaoh rather than to the LORD. It is not wrong to appeal to authorities (Acts 25:11), but deliverance will come from God.

In everyday life. Use proper channels for justice, but pray first and trust God most.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said, "You are idle, you are idle; that is why you say, 'Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.' Go now and work. No straw will be given you, but you must still deliver the same number of bricks." The foremen of the people of Israel saw that they were in trouble when they said, "You shall by no means reduce your number of bricks, your daily task each day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mocked as lazy and sent back to an impossible task, the foremen see that they are trapped.

You are idle, you are idle. Pharaoh repeats the word in contempt, linking their desire to sacrifice with laziness.

In trouble is literally “in evil”, in a bad place. Scripture records their despair honestly, yet God has not lost control: he had told Moses that Pharaoh would refuse (3:19).

verseByVerse.quote: They met Moses and Aaron, who were waiting for them, as they came out from Pharaoh; and they said to them, "The LORD look on you and judge, because you have made us stink in the sight of Pharaoh and his servants, and have put a sword in their hand to kill us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beaten foremen turn on Moses and Aaron and call down God’s judgment on them.

The LORD look on you and judge. This is more than a complaint; it is a curse, invoking God against the men he sent.

Made us stink means made us hateful to Pharaoh, and the sword in their hand is an excuse to kill us. Moses is rejected by his own people again, as he was forty years before (2:14) (compare Acts 7:35).

Real pain, wrong judgment. Their pain is real, but their judgment is wrong: hardship is not proof that God’s messenger is false. If people blame you for trouble that came from obeying God, take it to God rather than hitting back at them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses neither quits nor hits back; he turns to the LORD and pours out his complaint. His words sound more like accusation than prayer: why have you done evil to this people, and why did you send me? He has obeyed exactly, and Pharaoh has only grown crueller (vv. 22–23). Yet the complaint is spoken to God, and that is faith still talking. God’s answer comes at once in the next chapter: “Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh” (6:1).
verseByVerse.theology:
Moses' Honest Complaint

Lament brought to God is still faith talking to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God answers with a promise, not a rebuke (6:1). Now: obedience sometimes makes things worse for a while, and the protest taken to God is itself evidence of faith (Ps. 13:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses turned to the LORD and said, "O Lord, why have you done evil to this people? Why did you ever send me? For since I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has done evil to this people, and you have not delivered your people at all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses brings his bewildered complaint straight to God: he obeyed, and things only got worse.

Moses turned to the LORD. He does not quit or hit back; he prays.

Why have you done evil? Literally “brought harm on”. It is an accusation, honestly spoken, and “you have not delivered” is true as far as Moses can see: he obeyed exactly, and things got worse.

God’s answer. No rebuke follows. God answers, “Now you shall see what I will do” (6:1). Lament is a form of faith that keeps talking to God (Psalm 13:1; Habakkuk 1:2).

He was not rescued. On the cross Jesus also cried “Why?” (Mark 15:34). He was not rescued, so that we could be.

What it does not mean. God does not do evil. Moses speaks from pain, and God will show his purpose; yet complaint is not rebellion when it is brought to God.

In everyday life. Bring your “why” to God. He can bear it.

5.theology:
The defiance of unbelief. “Who is the LORD?” exposes the heart of rebellion: a refusal to acknowledge God’s right to rule.

The cost of obedience. Following God's word can bring immediate hardship. Things often get darker just before God delivers.

Honest lament. Moses brings his bewilderment to God himself. Faith may wrestle in the dark, so long as it wrestles with God.
5.examples:
Then: The first obedience to God's command brought heavier chains, not freedom, and the deliverer was blamed by the very people he came to save.

Now: When obedience seems to make life harder and prayers seem to go unanswered, we are exactly where Moses stood, and the lowest point may come just before God’s mightiest work.

keyVerse.quote: But Pharaoh said, “Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and moreover, I will not let Israel go.”
keyVerse.note: Pharaoh’s question sets the agenda for the plagues: God will answer it in act after act until Egypt knows that he is the LORD (7:5; 14:4). It is also the voice of every heart that refuses God’s claim, and the chapter shows what life looks like under a master who does not know him.

5.reflection:
Pharaoh asks, “Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice?” (v. 2). Where do you hear that question asked today, openly or quietly, and how does God answer it in the rest of Exodus and in Christ?

Pharaoh called a desire to worship and rest “idle” (vv. 8, 17). In what ways does our culture, or your own heart, treat rest and worship as wasted time, and what would it look like to rest as people who have been redeemed?

Moses obeyed and things got worse (vv. 20–23). Have you known a time when doing right brought trouble? How did it affect your trust in God?

Moses brought his “why” straight to God. What can we learn from his honesty, and how does Jesus’ cry on the cross (Mark 15:34) shape the way we lament?

6.title: I Will Redeem You with an Outstretched Arm
6.text: <sup>1</sup>But the LORD said to Moses, "Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh; for with a strong hand he will send them out, and with a strong hand he will drive them out of his land."<sup>2</sup>God spoke to Moses and said to him, "I am the LORD.<sup>3</sup>I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, as God Almighty, but by my name the LORD I did not make myself known to them.<sup>4</sup>I also established my covenant with them to give them the land of Canaan, the land in which they lived as sojourners.<sup>5</sup>Moreover, I have heard the groaning of the people of Israel whom the Egyptians hold as slaves, and I have remembered my covenant.<sup>6</sup>Say therefore to the people of Israel, 'I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will deliver you from slavery to them, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment.<sup>7</sup>I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God, and you shall know that I am the LORD your God, who has brought you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians.<sup>8</sup>I will bring you into the land that I swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob. I will give it to you for a possession. I am the LORD.'"<sup>9</sup>Moses spoke thus to the people of Israel, but they did not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery.<sup>10</sup>So the LORD said to Moses,<sup>11</sup>"Go in, tell Pharaoh king of Egypt to let the people of Israel go out of his land."<sup>12</sup>But Moses said to the LORD, "Behold, the people of Israel have not listened to me. How then shall Pharaoh listen to me, for I am of uncircumcised lips?"<sup>13</sup>But the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them a charge about the people of Israel and about Pharaoh king of Egypt: to bring the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt.<sup>14</sup>These are the heads of their fathers' houses: the sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi; these are the clans of Reuben.<sup>15</sup>The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman; these are the clans of Simeon.<sup>16</sup>These are the names of the sons of Levi according to their generations: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, the years of the life of Levi being 137 years.<sup>17</sup>The sons of Gershon: Libni and Shimei, by their clans.<sup>18</sup>The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, the years of the life of Kohath being 133 years.<sup>19</sup>The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites according to their generations.<sup>20</sup>Amram took as his wife Jochebed his father's sister, and she bore him Aaron and Moses, the years of the life of Amram being 137 years.<sup>21</sup>The sons of Izhar: Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri.<sup>22</sup>The sons of Uzziel: Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri.<sup>23</sup>Aaron took as his wife Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab and the sister of Nahshon, and she bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.<sup>24</sup>The sons of Korah: Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph; these are the clans of the Korahites.<sup>25</sup>Eleazar, Aaron's son, took as his wife one of the daughters of Putiel, and she bore him Phinehas. These are the heads of the fathers' houses of the Levites by their clans.<sup>26</sup>These are the Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said: "Bring out the people of Israel from the land of Egypt by their hosts."<sup>27</sup>It was they who spoke to Pharaoh king of Egypt about bringing out the people of Israel from Egypt, this Moses and this Aaron.<sup>28</sup>On the day when the LORD spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt,<sup>29</sup>the LORD said to Moses, "I am the LORD; tell Pharaoh king of Egypt all that I say to you."<sup>30</sup>But Moses said to the LORD, "Behold, I am of uncircumcised lips. How will Pharaoh listen to me?"
6.overview:
Where we are. Moses’ first appeal to Pharaoh has failed. The work is heavier, the foremen have cursed him, and he has asked God, “Why did you ever send me?” (5:22). This chapter is God’s reply.

The message. God answers despair not with a new plan but with himself. “I am the LORD” opens and closes his speech (vv. 2, 8), and between them he recalls his covenant with the fathers and makes seven promises, each beginning “I will”. Salvation rests on who God is and what he has sworn, not on the strength of the people or the eloquence of his messenger.

Why it was said. The generation that left Egypt, and their children on the edge of Canaan, needed to know that their rescue and their land came from a promise God made centuries before and kept (see the introduction). Their own faith had failed at the start (v. 9); God’s faithfulness had not.

How the chapter makes its case. God promises that Pharaoh will drive Israel out, and declares his name and his covenant: the God who appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob has heard the groaning and remembered (vv. 1–5). He gives Moses seven “I wills”: bring out, deliver, redeem, take as my people, be your God, bring in, give the land (vv. 6–8). But the people, crushed by slavery, cannot listen, and Moses doubts Pharaoh will (vv. 9–13). A family record roots Moses and Aaron in the tribe of Levi (vv. 14–27), and the chapter returns to Moses’ objection, ready for God’s answer in chapter 7 (vv. 28–30).

Where it leads. By promise and covenant. God binds himself as Israel’s Redeemer, the next-of-kin who buys back his family from slavery. That promise reaches its fullness in Christ, who was “born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Galatians 4:4–5). The covenant formula, “I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God”, runs through Scripture to its end, when “they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:3).

For us. When you are too worn out to believe, God’s promises do not depend on the strength of your faith but on his name. In Christ he has done every “I will”: he has brought us out, redeemed us at the cost of his blood, and made us his own. Rest on who he is.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers Moses’ accusation by revealing who he is and what he has bound himself to do. He promises that Pharaoh will not merely release Israel but drive them out with a strong hand (v. 1). He declares “I am the LORD”, the God who appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as God Almighty, though they had not known the full meaning of his name in mighty acts of rescue (vv. 2–3). He established his covenant to give them Canaan, he has heard Israel’s groaning, and he has remembered that covenant (vv. 4–5). The answer to despair is God himself.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Remembers His Covenant

The patriarchs had the promise; these slaves will see it kept, and so learn what the name means.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God answers Moses by telling him when he will act and who he is. Now: God rarely answers the "why" we ask, and gives instead a promise that can be leaned on while the trouble lasts.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD said to Moses, "Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh; for with a strong hand he will send them out, and with a strong hand he will drive them out of his land." God spoke to Moses and said to him, "I am the LORD. I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, as God Almighty, but by my name the LORD I did not make myself known to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers Moses’ despair with a promise and with his name: he is the LORD, and Israel will now see what that name means.

A strong hand. Pharaoh will not merely let Israel go; under God’s power he will drive them out (12:31–33).

I am the LORD is repeated four times in vv. 2–8. God’s answer to despair is himself.

God Almighty (El Shaddai, see the note) was the name under which God promised Abraham and Jacob offspring and land when it seemed impossible (Genesis 17:1; 35:11).

Did not make myself known. The patriarchs used the name LORD (Genesis 15:7; 28:13). To “know” the name is to experience what it means: God keeping his covenant in mighty acts of redemption.

Where Christians differ. Critical scholars read v. 3 as proof that Genesis came from different sources, one of them unaware of the name.

This commentary’s view. The verse concerns knowing the name’s meaning in experience, not hearing the word. Genesis uses the name freely; to know a name in Scripture is to know the character it reveals (34:5–7).

Uncertain wording. The origin of Shaddai is uncertain. The ESV follows the traditional “Almighty”; some link the word to “mountain”, others to “breast” (God who nourishes, Genesis 49:25). The Genesis uses make the sense clear enough: God with power to keep his promises.
verseByVerse.note: “God Almighty” is El Shaddai (ESV note). The patriarchs knew the name LORD, but had not seen what it means in great acts of redemption.

verseByVerse.quote: I also established my covenant with them to give them the land of Canaan, the land in which they lived as sojourners. Moreover, I have heard the groaning of the people of Israel whom the Egyptians hold as slaves, and I have remembered my covenant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has bound himself by covenant to give the land, and hearing Israel’s groaning, he will act on it.

I also established my covenant with them. God had set up his binding promise (Genesis 17:7–8), though the patriarchs lived in the land as sojourners, resident foreigners owning only a burial plot (Genesis 23).

Remembered means to act on a promise, not to recall something forgotten (2:24). Four hundred years have passed, and the covenant still binds him. In Christ he kept it still (Luke 1:72). Thank God that his promises to you in Christ do not grow old.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Seven promises, each beginning “I will”, set out everything God means to do for his people, framed by “I am the LORD” at the start and the end. He will bring them out from their burdens, deliver them from slavery and redeem them with an outstretched arm and great acts of judgment (v. 6). He will take them as his people and be their God, so that they know him (v. 7). He will bring them into the land sworn to the fathers and give it as their possession (v. 8). From first to last God does the saving.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Seven "I Wills"

God promises rescue, adoption and inheritance, each with “I will”.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: these were promises to slaves who could not yet see any of them. Now: Christ shared our flesh and blood to set us free (Heb. 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: Say therefore to the people of Israel, 'I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will deliver you from slavery to them, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment. I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God, and you shall know that I am the LORD your God, who has brought you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises to free Israel, to buy them back as their Redeemer and to make them his own people.

I will bring you out … deliver you … redeem you. Three verbs for one rescue. Redeem is Hebrew ga’al: the act of the next-of-kin, the go’el, who bought back a relative from slavery or debt (Leviticus 25:47–49; Ruth 4). God acts as Israel’s family Redeemer.

Outstretched arm pictures God’s power reaching out to act. The great acts of judgment are the plagues, judgments on Egypt and its gods (12:12).

My people … your God. The covenant formula, repeated across Scripture (Leviticus 26:12; Jeremiah 31:33) and fulfilled at the end (Revelation 21:3). You shall know that I am the LORD your God: knowing God personally is the goal of redemption.

As family, not as hired labour. Jesus became our near kinsman to redeem us (Galatians 4:4–5), and the outstretched arm reached its fullest stretch on the cross, where the Redeemer’s arms were stretched out to purchase a people at the cost of his blood. He redeemed you as family, not as hired labour.

verseByVerse.quote: I will bring you into the land that I swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob. I will give it to you for a possession. I am the LORD.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Redemption has a destination: the land God swore to the fathers.

Swore is literally “lifted my hand”, the gesture of an oath: God bound himself (Genesis 22:16; Hebrews 6:13).

I will give it to you for a possession. God brings his people out of Egypt and into a lasting inheritance. For the church, the inheritance is the new creation (1 Peter 1:4; Hebrews 11:16).

I am the LORD. The speech ends as it began: the promises rest on who God is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9-30 — Unbelief, Genealogy, and a Reluctant Mediator
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s promises meet a people too crushed to hear them and a messenger who still feels unfit, yet God’s purpose does not move. Israel does not listen, because of broken spirit and harsh slavery, and Moses asks how Pharaoh could listen to one of “uncircumcised lips” (vv. 9–13). God simply repeats his charge. A selective family record then traces Moses and Aaron through Levi, naming the clans and the future priests (vv. 14–27). The chapter ends by restating Moses’ objection (vv. 28–30), setting up God’s answer in chapter 7.
verseByVerse.theology:
Unbelief, Genealogy, and a Reluctant Mediator

God's plan does not pause for a people too broken to hear.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God renews the charge to Moses rather than arguing with him. Now: what God has promised never depended on our ability to feel encouraged by it.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses spoke thus to the people of Israel, but they did not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery. So the LORD said to Moses, "Go in, tell Pharaoh king of Egypt to let the people of Israel go out of his land." But Moses said to the LORD, "Behold, the people of Israel have not listened to me. How then shall Pharaoh listen to me, for I am of uncircumcised lips?" But the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them a charge about the people of Israel and about Pharaoh king of Egypt: to bring the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel is too crushed to listen, Moses doubts Pharaoh will, and God simply renews the command.

Broken spirit is literally “shortness of breath (or spirit)”: exhaustion and discouragement so deep that hope cannot get in. This was not stubborn defiance; they were crushed. Some people cannot take in good news because of long pain. Be patient with them; God was (Isaiah 42:3).

Uncircumcised lips is a new way of saying “I cannot speak” (compare 4:10). God does not argue with him. He simply repeats the charge to Moses and Aaron.

In everyday life. If you are too worn out to believe the promises, let others hold them for you, and keep listening.

Uncertain wording. The exact sense of “uncircumcised lips” is uncertain: lips unfit for God’s service, or, as with ears that are “uncircumcised” (Jeremiah 6:10), lips that do not work properly. Either way, Moses feels unqualified.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the heads of their fathers' houses: the sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi; these are the clans of Reuben. The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman; these are the clans of Simeon. These are the names of the sons of Levi according to their generations: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, the years of the life of Levi being 137 years. The sons of Gershon: Libni and Shimei, by their clans. The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, the years of the life of Kohath being 133 years. The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites according to their generations. Amram took as his wife Jochebed his father's sister, and she bore him Aaron and Moses, the years of the life of Amram being 137 years. The sons of Izhar: Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri. The sons of Uzziel: Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri. Aaron took as his wife Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab and the sister of Nahshon, and she bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. The sons of Korah: Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph; these are the clans of the Korahites. Eleazar, Aaron's son, took as his wife one of the daughters of Putiel, and she bore him Phinehas. These are the heads of the fathers' houses of the Levites by their clans. These are the Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said: "Bring out the people of Israel from the land of Egypt by their hosts." It was they who spoke to Pharaoh king of Egypt about bringing out the people of Israel from Egypt, this Moses and this Aaron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A family record roots Moses and Aaron in Levi: real men from a flawed family, chosen by grace.

Why a genealogy here? Before the contest with Pharaoh begins, the text roots the deliverers in Israel’s families. They are real men with real ancestors: “this Moses and this Aaron” (v. 27).

Reuben, Simeon, Levi were Jacob’s first three sons. Reuben slept with his father’s concubine; Simeon and Levi massacred Shechem, and Jacob cursed their anger (Genesis 34; 49:5–7). God’s deliverers come from a disgraced line.

Amram and Jochebed, Moses’ parents, are named at last (2:1). Amram married his father’s sister, which the later law forbade (Leviticus 18:12); the law had not yet been given.

Future names. It names men who matter later: the rebel Korah (Numbers 16), Nadab and Abihu (Leviticus 10:1–2) and Phinehas (Numbers 25:7–13). The future priests and Levites are already in view.

A selective list. Four hundred years are spanned by a few key names, not every generation.

Grace, not lineage. Lineage does not earn God’s favour. His grace chooses sinners, as Jesus’ family list in Matthew 1 also shows, and writes their failures into his story.
verseByVerse.note: The family list traces Moses and Aaron to Levi.

verseByVerse.quote: On the day when the LORD spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt, the LORD said to Moses, "I am the LORD; tell Pharaoh king of Egypt all that I say to you." But Moses said to the LORD, "Behold, I am of uncircumcised lips. How will Pharaoh listen to me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The story resumes: God sends Moses to speak all his words, and Moses again pleads that he is unfit.

Tell Pharaoh king of Egypt all that I say to you. Moses’ task is to deliver God’s whole word, and again he pleads his uncircumcised lips. He is no hero, so God’s power will be the more obvious. God does not accept the excuse: in the next chapter he commissions Moses again, with Aaron as his prophet (7:1–2).

In everyday life. You can serve God while still feeling unfit. He works through weak servants (2 Corinthians 12:9).

6.theology:
Redemption is God's work. In the seven “I wills” God does every saving act himself. We are brought out, delivered, redeemed and taken: salvation from first to last is God’s doing, not a partnership.

The covenant relationship. The goal of redemption is not just rescue from bondage but belonging to God.

God's faithfulness over our unbelief. The people cannot believe, yet God will save. His promises rest on his character, not our capacity to receive them.
6.examples:
Then: To a people too broken by slavery to listen, God pledged redemption purely on the basis of his covenant.

Now: When our spirits are too crushed to believe the gospel, the ground of our hope is not the strength of our faith but the faithfulness of our Redeemer, who has already secured the "I wills" of our salvation at the cross.

keyVerse.quote: I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will deliver you from slavery to them, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment.
keyVerse.note: Here the great word “redeem” enters the story of salvation: God acts as Israel’s next-of-kin, buying his family back from slavery. Every verb has God as its subject, and the promise rests on “I am the LORD”. It is the pattern for the redemption Christ accomplished at the cost of his own blood.

6.reflection:
God answered Moses’ despair by saying “I am the LORD” and recalling his promises (vv. 2–8). When you are discouraged, how does remembering who God is and what he has promised change things?

The seven promises all begin “I will”. What does it mean that God does all the saving, and how do these promises find their fulfilment in Christ?

Israel could not listen “because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery” (v. 9). How can we care for people who are too worn down to take in good news?

God’s deliverers came from a family with a troubled past (vv. 14–27). What encouragement does that give you about how God uses people like us?

7.title: The Battle of the Gods Begins
7.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron shall be your prophet.<sup>2</sup>You shall speak all that I command you, and your brother Aaron shall tell Pharaoh to let the people of Israel go out of his land.<sup>3</sup>But I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and though I multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt,<sup>4</sup>Pharaoh will not listen to you. Then I will lay my hand on Egypt and bring my hosts, my people the children of Israel, out of the land of Egypt by great acts of judgment.<sup>5</sup>The Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out my hand against Egypt and bring out the people of Israel from among them."<sup>6</sup>Moses and Aaron did so; they did just as the LORD commanded them.<sup>7</sup>Now Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three years old, when they spoke to Pharaoh.<sup>8</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron,<sup>9</sup>"When Pharaoh says to you, 'Prove yourselves by working a miracle,' then you shall say to Aaron, 'Take your staff and cast it down before Pharaoh, that it may become a serpent.'"<sup>10</sup>So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and did just as the LORD commanded. Aaron cast down his staff before Pharaoh and his servants, and it became a serpent.<sup>11</sup>Then Pharaoh summoned the wise men and the sorcerers, and they, the magicians of Egypt, also did the same by their secret arts.<sup>12</sup>For each man cast down his staff, and they became serpents. But Aaron's staff swallowed up their staffs.<sup>13</sup>Still Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.<sup>14</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh's heart is hardened; he refuses to let the people go.<sup>15</sup>Go to Pharaoh in the morning, as he is going out to the water, and stand on the bank of the Nile to meet him. Take in your hand the staff that turned into a serpent.<sup>16</sup>And you shall say to him, 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, sent me to you, saying, "Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness." But so far, you have not obeyed.<sup>17</sup>Thus says the LORD, "By this you shall know that I am the LORD: behold, with the staff that is in my hand I will strike the water that is in the Nile, and it shall turn into blood.<sup>18</sup>The fish in the Nile shall die, and the Nile will stink, and the Egyptians will grow weary of drinking water from the Nile."'"<sup>19</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers, their canals, and their ponds, and all their pools of water, so that they may become blood, and there shall be blood throughout all the land of Egypt, even in vessels of wood and in vessels of stone.'"<sup>20</sup>Moses and Aaron did as the LORD commanded. In the sight of Pharaoh and in the sight of his servants he lifted up the staff and struck the water in the Nile, and all the water in the Nile turned into blood.<sup>21</sup>And the fish in the Nile died, and the Nile stank, so that the Egyptians could not drink water from the Nile. There was blood throughout all the land of Egypt.<sup>22</sup>But the magicians of Egypt did the same by their secret arts. So Pharaoh's heart remained hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.<sup>23</sup>Pharaoh turned and went into his house, and he did not take even this to heart.<sup>24</sup>And all the Egyptians dug along the Nile for water to drink, for they could not drink the water of the Nile.<sup>25</sup>Seven full days passed after the LORD had struck the Nile.
7.overview:
Where we are. God has answered Moses’ despair with his name and seven promises (chapter 6), but Moses still protests that Pharaoh will not listen to a man of “uncircumcised lips” (6:30). Now God sends him back, and the contest with Pharaoh begins in earnest.

The message. The LORD is the true God, and he will make himself known, even to those who refuse him. Before a single plague falls, God states his purpose: “The Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD” (v. 5). The plagues are not random disasters but judgments on Egypt’s gods (12:12), beginning with the Nile, the river Egypt worshipped and the river where Pharaoh drowned Hebrew boys.

Why it was said. Israel had lived for generations among Egypt’s gods and would be tempted by idols again (32:1–6). They needed to see that Egypt’s power, magic and gods could imitate a little but win nothing, and that the God who rescued them rules the whole earth (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. God makes Moses “like God to Pharaoh”, with Aaron as his prophet, and declares that he will harden Pharaoh’s heart and multiply signs until Egypt knows him; Moses and Aaron, aged eighty and eighty-three, obey (vv. 1–7). Aaron’s staff becomes a serpent; the magicians copy it, but his staff swallows theirs, and Pharaoh’s heart stays hard (vv. 8–13). At the riverbank God announces the first plague, and the Nile and every water in Egypt turn to blood (vv. 14–21). The magicians copy even this, Pharaoh walks away unmoved, and the people dig for water for seven days (vv. 22–25).

Where it leads. By the character of God revealed in Christ, and by contrast. The God who judges Egypt’s gods is the God who in Christ “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame” (Colossians 2:15). Moses’ first sign turned water into blood and death; Jesus’ first sign turned water into wine at a wedding (John 2:1–11). Judgment is real, but “grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17), who bore God’s judgment himself so that those who turn to him need not.

For us. The idols of our age, wealth, success, pleasure, the state, promise life and cannot give it; they can imitate a little but cannot undo death. Take God’s warnings to heart, as Pharaoh would not, and trust the One whose power is greater than every rival and whose mercy gives time to repent.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-7 — Moses as God to Pharaoh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the plagues begin, God sets out who Moses is, what Pharaoh will do and why it is happening. Moses is made “like God to Pharaoh”, speaking with God’s authority, with Aaron as his prophet (vv. 1–2). God will harden Pharaoh’s heart and multiply signs, then bring Israel out by great acts of judgment, so that the Egyptians will know that he is the LORD (vv. 3–5). The purpose is stated before a single blow falls. Moses and Aaron, eighty and eighty-three years old, do just as the LORD commands (vv. 6–7). After five objections, simple obedience.
verseByVerse.theology:
Moses as God to Pharaoh

Everything that follows answers Pharaoh's "Who is the LORD?"
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the deliverer's real work began at eighty. Now: God is not bound by our sense of when a life's best years are past.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron shall be your prophet. You shall speak all that I command you, and your brother Aaron shall tell Pharaoh to let the people of Israel go out of his land. But I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and though I multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, Pharaoh will not listen to you. Then I will lay my hand on Egypt and bring my hosts, my people the children of Israel, out of the land of Egypt by great acts of judgment. The Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out my hand against Egypt and bring out the people of Israel from among them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends Moses with his own authority and announces his purpose: through judgment, Egypt will know that he is the LORD.

Like God to Pharaoh. The Hebrew word is elohim, “God”. Moses will speak with God’s authority over Pharaoh, who claimed to be divine. Aaron will be his prophet, his spokesman (4:16).
