I will harden. As at 4:21, God’s purpose and Pharaoh’s own will are both at work, and Pharaoh’s guilt is real (see the introduction, “Who hardened Pharaoh’s heart?”). Paul draws on this story in Romans 9:17–18.

Signs and wonders are the plagues: signs point to who God is, and wonders are acts that astonish.

The Egyptians shall know. This is the answer to Pharaoh’s “Who is the LORD?” (5:2). God’s goal includes Egypt’s knowing him, not only Israel’s rescue.

What it does not mean. Moses does not become divine. He represents God, as ambassadors represent kings.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses and Aaron did so; they did just as the LORD commanded them. Now Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three years old, when they spoke to Pharaoh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After all his objections, Moses, now eighty, simply does what God commands.

Moses and Aaron did so. After five objections comes simple obedience: just as the LORD commanded.

Eighty years old. Everything Moses is remembered for still lies ahead of him. Forty years in Egypt made a fugitive; forty in Midian made a shepherd (Acts 7:23, 30); the last forty God will use to lead his people.

In everyday life. Age neither disqualifies anyone nor guarantees usefulness; God chooses his time. If you are older, he may not have finished using you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-13 — Aaron's Staff Swallows the Magicians'
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first confrontation is a sign that shows whose power is real. Pharaoh demands a miracle, and Aaron’s staff becomes a serpent, the creature that pictured Egypt’s own might (vv. 8–10). The magicians do the same by their secret arts, but Aaron’s staff swallows up theirs (vv. 11–12). Egypt can imitate God’s sign but cannot survive it. Yet Pharaoh’s heart is hardened and he will not listen, exactly as the LORD had said (v. 13). The contest has begun, and its outcome is already shown in miniature.
verseByVerse.theology:
Aaron's Staff Swallows the Magicians'

God lets Egypt's experts match his sign, then shows whose power prevails.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the magicians could copy the sign, but their staffs were swallowed (2 Tim. 3:8-9). Now: a thing can be supernatural and still worthless; the test is whether it lasts.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "When Pharaoh says to you, 'Prove yourselves by working a miracle,' then you shall say to Aaron, 'Take your staff and cast it down before Pharaoh, that it may become a serpent.'" So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and did just as the LORD commanded. Aaron cast down his staff before Pharaoh and his servants, and it became a serpent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aaron’s staff becomes a serpent: God holds even the creature that pictured Egypt’s power.

Prove yourselves means “show a credential”, and God knows in advance that Pharaoh will demand it.

A serpent. Not the ordinary word for snake used at the bush (4:3) but tannin, the creature that pictured Egypt and Pharaoh (Ezekiel 29:3). The sign is a picture of Pharaoh’s own power in God’s hand.

What it does not mean. This is not a magic show. The point is who controls the creature.

Uncertain wording. Which creature tannin means here is uncertain: elsewhere it can be a great serpent, a crocodile or a sea monster. “Serpent” fits the earlier sign (4:3); “crocodile” would sharpen the link to Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh summoned the wise men and the sorcerers, and they, the magicians of Egypt, also did the same by their secret arts. For each man cast down his staff, and they became serpents. But Aaron's staff swallowed up their staffs. Still Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt’s magicians copy the sign, but Aaron’s staff swallows theirs.

Wise men, sorcerers, magicians were Egypt’s professional priests and experts in ritual, and their secret arts were their spells and techniques.

Swallowed up. Egypt can imitate God’s sign but cannot survive it. Later the earth “swallowed” Egypt’s army (15:12).

Jannes and Jambres. Jewish tradition names two of these magicians; Paul uses them as examples of those who oppose the truth (2 Timothy 3:8).

Testing every wonder. Not every wonder comes from God. Counterfeit signs exist; test everything by God’s word (Deuteronomy 13:1–3).

Where Christians differ: what did the magicians do? Some see sleight of hand: snake-charmers can make a cobra rigid like a stick. Others see real demonic power (2 Thessalonians 2:9).

This commentary’s view. The text does not say; either way, their power was real enough to deceive and too weak to win.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14-25 — The Nile Turned to Blood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first plague strikes the Nile, the source of Egypt’s life and an object of its worship. God sends Moses to meet Pharaoh at the river with the staff that became a serpent, and to announce that by this Pharaoh will know the LORD (vv. 14–18). Aaron stretches out the staff, and the Nile and every water in Egypt, even in vessels of wood and stone, turn to blood; the fish die and the river stinks (vv. 19–21). The magicians copy it, so Pharaoh turns away without taking it to heart, while the Egyptians dig for water through seven days (vv. 22–25).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Nile Turned to Blood

The first blow falls on Egypt's source of life and its god.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the river Egypt trusted for life is struck first. Now: Jesus came to bear judgment rather than pour it out (John 2:1-11 records his first sign, the joyful reverse of this one).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh's heart is hardened; he refuses to let the people go. Go to Pharaoh in the morning, as he is going out to the water, and stand on the bank of the Nile to meet him. Take in your hand the staff that turned into a serpent. And you shall say to him, 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, sent me to you, saying, "Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness." But so far, you have not obeyed. Thus says the LORD, "By this you shall know that I am the LORD: behold, with the staff that is in my hand I will strike the water that is in the Nile, and it shall turn into blood. The fish in the Nile shall die, and the Nile will stink, and the Egyptians will grow weary of drinking water from the Nile."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the riverbank God announces that the Nile, Egypt’s life and object of worship, will turn to blood.

Stand on the bank of the Nile. Moses meets Pharaoh in the morning, perhaps when the king went to the river for worship or inspection.

The Nile was Egypt’s life: almost no rain falls, and every crop depended on the river’s yearly flood. Egypt honoured Hapi, god of the flood (see the note).

It shall turn into blood. Pharaoh had made the Nile a grave for Hebrew boys (1:22). The river where he drowned them now turns to blood: God is calling Egypt to account.

Where Christians differ: natural or miraculous? Some explain the plagues as a natural chain: red silt or algae, then frogs, insects, disease.

This commentary’s view. God can use natural processes, but here the timing, the announcement in advance, the distinction made for Goshen (8:22) and the scale make them God’s direct acts of judgment.
verseByVerse.note: The Nile was worshipped as a source of life: the plagues strike at Egypt’s gods.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers, their canals, and their ponds, and all their pools of water, so that they may become blood, and there shall be blood throughout all the land of Egypt, even in vessels of wood and in vessels of stone.'" Moses and Aaron did as the LORD commanded. In the sight of Pharaoh and in the sight of his servants he lifted up the staff and struck the water in the Nile, and all the water in the Nile turned into blood. And the fish in the Nile died, and the Nile stank, so that the Egyptians could not drink water from the Nile. There was blood throughout all the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every water in Egypt turns to blood: the judgment is total and cannot be hidden.

Blood throughout all the land of Egypt. Even water stored in vessels of wood and stone is struck. It is done in Pharaoh’s presence, so there is no hiding it. The fish die, a food source fails, and the stink of death fills the land.

Water to blood, water to wine. Moses’ first sign brought death; Jesus’ first sign, water to wine, brought joy (John 2:1–11). The law came through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John 1:17).

verseByVerse.quote: But the magicians of Egypt did the same by their secret arts. So Pharaoh's heart remained hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said. Pharaoh turned and went into his house, and he did not take even this to heart. And all the Egyptians dug along the Nile for water to drink, for they could not drink the water of the Nile. Seven full days passed after the LORD had struck the Nile.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh walks away unmoved while his people dig for water.

The magicians of Egypt did the same. They could make more blood but could not turn it back to water; their power only adds to the misery.

Did not take even this to heart. Pharaoh refuses to reflect on what has happened. Hardening shows itself as indifference: he “turned and went into his house”.

All the Egyptians dug along the Nile, because water filtered through the soil was drinkable. Ordinary people suffer for their king’s pride.

Seven full days. A week passes before the next blow, a week to reconsider: God gives time for repentance (2 Peter 3:9). When his warnings come, take them to heart.

7.theology:
The LORD over all gods. The LORD alone is God; every idol is exposed as powerless.

The hardening of the heart. Pharaoh hardens himself, and God hardens Pharaoh, a mystery Scripture holds together (Rom. 9). Human rebellion and divine sovereignty are both fully true.

Judgment as revelation. "That they may know that I am the LORD." Even God's acts of judgment serve to make his glory known.
7.examples:
Then: God began to dismantle the gods of the world's greatest empire, while Pharaoh hardened his heart.

Now: Our culture’s idols (wealth, power, self) are no more able to save than Egypt's Nile. God still exposes every counterfeit and calls every heart to know that he alone is the LORD. The question is whether we will be softened or, like Pharaoh, hardened.

keyVerse.quote: The Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out my hand against Egypt and bring out the people of Israel from among them.
keyVerse.note: This verse states the purpose of the plagues before the first one falls. It answers Pharaoh’s defiant “Who is the LORD?” (5:2): God will make himself known, in judgment on Egypt and in rescue for Israel. The same God is made known supremely in Christ, judging evil and saving his people at the cross.

7.reflection:
God says, “The Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD” (v. 5). Why does it matter that God’s aim in the plagues was to make himself known, and not only to rescue Israel?

The magicians could copy the signs but could not undo them (vv. 11–12, 22). What “counterfeits” today imitate God’s power or promise life, and how can we test them?

Moses was eighty when God’s great work through him began (v. 7). What does that say to people who feel too old, too late or too ordinary to be used by God?

Pharaoh “did not take even this to heart” (v. 23). How can we avoid becoming indifferent to God’s warnings, and how does the patience of God in Christ invite us to respond?

8.title: Escalating Judgment and a Line Drawn
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, "Let my people go, that they may serve me.<sup>2</sup>But if you refuse to let them go, behold, I will plague all your country with frogs.<sup>3</sup>The Nile shall swarm with frogs that shall come up into your house and into your bedroom and on your bed and into the houses of your servants and your people, and into your ovens and your kneading bowls.<sup>4</sup>The frogs shall come up on you and on your people and on all your servants."'"<sup>5</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers, over the canals and over the pools, and make frogs come up on the land of Egypt!'"<sup>6</sup>So Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt.<sup>7</sup>But the magicians did the same by their secret arts and made frogs come up on the land of Egypt.<sup>8</sup>Then Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said, "Plead with the LORD to take away the frogs from me and from my people, and I will let the people go to sacrifice to the LORD."<sup>9</sup>Moses said to Pharaoh, "Be pleased to command me when I am to plead for you and for your servants and for your people, that the frogs be cut off from you and your houses and be left only in the Nile."<sup>10</sup>And he said, "Tomorrow." Moses said, "Be it as you say, so that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God.<sup>11</sup>The frogs shall go away from you and your houses and your servants and your people. They shall be left only in the Nile."<sup>12</sup>So Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh, and Moses cried to the LORD about the frogs, as he had agreed with Pharaoh.<sup>13</sup>And the LORD did according to the word of Moses. The frogs died out in the houses, the courtyards, and the fields.<sup>14</sup>And they gathered them together in heaps, and the land stank.<sup>15</sup>But when Pharaoh saw that there was a respite, he hardened his heart and would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.<sup>16</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth, so that it may become gnats in all the land of Egypt.'"<sup>17</sup>And they did so. Aaron stretched out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the earth, and there were gnats on man and beast. All the dust of the earth became gnats in all the land of Egypt.<sup>18</sup>The magicians tried by their secret arts to produce gnats, but they could not. So there were gnats on man and beast.<sup>19</sup>Then the magicians said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God." But Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.<sup>20</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Rise up early in the morning and present yourself to Pharaoh, as he goes out to the water, and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, "Let my people go, that they may serve me.<sup>21</sup>Or else, if you will not let my people go, behold, I will send swarms of flies on you and your servants and your people, and into your houses. And the houses of the Egyptians shall be filled with swarms of flies, and also the ground on which they stand.<sup>22</sup>But on that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people dwell, so that no swarms of flies shall be there, that you may know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth.<sup>23</sup>Thus I will put a division between my people and your people. Tomorrow this sign shall happen."'"<sup>24</sup>And the LORD did so. There came great swarms of flies into the house of Pharaoh and into his servants' houses. Throughout all the land of Egypt the land was ruined by the swarms of flies.<sup>25</sup>Then Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said, "Go, sacrifice to your God within the land."<sup>26</sup>But Moses said, "It would not be right to do so, for the offerings we shall sacrifice to the LORD our God are an abomination to the Egyptians. If we sacrifice offerings abominable to the Egyptians before their eyes, will they not stone us?<sup>27</sup>We must go three days' journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God as he tells us."<sup>28</sup>So Pharaoh said, "I will let you go to sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness; only you must not go very far away. Plead for me."<sup>29</sup>Then Moses said, "Behold, I am going out from you and I will plead with the LORD that the swarms of flies may depart from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people, tomorrow. Only let not Pharaoh cheat again by not letting the people go to sacrifice to the LORD."<sup>30</sup>So Moses went out from Pharaoh and prayed to the LORD.<sup>31</sup>And the LORD did as Moses asked, and removed the swarms of flies from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people; not one remained.<sup>32</sup>But Pharaoh hardened his heart this time also, and did not let the people go.
8.overview:
Where we are. The Nile has turned to blood, and Pharaoh has walked away unmoved (7:23). Seven days later God sends Moses back, and three more plagues follow in quick succession: frogs, gnats and flies.

The message. There is no one like the LORD our God (v. 10): he rules over creation, Egypt’s experts reach their limit, and he draws a line between his people and the world under judgment. Pharaoh begins to bargain, wanting relief without surrender, and every relief only hardens him further. God’s mercy is real, but it is not to be played with.

Why it was said. Israel needed to see that their God was “the LORD in the midst of the earth” (v. 22), not a local deity, and that they had been spared by grace, not by merit (see the introduction). They would also face the same temptation as Pharaoh: to cry to God in trouble and forget him when it passes.

How the chapter makes its case. God sends frogs over the land, into bedrooms and kneading bowls; the magicians add more but cannot remove them (vv. 1–7). Pharaoh asks Moses to pray and promises release, and Moses lets him name the time so that he may know there is no one like the LORD (vv. 8–11). God removes the frogs, but at the first respite Pharaoh hardens his heart (vv. 12–15). Gnats come from the dust without warning, the magicians fail and confess, “This is the finger of God” (vv. 16–19). Then come swarms of flies, but Goshen is set apart (vv. 20–24). Pharaoh offers to let Israel worship inside Egypt, then not far away; Moses prays, the flies go, and Pharaoh hardens his heart again (vv. 25–32).

Where it leads. By pattern and by the character of God revealed in Christ. Jesus said that he cast out demons “by the finger of God”, so “the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Luke 11:20): the same power that humbled Egypt’s magicians was at work in him. And the line God drew around Goshen points ahead to the Passover and the cross, where Christ bore God’s judgment so that his people are sheltered from it (1 Thessalonians 1:10).

For us. Do not bargain with God, offering him a little while keeping your life under another master. Regret over trouble is not repentance; true repentance lasts when the pressure lifts. And if you belong to Christ, rejoice that God has set you apart by grace, not because you were better than others.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-15 — Frogs and a Hollow Repentance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second plague invades every corner of Egyptian life, and Pharaoh’s first plea for prayer turns out to be hollow. Frogs swarm from the Nile into houses, bedrooms, ovens and kneading bowls; the magicians add more but cannot take any away (vv. 1–7). Pharaoh begs Moses to plead with the LORD and promises to let the people go, and Moses lets him choose the time so that he may know there is no one like the LORD (vv. 8–11). God answers Moses’ prayer exactly, the frogs die in stinking heaps, and as soon as there is respite Pharaoh hardens his heart (vv. 12–15).
verseByVerse.theology:
Frogs and a Hollow Repentance

Pressure produces promises; relief shows what they were worth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the test of repentance is not what is said under pressure but what is done in the respite. Now: "now is the day of salvation" (2 Cor. 6:2), not tomorrow.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, "Let my people go, that they may serve me. But if you refuse to let them go, behold, I will plague all your country with frogs. The Nile shall swarm with frogs that shall come up into your house and into your bedroom and on your bed and into the houses of your servants and your people, and into your ovens and your kneading bowls. The frogs shall come up on you and on your people and on all your servants."'" And the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers, over the canals and over the pools, and make frogs come up on the land of Egypt!'" So Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt. But the magicians did the same by their secret arts and made frogs come up on the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Frogs invade every corner of Egyptian life, and the magicians can add to them but not remove them.

That they may serve me. “Serve” is the Hebrew word for worship and also for slave labour. The question is whom Israel will serve: Pharaoh or the LORD.

I will plague all your country with frogs. Egyptians linked frogs with fertility and with the goddess Heqet, shown with a frog’s head. The sign of life becomes a plague.

Into your bedroom and on your bed. The frogs reach the most private places of life, sleep and food. No one is beyond the judgment, not even the king. The magicians can add frogs, but again they cannot remove the trouble.

What it does not mean. God is not mocking for amusement. The plagues expose powerless gods so that Egypt may know the LORD.
verseByVerse.note: Exodus 8:1–4 is 7:26–29 in the Hebrew numbering (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said, "Plead with the LORD to take away the frogs from me and from my people, and I will let the people go to sacrifice to the LORD." Moses said to Pharaoh, "Be pleased to command me when I am to plead for you and for your servants and for your people, that the frogs be cut off from you and your houses and be left only in the Nile." And he said, "Tomorrow." Moses said, "Be it as you say, so that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God. The frogs shall go away from you and your houses and your servants and your people. They shall be left only in the Nile."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh asks for prayer and promises release, and Moses lets him name the time.

Plead with the LORD. The man who asked “Who is the LORD?” (5:2) now asks for prayer.

Be pleased to command me. Moses lets Pharaoh choose the time, so that the answer cannot be called chance: “that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God”.

Tomorrow. Offered relief now, Pharaoh chooses one more night with the frogs: pride delaying what it needs. Do not say “tomorrow” to God about what he asks today (Hebrews 3:15).

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh, and Moses cried to the LORD about the frogs, as he had agreed with Pharaoh. And the LORD did according to the word of Moses. The frogs died out in the houses, the courtyards, and the fields. And they gathered them together in heaps, and the land stank. But when Pharaoh saw that there was a respite, he hardened his heart and would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God removes the frogs, but as soon as the pressure lifts, Pharaoh breaks his word.

Moses cried to the LORD. Moses prays for his enemy, and God answers precisely. The dead frogs lie in heaps and the land stinks, so even the relief is a reminder of the judgment.

A respite, a breathing space, and the promise is dropped. Here Pharaoh hardened his heart himself; the word is literally “made heavy”, dull and insensitive.

Not real repentance. Regret over pain is not turning from sin (2 Corinthians 7:10), and true repentance remains when the pressure goes. Keep the promises you make to God in a crisis, and if you have broken them, he still receives the one who comes back.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The third plague comes without warning and brings Egypt’s experts to the end of their power. At God’s word Aaron strikes the dust, and gnats cover man and beast throughout the land (vv. 16–17). The magicians try to copy it and cannot (v. 18). They confess to Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God”, admitting that this is God’s own direct work (v. 19). But recognising God’s power is not the same as trusting him, and Pharaoh’s heart stays hard, as the LORD had said.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Finger of God

Counterfeit power reaches its limit.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the magicians reached the end of their power. Now: Jesus used their words of his own work: “if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons” (Luke 11:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth, so that it may become gnats in all the land of Egypt.'" And they did so. Aaron stretched out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the earth, and there were gnats on man and beast. All the dust of the earth became gnats in all the land of Egypt. The magicians tried by their secret arts to produce gnats, but they could not. So there were gnats on man and beast. Then the magicians said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God." But Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gnats spring from the dust, and the magicians, unable to copy it, confess that this is God’s work.

The dust of the earth. The gnats come from the dust of the ground, recalling the dust from which God formed man (Genesis 2:7).

Without warning. The third plague in each set of three comes without warning (also 9:8; 10:21).

But they could not. Egypt’s experts reach their limit, for bringing life from dust belongs to God alone: the counterfeit power of darkness collapses before the living God.

The finger of God means God’s direct power, exercised with little effort; the tablets of the law were written by it (31:18). Jesus used the same phrase of his own power over demons (Luke 11:20).

Recognition is not faith. The magicians did not convert. Recognising God’s power is not the same as trusting him (James 2:19).

Uncertain wording. The exact insect is unknown: gnats, mosquitoes or lice. What matters is clear: tiny, biting and everywhere.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20-32 — Flies and the Setting Apart of Goshen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the fourth plague God draws a line between his people and Egypt, and Pharaoh begins to bargain. Swarms of flies ruin the land, but Goshen, where Israel lives, is spared, so that Pharaoh may know the LORD rules “in the midst of the earth” (vv. 20–24). Pharaoh offers worship inside Egypt; Moses refuses, since Israel’s sacrifices would provoke the Egyptians, and insists on three days’ journey (vv. 25–27). Pharaoh agrees, “only you must not go very far away”, and asks for prayer (vv. 28–29). God removes every fly, and Pharaoh hardens his heart once more (vv. 30–32).
verseByVerse.theology:
Flies and the Setting Apart of Goshen

God draws a line between his people and Egypt, and Pharaoh tries to redraw God's terms.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: each compromise adjusted terms that were God's to set. Now: God keeps showing mercy even to people who have already misused it (Rom. 5:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Rise up early in the morning and present yourself to Pharaoh, as he goes out to the water, and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, "Let my people go, that they may serve me. Or else, if you will not let my people go, behold, I will send swarms of flies on you and your servants and your people, and into your houses. And the houses of the Egyptians shall be filled with swarms of flies, and also the ground on which they stand. But on that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people dwell, so that no swarms of flies shall be there, that you may know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth. Thus I will put a division between my people and your people. Tomorrow this sign shall happen."'" And the LORD did so. There came great swarms of flies into the house of Pharaoh and into his servants' houses. Throughout all the land of Egypt the land was ruined by the swarms of flies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends flies on Egypt but spares Goshen, drawing a line between his people and Egypt.

Set apart means to make a distinction, to treat differently. From now on the plagues fall on Egypt and not on Israel (9:4, 26; 10:23; 11:7). By separating his people, God shows that he is the LORD “in the midst of the earth”, not a merely local god.

Grace, not merit. Israel was not more deserving. The distinction is grace, as the Passover will make plain (12:13). The God who pours out wrath also shelters his people from it, and beyond the Passover stands the cross, where Christ bore the judgment so that none should fall on us.

Uncertain wording. The insects in the swarms of flies are not named exactly: perhaps biting dog-flies, or beetles such as the scarab sacred to Egypt. In v. 23 the Hebrew reads “redemption” where the ESV, following some ancient translations, has division (see the ESV footnote). Either way, God sets his people apart.
verseByVerse.note: Goshen was the region of the eastern Nile delta where Israel lived.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said, "Go, sacrifice to your God within the land." But Moses said, "It would not be right to do so, for the offerings we shall sacrifice to the LORD our God are an abomination to the Egyptians. If we sacrifice offerings abominable to the Egyptians before their eyes, will they not stone us? We must go three days' journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God as he tells us." So Pharaoh said, "I will let you go to sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness; only you must not go very far away. Plead for me." Then Moses said, "Behold, I am going out from you and I will plead with the LORD that the swarms of flies may depart from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people, tomorrow. Only let not Pharaoh cheat again by not letting the people go to sacrifice to the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh tries to bargain, but Moses holds to what God commanded.

Within the land. Pharaoh’s first compromise is worship that stays in Egypt. Moses refuses: Israel’s sacrifices would include animals Egyptians held sacred or found offensive (compare Genesis 46:34), and that could provoke violence.

Only you must not go very far away. The second compromise is to go, but stay within reach. Pharaoh will keep offering partial freedom: leave your children (10:10–11), leave your flocks (10:24). The world often allows faith if it is kept small and private.

We must go three days’ journey into the wilderness. Moses holds to God’s instruction (3:18). It was a real request, and Pharaoh never granted even that.

In everyday life. Beware of compromises that let you keep God close while you still live under Pharaoh’s rule.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses went out from Pharaoh and prayed to the LORD. And the LORD did as Moses asked, and removed the swarms of flies from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people; not one remained. But Pharaoh hardened his heart this time also, and did not let the people go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God removes every fly, and Pharaoh hardens his heart again.

Not one remained. God answers the prayer exactly. Yet twice now Pharaoh has asked for prayer and broken his word, and hardening deepens with every relief.

Mercy not wasted. He answers prayer even for those who will abuse it (Matthew 5:45), and their guilt grows with every mercy refused (Romans 2:4–5).

In everyday life. An answered prayer is more than an escape from trouble: it is a call to keep your word to God.

8.theology:
There is no one like the LORD. The plagues expose every rival as powerless; even the magicians confess "the finger of God."

Distinguishing grace. God sets apart Goshen, sheltering his people in the day of judgment, a foreshadowing of Passover and the cross.

The hardened heart and false repentance. Pharaoh is sorry only for the consequences, bargains for partial obedience, and hardens again when relief comes.
8.examples:
Then: As the plagues escalated, Pharaoh offered the half-repentance and compromised obedience typical of a hardened heart.

Now: The world still offers God a partial obedience: do not go too far. But God draws a line between his people and the world, and in Christ he shelters us wholly from the judgment to come. He calls not for bargaining but for surrender.

keyVerse.quote: But on that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people dwell, so that no swarms of flies shall be there, that you may know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth.
keyVerse.note: From this plague on, God draws a line between his people and Egypt, and the line is grace, not merit. It shows that the LORD is no local god but rules “in the midst of the earth”, and it points ahead to the Passover and to the cross, where God shelters his people from the judgment they deserve.

8.reflection:
Pharaoh asked for prayer when the frogs came, then hardened his heart at the first respite (vv. 8–15). How can we tell the difference between regret over trouble and real repentance?

The magicians confessed, “This is the finger of God” (v. 19), yet did not turn to him. Why is recognising God’s power not the same as trusting him? Compare Jesus’ words in Luke 11:20.

God set Goshen apart from the plague (vv. 22–23). What does it mean for Christians to be set apart by grace, and how should that shape our attitude toward others?

Pharaoh offered compromises: worship within the land, or not too far away (vv. 25–28). What compromises does the world offer believers today, and how can we answer them?

9.title: That My Name May Be Proclaimed in All the Earth
9.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, "Let my people go, that they may serve me.<sup>2</sup>For if you refuse to let them go and still hold them,<sup>3</sup>behold, the hand of the LORD will fall with a very severe plague upon your livestock that are in the field, the horses, the donkeys, the camels, the herds, and the flocks.<sup>4</sup>But the LORD will make a distinction between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt, so that nothing of all that belongs to the people of Israel shall die."'"<sup>5</sup>And the LORD set a time, saying, "Tomorrow the LORD will do this thing in the land."<sup>6</sup>And the next day the LORD did this thing. All the livestock of the Egyptians died, but not one of the livestock of the people of Israel died.<sup>7</sup>And Pharaoh sent, and behold, not one of the livestock of Israel was dead. But the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not let the people go.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "Take handfuls of soot from the kiln, and let Moses throw them in the air in the sight of Pharaoh.<sup>9</sup>It shall become fine dust over all the land of Egypt, and become boils breaking out in sores on man and beast throughout all the land of Egypt."<sup>10</sup>So they took soot from the kiln and stood before Pharaoh. And Moses threw it in the air, and it became boils breaking out in sores on man and beast.<sup>11</sup>And the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils, for the boils came upon the magicians and upon all the Egyptians.<sup>12</sup>But the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and he did not listen to them, as the LORD had spoken to Moses.<sup>13</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Rise up early in the morning and present yourself before Pharaoh and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, "Let my people go, that they may serve me.<sup>14</sup>For this time I will send all my plagues on you yourself, and on your servants and your people, so that you may know that there is none like me in all the earth.<sup>15</sup>For by now I could have put out my hand and struck you and your people with pestilence, and you would have been cut off from the earth.<sup>16</sup>But for this purpose I have raised you up, to show you my power, so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth.<sup>17</sup>You are still exalting yourself against my people and will not let them go.<sup>18</sup>Behold, about this time tomorrow I will cause very heavy hail to fall, such as never has been in Egypt from the day it was founded until now.<sup>19</sup>Now therefore send, get your livestock and all that you have in the field into safe shelter, for every man and beast that is in the field and is not brought home will die when the hail falls on them."'"<sup>20</sup>Then whoever feared the word of the LORD among the servants of Pharaoh hurried his slaves and his livestock into the houses,<sup>21</sup>but whoever did not pay attention to the word of the LORD left his slaves and his livestock in the field.<sup>22</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward heaven, so that there may be hail in all the land of Egypt, on man and beast and every plant of the field, in the land of Egypt."<sup>23</sup>Then Moses stretched out his staff toward heaven, and the LORD sent thunder and hail, and fire ran down to the earth. And the LORD rained hail upon the land of Egypt.<sup>24</sup>There was hail and fire flashing continually in the midst of the hail, very heavy hail, such as had never been in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation.<sup>25</sup>The hail struck down everything that was in the field in all the land of Egypt, both man and beast. And the hail struck down every plant of the field and broke every tree of the field.<sup>26</sup>Only in the land of Goshen, where the people of Israel were, was there no hail.<sup>27</sup>Then Pharaoh sent and called Moses and Aaron and said to them, "This time I have sinned; the LORD is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong.<sup>28</sup>Plead with the LORD, for there has been enough of God's thunder and hail. I will let you go, and you shall stay no longer."<sup>29</sup>Moses said to him, "As soon as I have gone out of the city, I will stretch out my hands to the LORD. The thunder will cease, and there will be no more hail, so that you may know that the earth is the LORD's.<sup>30</sup>But as for you and your servants, I know that you do not yet fear the LORD God."<sup>31</sup>(The flax and the barley were struck down, for the barley was in the ear and the flax was in bud.<sup>32</sup>But the wheat and the emmer were not struck down, for they are late in coming up.)<sup>33</sup>So Moses went out of the city from Pharaoh and stretched out his hands to the LORD, and the thunder and the hail ceased, and the rain no longer poured upon the earth.<sup>34</sup>But when Pharaoh saw that the rain and the hail and the thunder had ceased, he sinned yet again and hardened his heart, he and his servants.<sup>35</sup>So the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not let the people of Israel go, just as the LORD had spoken through Moses.
9.overview:
Where we are. The Nile, the frogs, the gnats and the flies have come and gone (chapters 7–8), and each time Pharaoh has bargained and then hardened his heart. Now the plagues move from nuisance towards life and death: first Egypt’s livestock, then Egyptian bodies, then a storm that kills whatever stands in the open.

The message. The LORD is not a local god to be bargained with: “there is none like me in all the earth” (v. 14). He has kept Pharaoh standing for one purpose, “so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth” (v. 16), and even the proudest rebel ends up serving the display of God’s glory. Yet in the middle of judgment God offers shelter to anyone, Egyptian or Israelite, who takes his word seriously.

Why it was said. Israel would remember these plagues as slaves who had watched the world’s greatest king humbled by their God (see the introduction). They needed to know that their rescue rested on God’s purpose, not on Pharaoh’s goodwill, and to be warned against Pharaoh’s way of confessing sin in the storm and returning to it when the sky clears.

How the chapter makes its case. Disease kills Egypt’s livestock in the field while not one of Israel’s dies, and Pharaoh checks the facts and still refuses (vv. 1–7). Soot from the kiln becomes boils on man and beast; the magicians cannot even stand, and for the first time the LORD hardens Pharaoh’s heart (vv. 8–12). Before the hail God explains himself: he could have wiped Egypt out, but he has raised Pharaoh up to show his power; and he warns everyone to take shelter, and some of Pharaoh’s servants listen (vv. 13–21). Hail and fire strike everything in the open except Goshen (vv. 22–26). Pharaoh makes his fullest confession yet, Moses prays, the storm stops, and Pharaoh sins yet again (vv. 27–35).

Where it leads. Chiefly by revealing the character of God, which is shown in full in Christ. Paul quotes verse 16 in Romans 9:17: the God who raised up Pharaoh is the God who has mercy on whom he wills, and that mercy takes its fullest shape at the cross, where God is shown to be both “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). The pattern of shelter points the same way: the only safe place from the hail was the one God named, and the shelter he names now is his Son, “who delivers us from the wrath to come” (1 Thessalonians 1:10).

For us. Hear God’s warnings as mercies and take the shelter he gives. Do not confuse fear of consequences with the fear of God: a confession that vanishes with the storm was never repentance. And take heart: no ruler, however proud, stands outside God’s purpose for his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-12 — Livestock, Boils, and a Deeper Distinction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The plagues now strike life itself, and God hardens a heart that has already hardened itself. A deadly disease kills Egypt’s livestock in the field, while God keeps his word that not one of Israel’s animals will die; Pharaoh sends to check, sees the proof, and still refuses (vv. 1–7). Then soot from the kiln, where Israel’s bricks were fired, becomes festering boils on people and animals. The magicians, who once copied Moses’ signs, cannot even stand before him, and for the first time the text says that the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, as he had told Moses he would (vv. 8–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
Livestock, Boils, and a Deeper Distinction

Pharaoh sees the evidence and refuses it, and is confirmed in the hardness he chose.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: through five plagues Pharaoh hardened his own heart; now God confirms him in the hardness he chose. Now: more evidence cannot change a heart that has decided not to be moved by evidence.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, "Let my people go, that they may serve me. For if you refuse to let them go and still hold them, behold, the hand of the LORD will fall with a very severe plague upon your livestock that are in the field, the horses, the donkeys, the camels, the herds, and the flocks. But the LORD will make a distinction between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt, so that nothing of all that belongs to the people of Israel shall die."'" And the LORD set a time, saying, "Tomorrow the LORD will do this thing in the land." And the next day the LORD did this thing. All the livestock of the Egyptians died, but not one of the livestock of the people of Israel died. And Pharaoh sent, and behold, not one of the livestock of Israel was dead. But the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not let the people go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God strikes Egypt’s livestock and spares every animal of Israel’s, yet Pharaoh refuses with the proof before his eyes.

A very severe plague. A deadly animal disease, perhaps anthrax, strikes horses, donkeys, camels, herds and flocks in the field. God sets the time (v. 5), so no one can call it chance.

Egypt’s animal gods. Many of Egypt’s gods were pictured as animals: Apis the sacred bull, Hathor the cow goddess. The plague exposes them as powerless.

All the livestock of the Egyptians died. Yet there are cattle for the hail (v. 19) and horses for the chariots (14:9). “All” here means all kinds, and all in the field (v. 3), a common biblical way of speaking, not every single animal.

Not one of the livestock of Israel was dead. Pharaoh sends to check, sees the evidence, and still refuses. Evidence alone does not produce faith: a hardened heart can see the facts and still say no (Luke 16:31).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "Take handfuls of soot from the kiln, and let Moses throw them in the air in the sight of Pharaoh. It shall become fine dust over all the land of Egypt, and become boils breaking out in sores on man and beast throughout all the land of Egypt." So they took soot from the kiln and stood before Pharaoh. And Moses threw it in the air, and it became boils breaking out in sores on man and beast. And the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils, for the boils came upon the magicians and upon all the Egyptians. But the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and he did not listen to them, as the LORD had spoken to Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The plague reaches Egyptian bodies, the magicians are driven from the contest, and God confirms Pharaoh in his chosen hardness.

Soot from the kiln came from the furnace where Israel’s bricks were fired, so the furnace of slavery becomes the source of judgment.

Boils breaking out in sores. For the first time the plagues strike Egyptian bodies. The same disease is later threatened on covenant breakers (Deuteronomy 28:27).

The magicians could not stand before Moses. Unable to cure themselves, they leave the contest for good.

The LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh. This is the first time in the plagues that God is said to harden, “as the LORD had spoken to Moses” (4:21). Pharaoh had hardened himself repeatedly; now God confirms him in it, giving him over to what he has chosen (Romans 1:24).

What it does not mean. God does not harden an innocent man against his will. He gives a rebel over to his rebellion (see the introduction).

Uncertain wording. The word for soot occurs only here (some render it “ashes”), and the disease cannot be named with certainty: the words describe swellings that burst into blisters. The point is clear either way.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13-21 — The Warning and the God-Fearers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the worst storm in Egypt’s history, God explains what he is doing and opens a door of mercy. He could have cut Egypt off already; he has kept Pharaoh standing for one purpose, to show his power so that his name may be proclaimed in all the earth (vv. 13–17). Then he announces the hail for the next day and tells everyone to bring people and animals under cover. Some of Pharaoh’s own servants fear the word of the LORD and obey; others ignore it. The difference is not race but whether they believe what God has said (vv. 18–21).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Warning and the God-Fearers

Judgment comes with a way of escape for anyone who believes God's word.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the name was proclaimed, and forty years later Rahab in Jericho had heard what the LORD did for Israel (Josh. 2:10). Now: the line God draws runs between those who fear his word and those who do not (12:38).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Rise up early in the morning and present yourself before Pharaoh and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, "Let my people go, that they may serve me. For this time I will send all my plagues on you yourself, and on your servants and your people, so that you may know that there is none like me in all the earth. For by now I could have put out my hand and struck you and your people with pestilence, and you would have been cut off from the earth. But for this purpose I have raised you up, to show you my power, so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth. You are still exalting yourself against my people and will not let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God could have destroyed Pharaoh already; he has kept him standing so that the whole world will hear of the LORD’s power.

All my plagues on you yourself. The Hebrew says “to your heart”: the remaining plagues will strike Pharaoh’s very self.

For this purpose I have raised you up. Literally “caused you to stand”, kept alive and in power; that Pharaoh still lives is mercy, not weakness. Paul quotes it in Romans 9:17 to show that God has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills.

That my name may be proclaimed in all the earth. It came true: Rahab in Jericho had heard of it (Joshua 2:10), and so had the Philistines (1 Samuel 4:8). The same name is now proclaimed to the nations in the gospel of Christ (Philippians 2:9–11).

Where Christians differ: did God make Pharaoh to destroy him? Some read only “kept you alive through the plagues”; others see God’s sovereign purpose in raising Pharaoh to power at all. This commentary’s view: both are true. God ordained Pharaoh’s place in history for his glory, and Pharaoh freely exalted himself against God’s people (v. 17). God’s purpose does not excuse Pharaoh’s sin.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, about this time tomorrow I will cause very heavy hail to fall, such as never has been in Egypt from the day it was founded until now. Now therefore send, get your livestock and all that you have in the field into safe shelter, for every man and beast that is in the field and is not brought home will die when the hail falls on them."'" Then whoever feared the word of the LORD among the servants of Pharaoh hurried his slaves and his livestock into the houses, but whoever did not pay attention to the word of the LORD left his slaves and his livestock in the field.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God announces the worst storm in Egypt’s history and tells everyone how to escape it.

Into safe shelter. Here is mercy within judgment: any Egyptian could escape by believing God’s word and bringing his livestock in.

Whoever feared the word of the LORD. Some of Pharaoh’s own officials believed God and acted. They may be among the “mixed multitude” who left with Israel (12:38). Others ignored the warning and lost everything.

Refuge for any who feared. The plagues were not aimed at Egyptians as a race. God’s warnings are mercies still, and the refuge he names today is Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22-35 — Hail and a Confession That Melts
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The hail falls as God said, and Pharaoh’s confession falls apart as soon as it stops. Moses stretches out his staff, and hail with fire running along the ground destroys people, animals, crops and trees in the open, everywhere but Goshen (vv. 22–26). Pharaoh admits, “This time I have sinned; the LORD is in the right”, and begs for prayer. Moses agrees, so that Pharaoh may know the earth is the LORD’s, but he sees that Pharaoh does not yet fear God (vv. 27–30). A note on the crops shows what was lost and what remained (vv. 31–32). When the storm ends, Pharaoh sins yet again (vv. 33–35).
verseByVerse.theology:
Hail and a Confession That Melts

Pharaoh wants the thunder to stop, not his sin.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the wheat left standing showed how much Egypt still had to lose. Now: worldly grief only wants the trouble to stop; godly grief leads to repentance (2 Cor. 7:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward heaven, so that there may be hail in all the land of Egypt, on man and beast and every plant of the field, in the land of Egypt." Then Moses stretched out his staff toward heaven, and the LORD sent thunder and hail, and fire ran down to the earth. And the LORD rained hail upon the land of Egypt. There was hail and fire flashing continually in the midst of the hail, very heavy hail, such as had never been in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation. The hail struck down everything that was in the field in all the land of Egypt, both man and beast. And the hail struck down every plant of the field and broke every tree of the field. Only in the land of Goshen, where the people of Israel were, was there no hail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hail falls as God said, destroying everything in the open except in Goshen.

Fire ran down to the earth. Lightning runs along the ground with the hail, a storm unlike any in Egypt, where rain is rare. Nut the sky goddess, Seth the storm god and Osiris the god of crops are all helpless.

The LORD sent thunder and hail. The weather itself does his bidding (Psalm 148:8).

Only in the land of Goshen. God protects his people in the midst of judgment, as at the flies (8:22).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh sent and called Moses and Aaron and said to them, "This time I have sinned; the LORD is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong. Plead with the LORD, for there has been enough of God's thunder and hail. I will let you go, and you shall stay no longer." Moses said to him, "As soon as I have gone out of the city, I will stretch out my hands to the LORD. The thunder will cease, and there will be no more hail, so that you may know that the earth is the LORD's. But as for you and your servants, I know that you do not yet fear the LORD God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh confesses more fully than ever, but he fears the storm, not God.

This time I have sinned. Pharaoh uses God’s name and calls him just in his judgments: “the LORD is in the right”. His question “Who is the LORD?” (5:2) has been answered by his own mouth.

The earth is the LORD’s. The answered prayer will show that the LORD is no local god of the Hebrews (Psalm 24:1).

You do not yet fear the LORD God. The fear of God is reverent submission that changes behaviour. Pharaoh feared the consequences, not God. Confessing sin is never useless, but true repentance turns from sin, not only from its pain (2 Corinthians 7:10).

verseByVerse.quote: (The flax and the barley were struck down, for the barley was in the ear and the flax was in bud. But the wheat and the emmer were not struck down, for they are late in coming up.) So Moses went out of the city from Pharaoh and stretched out his hands to the LORD, and the thunder and the hail ceased, and the rain no longer poured upon the earth. But when Pharaoh saw that the rain and the hail and the thunder had ceased, he sinned yet again and hardened his heart, he and his servants. So the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not let the people of Israel go, just as the LORD had spoken through Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the storm ends, Pharaoh sins again and hardens his heart.

The flax and the barley were struck down. Flax (for linen) was in bud and barley in the ear, while wheat and emmer come up later. The detail fits Egypt’s farming year, perhaps January or February.

The wheat and the emmer. The surviving crops give Egypt one more thing to lose, to the locusts (10:5, 15), but they also leave room to repent.

He sinned yet again. Scripture calls his hardening sin, and his servants harden their hearts with him, just as the LORD had spoken through Moses: Pharaoh’s choice and God’s word stand together.

In everyday life. When trouble passes, do you go back to the sin it exposed? If so, the repentance Pharaoh refused is still open to you.

Uncertain wording. The grain called emmer is “spelt” or “rye” in older versions; emmer, a hardy wheat grown widely in Egypt, is the likely meaning.
verseByVerse.note: “Emmer” is a type of wheat (ESV note). The details date the hail to late winter.

9.theology:
The sovereignty of God in hardening. The LORD himself now hardens Pharaoh (v. 12), and declares that Pharaoh exists for the display of God's power (v. 16).

The glory of God as the goal of all things. "That my name may be proclaimed in all the earth" is the supreme purpose behind the plagues and behind history itself.

The futility of false repentance. Pharaoh’s confession sounds perfect, but it melts away when the pressure lifts. Words without a changed heart save no one.
9.examples:
Then: God brought Egypt to its knees with disease and the worst hailstorm in its history.

Now: God still governs even the hardest hearts toward the proclamation of his glory. And we are warned: it is possible to confess sin with flawless words in a crisis and remain unchanged. True repentance bears fruit when the storm has passed.

keyVerse.quote: But for this purpose I have raised you up, to show you my power, so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth.
keyVerse.note: This verse explains the whole contest with Pharaoh: God could have ended it with one blow (v. 15), but he kept Pharaoh standing so that his power and name would be known worldwide. Paul quotes it in Romans 9:17, and its purpose is still being fulfilled wherever the gospel makes the LORD’s name known.

9.reflection:
Pharaoh sent to check that Israel’s livestock had survived, saw the proof, and still refused (v. 7). Why does evidence alone not produce faith? Compare Luke 16:31.

God says he has raised Pharaoh up “so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth” (v. 16). How does it help you to know that God’s purpose stands even behind those who oppose him, and how does Paul use this verse in Romans 9?

Before the hail, God told everyone how to find shelter, and some of Pharaoh’s servants “feared the word of the LORD” (v. 20). What does this show about God’s character in judgment, and what shelter does he offer us?

Pharaoh said, “This time I have sinned”, yet Moses knew he did not fear God (vv. 27–30, 34). How can we tell sorrow over consequences from true repentance in our own lives?

10.title: Darkness Over the Land
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart and the heart of his servants, that I may show these signs of mine among them,<sup>2</sup>and that you may tell in the hearing of your son and of your grandson how I have dealt harshly with the Egyptians and what signs I have done among them, that you may know that I am the LORD."<sup>3</sup>So Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, 'How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me? Let my people go, that they may serve me.<sup>4</sup>For if you refuse to let my people go, behold, tomorrow I will bring locusts into your country,<sup>5</sup>and they shall cover the face of the land, so that no one can see the land. And they shall eat what is left to you after the hail, and they shall eat every tree of yours that grows in the field,<sup>6</sup>and they shall fill your houses and the houses of all your servants and of all the Egyptians, as neither your fathers nor your grandfathers have seen, from the day they came on earth to this day.'" Then he turned and went out from Pharaoh.<sup>7</sup>Then Pharaoh's servants said to him, "How long shall this man be a snare to us? Let the men go, that they may serve the LORD their God. Do you not yet understand that Egypt is ruined?"<sup>8</sup>So Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh. And he said to them, "Go, serve the LORD your God. But which ones are to go?"<sup>9</sup>Moses said, "We will go with our young and our old. We will go with our sons and daughters and with our flocks and herds, for we must hold a feast to the LORD."<sup>10</sup>But he said to them, "The LORD be with you, if ever I let you and your little ones go! Look, you have some evil purpose in mind.<sup>11</sup>No! Go, the men among you, and serve the LORD, for that is what you are asking." And they were driven out from Pharaoh's presence.<sup>12</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt for the locusts, so that they may come upon the land of Egypt and eat every plant in the land, all that the hail has left."<sup>13</sup>So Moses stretched out his staff over the land of Egypt, and the LORD brought an east wind upon the land all that day and all that night. When it was morning, the east wind had brought the locusts.<sup>14</sup>The locusts came up over all the land of Egypt and settled on the whole country of Egypt, such a dense swarm of locusts as had never been before, nor ever will be again.<sup>15</sup>They covered the face of the whole land, so that the land was darkened, and they ate all the plants in the land and all the fruit of the trees that the hail had left. Not a green thing remained, neither tree nor plant of the field, through all the land of Egypt.<sup>16</sup>Then Pharaoh hastily called Moses and Aaron and said, "I have sinned against the LORD your God, and against you.<sup>17</sup>Now therefore, forgive my sin, please, only this once, and plead with the LORD your God only to remove this death from me."<sup>18</sup>So he went out from Pharaoh and pleaded with the LORD.<sup>19</sup>And the LORD turned the wind into a very strong west wind, which lifted the locusts and drove them into the Red Sea. Not a single locust was left in all the country of Egypt.<sup>20</sup>But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the people of Israel go.<sup>21</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, a darkness to be felt."<sup>22</sup>So Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and there was pitch darkness in all the land of Egypt three days.<sup>23</sup>They did not see one another, nor did anyone rise from his place for three days, but all the people of Israel had light where they lived.<sup>24</sup>Then Pharaoh called Moses and said, "Go, serve the LORD; your little ones also may go with you; only let your flocks and your herds remain behind."<sup>25</sup>But Moses said, "You must also let us have sacrifices and burnt offerings, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God.<sup>26</sup>Our livestock also must go with us; not a hoof shall be left behind, for we must take of them to serve the LORD our God, and we do not know with what we must serve the LORD until we arrive there."<sup>27</sup>But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he would not let them go.<sup>28</sup>Then Pharaoh said to him, "Get away from me; take care never to see my face again, for on the day you see my face you shall die."<sup>29</sup>Moses said, "As you say! I will not see your face again."
10.overview:
Where we are. The hail has flattened Egypt’s flax and barley, and Pharaoh has confessed his sin and taken it back as soon as the sky cleared (9:27–35). Two plagues remain before the last: locusts and darkness.

The message. God is making himself known, to Egypt and to Israel’s children and grandchildren, as the LORD before whom the proud must bow (vv. 2–3). He will not accept a partial surrender: Pharaoh offers to let some go, then all but the flocks, but God claims his whole people and everything they have for his worship. Meanwhile his creation turns against Egypt: not a green thing remains, and a darkness falls that can be felt, while Israel has light.

Why it was said. Israel was told to retell these signs to their sons and grandsons (v. 2), and this chapter is part of that telling. Generations who never saw Egypt needed to know what their God had done, and to be warned that the LORD will not share his people with another master (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. God states his purpose, to show his signs and to give Israel a story to tell, and asks Pharaoh how long he will refuse to humble himself (vv. 1–6). Pharaoh’s officials beg him to give way, and he offers to let only the men go (vv. 7–11). Locusts strip everything the hail left (vv. 12–15). Pharaoh hurriedly confesses, Moses prays, a west wind removes every locust, and the LORD hardens Pharaoh’s heart (vv. 16–20). Darkness covers Egypt for three days, but Israel has light (vv. 21–23). Pharaoh’s last offer, to keep the flocks, is refused: “not a hoof shall be left behind”; he threatens Moses with death, and Moses leaves his presence for good (vv. 24–29).

Where it leads. By pattern. In Egypt darkness came first and then the death of the firstborn (chapters 11–12). At the cross darkness covered all the land for three hours (Matthew 27:45), and then God’s own firstborn Son died; but there the darkness fell on him in our place, so that his people have light. “Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness,” Jesus said (John 8:12). And the God who would not leave a hoof in Egypt has bought his people whole: “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

For us. Tell your children and grandchildren what God has done; faith is still passed on by stories told at home. Do not bargain with God over how much of your life he may have. The God who redeemed all of you can be trusted with all of it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pharaoh will not humble himself, so God strips his land bare while giving Israel a story to tell for generations. God sends Moses with a purpose that reaches beyond Egypt: to show his signs and to give Israel something to tell their grandchildren (vv. 1–6). Pharaoh’s officials, seeing Egypt ruined, urge him to give way, but he offers to release only the men, keeping the children as hostages (vv. 7–11). Locusts brought by an east wind devour every green thing the hail left (vv. 12–15). Pharaoh hurries to confess and ask for prayer; God removes every locust with a west wind, and then hardens Pharaoh’s heart (vv. 16–20).
verseByVerse.theology:
Locusts Devour the Land

Pharaoh’s own officials give way, but he will let only the men go.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the plagues were done for an audience not yet born. Now: worship that is not passed on to the next generation dies within a lifetime; no one needs to abolish it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart and the heart of his servants, that I may show these signs of mine among them, and that you may tell in the hearing of your son and of your grandson how I have dealt harshly with the Egyptians and what signs I have done among them, that you may know that I am the LORD." So Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, 'How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me? Let my people go, that they may serve me. For if you refuse to let my people go, behold, tomorrow I will bring locusts into your country, and they shall cover the face of the land, so that no one can see the land. And they shall eat what is left to you after the hail, and they shall eat every tree of yours that grows in the field, and they shall fill your houses and the houses of all your servants and of all the Egyptians, as neither your fathers nor your grandfathers have seen, from the day they came on earth to this day.'" Then he turned and went out from Pharaoh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends Moses back with a purpose that reaches beyond Egypt, a story for Israel to tell its children, and he names Pharaoh’s real problem: pride.

I have hardened his heart. As at 4:21: God’s purpose and Pharaoh’s own will are both at work, and Pharaoh’s guilt is real.

Tell your son and grandson. The plagues are also for future generations: the story is meant to be retold (Psalm 78:4–7), and faith is still passed on by stories told to children and grandchildren.

How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me? The issue is pride: Pharaoh refuses to bow before God.

Tomorrow I will bring locusts. Desert locusts can form swarms of billions, stripping every green thing. They will eat what the hail left (9:32) and fill the houses of Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh's servants said to him, "How long shall this man be a snare to us? Let the men go, that they may serve the LORD their God. Do you not yet understand that Egypt is ruined?" So Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh. And he said to them, "Go, serve the LORD your God. But which ones are to go?" Moses said, "We will go with our young and our old. We will go with our sons and daughters and with our flocks and herds, for we must hold a feast to the LORD." But he said to them, "The LORD be with you, if ever I let you and your little ones go! Look, you have some evil purpose in mind. No! Go, the men among you, and serve the LORD, for that is what you are asking." And they were driven out from Pharaoh's presence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh’s own officials see that Egypt is ruined and urge him to give way, but he offers only a half-release: the men may go, the children stay.

A snare to us. To Pharaoh’s officials Moses has become a trap that ruins. Egypt is ruined: they see what Pharaoh will not.

Which ones are to go? Moses answers: young and old, sons and daughters, flocks and herds. Worship involves the whole people.

The LORD be with you is sarcasm: “As if I would let your little ones go!” By you have some evil purpose in mind Pharaoh means, “You plan to escape.”

Go, the men among you. His third compromise is to let only the men go, since families left in Egypt would draw the men back. But faith is not only for adults. Children belong among God’s worshipping people (Deuteronomy 31:12; Mark 10:14); do not leave yours in Egypt.

Uncertain wording. Verse 10 is literally “evil is before your faces”. Most take it as the ESV does, an accusation of a plot; others read a threat, “trouble awaits you” if you try. Some have heard a play on the name of the sun god Ra, but that is guesswork. Either way, Pharaoh refuses.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt for the locusts, so that they may come upon the land of Egypt and eat every plant in the land, all that the hail has left." So Moses stretched out his staff over the land of Egypt, and the LORD brought an east wind upon the land all that day and all that night. When it was morning, the east wind had brought the locusts. The locusts came up over all the land of Egypt and settled on the whole country of Egypt, such a dense swarm of locusts as had never been before, nor ever will be again. They covered the face of the whole land, so that the land was darkened, and they ate all the plants in the land and all the fruit of the trees that the hail had left. Not a green thing remained, neither tree nor plant of the field, through all the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Moses’ signal God brings the worst locust swarm Egypt will ever see, and it finishes off what the hail left.

An east wind upon the land. God rules the winds: an east wind from the desert brings the swarm.

Such a dense swarm. The swarm is so thick that “the land was darkened”, a foretaste of the darkness to come (v. 21). The wheat and emmer that survived the hail (9:32) are eaten too: “not a green thing remained”, and with the crops goes Egypt’s food for the coming year.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh hastily called Moses and Aaron and said, "I have sinned against the LORD your God, and against you. Now therefore, forgive my sin, please, only this once, and plead with the LORD your God only to remove this death from me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh’s quickest and most religious confession yet still asks for relief from the plague, not freedom from sin.

Hastily … only this once. Pharaoh sends for Moses as fast as the swarm came. He has said “I have sinned” before (9:27), and “only this once” is a bargain, as if this will be the last time he needs to ask. He admits wronging Moses and Aaron as well as their God, but he still does not let the people go.

Only to remove this death from me. He asks God to take away “this death”, not his sin. Words of repentance are not always false, but repentance shows itself in turning, not only in asking for relief.

verseByVerse.quote: So he went out from Pharaoh and pleaded with the LORD. And the LORD turned the wind into a very strong west wind, which lifted the locusts and drove them into the Red Sea. Not a single locust was left in all the country of Egypt. But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the people of Israel go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers Moses’ prayer completely and removes every locust, but Pharaoh’s relief turns again into hardness.

He pleaded with the LORD. Moses prays at once for the man who has broken his word to him twice before (8:28–32; 9:28–35). The answer is as complete as the plague, “Not a single locust was left”, so that no one could put either the coming or the going down to chance.

Into the Red Sea. A west wind drives the locusts into the sea where Egypt’s army will also end (14:28).

But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart. Relief that should have led to obedience leads to hardening, as after each plague before (see the note on vv. 1–6). A confession made in a crisis is often withdrawn when the crisis passes.

Uncertain wording. The Red Sea is in Hebrew yam suph, “Sea of Reeds”. The same name is used of the Gulf of Aqaba (1 Kings 9:26), so it can cover the Red Sea and its gulfs; which stretch of water Israel crossed is debated (see chapter 14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21-29 — A Darkness to Be Felt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Egypt sits in a darkness it can feel while Israel has light, and Pharaoh’s final bargain fails. With no warning, Moses stretches out his hand, and for three days no Egyptian can see another or leave his place; yet in Israel’s homes there is light (vv. 21–23). Pharaoh now offers to let everyone go, even the children, if only the flocks stay behind. Moses refuses: they need the animals for worship, and they do not yet know what God will ask. Not a hoof will remain. Pharaoh threatens Moses with death, and Moses agrees that he will not see Pharaoh’s face again (vv. 24–29).
verseByVerse.theology:
A Darkness to Be Felt

Egypt’s chief god, the sun, is dethroned, and not a hoof is left behind.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the sun Egypt worshipped did not rise. Now: the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it (John 1:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, a darkness to be felt." So Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and there was pitch darkness in all the land of Egypt three days. They did not see one another, nor did anyone rise from his place for three days, but all the people of Israel had light where they lived.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without warning God covers Egypt in a darkness so thick it can be felt, while every Israelite home has light.

Darkness over the land of Egypt. Like the gnats and the boils, this plague comes unannounced. It is a blow against Ra, the sun god, and against Pharaoh, who was called the son of Ra.

A darkness to be felt. It was so dense it pressed in: no one could see another or rise from his place, and life stopped. The God who said “Let there be light” now says, in effect, let there be darkness, and the world of Egypt unravels.

Light where they lived. Yet Israel has light: God’s people have light in a dark world (John 8:12).

Darkness on his own Son. At the cross darkness covered the land for three hours (Matthew 27:45; Mark 15:33). There it fell not on God’s enemies but on his own Son, in our place, so that we might have light.
verseByVerse.note: The sun god Ra was among Egypt’s chief gods.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh called Moses and said, "Go, serve the LORD; your little ones also may go with you; only let your flocks and your herds remain behind." But Moses said, "You must also let us have sacrifices and burnt offerings, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God. Our livestock also must go with us; not a hoof shall be left behind, for we must take of them to serve the LORD our God, and we do not know with what we must serve the LORD until we arrive there." But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he would not let them go. Then Pharaoh said to him, "Get away from me; take care never to see my face again, for on the day you see my face you shall die." Moses said, "As you say! I will not see your face again."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh’s last compromise is refused, because God claims his people and all they have, and the audience ends with a threat of death.

Only let your flocks and your herds remain behind. Pharaoh’s fourth and last compromise: something must stay in Egypt.

Not a hoof shall be left behind. Every animal must go, because they do not yet know what God will require for worship. Full obedience leaves nothing behind.

The day you see my face you shall die. Moses accepts Pharaoh’s threat: after one last announcement (11:4–8) he will not come again.

In everyday life. Christians need not reject every compromise in practical matters. But in what God requires, partial obedience is disobedience. Is there one area of life you want to keep in Egypt? The God who redeemed all of you can be trusted with all of it.

10.theology:
The undoing of creation. Locusts and a darkness that could be felt reverse the order God established and show the LORD's mastery over creation itself.

The darkness that points to Calvary. There, in darkness, the true Firstborn bore judgment so his people might have light.

Generational testimony. God designs the exodus to be retold, that every generation may know he is the LORD.
10.examples:
Then: God stripped Egypt bare and dethroned the sun-god, yet Pharaoh still bargained and hardened.

Now: Those in Christ are children of light. And we, like Israel, are called to tell our children how the LORD has saved, that they too may know him.

keyVerse.quote: and that you may tell in the hearing of your son and of your grandson how I have dealt harshly with the Egyptians and what signs I have done among them, that you may know that I am the LORD.
keyVerse.note: God gives the plagues a second audience: not only Pharaoh, but Israel’s children and grandchildren. The signs were meant to be retold, so that every generation would know the LORD, and the chapter itself is part of that retelling, reaching us too.

10.reflection:
God told Israel to retell his signs to their sons and grandsons (v. 2). What stories of God’s faithfulness, in Scripture and in your own life, are you passing on, and how could you do it better?

Pharaoh offered to let only the men go, then everyone but the flocks (vv. 11, 24). Why does God refuse every partial release? Is there an area of your life you are keeping back from him?

Pharaoh asked forgiveness “only this once” but wanted God only to “remove this death” (v. 17). What is the difference between wanting relief and wanting God?

Israel had light while Egypt sat in darkness (v. 23), and darkness covered the land when Jesus died (Matthew 27:45). How does the cross help you understand this plague, and what does it mean to have light in a dark world?

11.title: The Announcement of the Last Plague
11.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Moses, "Yet one plague more I will bring upon Pharaoh and upon Egypt. Afterward he will let you go from here. When he lets you go, he will drive you away completely.<sup>2</sup>Speak now in the hearing of the people, that they ask, every man of his neighbor and every woman of her neighbor, for silver and gold jewelry."<sup>3</sup>And the LORD gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians.
