Moreover, the man Moses was very great in the land of Egypt, in the sight of Pharaoh's servants and in the sight of the people.<sup>4</sup>So Moses said, "Thus says the LORD: 'About midnight I will go out in the midst of Egypt,<sup>5</sup>and every firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne, even to the firstborn of the slave girl who is behind the handmill, and all the firstborn of the cattle.<sup>6</sup>There shall be a great cry throughout all the land of Egypt, such as there has never been, nor ever will be again.<sup>7</sup>But not a dog shall growl against any of the people of Israel, either man or beast, that you may know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel.'<sup>8</sup>And all these your servants shall come down to me and bow down to me, saying, 'Get out, you and all the people who follow you.' And after that I will go out." And he went out from Pharaoh in hot anger.<sup>9</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh will not listen to you, that my wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt."<sup>10</sup>Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh, and the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the people of Israel go out of his land.
11.overview:
Where we are. Moses has just been ordered out of Pharaoh’s presence on pain of death (10:28–29). Nine plagues are over, and this short chapter is the hush before the last one.

The message. God announces his final blow: at midnight every firstborn in Egypt will die, from Pharaoh’s heir to the slave girl’s son. Pharaoh refused to release God’s firstborn son, Israel, and was warned that his own firstborn would pay (4:22–23); now that word will be kept. Yet the heart of the chapter is the line God draws: “the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel” (v. 7). Chapter 12 will show that the line is drawn not by merit but by the blood of a lamb.

Why it was said. Israel needed to know that their freedom was God’s doing, not the fruit of a slave revolt, and that the wealth they carried out was his promised gift, not plunder seized by force (3:21–22; Genesis 15:14). They also needed to feel the weight of the judgment from which they alone were spared (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. God tells Moses that one plague more will make Pharaoh drive Israel out, and tells the people to ask their neighbours for silver and gold; God gives them favour, and Moses is held in honour even in Egypt (vv. 1–3). Moses delivers his last message to Pharaoh: at midnight the LORD will go out, every firstborn will die, and a great cry will fill Egypt, while not a dog growls against Israel; then he leaves in hot anger (vv. 4–8). The narrator sums up the whole contest: Pharaoh would not listen, and God used even that to multiply his wonders (vv. 9–10).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and then by pattern. Israel’s firstborn deserved death no less than Egypt’s, so the chapter raises a question it leaves open: how can God spare them and still be just? Chapter 12 answers with a lamb dying in their place, and the gospel with God’s own firstborn Son, whom the Father “did not spare” but “gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). In Egypt the firstborn of the guilty died; at the cross the innocent Firstborn died for the guilty.

For us. God’s patience is long, but it is not endless: nine warnings came before the tenth plague (2 Peter 3:9). If you belong to Christ, you are not spared because you are better than others, but because you are covered. Let that make you humble, grateful and urgent in warning others.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-3 — Favor in the Eyes of the Egyptians
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the last plague, God tells Moses how it will end and arranges for Israel to leave honoured and enriched. One more blow will make Pharaoh not merely let them go but drive them out (v. 1). The people are to ask their Egyptian neighbours for silver and gold jewellery, and God gives them favour, so that what was promised to Moses at the burning bush, and to Abraham long before, comes true (v. 2). Even Moses, once a fugitive, is now held in great honour by Pharaoh’s servants and people (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology:
Favor in the Eyes of the Egyptians

The fugitive is now honoured in the land that hunted him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God now keeps the promise of 3:21-22. Now: God sometimes answers our fears by events, not arguments: the man who feared no one would listen is now honoured.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Yet one plague more I will bring upon Pharaoh and upon Egypt. Afterward he will let you go from here. When he lets you go, he will drive you away completely. Speak now in the hearing of the people, that they ask, every man of his neighbor and every woman of her neighbor, for silver and gold jewelry." And the LORD gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians. Moreover, the man Moses was very great in the land of Egypt, in the sight of Pharaoh's servants and in the sight of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God announces that the end is near and arranges for Israel to leave not as runaways but honoured and enriched, as he had promised.

Yet one plague more. Pharaoh will not merely permit them to go; he will drive you away completely.

Silver and gold jewelry. The jewellery was asked for, not stolen (3:21–22): back wages for generations of slavery, given because God turned Egyptian hearts towards Israel. God had promised Abraham that his descendants would come out “with great possessions” (Genesis 15:14).

Moses was very great. The fugitive is now respected by Pharaoh’s own officials and people. This was God’s gift, not his own achievement.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4-8 — The Death of the Firstborn Announced
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses delivers God’s final warning: at midnight every firstborn in Egypt will die, and the LORD will show the distinction between Egypt and Israel. The LORD himself will go out; no household is exempt, from Pharaoh’s heir to the son of the slave girl at the handmill, and even the firstborn of the cattle (vv. 4–5). A cry like no other will rise through Egypt, while against Israel not a dog will growl (vv. 6–7). Pharaoh’s own officials will bow and beg Israel to go, and Moses walks out in hot anger at the hardness that will cost so much (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Death of the Firstborn Announced

Rank gives no protection; only God's distinction does.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a way of escape was about to be announced to Israel. Now: the only distinction that saves is the blood of the Lamb.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses said, "Thus says the LORD: 'About midnight I will go out in the midst of Egypt, and every firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne, even to the firstborn of the slave girl who is behind the handmill, and all the firstborn of the cattle. There shall be a great cry throughout all the land of Egypt, such as there has never been, nor ever will be again. But not a dog shall growl against any of the people of Israel, either man or beast, that you may know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel.' And all these your servants shall come down to me and bow down to me, saying, 'Get out, you and all the people who follow you.' And after that I will go out." And he went out from Pharaoh in hot anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses’ last words to Pharaoh announce the death of every firstborn in Egypt, and a distinction that will leave Israel untouched.

I will go out. This is God himself acting, not a natural disaster.

Every firstborn. The firstborn son was the heir, the family’s future and pride, and from the throne to the handmill no family is exempt.

Why this judgment? Egypt had drowned Israel’s sons (1:22), and God had warned Pharaoh, “Israel is my firstborn son”: refuse to let him go, and God would kill Pharaoh’s firstborn (4:22–23). Nine plagues gave time to repent.

A great cry throughout all the land of Egypt. The cry Israel raised under slavery (3:7) will now fill Egypt, while against Israel not a dog shall growl (literally, not a dog will so much as move its tongue): the distinction between Egypt and Israel at its sharpest. Pharaoh’s servants will soon bow and beg Israel to leave, as Moses says (12:31–33), and he goes out in hot anger at the stubbornness that will bring such grief.

A hard judgment. This is one of the hardest judgments in Scripture: children and young men die for a king’s refusal, and every grieving Egyptian home is a real grief. God does not delight in death (Ezekiel 33:11), and these children are not punished for their own sin. A whole nation shares its ruler’s judgment, as Israel’s firstborn would too without the Passover lamb (12:13).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The narrator steps back and sums up the whole contest of the plagues. God had told Moses that Pharaoh would not listen, and that his refusal would serve to multiply God’s wonders in Egypt (v. 9). Moses and Aaron did every sign; Pharaoh did not let the people go; and behind both stands the LORD, who hardened Pharaoh’s heart (v. 10). The scene is set for the night that will change everything.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Hardening Completed

God used each refusal to show another wonder.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Pharaoh's will and God's purpose ran together to the end. Now: the story stops on the edge of the worst night and turns to a lamb.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh will not listen to you, that my wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt." Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh, and the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the people of Israel go out of his land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator sums up the whole contest: Pharaoh would not listen, and God used his refusal to multiply his wonders.

That my wonders may be multiplied. Pharaoh’s refusal was foreseen (3:19–20) and used for God’s purpose, to display his power and name.

The contest summed up. Pharaoh hardened himself, and God hardened him. God is not unjust in this (Romans 9:14). Pharaoh had every warning and chose rebellion; God’s hardening was justice, not cruelty.

11.theology:
The wages of sin is death. The final plague confronts us with judgment in its starkest form.

Distinguishing grace. God makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel, not by merit but, as ch. 12 reveals, by the blood of a substitute.

God's faithfulness to ancient promises. The plundering of Egypt fulfills the word given to Abraham four centuries earlier (Gen. 15:14).
11.examples:
Then: God announced a judgment that would fall on all Egypt, palace and hovel alike, and could be escaped only by the distinction God himself would make.

Now: None can escape judgment on the basis of merit. Christ, the true Firstborn, died that we might live.

keyVerse.quote: But not a dog shall growl against any of the people of Israel, either man or beast, that you may know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel.
keyVerse.note: On the night of Egypt’s greatest grief, Israel will be so untouched that not even a dog will growl at them. The verse names the theme of the whole chapter, God’s distinction between his people and the world under judgment, and chapter 12 shows that the distinction rests on the blood of a lamb, not on Israel’s merit.

11.reflection:
The Israelites asked for silver and gold, and God gave them favour with the Egyptians (vv. 2–3; Genesis 15:14). How does this show God keeping a promise made centuries before? Where have you seen him keep his word slowly but surely?

The death of the firstborn is one of the hardest judgments in Scripture (vv. 4–6). How do the long warnings that came before it, and God’s words in Ezekiel 33:11, help us think about it honestly?

“The LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel” (v. 7). On what basis does God make that distinction, according to chapter 12? How should that shape the way Christians see themselves and others?

Moses left Pharaoh “in hot anger” (v. 8). When is anger at sin right, and how can we tell it from anger that is merely wounded pride?

12.title: Christ Our Passover
12.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt,<sup>2</sup>"This month shall be for you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year for you.<sup>3</sup>Tell all the congregation of Israel that on the tenth day of this month every man shall take a lamb according to their fathers' houses, a lamb for a household.<sup>4</sup>And if the household is too small for a lamb, then he and his nearest neighbor shall take according to the number of persons; according to what each can eat you shall make your count for the lamb.<sup>5</sup>Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male a year old. You may take it from the sheep or from the goats,<sup>6</sup>and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month, when the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill their lambs at twilight.<sup>7</sup>"Then they shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and the lintel of the houses in which they eat it.<sup>8</sup>They shall eat the flesh that night, roasted on the fire; with unleavened bread and bitter herbs they shall eat it.<sup>9</sup>Do not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but roasted, its head with its legs and its inner parts.<sup>10</sup>And you shall let none of it remain until the morning; anything that remains until the morning you shall burn.<sup>11</sup>In this manner you shall eat it: with your belt fastened, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand. And you shall eat it in haste. It is the LORD's Passover.<sup>12</sup>For I will pass through the land of Egypt that night, and I will strike all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both man and beast; and on all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments: I am the LORD.<sup>13</sup>The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague will befall you to destroy you, when I strike the land of Egypt.<sup>14</sup>"This day shall be for you a memorial day, and you shall keep it as a feast to the LORD; throughout your generations, as a statute forever, you shall keep it as a feast.<sup>15</sup>Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. On the first day you shall remove leaven out of your houses, for if anyone eats what is leavened, from the first day until the seventh day, that person shall be cut off from Israel.<sup>16</sup>On the first day you shall hold a holy assembly, and on the seventh day a holy assembly. No work shall be done on those days. But what everyone needs to eat, that alone may be prepared by you.<sup>17</sup>And you shall observe the Feast of Unleavened Bread, for on this very day I brought your hosts out of the land of Egypt. Therefore you shall observe this day, throughout your generations, as a statute forever.<sup>18</sup>In the first month, from the fourteenth day of the month at evening, you shall eat unleavened bread until the twenty-first day of the month at evening.<sup>19</sup>For seven days no leaven is to be found in your houses. If anyone eats what is leavened, that person will be cut off from the congregation of Israel, whether he is a sojourner or a native of the land.<sup>20</sup>You shall eat nothing leavened; in all your dwelling places you shall eat unleavened bread."<sup>21</sup>Then Moses called all the elders of Israel and said to them, "Go and select lambs for yourselves according to your clans, and kill the Passover lamb.<sup>22</sup>Take a bunch of hyssop and dip it in the blood that is in the basin, and touch the lintel and the two doorposts with the blood that is in the basin. None of you shall go out of the door of his house until the morning.<sup>23</sup>For the LORD will pass through to strike the Egyptians, and when he sees the blood on the lintel and on the two doorposts, the LORD will pass over the door and will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses to strike you.<sup>24</sup>You shall observe this rite as a statute for you and for your sons forever.<sup>25</sup>And when you come to the land that the LORD will give you, as he has promised, you shall keep this service.<sup>26</sup>And when your children say to you, 'What do you mean by this service?'<sup>27</sup>you shall say, 'It is the sacrifice of the LORD's Passover, for he passed over the houses of the people of Israel in Egypt, when he struck the Egyptians but spared our houses.'" And the people bowed their heads and worshiped.<sup>28</sup>Then the people of Israel went and did so; as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron, so they did.<sup>29</sup>At midnight the LORD struck down all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on his throne to the firstborn of the captive who was in the dungeon, and all the firstborn of the livestock.<sup>30</sup>And Pharaoh rose up in the night, he and all his servants and all the Egyptians. And there was a great cry in Egypt, for there was not a house where someone was not dead.<sup>31</sup>Then he summoned Moses and Aaron by night and said, "Up, go out from among my people, both you and the people of Israel; and go, serve the LORD, as you have said.<sup>32</sup>Take your flocks and your herds, as you have said, and be gone, and bless me also!"<sup>33</sup>The Egyptians were urgent with the people to send them out of the land in haste. For they said, "We shall all be dead."<sup>34</sup>So the people took their dough before it was leavened, their kneading bowls being bound up in their cloaks on their shoulders.<sup>35</sup>The people of Israel had also done as Moses told them, for they had asked the Egyptians for silver and gold jewelry and for clothing.<sup>36</sup>And the LORD had given the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, so that they let them have what they asked. Thus they plundered the Egyptians.<sup>37</sup>And the people of Israel journeyed from Rameses to Succoth, about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides women and children.<sup>38</sup>A mixed multitude also went up with them, and very much livestock, both flocks and herds.<sup>39</sup>And they baked unleavened cakes of the dough that they had brought out of Egypt, for it was not leavened, because they were thrust out of Egypt and could not wait, nor had they prepared any provisions for themselves.<sup>40</sup>The time that the people of Israel lived in Egypt was 430 years.<sup>41</sup>At the end of 430 years, on that very day, all the hosts of the LORD went out from the land of Egypt.<sup>42</sup>It was a night of watching by the LORD, to bring them out of the land of Egypt; so this same night is a night of watching kept to the LORD by all the people of Israel throughout their generations.<sup>43</sup>And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "This is the statute of the Passover: no foreigner shall eat of it,<sup>44</sup>but every slave that is bought for money may eat of it after you have circumcised him.<sup>45</sup>No foreigner or hired worker may eat of it.<sup>46</sup>It shall be eaten in one house; you shall not take any of the flesh outside the house, and you shall not break any of its bones.<sup>47</sup>All the congregation of Israel shall keep it.<sup>48</sup>If a stranger shall sojourn with you and would keep the Passover to the LORD, let all his males be circumcised. Then he may come near and keep it; he shall be as a native of the land. But no uncircumcised person shall eat of it.<sup>49</sup>There shall be one law for the native and for the stranger who sojourns among you."<sup>50</sup>All the people of Israel did just as the LORD commanded Moses and Aaron.<sup>51</sup>And on that very day the LORD brought the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt by their hosts.
12.overview:
Where we are. The last plague has been announced (chapter 11), and Moses has left Pharaoh for the last time. Before the blow falls, God pauses the story to give Israel a new calendar, a lamb, a sign in blood and a meal, and then the night itself arrives.

The message. God saves his people from his own judgment by the blood of a substitute. Israel’s firstborn were no more innocent than Egypt’s; they lived because a lamb died in their place and its blood marked their doors: “when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (v. 13). The question that night was not “Are you better?” but “Are you covered?” And God made the night a feast for ever, so that every generation would know itself redeemed.

Why it was said. Israel’s whole life as a people was to rest on this night: their year began with it (v. 2), their children would ask about it (v. 26), and in the land they would keep it every spring (see the introduction). The chapter gave later generations both the story and the rite, and taught them that they were free not because they had earned it but because God had provided a lamb.

How the chapter makes its case. God resets the calendar and gives the instructions: a flawless lamb for each household, its blood on the doorposts, its flesh eaten in haste, and his promise to pass over (vv. 1–13). The night becomes a yearly memorial, with a week of unleavened bread (vv. 14–20). Moses passes the instructions to the elders, and tells them what to say when their children ask (vv. 21–28). At midnight the firstborn of Egypt die, and Pharaoh drives Israel out, while the Egyptians hand over silver and gold (vv. 29–36). A great company leaves on the very day the 430 years end (vv. 37–42). Last come the rules for who may eat: every Israelite, and any outsider who takes the covenant sign (vv. 43–51).

Where it leads. By pattern and promise, as clearly as anywhere in the Old Testament. “For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Jesus died at Passover, a lamb “without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19), with not one bone broken (John 19:36), and at his last Passover he gave the meal new meaning in the Lord’s Supper (Luke 22:15–20). The blood that turned judgment aside in Egypt points to the blood by which we are “saved by him from the wrath of God” (Romans 5:9).

For us. Do not rest your hope on being better than others; rest it on the blood of Christ. Come to the Lord’s Supper as people who remember a rescue, and tell your children what it means. Then live as the redeemed: belt fastened, ready to follow wherever God leads.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-13 — The Lamb and the Blood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God saves his people from his own judgment by the blood of a substitute. He begins Israel’s year with the month of their redemption (vv. 1–2). Each household is to choose a flawless young lamb, keep it four days and kill it at twilight (vv. 3–6). Its blood goes on the doorposts and lintel, and the family eats it roasted, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, dressed to travel (vv. 7–11). That night the LORD will strike Egypt’s firstborn and judge all its gods, but where he sees the blood he will pass over (vv. 12–13).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lamb and the Blood

Redemption begins at home, with a substitute God himself appoints.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a house was safe if the blood was on its doorframe, and only then. Now: the decisive question is whether we are covered by Christ's blood.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, "This month shall be for you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God makes the month of redemption the first month of Israel’s year: their life as a people is to be counted from his rescue.

The beginning of months. Israel will count its year from its redemption (see the Jewish calendar). A civil year still began in autumn, but the religious year began with the exodus.

Where your story begins. Christians, too, date their lives from their redemption in Christ. That is where your story really begins (2 Corinthians 5:17).
verseByVerse.note: The month was Abib (later Nisan), in March–April.

verseByVerse.quote: Tell all the congregation of Israel that on the tenth day of this month every man shall take a lamb according to their fathers' houses, a lamb for a household. And if the household is too small for a lamb, then he and his nearest neighbor shall take according to the number of persons; according to what each can eat you shall make your count for the lamb. Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male a year old. You may take it from the sheep or from the goats, and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month, when the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill their lambs at twilight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each household chooses a flawless young lamb, keeps it four days and kills it at the appointed time: a substitute chosen with care.

Congregation is used here for the first time: the whole assembly of Israel, a people gathered before God.

A lamb for a household. The Hebrew seh means a young sheep or goat. Redemption begins at home, not in a temple, and small households share with neighbours.

Without blemish, a male a year old. The lamb has no defect and is in its prime. It is kept four days with the family, time to see that it had no flaw, and then killed.

Examined and found without fault. Jesus entered Jerusalem before Passover and was questioned and examined for days, and Pilate found no guilt in him (John 18:38). He is “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29), a lamb “without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19).

Uncertain wording. At twilight is literally “between the two evenings”. The exact time is uncertain: perhaps between sunset and dark, or, as later practice at the temple took it, from mid-afternoon until sunset.
verseByVerse.note: “At twilight” is literally “between the two evenings” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and the lintel of the houses in which they eat it. They shall eat the flesh that night, roasted on the fire; with unleavened bread and bitter herbs they shall eat it. Do not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but roasted, its head with its legs and its inner parts. And you shall let none of it remain until the morning; anything that remains until the morning you shall burn. In this manner you shall eat it: with your belt fastened, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand. And you shall eat it in haste. It is the LORD's Passover.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blood goes on the doorway, the lamb is eaten whole, and the family eats dressed to leave, trusting God for a rescue not yet seen.

The blood is life given in death (Leviticus 17:11), and it goes on the outside of the house, where God would see it: on the sides and top of the doorway, not the threshold, so that no one would tread on it (Hebrews 10:29).

Roasted on the fire. The lamb is roasted whole. The unleavened bread is flat bread made without yeast, because there was no time for dough to rise (v. 39), and the bitter herbs recall the bitterness of slavery (1:14).

With your belt fastened. They eat dressed to travel, belt fastened and sandals on, by faith in a deliverance not yet seen.

What it does not mean. The blood was not a magic charm, and safety was not a reward for being Israelite. Any Israelite house without blood would have lost its firstborn too. Safety lay in God’s provision, received by obedient faith (Hebrews 11:28).

Uncertain wording. The LORD’s Passover translates pesach, from the verb “pass over” (vv. 13, 23). Some think the verb also carries the sense of shielding or protecting, as in Isaiah 31:5, where the LORD will “spare and rescue” Jerusalem. Either way God spares the house marked with blood.

verseByVerse.quote: For I will pass through the land of Egypt that night, and I will strike all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both man and beast; and on all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments: I am the LORD. The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague will befall you to destroy you, when I strike the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself will judge Egypt and its gods that night, but where he sees the blood he will pass over: safety lies in the substitute, not in the family’s goodness.

On all the gods of Egypt. The night exposes every idol. Pharaoh, honoured as a god, cannot protect even his own son.

When I see the blood. The lamb has died instead of the firstborn. “For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7), and his blood shields us from God’s judgment (Romans 5:9). Thank God that he sees the blood of Christ over you.

Isn’t a blood sacrifice primitive? To a modern reader the Passover can look like the worst of ancient religion: an angry deity who must see blood before he calms down. Some have called the cross itself a kind of cosmic child abuse, a Father punishing an unwilling Son. If that were the picture it would be monstrous. But look at what this night teaches. The firstborn of Israel were not spared because they were innocent; they were spared because something died in their place. Justice is not satisfied by looking the other way; the cost of the wrong has to land somewhere. And at Calvary the one on whom it lands is not a third party dragged in. John Stott called it the self-substitution of God: the Judge himself, in the person of the Son, stepping under his own sentence. Jesus said of his life, “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18). That is not primitive. It is the only kind of love that can be holy and kind at once.

How Jewish readers take it. For Jewish families Passover is above all the festival of redemption, kept at the Seder, where each generation is to see itself as brought out of Egypt (Mishnah Pesachim 10:5). Since the temple fell no lamb is sacrificed; a roasted bone on the Seder plate recalls it. Many Jewish interpreters see the blood as a sign of obedience and belonging rather than an offering for sin. Both traditions look back to the God who rescues his people and forward to a greater redemption. This commentary hears that hope answered in Christ, our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the night has even happened, God makes it a feast to be kept for ever. For seven days each year Israel is to eat unleavened bread and clear every trace of leaven from their homes, with a holy assembly at each end of the week (vv. 14–20). Moses passes the instructions to the elders: blood applied with hyssop, no one out of doors until morning, and the LORD will not let the destroyer in (vv. 21–24). In the land they are to keep the rite and explain it when their children ask, and the people bow down in worship and obey (vv. 25–28).
verseByVerse.theology:
A Memorial Forever

Each generation is to receive the rescue as its own.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the strange meal was built to make children ask. Now: the redeemed clear the old leaven, sin, out of their lives (1 Cor. 5:6-8), and the Lord's Supper recalls the Lamb until he comes.

verseByVerse.quote: "This day shall be for you a memorial day, and you shall keep it as a feast to the LORD; throughout your generations, as a statute forever, you shall keep it as a feast. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. On the first day you shall remove leaven out of your houses, for if anyone eats what is leavened, from the first day until the seventh day, that person shall be cut off from Israel. On the first day you shall hold a holy assembly, and on the seventh day a holy assembly. No work shall be done on those days. But what everyone needs to eat, that alone may be prepared by you. And you shall observe the Feast of Unleavened Bread, for on this very day I brought your hosts out of the land of Egypt. Therefore you shall observe this day, throughout your generations, as a statute forever. In the first month, from the fourteenth day of the month at evening, you shall eat unleavened bread until the twenty-first day of the month at evening. For seven days no leaven is to be found in your houses. If anyone eats what is leavened, that person will be cut off from the congregation of Israel, whether he is a sojourner or a native of the land. You shall eat nothing leavened; in all your dwelling places you shall eat unleavened bread."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God makes the night a feast before it has even happened: a week without leaven every year, so that each generation relives its redemption.

A memorial day is a day of remembrance that makes the past present to each generation.

Leaven was yeast, or a piece of old fermented dough used to raise new dough. A little spreads through the whole batch, which is why it became a picture of sin (1 Corinthians 5:6–8; see the Feast of Unleavened Bread).

Cut off … a holy assembly. To be cut off meant exclusion from Israel, or death at God’s hand: disregarding his ordinance was serious. A holy assembly was a sacred gathering for worship, on which no ordinary work was done.

In everyday life. Clear out the “old leaven” in your life, not to earn redemption but because you have been redeemed.

Where Christians differ: should Christians keep Passover? Some keep a Christian Seder. This commentary’s view: Passover is fulfilled in Christ, and Jesus made his last Passover the Lord’s Supper (Luke 22:15–20). Learning from a Seder can be helpful, but it is not required (Colossians 2:16–17).
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) became a picture of sin spreading through a whole lump of dough.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses called all the elders of Israel and said to them, "Go and select lambs for yourselves according to your clans, and kill the Passover lamb. Take a bunch of hyssop and dip it in the blood that is in the basin, and touch the lintel and the two doorposts with the blood that is in the basin. None of you shall go out of the door of his house until the morning. For the LORD will pass through to strike the Egyptians, and when he sees the blood on the lintel and on the two doorposts, the LORD will pass over the door and will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses to strike you. You shall observe this rite as a statute for you and for your sons forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses passes the instructions to the elders: the blood applied with hyssop, everyone indoors till morning, and the destroyer kept out of every marked house.

A bunch of hyssop. Hyssop, a small bushy plant, was used like a brush (Leviticus 14:4; Numbers 19:18). David prays, “Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean” (Psalm 51:7), and at the cross a sponge on hyssop was lifted to Jesus (John 19:29).

None of you shall go out. Safety was inside the blood-marked house, nowhere else.

The destroyer. God says he strikes (v. 12) and that he will not let the destroyer enter (v. 23). This commentary’s view: the destroyer is God’s agent, perhaps an angel (2 Samuel 24:16; Hebrews 11:28), acting under his command. The judgment is God’s.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew word for basin may instead mean “threshold”, so that the blood was caught at the doorway itself. The meaning of the rite is the same either way.
verseByVerse.note: Hyssop was a small bushy plant used for sprinkling.

verseByVerse.quote: And when you come to the land that the LORD will give you, as he has promised, you shall keep this service. And when your children say to you, 'What do you mean by this service?' you shall say, 'It is the sacrifice of the LORD's Passover, for he passed over the houses of the people of Israel in Egypt, when he struck the Egyptians but spared our houses.'" And the people bowed their heads and worshiped. Then the people of Israel went and did so; as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron, so they did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rite is to continue in the promised land and be explained to every child who asks, and the people answer with worship and obedience.

When your children say. Worship is meant to raise questions, and the Jewish Passover Seder still includes the children’s questions. The answer is the story of what God did: a sacrifice that spared them.

The people bowed their heads and worshiped, and then went and did so, acting in faith before they saw the result.

In everyday life. When children ask about baptism or the Lord’s Supper, tell them the story of the cross.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps his word to the minute, and Israel walks out of Egypt free. At midnight every firstborn dies, a great cry rises, and Pharaoh, who would not let them go, now begs them to leave and asks for a blessing (vv. 29–32). The Egyptians hurry them out, and they carry unleavened dough and the silver and gold the Egyptians gave them (vv. 33–36). A vast company, with outsiders among them, sets out on the very day the 430 years end (vv. 37–42). Finally God sets the rules for the meal: it belongs to the covenant household, but any outsider may join by taking the covenant sign (vv. 43–51).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Exodus at Midnight

Every condition Pharaoh set is surrendered, and the door is opened to any foreigner who joins the covenant.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: membership was by covenant sign, not bloodline. Now: the redeemed come from every nation (Rev. 7:9).

verseByVerse.quote: At midnight the LORD struck down all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on his throne to the firstborn of the captive who was in the dungeon, and all the firstborn of the livestock. And Pharaoh rose up in the night, he and all his servants and all the Egyptians. And there was a great cry in Egypt, for there was not a house where someone was not dead. Then he summoned Moses and Aaron by night and said, "Up, go out from among my people, both you and the people of Israel; and go, serve the LORD, as you have said. Take your flocks and your herds, as you have said, and be gone, and bless me also!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At midnight God does exactly what he said, and the king who would not let Israel go now begs them to leave and asks for their blessing.

A great cry in Egypt. Egypt drowned Israel’s sons; now its own sons die, and a cry goes up from every house.

Up, go out. Every condition Pharaoh made is gone: children, flocks, everything. In bless me also the king who claimed to be a god asks a blessing from the slaves’ God.

Three kinds of firstborn. Three kinds of firstborn meet in this night. Egypt’s firstborn died. Israel’s firstborn was spared by a lamb. God’s own firstborn Son was not spared, so that we might be (Romans 8:32).

What it does not mean. God does not delight in suffering, and the grief of that night was real. Nine warnings preceded it, and judgment came only when mercy was refused (Romans 2:4–5).

verseByVerse.quote: The Egyptians were urgent with the people to send them out of the land in haste. For they said, "We shall all be dead." So the people took their dough before it was leavened, their kneading bowls being bound up in their cloaks on their shoulders. The people of Israel had also done as Moses told them, for they had asked the Egyptians for silver and gold jewelry and for clothing. And the LORD had given the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, so that they let them have what they asked. Thus they plundered the Egyptians.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt hurries Israel out, and they leave with unleavened dough and Egyptian silver and gold, as God had promised.

Their dough before it was leavened. This is the origin of the unleavened bread of the feast (v. 39).

Asked … plundered. This was not theft. As foretold (3:21–22; Genesis 15:14), Israel asked, God gave them favour, and the Egyptians gave willingly: spoil won without battle, and wages for unpaid labour. God keeps his promises to the letter.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel journeyed from Rameses to Succoth, about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides women and children. A mixed multitude also went up with them, and very much livestock, both flocks and herds. And they baked unleavened cakes of the dough that they had brought out of Egypt, for it was not leavened, because they were thrust out of Egypt and could not wait, nor had they prepared any provisions for themselves. The time that the people of Israel lived in Egypt was 430 years. At the end of 430 years, on that very day, all the hosts of the LORD went out from the land of Egypt. It was a night of watching by the LORD, to bring them out of the land of Egypt; so this same night is a night of watching kept to the LORD by all the people of Israel throughout their generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great company, outsiders among them, leaves Egypt on the very day God had set, and the night becomes one Israel is to keep for ever.

From Rameses to Succoth. They travel from Rameses, the store city (1:11), to Succoth, a camp to the east in the delta whose name means “booths”.

A mixed multitude. Non-Israelites joined them, perhaps Egyptians who had feared God’s word (9:20). God’s people was never a pure bloodline.

At the end of 430 years. Genesis 15:13 rounds the figure to 400, and the exodus comes on that very day: God’s timetable is exact. As the LORD kept watch over them that night, Israel is to keep watch on it every year in remembrance.

Where Christians differ: the numbers. Some read the Hebrew elef (“thousand”) as “clan” or “military unit”, giving far smaller numbers. Others hold the large figure, supported by the census totals (Numbers 1:46; Exodus 38:25–26). This commentary’s view: the plain reading is a very large company; the alternative is held by faithful scholars and does not affect the truth of the event.

Textual note. In verse 40 some ancient copies and translations read that the 430 years covered Israel’s time in Canaan as well as in Egypt, counting from Abraham, as Paul’s 430 years from the promise to the law may also do (Galatians 3:17). The standard Hebrew text, followed by the ESV, counts the years in Egypt alone.
verseByVerse.note: Six hundred thousand men implies a total population of perhaps two million, though some take the numbers differently.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "This is the statute of the Passover: no foreigner shall eat of it, but every slave that is bought for money may eat of it after you have circumcised him. No foreigner or hired worker may eat of it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Passover belongs to the covenant household: outsiders may share it, but only by joining God’s people through the covenant sign.

No foreigner. The line is not race but covenant: a foreigner here is an outsider who has not joined God’s people. A slave or a resident foreigner who took the sign given to Abraham, circumcision (Genesis 17), could eat as one born in the land.

Slave … hired worker. A slave bought for money belonged to the household for good and could be circumcised into it. The hired worker and the passing foreigner were temporary and stood outside it. Passover was the meal of the covenant household, not a public festival anyone could drop in on.

verseByVerse.quote: It shall be eaten in one house; you shall not take any of the flesh outside the house, and you shall not break any of its bones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lamb is eaten whole in one house and none of its bones is broken, a detail John saw fulfilled at the cross.

In one house. None of the flesh is carried outside or shared out in pieces. On the first night no one was to go out of the door until morning (v. 22), and the meal keeps that shape: one family together under the blood.

Not break any of its bones. Fulfilled at the cross: the soldiers did not break Jesus’ legs, “that the Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘Not one of his bones will be broken’” (John 19:36).

verseByVerse.quote: All the congregation of Israel shall keep it. If a stranger shall sojourn with you and would keep the Passover to the LORD, let all his males be circumcised. Then he may come near and keep it; he shall be as a native of the land. But no uncircumcised person shall eat of it. There shall be one law for the native and for the stranger who sojourns among you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every Israelite must keep the Passover, and any stranger who takes the covenant sign may keep it as one born in the land: one law for both.

All the congregation of Israel shall keep it. No Israelite is excused; later the law says that a man able to keep it who neglects it is to be cut off (Numbers 9:13). Nor is the outsider shut out for ever: he may come near by receiving the covenant sign, and then stands on equal ground (see the note on vv. 43–45).

Outsiders brought near. The gospel does not exclude outsiders. In Christ, Gentiles who were far off are brought near (Ephesians 2:12–13); faith, not ancestry, is the condition. Thank God for the Lamb whose death was planned and foretold in every detail.

verseByVerse.quote: All the people of Israel did just as the LORD commanded Moses and Aaron. And on that very day the LORD brought the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt by their hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel obeys, and on the very day God appointed he brings them out of Egypt, ordered like an army.

On that very day. The chapter closes with obedience, then deliverance. The narrator repeats verse 41: God brought them out by their hosts, ordered like an army rather than fleeing like a rabble. The chapter that began by resetting Israel’s calendar (v. 2) ends with God keeping his own date.

12.theology:
Substitution. The lamb dies in the place of the firstborn: salvation is by a substitute's blood, not by merit.

Christ our Passover. The spotless lamb, the applied blood, the unbroken bones: all are fulfilled in Jesus.

Redemption remembered. The Passover becomes a perpetual memorial, fulfilled in the Lord's Supper, by which the church proclaims Christ's death until he comes.
12.examples:
Then: On the night of judgment God's people went free, not by their worth but by the blood.

Now: Whoever trusts Christ is covered by his blood, and the judgment passes over them for ever. Every Lord's Supper recalls this redemption until he comes.

keyVerse.quote: The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague will befall you to destroy you, when I strike the land of Egypt.
keyVerse.note: Here is the hinge of the whole exodus: safety depends not on who lives in the house but on the blood on the door. It is the clearest Old Testament picture of substitution, and the New Testament sees it fulfilled when Christ, our Passover lamb, was sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7).

12.reflection:
Israel’s firstborn were spared not because they were better than Egypt’s but because a lamb died in their place (vv. 12–13). How does this picture help you understand what Christ has done for you?

God told Israel to begin their year with the month of their redemption (v. 2). What would it look like to “date” your life, and shape your priorities, from your redemption in Christ?

When children ask, “What do you mean by this service?” (v. 26), parents are to tell the story of the Passover. How can we use baptism and the Lord’s Supper to tell our children the gospel?

A mixed multitude went out with Israel, and a stranger could keep the Passover by joining the covenant (vv. 38, 48–49). What does this show about who may belong to God’s people, and how should it shape our welcome of outsiders?

13.title: Consecration and the Guiding Presence
13.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Moses,<sup>2</sup>"Consecrate to me all the firstborn. Whatever is the first to open the womb among the people of Israel, both of man and of beast, is mine."<sup>3</sup>Then Moses said to the people, "Remember this day in which you came out from Egypt, out of the house of slavery, for by a strong hand the LORD brought you out from this place. No leavened bread shall be eaten.<sup>4</sup>Today, in the month of Abib, you are going out.<sup>5</sup>And when the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, which he swore to your fathers to give you, a land flowing with milk and honey, you shall keep this service in this month.<sup>6</sup>Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a feast to the LORD.<sup>7</sup>Unleavened bread shall be eaten for seven days; no leavened bread shall be seen with you, and no leaven shall be seen with you in all your territory.<sup>8</sup>You shall tell your son on that day, 'It is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt.'<sup>9</sup>And it shall be to you as a sign on your hand and as a memorial between your eyes, that the law of the LORD may be in your mouth. For with a strong hand the LORD has brought you out of Egypt.<sup>10</sup>You shall therefore keep this statute at its appointed time from year to year.<sup>11</sup>"When the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as he swore to you and your fathers, and shall give it to you,<sup>12</sup>you shall set apart to the LORD all that first opens the womb. All the firstborn of your animals that are males shall be the LORD's.<sup>13</sup>Every firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb, or if you will not redeem it you shall break its neck. Every firstborn of man among your sons you shall redeem.<sup>14</sup>And when in time to come your son asks you, 'What does this mean?' you shall say to him, 'By a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, from the house of slavery.<sup>15</sup>For when Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let us go, the LORD killed all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both the firstborn of man and the firstborn of animals. Therefore I sacrifice to the LORD all the males that first open the womb, but all the firstborn of my sons I redeem.'<sup>16</sup>It shall be as a mark on your hand or frontlets between your eyes, for by a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt."<sup>17</sup>When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them by way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near. For God said, "Lest the people change their minds when they see war and return to Egypt."<sup>18</sup>But God led the people around by the way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea. And the people of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt equipped for battle.<sup>19</sup>Moses took the bones of Joseph with him, for Joseph had made the sons of Israel solemnly swear, saying, "God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones with you from here."<sup>20</sup>And they moved on from Succoth and encamped at Etham, on the edge of the wilderness.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them along the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light, that they might travel by day and by night.<sup>22</sup>The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night did not depart from before the people.
13.overview:
Where we are. Passover night is over and Israel has left Egypt (12:37–42). Before the journey goes far, God claims the firstborn, fixes the feast for the generations to come, and takes the lead himself in a pillar of cloud and fire.

The message. Those whom God has redeemed belong to him, and he goes with them. The firstborn spared by the lamb’s blood are now his, and the rescue is to be kept every year and told to every child. And the God who brought them out does not leave them to find their own way: he chooses the road they can bear and walks it in front of them.

Why it was said. Israel would soon live in a land of plenty where memory fades and other gods beckon (see the introduction). Twice the instructions look ahead, “when the LORD brings you into the land” (vv. 5, 11), so that the feast, the redemption of every firstborn son and the child’s question would carry the exodus to generations who never saw Egypt.

How the chapter makes its case. God claims every firstborn as his (vv. 1–2). Moses tells the people to remember the day and, once in the land, to keep seven days of unleavened bread and tell their sons why (vv. 3–10). Firstborn animals are given to the LORD, and the donkey and every firstborn son are redeemed (vv. 11–13). When a child asks what it means, the answer is the night Egypt’s firstborn died and Israel’s were spared (vv. 14–16). Then God leads them away from the short road to war and round by the wilderness, Moses carries Joseph’s bones, and the LORD goes before them in a pillar that never leaves (vv. 17–22).

Where it leads. By pattern, and the New Testament draws the lines. Jesus, Mary’s firstborn, was brought to the temple under this very law (Luke 2:22–23), the firstborn redeemed as a baby who would give “his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). Those he redeems become “the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven” (Hebrews 12:23). And the God who went before Israel in light came among us in person: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12).

For us. “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20): the redeemed belong wholly to their Redeemer. Build habits that remember the cross, and tell your children what it means. And when God leads you by a longer road than you wanted, trust that he has chosen it, and that he is on it ahead of you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Redeemed people belong to the God who redeemed them, and must never forget it. God claims every firstborn of man and beast, because he spared Israel’s firstborn on the night Egypt’s died (vv. 1–2, 15). Moses ties this to remembering: in the land, seven days of unleavened bread each spring, and a father telling his son what the LORD did for him (vv. 3–10). Firstborn animals are given to God, the unclean donkey is redeemed with a lamb, and every firstborn son is bought back (vv. 11–13). When a child asks what it means, the answer is the story of God’s strong hand and the night of judgment (vv. 14–16). Twice the rite is called a sign on the hand and between the eyes (vv. 9, 16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Consecrate the Firstborn

Those God has redeemed now belong to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the firstborn were claimed not as a tax but because God had bought them back. Now: "you are not your own, for you were bought with a price" (1 Cor. 6:19-20), and the unclean live because the clean died for them (1 Pet. 3:18).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Consecrate to me all the firstborn. Whatever is the first to open the womb among the people of Israel, both of man and of beast, is mine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every firstborn in Israel, human and animal, belongs to God, because he spared them on Passover night.

Consecrate means to set apart as holy, belonging to God. The claim covers the firstborn male of people and animals.

It is mine. Israel is God’s “firstborn son” (4:22), and Egypt lost its firstborn for refusing to let him go. Israel’s firstborn were spared by the lamb’s blood; their lives now belong to the one who redeemed them (Numbers 3:13).

What it does not mean. This never meant that firstborn children were to be sacrificed. Israel’s firstborn sons were redeemed by a payment (v. 13; Numbers 18:15–16). Child sacrifice was an abomination (Leviticus 18:21).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses said to the people, "Remember this day in which you came out from Egypt, out of the house of slavery, for by a strong hand the LORD brought you out from this place. No leavened bread shall be eaten. Today, in the month of Abib, you are going out. And when the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, which he swore to your fathers to give you, a land flowing with milk and honey, you shall keep this service in this month. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a feast to the LORD. Unleavened bread shall be eaten for seven days; no leavened bread shall be seen with you, and no leaven shall be seen with you in all your territory. You shall tell your son on that day, 'It is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt.' And it shall be to you as a sign on your hand and as a memorial between your eyes, that the law of the LORD may be in your mouth. For with a strong hand the LORD has brought you out of Egypt. You shall therefore keep this statute at its appointed time from year to year.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel is to remember its rescue every year with a week of unleavened bread, and each generation is to tell its children that God did it “for me”.

Remember is the key word: remembering what God did keeps faith alive. Abib means “ear of grain”, the spring month when barley ripened (see the Jewish calendar). And four times the chapter says by a strong hand (vv. 3, 9, 14, 16): the rescue was all God’s doing.

What the LORD did for me. The son never saw Egypt, yet he is taught to count himself among the redeemed.

A sign on your hand … between your eyes. The feast is a reminder that shapes what you do (the hand) and how you think (the mind).

In everyday life. Obedience did not earn the rescue; they obey because God has already brought them out. Christians keep the feast with “the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth”, because Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7–8). Build habits of remembering: Scripture, the Lord’s Day, the Lord’s Supper. You will forget otherwise.

Where Christians differ: literal or figurative? Later Judaism wore tefillin, small boxes holding these words, on arm and forehead. This commentary’s view: the purpose clause, “that the law of the LORD may be in your mouth”, shows the main aim: God’s word governing life. Jesus condemned wearing them for show (Matthew 23:5), not the practice itself.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as he swore to you and your fathers, and shall give it to you, you shall set apart to the LORD all that first opens the womb. All the firstborn of your animals that are males shall be the LORD's. Every firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb, or if you will not redeem it you shall break its neck. Every firstborn of man among your sons you shall redeem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Firstborn animals are given to God, but the unclean donkey and every firstborn son must be bought back by a substitute or a price.

Every firstborn of a donkey. Clean firstborn animals were sacrificed. The donkey was unclean, unfit for the altar, so it must be redeemed with a lamb or have its neck broken. Redeem here is Hebrew padah, to release by paying a price: a lamb dies in the donkey’s place.

Every firstborn of man. Israel’s sons stand where the donkey stands: unable to be offered, needing a substitute. Later they were redeemed with five shekels (Numbers 18:16), and the Levites were taken in their place (Numbers 3:12).

Redeemed as a baby, then the ransom. Jesus, the firstborn, was himself presented and redeemed as a baby (Luke 2:22–24), and then gave his life as the ransom for us (Mark 10:45).

verseByVerse.quote: And when in time to come your son asks you, 'What does this mean?' you shall say to him, 'By a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, from the house of slavery. For when Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let us go, the LORD killed all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both the firstborn of man and the firstborn of animals. Therefore I sacrifice to the LORD all the males that first open the womb, but all the firstborn of my sons I redeem.' It shall be as a mark on your hand or frontlets between your eyes, for by a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When children ask, parents answer with the whole story: God’s strong hand, the judgment on Egypt, and a redemption that cost a life.

When your son asks. The faith is taught by answering children’s questions, and the answer includes judgment as well as rescue: Pharaoh’s refusal and the death of Egypt’s firstborn. The cost explains the redemption. Parents, do not leave out the hard parts when you tell children the gospel: sin, judgment and the cost of the cross.

Shouldn’t children be left to decide for themselves? Many thoughtful parents feel that handing on a faith is an imposition, and that the respectful thing is to keep children neutral until they can choose. It is a generous instinct, but there is no neutral upbringing. Every home teaches what matters by what it celebrates, worries about and spends on, and a child not given the story of the exodus will still be given a story: that life is about achievement, or comfort, or being liked. The poet Samuel Taylor Coleridge is reported to have answered a visitor who held this view by showing him a garden full of weeds: he had not wished to prejudice the soil towards roses and strawberries. And notice what Israel’s children were given: not a list of rules first, but an answer to “What does this mean?”: “By a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, from the house of slavery.” Christian parents hand on a rescue, not a regime, and a child who knows he has been loved like that is freer to choose, not less.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17-22 — The Pillar of Cloud and Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God leads his redeemed people himself, choosing the road they can bear and never leaving them. He turns them away from the short coastal road, where they would meet war and lose heart, and leads them round by the wilderness towards the Red Sea (vv. 17–18). Moses carries Joseph’s bones, keeping a promise made centuries before in faith that God would bring Israel out (v. 19). They camp at the edge of the wilderness (v. 20), and the LORD goes before them in a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night, a presence that never leaves its place in front of the people (vv. 21–22).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pillar of Cloud and Fire

God chooses the road his people can bear, and goes on it with them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a promise made to a dying man was kept through the long years. Now: God’s detours do not mean that he has lost the way, and he guides us by going with us himself.

verseByVerse.quote: When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them by way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near. For God said, "Lest the people change their minds when they see war and return to Egypt." But God led the people around by the way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea. And the people of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt equipped for battle. Moses took the bones of Joseph with him, for Joseph had made the sons of Israel solemnly swear, saying, "God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones with you from here." And they moved on from Succoth and encamped at Etham, on the edge of the wilderness. And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them along the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light, that they might travel by day and by night. The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night did not depart from before the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God leads his people by a longer road they can bear, and goes in front of them himself, day and night, without ever leaving.

The land of the Philistines. The coastal road was guarded by Egyptian forts. It was perhaps two weeks’ march to Canaan, but they would meet war at once, and God knew their weakness.

The bones of Joseph. Moses carries them, as Joseph had made Israel’s sons swear (Genesis 50:25). Hebrews calls it faith (Hebrews 11:22).

The pillar of cloud and fire was the visible sign of God’s presence, leading by day and giving light by night. It did not depart for forty years, through every grumbling and rebellion. The God who led them so came among us in his Son, “the light of the world” (John 8:12).

Around by the way of the wilderness. The longer road was not punishment: God chose the way they could bear (1 Corinthians 10:13). When he leads you by a longer road than you wanted, he may be sparing you a battle you were not ready for. Thank God who goes before you and never leaves (Hebrews 13:5).

Uncertain wording. Equipped for battle translates a rare word that seems related to the number five. It may mean “armed” or “in ranks” (perhaps five divisions): organised, but not yet ready to fight.
verseByVerse.note: “The way of the land of the Philistines” was the coastal military road; God led them away from war. Moses took Joseph’s bones as promised.

13.theology:
Redemption and consecration. Those whom God redeems, he claims. The firstborn are his; we who are redeemed by Christ are not our own.

The wisdom of God's leading. God chooses the road his people can bear, and his detours are mercies.

The guiding presence of God. The pillar of cloud and fire reveals a God who never departs from his people, a presence fulfilled in Christ and the Spirit who lives in us.
13.examples:
Then: Having redeemed his people, God claimed their firstborn as his own and led them out himself.

Now: Redeemed by Christ, we belong wholly to God. And we are never left to find our own way: he leads us by his Word and Spirit, choosing wise paths, promising never to leave us nor forsake us.

keyVerse.quote: And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them along the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light, that they might travel by day and by night.
keyVerse.note: The God who redeemed Israel does not send them on alone: he goes in front, by day and by night. The chapter’s claim that the redeemed belong to God is matched by this promise that God goes with the redeemed, and the pillar that “did not depart” (v. 22) through forty years of grumbling is a picture of the faithfulness we meet fully in Christ.

13.reflection:
God claims Israel’s firstborn because he spared them on Passover night (vv. 1–2, 15). What does it mean in practice that you are “not your own” but bought by Christ? Which part of your life do you find hardest to hand over?

The son who never saw Egypt is taught to say, “what the LORD did for me” (v. 8). How can we help our children, and new believers, to see the gospel story as their own story?

Moses’ answer to the child’s question includes judgment as well as rescue (vv. 14–15). Why is it important not to leave the hard parts out when we explain the gospel?

God led Israel by the longer road because the short one meant war they could not face (vv. 17–18). Can you look back on a “longer road” in your own life and see God’s care in it? How does the pillar that never departed (v. 22) help you on the road you are on now?

14.title: The LORD Will Fight for You
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses,<sup>2</sup>"Tell the people of Israel to turn back and encamp in front of Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, in front of Baal-zephon; you shall encamp facing it, by the sea.<sup>3</sup>For Pharaoh will say of the people of Israel, 'They are wandering in the land; the wilderness has shut them in.'<sup>4</sup>And I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and he will pursue them, and I will get glory over Pharaoh and all his host, and the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD." And they did so.<sup>5</sup>When the king of Egypt was told that the people had fled, the mind of Pharaoh and his servants was changed toward the people, and they said, "What is this we have done, that we have let Israel go from serving us?"<sup>6</sup>So he made ready his chariot and took his army with him,<sup>7</sup>and took six hundred chosen chariots and all the other chariots of Egypt with officers over all of them.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and he pursued the people of Israel while the people of Israel were going out defiantly.<sup>9</sup>The Egyptians pursued them, all Pharaoh's horses and chariots and his horsemen and his army, and overtook them encamped at the sea, by Pi-hahiroth, in front of Baal-zephon.<sup>10</sup>When Pharaoh drew near, the people of Israel lifted up their eyes, and behold, the Egyptians were marching after them, and they feared greatly. And the people of Israel cried out to the LORD.<sup>11</sup>They said to Moses, "Is it because there are no graves in Egypt that you have taken us away to die in the wilderness? What have you done to us in bringing us out of Egypt?<sup>12</sup>Is not this what we said to you in Egypt: 'Leave us alone that we may serve the Egyptians'? For it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness."<sup>13</sup>And Moses said to the people, "Fear not, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will work for you today. For the Egyptians whom you see today, you shall never see again.<sup>14</sup>The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent."<sup>15</sup>The LORD said to Moses, "Why do you cry to me? Tell the people of Israel to go forward.<sup>16</sup>Lift up your staff, and stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it, that the people of Israel may go through the sea on dry ground.<sup>17</sup>And I will harden the hearts of the Egyptians so that they shall go in after them, and I will get glory over Pharaoh and all his host, his chariots, and his horsemen.<sup>18</sup>And the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I have gotten glory over Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen."<sup>19</sup>Then the angel of God who was going before the host of Israel moved and went behind them, and the pillar of cloud moved from before them and stood behind them,<sup>20</sup>coming between the host of Egypt and the host of Israel. And there was the cloud and the darkness. And it lit up the night without one coming near the other all night.<sup>21</sup>Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the LORD drove the sea back by a strong east wind all night and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided.<sup>22</sup>And the people of Israel went into the midst of the sea on dry ground, the waters being a wall to them on their right hand and on their left.<sup>23</sup>The Egyptians pursued and went in after them into the midst of the sea, all Pharaoh's horses, his chariots, and his horsemen.<sup>24</sup>And in the morning watch the LORD in the pillar of fire and of cloud looked down on the Egyptian forces and threw the Egyptian forces into a panic,<sup>25</sup>clogging their chariot wheels so that they drove heavily. And the Egyptians said, "Let us flee from before Israel, for the LORD fights for them against the Egyptians."<sup>26</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the sea, that the water may come back upon the Egyptians, upon their chariots, and upon their horsemen."<sup>27</sup>So Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the sea returned to its normal course when the morning appeared. And as the Egyptians fled into it, the LORD threw the Egyptians into the midst of the sea.<sup>28</sup>The waters returned and covered the chariots and the horsemen; of all the host of Pharaoh that had followed them into the sea, not one of them remained.<sup>29</sup>But the people of Israel walked on dry ground through the sea, the waters being a wall to them on their right hand and on their left.<sup>30</sup>Thus the LORD saved Israel that day from the hand of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore.<sup>31</sup>Israel saw the great power that the LORD used against the Egyptians, so the people feared the LORD, and they believed in the LORD and in his servant Moses.
14.overview:
Where we are. Israel has left Egypt, led by the pillar of cloud and fire (13:17–22). Now God turns them back to camp with the sea in front of them, and Pharaoh, his heart hardened once more, comes after them with every chariot in Egypt.

The message. Salvation belongs to the LORD. Trapped between the army and the sea, Israel can do nothing, and God does everything: “The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent” (v. 14). He opens a way through the waters of death for his people and closes them over their enemies, so that Egypt learns that he is the LORD, and Israel fears him and believes.

Why it was said. Israel would face many enemies stronger than themselves (see the introduction). This night became the memory their faith returned to, in psalms and prophets, whenever hope seemed gone: the God who “makes a way in the sea” (Isaiah 43:16) had done it once and could do it again.

How the chapter makes its case. God deliberately leads Israel into a dead end to draw Pharaoh out (vv. 1–4), and Pharaoh, regretting the loss of his slaves, pursues with his chariots (vv. 5–9). Israel panics and wishes they had stayed in Egypt, but Moses tells them to stand firm and watch the LORD save (vv. 10–14). God commands them forward; the pillar moves behind them, an east wind drives back the sea all night, and Israel walks through on dry ground (vv. 15–22). The Egyptians follow, and the LORD throws them into panic (vv. 23–25). The waters return, not one Egyptian remains, and Israel fears the LORD and believes (vv. 26–31).

Where it leads. By pattern, and the New Testament draws it. Paul calls the crossing a baptism into Moses “in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:2): God’s people united to their deliverer, passing through judgment safely while the enemy drowns behind them. Jesus spoke of his death as his “departure”, his exodus (Luke 9:31). He went down into the waters of judgment alone, and those joined to him pass with him from death to life, while their sins are cast “into the depths of the sea” (Micah 7:19). At the sea Israel only watched; at the cross Jesus said, “It is finished” (John 19:30).

For us. You cannot save yourself from sin and death, and you do not have to. Stop panicking and look at what God has done in Christ. Then, when he says “go forward”, walk into whatever he has opened for you, trusting the God who fights for his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-14 — Trapped, Terrified, and Told to Stand Still
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God leads his people into a trap so that he may show who he is, and their part is to stand still and watch him save. He turns Israel back to camp with the sea in front, so that Pharaoh will think them lost and pursue (vv. 1–4). Pharaoh regrets letting his slaves go and comes after them with six hundred chosen chariots and all the rest (vv. 5–9). Seeing the army, Israel cries out in terror and turns on Moses: it would have been better to serve Egypt than to die here (vv. 10–12). Moses answers with the chapter’s heart: fear not, stand firm and see the salvation of the LORD, who will fight for you (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology:
Trapped, Terrified, and Told to Stand Still

It looks like a trap for Israel, but it is God’s trap for Pharaoh.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the people remembered slavery as safety. Now: a known misery can feel safer than an unknown rescue, and sometimes God asks only that we stop struggling.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Tell the people of Israel to turn back and encamp in front of Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, in front of Baal-zephon; you shall encamp facing it, by the sea. For Pharaoh will say of the people of Israel, 'They are wandering in the land; the wilderness has shut them in.' And I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and he will pursue them, and I will get glory over Pharaoh and all his host, and the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD." And they did so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God deliberately leads Israel into a dead end by the sea, to draw Pharaoh out and win glory over him.

Turn back and encamp. With the sea in front of them, Israel looks lost and cornered, wandering and shut in: bait for Pharaoh. As before, Pharaoh’s own will and God’s purpose meet (see the introduction on the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart), and God will get glory, showing his greatness by defeating Pharaoh and his army.

The Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD. This is the aim of the whole manoeuvre. Pharaoh began by asking, “Who is the LORD?” (5:2); the sea will answer him. And Israel obeys an order that makes no military sense: “And they did so.”

Why God led them there. God does not lead his people into danger carelessly. He leads them where his power will be seen.

Uncertain wording. Pi-hahiroth, Migdol (“tower”, perhaps a border fort) and Baal-zephon (named after a Canaanite god) were places near the sea, but their sites are not known, and so the exact route and crossing point remain uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: When the king of Egypt was told that the people had fled, the mind of Pharaoh and his servants was changed toward the people, and they said, "What is this we have done, that we have let Israel go from serving us?" So he made ready his chariot and took his army with him, and took six hundred chosen chariots and all the other chariots of Egypt with officers over all of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt regrets, not its defiance of God, but the loss of its slaves, and sends its whole army after them.

What is this we have done? Egypt’s regret is not that it defied God for so long, but that it finally obeyed him. The question they should have asked after the first plague, they ask about losing their slaves.

He made ready his chariot. Egypt sends six hundred chosen chariots, its elite force, and all the rest: the grief of the tenth plague has given way to anger at the loss of their labour.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and he pursued the people of Israel while the people of Israel were going out defiantly. The Egyptians pursued them, all Pharaoh's horses and chariots and his horsemen and his army, and overtook them encamped at the sea, by Pi-hahiroth, in front of Baal-zephon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel marches out boldly, Egypt overtakes them exactly where God told them to camp, and the trap that closes is God’s.

Going out defiantly. Literally “with a high hand”: openly and boldly, like a victorious army, not slinking away (compare Numbers 33:3). Behind them comes the whole strength of Egypt, and it overtakes them “encamped at the sea, by Pi-hahiroth”, exactly where God had told them to camp (v. 2). The trap closes, but it is God’s trap, and Pharaoh is the one caught in it.

verseByVerse.quote: When Pharaoh drew near, the people of Israel lifted up their eyes, and behold, the Egyptians were marching after them, and they feared greatly. And the people of Israel cried out to the LORD. They said to Moses, "Is it because there are no graves in Egypt that you have taken us away to die in the wilderness? What have you done to us in bringing us out of Egypt? Is not this what we said to you in Egypt: 'Leave us alone that we may serve the Egyptians'? For it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness." And Moses said to the people, "Fear not, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will work for you today. For the Egyptians whom you see today, you shall never see again. The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Terrified Israel turns on Moses, and Moses answers that the LORD alone will save them: they have only to stand firm and watch.

No graves in Egypt? This is bitter sarcasm, for Egypt was famous for tombs. Already they speak of slavery as better than freedom.
