Fear not, stand firm, see. They are to stand their ground and watch what God will do. The salvation here is rescue from death, worked wholly by God, for the LORD will fight for you: the battle is his (2 Chronicles 20:15–17). To be silent is to stop panicking and complaining.

The exhausting religion of doing it yourself. Modern people are trained from childhood to believe that every problem has a solution and that the solution is up to us: plan harder, optimise, take control. It is a creed with real achievements, and a hidden cost. When the sea is in front and the chariots behind, the person who must save himself has nothing left but panic, which may be why an age of unprecedented control is also an age of anxiety. Religion often offers the same creed in holier clothes: pray more, try harder, and God will reward the effort. Moses’ words cut through both. Salvation here is not a joint venture; Israel contributes nothing but the walk through the gap God makes. That is the shape of the gospel. At the cross the decisive battle was fought while the disciples hid and the women watched from a distance, and Jesus did not say “Now you finish it” but “It is finished” (John 19:30). Silence before that is not passivity. It is relief.

What it does not mean. This is not a rule of passivity for every situation; next God says “go forward” (v. 15). It concerns the battle only God can win. In a crisis you cannot fix, stop the panic and look to God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God makes a way where there is none, protecting his people and confounding their enemies. He tells Moses to stop crying out and lead the people forward, and to stretch his staff over the sea (vv. 15–18). The angel of God and the pillar move behind Israel, standing between the two camps, darkness to one and light to the other (vv. 19–20). All night a strong east wind drives back the sea, and Israel walks through on dry ground with the waters as walls on either side (vv. 21–22). When the Egyptians follow, the LORD looks down from the pillar, throws them into panic and clogs their wheels, until they cry out that the LORD fights for Israel (vv. 23–25).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sea Divided

Israel walks through on dry ground, and Egypt confesses too late that the LORD fights for them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel had to step towards the water before it opened. Now: like the pillar, Christ is a fragrance of life to some and of death to others (2 Cor. 2:16).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Why do you cry to me? Tell the people of Israel to go forward. Lift up your staff, and stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it, that the people of Israel may go through the sea on dry ground. And I will harden the hearts of the Egyptians so that they shall go in after them, and I will get glory over Pharaoh and all his host, his chariots, and his horsemen. And the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I have gotten glory over Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen." Then the angel of God who was going before the host of Israel moved and went behind them, and the pillar of cloud moved from before them and stood behind them, coming between the host of Egypt and the host of Israel. And there was the cloud and the darkness. And it lit up the night without one coming near the other all night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The time for crying out gives way to obeying: Israel must go forward, while God himself stands between them and their enemies.

Why do you cry to me? Prayer is not wrong, but it does not replace obedience when God has spoken.

Go forward. They must walk towards the water before it parts: faith acts on God’s word.

The angel of God is God’s own presence in the pillar (23:20–21), and this commentary takes the angel who speaks and acts as God to be the Son before his incarnation (see 3:2). He moves from the front to the rear, darkness to the enemy and light to his people (2 Corinthians 2:15–16).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of v. 20 is compressed: literally, “there was the cloud and the darkness, and it lit up the night”. The likely sense is that the one cloud was darkness to Egypt and light to Israel, so that neither camp came near the other all night.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the LORD drove the sea back by a strong east wind all night and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided. And the people of Israel went into the midst of the sea on dry ground, the waters being a wall to them on their right hand and on their left. The Egyptians pursued and went in after them into the midst of the sea, all Pharaoh's horses, his chariots, and his horsemen. And in the morning watch the LORD in the pillar of fire and of cloud looked down on the Egyptian forces and threw the Egyptian forces into a panic, clogging their chariot wheels so that they drove heavily. And the Egyptians said, "Let us flee from before Israel, for the LORD fights for them against the Egyptians."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God drives back the sea by a wind he controls, his people walk through on dry ground, and their pursuers are thrown into panic.

A strong east wind all night. God uses means and takes time: a real event in the physical world, controlled by him.

The waters being a wall to them. The waters stood like a wall on both sides. Dry ground is the same word as Genesis 1:9: this is a new creation, as land emerges from the waters.

Threw the Egyptian forces into a panic. In the morning watch, the last part of the night before dawn, God looked down from the pillar and threw the army into panic, clogging their chariot wheels. Even Egypt confesses, “the LORD fights for them”.

Where Christians differ: the Red Sea or a Sea of Reeds? Hebrew yam suph can mean “sea of reeds”, and some place the crossing at a shallow lake in the delta. This commentary’s view: the location is uncertain, but the text describes deep water standing as walls and an army drowned. Whatever the place, it was a miracle, not a wade through marsh.
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew phrase behind “Red Sea” may mean “Sea of Reeds.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The same waters that saved Israel destroy their enemies, and the people who were terrified now fear the LORD and believe. At God’s word Moses stretches out his hand again, and at dawn the sea returns (vv. 26–27). Every chariot and horseman that followed into the sea is drowned; not one remains (v. 28). Israel, meanwhile, has walked through on dry ground (v. 29). The chapter ends with its verdict: the LORD saved Israel that day. They see the Egyptians dead on the shore, see the great power of the LORD, and respond with reverent fear and faith in the LORD and in his servant Moses (vv. 30–31).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Enemy Swallowed Up

The same waters save and judge.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore. Now: the enemies that owned us (sin, death and the accuser) lie defeated behind those who are in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the sea, that the water may come back upon the Egyptians, upon their chariots, and upon their horsemen." So Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the sea returned to its normal course when the morning appeared. And as the Egyptians fled into it, the LORD threw the Egyptians into the midst of the sea. The waters returned and covered the chariots and the horsemen; of all the host of Pharaoh that had followed them into the sea, not one of them remained. But the people of Israel walked on dry ground through the sea, the waters being a wall to them on their right hand and on their left. Thus the LORD saved Israel that day from the hand of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore. Israel saw the great power that the LORD used against the Egyptians, so the people feared the LORD, and they believed in the LORD and in his servant Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The waters return and destroy the whole army, and Israel, seeing what the LORD has done, fears him and believes.

Not one remained. The army that hunted them is gone, in the waters where Egypt drowned Israel’s sons (1:22). Saved is Hebrew yasha, the root of the name “Jesus”.

Feared the LORD and believed. Reverent awe and trust were the purpose of the trap, and they believed Moses, God’s servant, too.

A baptism into Moses. Paul calls the crossing a baptism into Moses (1 Corinthians 10:1–2): passing through judgment safely, united to the deliverer, with the old enemy drowned behind. Jesus passed through the waters of death for us (Luke 12:50), and in him we pass from death to life.

Faith not yet secure. Yet many who crossed fell later; being part of the crossing did not guarantee faithfulness, and three days later they grumble (15:24). A great experience must grow into steady trust. The God who saved them at the sea saves from enemies you could never defeat.

14.theology:
Salvation belongs to the LORD. Israel only watches; God does the saving.

The Red Sea as baptism. The crossing is the pattern of Christian baptism: through the waters from death to life, "baptized into Moses" (1 Cor. 10:2).

The same waters save and judge. Salvation and judgment flow from one hand.
14.examples:
Then: Trapped between army and sea, Israel was told to stand still and see God save.

Now: When we are cornered with no way out, the gospel call is the same: stand firm and see the salvation of the LORD. At the cross our true enemies were defeated, and in Christ we have passed through the waters of judgment into new life.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent.
keyVerse.note: This is the heart of the chapter and of the gospel: salvation is God’s work, received, not achieved. Israel contributes nothing but the walk through the gap God makes. The same is true at the cross, where Christ won the battle alone and his people receive the victory.

14.reflection:
Israel ended up trapped by the sea because God led them there (vv. 1–4). How does it change the way you see a hard situation to know that God may have led you into it for his glory and your good?

Within days of their rescue, Israel says slavery would have been better (vv. 11–12). Why is fear so quick to rewrite the past? Where are you tempted to look back on life before Christ as easier?

Moses says, “you have only to be silent” (v. 14), and then God says, “go forward” (v. 15). How do resting in what God does and obeying what God says fit together in the Christian life?

Paul calls the crossing a kind of baptism (1 Corinthians 10:1–2). What does the sea, with Israel saved and the enemy drowned, show you about what Christ has done for you?

15.title: The Song of the Redeemed
15.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Moses and the people of Israel sang this song to the LORD, saying, "I will sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea.<sup>2</sup>The LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation; this is my God, and I will praise him, my father's God, and I will exalt him.<sup>3</sup>The LORD is a man of war; the LORD is his name.<sup>4</sup>"Pharaoh's chariots and his host he cast into the sea, and his chosen officers were sunk in the Red Sea.<sup>5</sup>The floods covered them; they went down into the depths like a stone.<sup>6</sup>Your right hand, O LORD, glorious in power, your right hand, O LORD, shatters the enemy.<sup>7</sup>In the greatness of your majesty you overthrow your adversaries; you send out your fury; it consumes them like stubble.<sup>8</sup>At the blast of your nostrils the waters piled up; the floods stood up in a heap; the deeps congealed in the heart of the sea.<sup>9</sup>The enemy said, 'I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil, my desire shall have its fill of them. I will draw my sword; my hand shall destroy them.'<sup>10</sup>You blew with your wind; the sea covered them; they sank like lead in the mighty waters.<sup>11</sup>"Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness, awesome in glorious deeds, doing wonders?<sup>12</sup>You stretched out your right hand; the earth swallowed them.<sup>13</sup>"You have led in your steadfast love the people whom you have redeemed; you have guided them by your strength to your holy abode.<sup>14</sup>The peoples have heard; they tremble; pangs have seized the inhabitants of Philistia.<sup>15</sup>Now are the chiefs of Edom dismayed; trembling seizes the leaders of Moab; all the inhabitants of Canaan have melted away.<sup>16</sup>Terror and dread fall upon them; because of the greatness of your arm, they are still as a stone, till your people, O LORD, pass by, till the people pass by whom you have purchased.<sup>17</sup>You will bring them in and plant them on your own mountain, the place, O LORD, which you have made for your abode, the sanctuary, O Lord, which your hands have established.<sup>18</sup>The LORD will reign forever and ever."<sup>19</sup>For when the horses of Pharaoh with his chariots and his horsemen went into the sea, the LORD brought back the waters of the sea upon them, but the people of Israel walked on dry ground in the midst of the sea.<sup>20</sup>Then Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women went out after her with tambourines and dancing.<sup>21</sup>And Miriam sang to them: "Sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea."<sup>22</sup>Then Moses made Israel set out from the Red Sea, and they went into the wilderness of Shur. They went three days in the wilderness and found no water.<sup>23</sup>When they came to Marah, they could not drink the water of Marah because it was bitter; therefore it was named Marah.<sup>24</sup>And the people grumbled against Moses, saying, "What shall we drink?"<sup>25</sup>And he cried to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a log, and he threw it into the water, and the water became sweet. There the LORD made for them a statute and a rule, and there he tested them,<sup>26</sup>saying, "If you will diligently listen to the voice of the LORD your God, and do that which is right in his eyes, and give ear to his commandments and keep all his statutes, I will put none of the diseases on you that I put on the Egyptians, for I am the LORD, your healer."<sup>27</sup>Then they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they encamped there by the water.
15.overview:
Where we are. Israel stands on the far shore with the Egyptians dead behind them (14:30–31). Their first act as a free people is to sing. Then the journey begins, and after three days in the wilderness there is no water.

The message. The God who saved his people deserves all their praise, and he can be trusted with what comes next. The song is about who he is: a warrior who fights for slaves, unlike any so-called god, majestic in holiness and steadfast in love, leading his redeemed people home to his sanctuary, and King for ever. At Marah that praise is tested, and God shows himself as “the LORD, your healer” (v. 26).

Why it was said. Israel would sing this song for generations (see the introduction), and songs shape memory more deeply than records do. Its second half looks ahead to the nations trembling and Israel planted on God’s mountain, so later generations living in the land could see their own life as its fulfilment. Marah warned every generation how quickly praise can sour into complaint.

How the chapter makes its case. Moses and Israel sing of the victory at the sea (vv. 1–5), of God’s right hand and the breath of his nostrils against an enemy full of boasts (vv. 6–10), and of his incomparable holiness (vv. 11–12). Then the song looks forward: God leading his people in steadfast love, the nations frozen with fear, Israel planted on his mountain and the LORD reigning for ever (vv. 13–18). Miriam leads the women in the refrain (vv. 19–21). Three days later, at Marah, praise turns to grumbling; God makes the bitter water sweet, tests his people, names himself their healer and brings them to the springs of Elim (vv. 22–27).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. The warrior who fought for slaves won his greatest victory at the cross, where Christ “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them” (Colossians 2:15). The LORD who heals walked among us: “He took our illnesses and bore our diseases” (Matthew 8:17). And at the end the redeemed stand beside another sea and sing “the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb” (Revelation 15:3).

For us. Make your songs about God and what he has done, not about yourself. Expect testing after deliverance, and when it comes, bring your need to the Lord rather than your grumbling to others. The one who sweetened Marah can be trusted in the wilderness you are in.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-12 — The LORD Is a Warrior
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD has fought for his people and won, and no one compares with him. The song opens with Israel’s response to rescue: God has thrown horse and rider into the sea, and he is my strength, my song and my salvation (vv. 1–3). It retells the battle: Pharaoh’s army sinking like a stone (vv. 4–5), God’s right hand shattering the enemy and the blast of his nostrils piling up the waters (vv. 6–8). The enemy’s six boasts are answered by one breath of God’s wind (vv. 9–10). So the song asks the question at its centre: who is like you, majestic in holiness, doing wonders (vv. 11–12)?
verseByVerse.theology:
The LORD Is a Warrior

The song celebrates what God has done, not what Israel did.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the first thing God's people are recorded singing is their rescue. Now: one act of God was both mercy to the slaves and judgment on their oppressors.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses and the people of Israel sang this song to the LORD, saying, "I will sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea. The LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation; this is my God, and I will praise him, my father's God, and I will exalt him. The LORD is a man of war; the LORD is his name. "Pharaoh's chariots and his host he cast into the sea, and his chosen officers were sunk in the Red Sea. The floods covered them; they went down into the depths like a stone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s first response to rescue is a song about God: he has thrown down Egypt’s army and has become his people’s strength, song and salvation.

I will sing to the LORD. Worship responds to redemption. Triumphed gloriously is literally “he is highly exalted”: the song is about God, not Israel.

My strength and my song. God gives the strength and is the theme of the song, and he is my rescue. The words are echoed in Psalm 118:14 and Isaiah 12:2. “My God … my father’s God” joins personal faith and inherited faith.

A man of war. God is a warrior who fights for his people. This is no violent God who loves bloodshed. He fights for slaves against their oppressor, and his warfare is justice. Christ fights the final battle by his word (Revelation 19:15).

Uncertain wording. My song (zimrat) may instead mean “my might” or “my protection”, as some translations have it. Either way, the LORD is all his people need.
verseByVerse.note: The first song the Bible calls a song: Israel’s hymn of victory.

verseByVerse.quote: Your right hand, O LORD, glorious in power, your right hand, O LORD, shatters the enemy. In the greatness of your majesty you overthrow your adversaries; you send out your fury; it consumes them like stubble. At the blast of your nostrils the waters piled up; the floods stood up in a heap; the deeps congealed in the heart of the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s own power, not Israel’s, broke the enemy: his right hand shattered them and his breath piled up the sea.

God’s power in action. God’s right hand, the hand of strength and skill, is his power in action, and his fury is his burning anger against those who rose against his people. The blast of your nostrils is the east wind of 14:21, and the waters that congealed are poetry for walls of water standing still.

In everyday life. His power is greater than every force you fear.

verseByVerse.quote: The enemy said, 'I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil, my desire shall have its fill of them. I will draw my sword; my hand shall destroy them.' You blew with your wind; the sea covered them; they sank like lead in the mighty waters. "Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness, awesome in glorious deeds, doing wonders? You stretched out your right hand; the earth swallowed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The enemy’s loud boasts are answered by one breath from God, and the song breaks out: no one is like the LORD.

I will pursue, I will overtake. The enemy makes six boasts in a row; pride speaks loudly. One breath from God answers them all.

Who is like you … among the gods? The plagues judged Egypt’s gods (12:12). God is majestic in holiness, unlike all else and pure.

What it does not mean. This does not make other gods real rivals. It means that no so-called god can be compared with him (Psalm 96:5; 1 Corinthians 8:4–6).

Uncertain wording. The earth swallowed them: “earth” here may mean the sea, or the grave.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who redeemed his people will finish what he began: he will bring them home and reign for ever. The song turns from the sea to the future, singing of it as though it were already done. God has led his redeemed people in steadfast love towards his holy dwelling (v. 13). The nations on the way, Philistia, Edom, Moab and Canaan, hear and freeze with dread until God’s people pass by (vv. 14–16). He will plant them on his own mountain, in the sanctuary his hands have made (v. 17). And the song ends with its climax: the LORD will reign forever and ever (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology:
Leading to the Sanctuary

The exodus is a beginning: it leads to worship where God dwells.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: "Who is like you, O LORD?" answers Pharaoh's "Who is the LORD?" Now: the redeemed still sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb (Rev. 15:3-4).

verseByVerse.quote: "You have led in your steadfast love the people whom you have redeemed; you have guided them by your strength to your holy abode. The peoples have heard; they tremble; pangs have seized the inhabitants of Philistia. Now are the chiefs of Edom dismayed; trembling seizes the leaders of Moab; all the inhabitants of Canaan have melted away. Terror and dread fall upon them; because of the greatness of your arm, they are still as a stone, till your people, O LORD, pass by, till the people pass by whom you have purchased. You will bring them in and plant them on your own mountain, the place, O LORD, which you have made for your abode, the sanctuary, O Lord, which your hands have established. The LORD will reign forever and ever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who redeemed his people in steadfast love will bring them all the way home, through every enemy, and reign for ever.

Steadfast love is Hebrew hesed, loyal covenant love that does not let go; this is its first appearance in Exodus.

Your holy abode … your sanctuary is the place where God will dwell among them: Sinai, the land, and finally Jerusalem’s temple (Psalm 78:54).

The peoples have heard. Philistia, Edom, Moab and Canaan hear and tremble (Joshua 2:9–11).

The LORD will reign forever and ever. The song climbs to its climax: the LORD is King for ever. The song begun on the shore of the Red Sea will be completed before the throne, where the victorious sing, “Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty!” (Revelation 15:3). Sing to the King who redeemed you and is leading you home.

Uncertain wording. Purchased (v. 16) may also be translated “created”, since the Hebrew verb can mean both. Either way, God has acquired a people for himself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Praise belongs to all God’s people, and the women take up the song. The narrator sums up the miracle once more: Pharaoh’s horses and chariots went into the sea and the waters came back on them, while Israel walked through on dry ground (v. 19). Then Miriam the prophetess, Aaron’s sister, takes a tambourine and leads the women out with tambourines and dancing (v. 20). She sings back to them the opening of the song: sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously (v. 21). Joyful, whole-hearted, even physical praise is the fitting response to God’s salvation.
verseByVerse.theology:
Miriam's Song

Joy in salvation overflows into the whole community.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the girl who watched the basket in the reeds sees the sea take an army. Now: not everyone writes the song, but everyone may sing it.

verseByVerse.quote: For when the horses of Pharaoh with his chariots and his horsemen went into the sea, the LORD brought back the waters of the sea upon them, but the people of Israel walked on dry ground in the midst of the sea. Then Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women went out after her with tambourines and dancing. And Miriam sang to them: "Sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Miriam leads the women in the refrain, and the whole people praise God with joy.

Miriam the prophetess is probably the sister who watched the basket (2:4). A prophetess speaks God’s word; here she leads praise.

A tambourine in her hand. Tambourine and dancing are joyful worship with the body, and Israel’s women often celebrated victories this way (1 Samuel 18:6). Not every service must include dancing, but whole-hearted, physical joy in God has its place (Psalm 149:3).
verseByVerse.note: Miriam is the first woman in the Bible called a prophetess.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Redeemed people are tested, and the God who saved them proves to be the God who heals them. Three days into the wilderness of Shur they find no water, and when they find it at Marah it is bitter (vv. 22–23). The people who sang now grumble against Moses (v. 24). Moses cries to the LORD, who shows him a log; thrown into the water, it makes it sweet (v. 25). There God tests them and sets out a statute: listen and obey, and he will keep from them the diseases of Egypt, for he is the LORD, their healer (vv. 25–26). Then he brings them to Elim, with twelve springs and seventy palms (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology:
Marah and Elim

The God who saved at the sea heals in the desert.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the same mouths sang on the shore and grumbled three days later. Now: God does not always take his people around the bitter place, but through it to the springs.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses made Israel set out from the Red Sea, and they went into the wilderness of Shur. They went three days in the wilderness and found no water. When they came to Marah, they could not drink the water of Marah because it was bitter; therefore it was named Marah. And the people grumbled against Moses, saying, "What shall we drink?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three days after singing, the people meet bitter water and turn on Moses.

The wilderness of Shur. Shur lay on the road to Sinai. After three days the same mouths that sang now complain, and the water at Marah is undrinkable, perhaps brackish.

What shall we drink? They grumbled against their leader, but in truth against God (16:8). Their need was not imaginary, for thirst in the desert is deadly; the sin is distrust, not need. When praise is quickly followed by trouble, bring your need to God, not your grumbling to others.
verseByVerse.note: “Marah” means bitterness (ESV note). Shur was the wilderness east of Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: And he cried to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a log, and he threw it into the water, and the water became sweet. There the LORD made for them a statute and a rule, and there he tested them, saying, "If you will diligently listen to the voice of the LORD your God, and do that which is right in his eyes, and give ear to his commandments and keep all his statutes, I will put none of the diseases on you that I put on the Egyptians, for I am the LORD, your healer." Then they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they encamped there by the water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God makes the bitter water sweet, tests his redeemed people, and reveals himself as the LORD who heals them.

A log, or “a tree”: God works through an ordinary thing. Some early Christian writers saw a picture of the cross, which makes bitter things sweet.

Tested after redemption. God tested a people he had already redeemed, to show whether they would trust and obey. The diseases of Egypt are the plagues: God, who struck Egypt, can keep Israel from such judgments.

I am the LORD, your healer. The God who restores and makes whole leads them on to Elim, with twelve springs and seventy palms: rest and plenty after bitterness. In Jesus the healer came among us, and “took our illnesses and bore our diseases” (Matthew 8:17). Thank God for every healing and for the final healing to come.

Where Christians differ: does God promise health to the obedient? Some teach that faith and obedience guarantee healing. This commentary’s view: the promise belongs to Israel’s covenant life in the land, set beside its curses (Deuteronomy 28). God does heal, and will heal fully at the resurrection, but faithful believers still get ill (2 Timothy 4:20).

15.theology:
Praise as the response to redemption. Salvation accomplished overflows into worship, and knowing God rightly ends in praising him.

No one is like God. The song magnifies the unique, holy, warrior-King.

The everlasting reign of God. "The LORD will reign forever and ever." The exodus points on to God’s eternal kingdom, which comes in Christ.
15.examples:
Then: Standing on the far shore with their enemies dead behind them, the redeemed people sang.

Now: We who have been brought through the waters in Christ join the song of Moses and the Lamb. Our worship now is the rehearsal of the eternal praise we will sing before the throne.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation; this is my God, and I will praise him, my father’s God, and I will exalt him.
keyVerse.note: Here the redeemed say in one breath what God has become to them: their strength, the theme of their singing and their salvation. The words are taken up again in Psalm 118:14 and Isaiah 12:2, and they join personal faith (“my God”) to the faith handed down (“my father’s God”). Every song of the redeemed, to the song of the Lamb, begins here.

15.reflection:
The song is almost entirely about God, not about Israel (vv. 1–18). What would change if more of our praise, sung and spoken, were about who God is and what he has done?

The song calls the LORD “a man of war” (v. 3). How do you respond to that picture of God? How does it help to see that he fights for the oppressed, and that Christ’s greatest victory was won on the cross?

Only three days after singing, the people grumble at Marah (vv. 22–24). Why does praise turn to complaint so quickly? What helps you trust God when a great answer to prayer is followed by fresh trouble?

God calls himself “the LORD, your healer” (v. 26). How should we pray for healing, and how should we hold on to God when healing does not come?

16.title: Bread from Heaven
16.text: <sup>1</sup>They set out from Elim, and all the congregation of the people of Israel came to the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after they had departed from the land of Egypt.<sup>2</sup>And the whole congregation of the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness,<sup>3</sup>and the people of Israel said to them, "Would that we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the meat pots and ate bread to the full, for you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger."<sup>4</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, I am about to rain bread from heaven for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day's portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law or not.<sup>5</sup>On the sixth day, when they prepare what they bring in, it will be twice as much as they gather daily."<sup>6</sup>So Moses and Aaron said to all the people of Israel, "At evening you shall know that it was the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt,<sup>7</sup>and in the morning you shall see the glory of the LORD, because he has heard your grumbling against the LORD. For what are we, that you grumble against us?"<sup>8</sup>And Moses said, "When the LORD gives you in the evening meat to eat and in the morning bread to the full, because the LORD has heard your grumbling that you grumble against him— what are we? Your grumbling is not against us but against the LORD."<sup>9</sup>Then Moses said to Aaron, "Say to the whole congregation of the people of Israel, 'Come near before the LORD, for he has heard your grumbling.'"<sup>10</sup>And as soon as Aaron spoke to the whole congregation of the people of Israel, they looked toward the wilderness, and behold, the glory of the LORD appeared in the cloud.<sup>11</sup>And the LORD said to Moses,<sup>12</sup>"I have heard the grumbling of the people of Israel. Say to them, 'At twilight you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread. Then you shall know that I am the LORD your God.'"<sup>13</sup>In the evening quail came up and covered the camp, and in the morning dew lay around the camp.<sup>14</sup>And when the dew had gone up, there was on the face of the wilderness a fine, flake-like thing, fine as frost on the ground.<sup>15</sup>When the people of Israel saw it, they said to one another, "What is it?" For they did not know what it was. And Moses said to them, "It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat.<sup>16</sup>This is what the LORD has commanded: 'Gather of it, each one of you, as much as he can eat. You shall each take an omer, according to the number of the persons that each of you has in his tent.'"<sup>17</sup>And the people of Israel did so. They gathered, some more, some less.<sup>18</sup>But when they measured it with an omer, whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack. Each of them gathered as much as he could eat.<sup>19</sup>And Moses said to them, "Let no one leave any of it over till the morning."<sup>20</sup>But they did not listen to Moses. Some left part of it till the morning, and it bred worms and stank. And Moses was angry with them.<sup>21</sup>Morning by morning they gathered it, each as much as he could eat; but when the sun grew hot, it melted.<sup>22</sup>On the sixth day they gathered twice as much bread, two omers each. And when all the leaders of the congregation came and told Moses,<sup>23</sup>he said to them, "This is what the LORD has commanded: 'Tomorrow is a day of solemn rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD; bake what you will bake and boil what you will boil, and all that is left over lay aside to be kept till the morning.'"<sup>24</sup>So they laid it aside till the morning, as Moses commanded them, and it did not stink, and there were no worms in it.<sup>25</sup>Moses said, "Eat it today, for today is a Sabbath to the LORD; today you will not find it in the field.<sup>26</sup>Six days you shall gather it, but on the seventh day, which is a Sabbath, there will be none."<sup>27</sup>On the seventh day some of the people went out to gather, but they found none.<sup>28</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "How long will you refuse to keep my commandments and my laws?<sup>29</sup>See! The LORD has given you the Sabbath; therefore on the sixth day he gives you bread for two days. Remain each of you in his place; let no one go out of his place on the seventh day."<sup>30</sup>So the people rested on the seventh day.<sup>31</sup>Now the house of Israel called its name manna. It was like coriander seed, white, and the taste of it was like wafers made with honey.<sup>32</sup>Moses said, "This is what the LORD has commanded: 'Let an omer of it be kept throughout your generations, so that they may see the bread with which I fed you in the wilderness, when I brought you out of the land of Egypt.'"<sup>33</sup>And Moses said to Aaron, "Take a jar, and put an omer of manna in it, and place it before the LORD to be kept throughout your generations."<sup>34</sup>As the LORD commanded Moses, so Aaron placed it before the testimony to be kept.<sup>35</sup>The people of Israel ate the manna forty years, till they came to a habitable land. They ate the manna till they came to the border of the land of Canaan.<sup>36</sup>(An omer is the tenth part of an ephah.)
16.overview:
Where we are. A month after leaving Egypt (v. 1), past the bitter water of Marah and the springs of Elim (15:22–27), Israel reaches the wilderness of Sin, and the food runs short. Sinai, where God will give his law, is still ahead.

The message. God answers ungrateful grumbling with grace, and teaches his people to live on him one day at a time. He rains bread from heaven, enough for each day and no more, and a double portion before the Sabbath, so that they learn he can be trusted for tomorrow and that his rest is a gift. As Moses later explains, God fed them “that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone” (Deuteronomy 8:3).

Why it was said. Israel ate manna for forty years and then lived in a land where bread came from fields and barns (see the introduction), and plenty makes people forget who feeds them. The jar of manna kept “throughout your generations” (vv. 32–33) shows that the story was told for those who never tasted it, so that every generation would remember its daily dependence on God.

How the chapter makes its case. The whole people grumble for Egypt’s meat pots (vv. 1–3). God promises bread from heaven as a daily test, and Moses and Aaron tell them their complaint is against the LORD (vv. 4–8). The glory of the LORD appears in the cloud, with a promise of meat and bread (vv. 9–12). Quail come in the evening and manna in the morning, and everyone has enough (vv. 13–18), but what is hoarded rots (vv. 19–21). On the sixth day a double portion keeps for the Sabbath, God’s gift of rest, and those who go out on the seventh find nothing (vv. 22–30). A jar of manna is kept as a memorial, and the manna lasts forty years, until Canaan (vv. 31–36).

Where it leads. By pattern, and Jesus draws it himself: “it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven” (John 6:32). “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger” (John 6:35). The manna kept people alive for a day, and those who ate it died (John 6:49), but whoever eats the living bread “will live forever” (John 6:51). The Sabbath rest given here points on to the rest Christ gives (Hebrews 4:9–10).

For us. Ask God for today’s bread, and trust him for tomorrow’s instead of grasping in fear. Notice how grumbling forgets grace, and give thanks instead. Receive the Lord’s Day as a gift. Above all, come to Christ, the bread from heaven, who alone satisfies.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God meets his people’s grumbling with grace, and his grace comes with a test. A month out of Egypt the whole congregation complains that they would rather have died in Egypt by the meat pots than starve in the wilderness (vv. 1–3). God does not answer with judgment but with a promise: he will rain bread from heaven, a day’s portion each day and double on the sixth, to test whether they will walk in his law (vv. 4–5). Moses and Aaron tell the people that their grumbling is against the LORD (vv. 6–8). Then the glory of the LORD appears in the cloud, and he promises meat at twilight and bread in the morning (vv. 9–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
Grumbling and Grace

God answers slander with provision, and counts complaint against his servants as against himself.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: hunger made slavery look like a feast. Now: God still meets our grumbling with patience before he corrects it.

verseByVerse.quote: They set out from Elim, and all the congregation of the people of Israel came to the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after they had departed from the land of Egypt. And the whole congregation of the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness, and the people of Israel said to them, "Would that we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the meat pots and ate bread to the full, for you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A month out of Egypt, the whole people grumble, remembering slavery as a full table and accusing their leaders of bringing them out to starve.

The fifteenth day of the second month. They left Egypt on the fifteenth day of the first month (Numbers 33:3), so this is exactly a month into freedom.

Meat pots and bread to the full. Memory edits the past. Egypt was whips and drowned sons, but under pressure they remember only food. They even accuse God’s servants of plotting to kill the whole assembly with hunger. Hunger is not sin; the sin is ingratitude and distrust after so many signs of God’s care. When you are tempted to romanticise life before Christ, remember what it really was.

Why do we miss our chains? It seems absurd that people a few weeks out of slavery should long to go back, but it is one of the most human things in the book. In 1941, watching Europe hand itself to dictators, the psychologist Erich Fromm wrote Escape from Freedom, arguing that freedom brings a loneliness and uncertainty many people cannot bear, so they go looking for a new master to relieve them of it. Egypt was cruel, but it was predictable: there was always a pot on the fire. The wilderness offers freedom with no guaranteed supper. Many of our idols hold us the same way. The job we resent but cannot leave, the relationship that diminishes us, the habit that shames us: each is a small Egypt, and what keeps us there is not love of the chains but fear of the open desert. God does not answer the grumbling with a lecture. He rains bread from heaven, the first of many signs that the God who frees you will also feed you, until the true bread from heaven says, “whoever comes to me shall not hunger” (John 6:35).
verseByVerse.note: The wilderness of Sin lay in the Sinai peninsula; the name is unrelated to the English word.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, I am about to rain bread from heaven for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day's portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law or not. On the sixth day, when they prepare what they bring in, it will be twice as much as they gather daily." So Moses and Aaron said to all the people of Israel, "At evening you shall know that it was the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt, and in the morning you shall see the glory of the LORD, because he has heard your grumbling against the LORD. For what are we, that you grumble against us?" And Moses said, "When the LORD gives you in the evening meat to eat and in the morning bread to the full, because the LORD has heard your grumbling that you grumble against him— what are we? Your grumbling is not against us but against the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers slander with grace: bread from heaven, given a day at a time to test and train his people’s trust.

Rain bread from heaven. God’s answer to their complaint is not judgment but a gift.

A day’s portion every day. Enough for today only: the daily provision teaches daily dependence, as Jesus taught us to pray for daily bread (Matthew 6:11). God gives it that I may test them, to reveal and train their hearts: will they trust and obey?

Your grumbling is against the LORD. Complaints against God’s servants reach God himself.

What it does not mean. Planning ahead is not wrong. Joseph stored grain for famine at God’s word (Genesis 41). The manna rule applied where God himself had promised daily supply.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses said to Aaron, "Say to the whole congregation of the people of Israel, 'Come near before the LORD, for he has heard your grumbling.'" And as soon as Aaron spoke to the whole congregation of the people of Israel, they looked toward the wilderness, and behold, the glory of the LORD appeared in the cloud. And the LORD said to Moses, "I have heard the grumbling of the people of Israel. Say to them, 'At twilight you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread. Then you shall know that I am the LORD your God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God summons the grumblers into his presence, shows them his glory, and promises to feed them so that they will know he is their God.

Come near before the LORD. The grumblers are summoned into God’s presence, and the glory of the LORD appeared, his visible majesty in the cloud. His answer to complaint is to show himself, and to promise a double provision: meat at twilight and bread in the morning.

Then you shall know that I am the LORD your God. The food is not only for their stomachs but for their knowledge of him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God provides exactly enough for each day, and his people must trust him for tomorrow. In the evening quail cover the camp, and in the morning fine flakes lie on the ground; the people ask, “What is it?”, and Moses tells them it is the bread the LORD has given (vv. 13–15). Each gathers according to the size of his household, and whether they gathered much or little, all have enough (vv. 16–18). Moses tells them to leave none till morning, but some keep it anyway, and it breeds worms and stinks (vv. 19–20). Every morning they gather, and what is left melts in the sun (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology:
Bread from Heaven

Provision that cannot be stockpiled teaches trust.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul used verse 18 to argue for generosity (2 Cor. 8:15). Now: what we cling to beyond the day God gave it for goes bad.

verseByVerse.quote: In the evening quail came up and covered the camp, and in the morning dew lay around the camp. And when the dew had gone up, there was on the face of the wilderness a fine, flake-like thing, fine as frost on the ground. When the people of Israel saw it, they said to one another, "What is it?" For they did not know what it was. And Moses said to them, "It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat. This is what the LORD has commanded: 'Gather of it, each one of you, as much as he can eat. You shall each take an omer, according to the number of the persons that each of you has in his tent.'" And the people of Israel did so. They gathered, some more, some less. But when they measured it with an omer, whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack. Each of them gathered as much as he could eat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends quail and manna, and however much or little each one gathers, everyone has exactly enough.

Quail came up and covered the camp. Quail are migrating birds that often land exhausted in Sinai.

What is it? Hebrew man hu, the origin of “manna”. Moses answers: “It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat.”

Whoever gathered much had nothing left over. An omer was a day’s ration. Whoever gathered much or little had exactly enough. Paul uses this to urge Christians to share (2 Corinthians 8:13–15).

Where Christians differ: what was manna? Some compare a sweet resin produced by tamarisk shrubs in Sinai. This commentary’s view: that resin is small, seasonal and local. Manna fell in quantity enough for a nation, daily for forty years, stopped on the Sabbath and ended when they entered Canaan (Joshua 5:12). It was God’s miraculous provision.
verseByVerse.note: An omer was about 2 quarts (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses said to them, "Let no one leave any of it over till the morning." But they did not listen to Moses. Some left part of it till the morning, and it bred worms and stank. And Moses was angry with them. Morning by morning they gathered it, each as much as he could eat; but when the sun grew hot, it melted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Manna kept overnight against God’s word rots: the gift could not be hoarded, only trusted for again tomorrow.

Let no one leave any of it over till the morning. The command asked them to trust God for tomorrow, and they disobeyed on the very first day. The hoarded manna bred worms and stank: greed and anxiety spoil good gifts.

What it does not mean. This is not a ban on saving or wise stewardship. It was a specific test of trust in God’s daily provision. But the lesson holds: hoarding in fear, instead of trusting, spoils what God gives. Is anxiety about tomorrow leading you to grasp more than you need (Matthew 6:34)?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22-36 — The Sabbath Provision and a Memorial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God gives his people rest, and he wants them to remember for ever that he fed them. On the sixth day they gather twice as much, and Moses explains that tomorrow is a holy Sabbath; the manna kept overnight does not spoil (vv. 22–24). Some go out on the seventh day anyway and find nothing, and God rebukes their refusal to keep his commands; the Sabbath is his gift, and the people rest (vv. 25–30). The narrator describes the manna and tells how a jar of it was kept before the testimony for later generations (vv. 31–34). Israel ate it for forty years, until they reached Canaan (vv. 35–36).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sabbath Provision and a Memorial

Rest arrives as a gift before it is a rule.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27). Now: Jesus is the bread from heaven that a man may eat and not die (John 6:31-51).

verseByVerse.quote: On the sixth day they gathered twice as much bread, two omers each. And when all the leaders of the congregation came and told Moses, he said to them, "This is what the LORD has commanded: 'Tomorrow is a day of solemn rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD; bake what you will bake and boil what you will boil, and all that is left over lay aside to be kept till the morning.'" So they laid it aside till the morning, as Moses commanded them, and it did not stink, and there were no worms in it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the sixth day God gives a double portion, and the manna kept for the Sabbath does not spoil: rest is his provision.

Twice as much bread. On the sixth day each person gathers two omers, double the daily ration (v. 16), as God had said they would (v. 5). The leaders come to Moses, perhaps because it looked like breaking the rule against keeping manna overnight (v. 19). He explains that the extra is for the Sabbath. “Bake what you will bake”: manna could be baked or boiled (Numbers 11:8), and the cooking is done the day before.

A day of solemn rest is a complete rest, a day set apart for God.

A Sabbath before Sinai. Israel keeps the Sabbath weeks before the Ten Commandments: rest rooted in creation (Genesis 2:2–3) and given as a gift.

It did not stink. The same food that rotted overnight on other days kept for the Sabbath, because God said it would.
verseByVerse.note: The first explicit mention of the Sabbath as a command to Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses said, "Eat it today, for today is a Sabbath to the LORD; today you will not find it in the field. Six days you shall gather it, but on the seventh day, which is a Sabbath, there will be none." On the seventh day some of the people went out to gather, but they found none.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sabbath is first a gift to receive, and those who go out to gather anyway find nothing.

Eat it today. The Sabbath is something to receive before it is something to refrain from. Moses states the pattern plainly: six days of gathering, and on the seventh none.

Some of the people went out. They were not hungry, for the double portion was waiting at home. They went because they did not quite believe the word, or wanted more than enough, and they found nothing. As with the manna kept overnight (vv. 19–20), unbelief shows itself in small, practical acts.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "How long will you refuse to keep my commandments and my laws? See! The LORD has given you the Sabbath; therefore on the sixth day he gives you bread for two days. Remain each of you in his place; let no one go out of his place on the seventh day." So the people rested on the seventh day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God rebukes his people’s repeated disobedience and reminds them that the Sabbath is his gift, and at last they rest.

How long will you refuse? God’s exasperated question at repeated disobedience. My commandments and my laws: the words are spoken to Moses, but the “you” is plural, aimed at the people after weeks of grumbling and disobedience (15:24; 16:2, 20). This is the test the manna was given for (v. 4): will they walk in God’s law?

The LORD has given you the Sabbath. The Sabbath is given: a gift to enjoy, not a burden to carry.

Remain each of you in his place. This forbids going out to gather, not all movement; later Jewish teaching drew from it a set distance that could be walked on the Sabbath, “a Sabbath day’s journey” (Acts 1:12). “So the people rested”: the gift was at last received.

Where Christians differ: is the Sabbath binding today? Some, with the Westminster Confession, say this pre-Sinai Sabbath shows a creation ordinance binding all people, now kept on the Lord’s Day as the Christian Sabbath; Seventh-day Adventists keep Saturday. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath was given to Israel as a sign of the covenant (31:13) and is fulfilled in Christ, who gives true rest (Hebrews 4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17). The Lord’s Day is a glad privilege for worship and rest, not a legal burden, and no one may bind another’s conscience.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the house of Israel called its name manna. It was like coriander seed, white, and the taste of it was like wafers made with honey. Moses said, "This is what the LORD has commanded: 'Let an omer of it be kept throughout your generations, so that they may see the bread with which I fed you in the wilderness, when I brought you out of the land of Egypt.'" And Moses said to Aaron, "Take a jar, and put an omer of manna in it, and place it before the LORD to be kept throughout your generations." As the LORD commanded Moses, so Aaron placed it before the testimony to be kept.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A jar of manna is kept before the LORD, so that later generations can see the bread with which he fed his people.

It was like coriander seed. Manna looked like coriander seed, small, round and white, and tasted sweet like wafers made with honey.

Let an omer of it be kept. A jar of manna was kept as a memorial, so that later generations could see the bread God gave.

Before the testimony means in front of the ark, which held “the testimony”, the tablets of the law (25:16). The jar was placed there later, with Aaron’s staff (Hebrews 9:4).

The hidden manna. The risen Christ promises, “To the one who conquers I will give some of the hidden manna” (Revelation 2:17): he himself will feed his people for ever.

In everyday life. Keep reminders of God’s past provision. They strengthen faith for the future.

verseByVerse.quote: The people of Israel ate the manna forty years, till they came to a habitable land. They ate the manna till they came to the border of the land of Canaan. (An omer is the tenth part of an ephah.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
God fed his people every morning for forty years, through every rebellion, until they reached the land, teaching them to live by his word.

Forty years. Every morning, through every rebellion, God fed them (Deuteronomy 8:3–4). An omer is a tenth of an ephah. The narrator adds the conversion probably because the omer was no longer a familiar measure to later readers.

Not by bread alone. The lesson is that “man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 8:3).

Those who ate manna died. Jesus said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). Those who ate manna died; whoever eats the living bread from heaven will live for ever (John 6:49–51). Thank God for daily bread, and for the Bread of Life.
verseByVerse.note: An ephah was about 3/5 bushel (ESV note).

16.theology:
The grumbling heart and patient grace. The redeemed forget grace and look back fondly on slavery, yet God answers grumbling with merciful provision.

Daily dependence. The manna teaches trust for each day, contentment and Sabbath rest.

Christ the bread of life. The manna is fulfilled in Jesus, the living bread from heaven who alone satisfies the soul's hunger for ever.
16.examples:
Then: When the redeemed grumbled and longed for Egypt's bread, God fed them daily for forty years.

Now: We still crave the security of our old slaveries and forget past mercies. God still calls us to daily dependence, and offers us himself, the true bread from heaven. Feeding on Christ by faith, we shall never hunger.

keyVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Behold, I am about to rain bread from heaven for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law or not.
keyVerse.note: God answers grumbling with bread from heaven, but the bread is also a school. Given one day at a time, it tests and trains his people to trust his word for tomorrow. Jesus taught us to pray for daily bread, and called himself the true bread from heaven (John 6:32–35).

16.reflection:
Only a month after the exodus, the people remember Egypt as a place of full meat pots (v. 3). Why do we romanticise the past when the present is hard? What “Egypt” are you tempted to look back on fondly?

God gave enough manna for each day, and what was hoarded rotted (vv. 16–20). How does this shape the way you think about money, saving, anxiety and trust? Where is the line between wise planning and fearful grasping?

God gave Israel the Sabbath as a gift before he gave it as a commandment (vv. 23–30). How can you receive the Lord’s Day as a gift rather than a burden or just another day?

Jesus said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). What does it mean in daily life to feed on Christ, and what other “bread” do you look to for satisfaction?

17.title: The Rock and the Uplifted Hands
17.text: <sup>1</sup>All the congregation of the people of Israel moved on from the wilderness of Sin by stages, according to the commandment of the LORD, and camped at Rephidim, but there was no water for the people to drink.<sup>2</sup>Therefore the people quarreled with Moses and said, "Give us water to drink." And Moses said to them, "Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test the LORD?"<sup>3</sup>But the people thirsted there for water, and the people grumbled against Moses and said, "Why did you bring us up out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and our livestock with thirst?"<sup>4</sup>So Moses cried to the LORD, "What shall I do with this people? They are almost ready to stone me."<sup>5</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Pass on before the people, taking with you some of the elders of Israel, and take in your hand the staff with which you struck the Nile, and go.<sup>6</sup>Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it, and the people will drink." And Moses did so, in the sight of the elders of Israel.<sup>7</sup>And he called the name of the place Massah and Meribah, because of the quarreling of the people of Israel, and because they tested the LORD by saying, "Is the LORD among us or not?"<sup>8</sup>Then Amalek came and fought with Israel at Rephidim.<sup>9</sup>So Moses said to Joshua, "Choose for us men, and go out and fight with Amalek. Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand."<sup>10</sup>So Joshua did as Moses told him, and fought with Amalek, while Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill.<sup>11</sup>Whenever Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed, and whenever he lowered his hand, Amalek prevailed.<sup>12</sup>But Moses' hands grew weary, so they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it, while Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on one side, and the other on the other side. So his hands were steady until the going down of the sun.<sup>13</sup>And Joshua overwhelmed Amalek and his people with the sword.<sup>14</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Write this as a memorial in a book and recite it in the ears of Joshua, that I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven."<sup>15</sup>And Moses built an altar and called the name of it, The LORD Is My Banner,<sup>16</sup>saying, "A hand upon the throne of the LORD! The LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation."
17.overview:
Where we are. Israel has crossed the sea, sung God’s victory, and been fed with manna in the wilderness of Sin (chapter 16). Now, moving towards Sinai, they meet two new trials at Rephidim: thirst, and an enemy army.

The message. The LORD is among his people, even when they doubt it and even when they deserve nothing but judgment. He gives water to people who were ready to stone his servant, and he wins their battle while they depend on him. Whether the trial is inside the camp or outside it, life and victory come from God, not from Israel.

Why it was said. Israel would remember this place by its names, Massah and Meribah, “testing” and “quarreling”, and later generations were warned not to repeat it (Psalm 95:8). They would also face Amalek again, and needed to know that the war was the LORD’s (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. At Rephidim there is no water, and the people accuse Moses and test the LORD (vv. 1–4). God stands on the rock at Horeb, Moses strikes it with the staff of judgment, and water flows for the guilty (vv. 5–7). Then Amalek attacks; Joshua fights in the valley while Moses holds up the staff on the hill, and when his hands grow weary Aaron and Hur hold them up until sunset (vv. 8–13). God has the victory written down, and Moses builds an altar called “The LORD Is My Banner” (vv. 14–16).

Where it leads. By pattern, and Paul names it: “the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). The judgment that should have fallen on a quarrelling people fell on the rock where God stood, and life flowed out; so Christ was struck for us, and from him flows the living water of the Spirit (John 7:37–39). The battle won by uplifted hands points, more faintly, to the Mediator who never grows weary, who “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

For us. When you are tempted to ask, “Is the LORD among us or not?”, look to the struck Rock: God has already answered that question at the cross. And in the long battles of the Christian life, pray, and hold up one another’s hands.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-7 — Water from the Struck Rock
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A quarrelling people is answered with water from a rock that God himself stands upon. At Rephidim there is no water, and the people do more than grumble: they bring a charge against Moses, test the LORD and are nearly ready to stone his servant (vv. 1–4). Moses cries to God, and God sends him ahead with the elders and the staff that struck the Nile. The LORD stands on the rock at Horeb, Moses strikes it, and water pours out for the people who had accused him (vv. 5–7). The place is named for their sin, Massah and Meribah, but the story is about God’s grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Water from the Struck Rock

A quarrelling people is answered with water, not with judgment.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the place was named for the people's testing, not for God's gift. Now: more proof rarely settles the question “Is the LORD among us or not?”

verseByVerse.quote: All the congregation of the people of Israel moved on from the wilderness of Sin by stages, according to the commandment of the LORD, and camped at Rephidim, but there was no water for the people to drink. Therefore the people quarreled with Moses and said, "Give us water to drink." And Moses said to them, "Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test the LORD?" But the people thirsted there for water, and the people grumbled against Moses and said, "Why did you bring us up out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and our livestock with thirst?" So Moses cried to the LORD, "What shall I do with this people? They are almost ready to stone me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people accuse Moses and test the LORD, and Moses takes the crisis to God.

Camped at Rephidim. God himself led them to a place without water. Rephidim lay near Sinai; its site is uncertain.

Quarreled is Hebrew riv, to bring a legal complaint, to accuse: this is worse than the grumbling of 15:24.

Why do you test the LORD? To test the LORD is to demand that he prove himself on our terms, doubting his presence and goodness (v. 7). Jesus refused to do it (Matthew 4:7).

Asking is not testing. Asking God for help is not testing him. The people did not ask; they accused. When you are desperate, pray as Moses did: “What shall I do?”

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Pass on before the people, taking with you some of the elders of Israel, and take in your hand the staff with which you struck the Nile, and go. Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it, and the people will drink." And Moses did so, in the sight of the elders of Israel. And he called the name of the place Massah and Meribah, because of the quarreling of the people of Israel, and because they tested the LORD by saying, "Is the LORD among us or not?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God stands on the rock, Moses strikes it, and water flows for the people who accused him.

Taking with you some of the elders of Israel. The elders come as witnesses, as in a court case, and the staff is the one that struck the Nile, the rod of judgment.

I will stand before you there on the rock. God places himself on the rock, and then Moses strikes it. The blow of judgment falls where God stands, and life flows to the guilty quarrellers.

Is the LORD among us or not? This is the real question behind the complaint: doubt of God’s presence. The place is named for it, Massah and Meribah, and Psalm 95:8 warns, “do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah”.

And the Rock was Christ. Paul says Israel “drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). Christ was struck for us, and from him flows the Spirit, living water (John 7:37–39).

Struck only once. Later, told to speak to a rock, Moses struck it in anger and was barred from Canaan (Numbers 20:8–12). The rock needed striking only once, as Christ was offered once (Hebrews 9:28).
verseByVerse.note: Massah means “testing” and Meribah “quarreling” (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-13 — The Uplifted Hands and the Battle with Amalek
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel wins its first battle while its leader’s hands are lifted up to God, and loses ground whenever they fall. Amalek attacks at Rephidim, and Moses sends Joshua to fight while he stands on the hill with the staff of God (vv. 8–10). The battle sways with Moses’ hands (v. 11). When he tires, Aaron and Hur seat him on a stone and hold up his hands until sunset, and Joshua overwhelms Amalek (vv. 12–13). The victory is God’s, given in answer to dependence, and even the leader’s dependence needs the help of others.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Uplifted Hands and the Battle with Amalek

Victory is God's, and the hands lifted to him need others to hold them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Joshua fought, Moses prayed, and Aaron and Hur held him up. Now: the work goes on because someone holds up the arms of the one who cannot, and Christ always lives to intercede (Heb. 7:25).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Amalek came and fought with Israel at Rephidim. So Moses said to Joshua, "Choose for us men, and go out and fight with Amalek. Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand." So Joshua did as Moses told him, and fought with Amalek, while Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill. Whenever Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed, and whenever he lowered his hand, Amalek prevailed. But Moses' hands grew weary, so they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it, while Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on one side, and the other on the other side. So his hands were steady until the going down of the sun. And Joshua overwhelmed Amalek and his people with the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel defeats Amalek while Moses’ hands are lifted to God, and Aaron and Hur hold them up when he grows weary.

Amalek was a desert people descended from Esau (Genesis 36:12) who attacked the weak stragglers at the rear (Deuteronomy 25:17–18).

Joshua, named here for the first time, will lead Israel into the land. His name means “the LORD saves”; in Greek it is Jesus.

The staff of God in my hand. The staff is a sign of dependence on God’s power, perhaps raised in prayer: the battle below is decided by dependence above.

Aaron and Hur held up his hands. When Moses’ hands grew weary, the leader needed others. Hur was a leader of the people (24:14), in Jewish tradition Miriam’s husband.

The intercessor who does not tire. Moses’ hands grew heavy; Christ’s do not, for he “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

What it does not mean. Raised hands do not work like magic. Victory comes from God, and the picture is of dependent prayer, which needs support. Hold up the hands of your pastor and leaders in prayer and practical help.
verseByVerse.note: Amalek descended from Esau. This is the first mention of Joshua.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14-16 — The LORD Is My Banner
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God makes the victory a lasting memorial, and Moses names the altar for the LORD himself. The LORD tells Moses to write the event in a book and to make sure Joshua hears it: Amalek’s memory will be blotted out (v. 14). Moses builds an altar and calls it “The LORD Is My Banner”, for the LORD is the standard Israel rallies to (v. 15). The war with Amalek is the LORD’s own war, from generation to generation (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology:
The LORD Is My Banner

God himself is Israel's rallying point.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the victory is written down and an altar built, so that it will not be forgotten. Now: God’s people rally to a banner the enemy cannot touch.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Write this as a memorial in a book and recite it in the ears of Joshua, that I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven." And Moses built an altar and called the name of it, The LORD Is My Banner, saying, "A hand upon the throne of the LORD! The LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has the victory written down and promises to blot out Amalek, and Moses names the altar for the LORD who fights for Israel.

Write this … in a book. The first command in the Bible to write something down. It is to be recited “in the ears of Joshua”, because he will lead Israel into the land, where the war with Amalek will go on (Deuteronomy 25:17–19).

Blot out the memory of Amalek. God will judge Amalek completely (1 Samuel 15:2–3).

The LORD Is My Banner. A banner was the standard raised in battle to rally troops. Israel’s standard is not Moses’ staff but the LORD himself.

Christ our banner. Rally to Christ, lifted up for us (John 12:32).

Where Christians differ: why perpetual war with Amalek? Some see harsh ethnic hostility. This commentary’s view: Amalek attacked a nation of fleeing slaves from behind, killing the weak, and set itself against God. The judgment is on a persistent enemy of God’s purpose, not on ethnicity, and it gives Christians no licence for violence: our battle is not against flesh and blood (Ephesians 6:12).

Uncertain wording. “A hand upon the throne of the LORD!” (v. 16) is obscure. It may be a hand raised to God’s throne in an oath, or Amalek’s hand raised against it. The word for “throne” (kes) is an unusual short form found only here, and some suggest reading the similar nes, “banner”, echoing v. 15. Either way, the war against Amalek is God’s cause.

17.theology:
Christ the struck Rock. Christ was struck by God's judgment that living water might flow to thirsting sinners.

The ministry of intercession. Moses’ uplifted hands point to Christ, who always lives to pray for us, and to the church’s call to keep praying.

The LORD our Banner. The battle and the victory are God's, and the triumph is credited to him alone.
17.examples:
Then: God gave water to a doubting people and victory to a weary one.

Now: Christ our Rock was struck that the living water of the Spirit might flow to us; he ever lives, with hands once outstretched on the cross, to intercede for us. And the church wins its battles under the LORD's banner, holding up one another in prayer.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it, and the people will drink.
keyVerse.note: God answers a people who were testing him not with judgment but with water, and he does it by standing on the very rock that is struck. Paul reads the scene as a pattern of Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4), struck in our place so that life might flow to the undeserving.

17.reflection:
The people asked, “Is the LORD among us or not?” (v. 7). When are you most tempted to ask that question, and what is the difference between bringing a need to God and putting him on trial?

God stood on the rock that Moses struck (v. 6). How does Paul’s statement that “the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4) help you understand what happened at the cross?

Moses could not keep his hands up alone (v. 12). Who are the Aarons and Hurs in your life, and whose hands could you help to hold up this week?

Moses called the altar “The LORD Is My Banner” (v. 15). What would it look like to fight your present battles under that banner rather than in your own strength?

18.title: Wise Counsel and Shared Burdens
18.text: <sup>1</sup>Jethro, the priest of Midian, Moses' father-in-law, heard of all that God had done for Moses and for Israel his people, how the LORD had brought Israel out of Egypt.<sup>2</sup>Now Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, had taken Zipporah, Moses' wife, after he had sent her home,<sup>3</sup>along with her two sons. The name of the one was Gershom (for he said, "I have been a sojourner in a foreign land"),<sup>4</sup>and the name of the other, Eliezer (for he said, "The God of my father was my help, and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh").<sup>5</sup>Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, came with his sons and his wife to Moses in the wilderness where he was encamped at the mountain of God.<sup>6</sup>And when he sent word to Moses, "I, your father-in-law Jethro, am coming to you with your wife and her two sons with her,"<sup>7</sup>Moses went out to meet his father-in-law and bowed down and kissed him. And they asked each other of their welfare and went into the tent.<sup>8</sup>Then Moses told his father-in-law all that the LORD had done to Pharaoh and to the Egyptians for Israel's sake, all the hardship that had come upon them in the way, and how the LORD had delivered them.<sup>9</sup>And Jethro rejoiced for all the good that the LORD had done to Israel, in that he had delivered them out of the hand of the Egyptians.<sup>10</sup>Jethro said, "Blessed be the LORD, who has delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians and out of the hand of Pharaoh and has delivered the people from under the hand of the Egyptians.<sup>11</sup>Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods, because in this affair they dealt arrogantly with the people."<sup>12</sup>And Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, brought a burnt offering and sacrifices to God; and Aaron came with all the elders of Israel to eat bread with Moses' father-in-law before God.<sup>13</sup>The next day Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood around Moses from morning till evening.<sup>14</sup>When Moses' father-in-law saw all that he was doing for the people, he said, "What is this that you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone, and all the people stand around you from morning till evening?"<sup>15</sup>And Moses said to his father-in-law, "Because the people come to me to inquire of God;<sup>16</sup>when they have a dispute, they come to me and I decide between one person and another, and I make them know the statutes of God and his laws."<sup>17</sup>Moses' father-in-law said to him, "What you are doing is not good.<sup>18</sup>You and the people with you will certainly wear yourselves out, for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to do it alone.<sup>19</sup>Now obey my voice; I will give you advice, and God be with you! You shall represent the people before God and bring their cases to God,<sup>20</sup>and you shall warn them about the statutes and the laws, and make them know the way in which they must walk and what they must do.<sup>21</sup>Moreover, look for able men from all the people, men who fear God, who are trustworthy and hate a bribe, and place such men over the people as chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens.<sup>22</sup>And let them judge the people at all times. Every great matter they shall bring to you, but any small matter they shall decide themselves. So it will be easier for you, and they will bear the burden with you.<sup>23</sup>If you do this, God will direct you, you will be able to endure, and all this people also will go to their place in peace."<sup>24</sup>So Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law and did all that he had said.<sup>25</sup>Moses chose able men out of all Israel and made them heads over the people, chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens.<sup>26</sup>And they judged the people at all times. Any hard case they brought to Moses, but any small matter they decided themselves.<sup>27</sup>Then Moses let his father-in-law depart, and he went away to his own country.
18.overview:
Where we are. The first part of Exodus, the story of rescue, is closing. Israel has been brought out of Egypt, fed, given water from the rock and defended against Amalek (chapters 14–17); next they will stand at Sinai to receive the covenant (chapter 19).

The message. What God has done for his people is meant to be told, and when it is told, outsiders come to worship him. And the people God has rescued are to be cared for by many faithful hands, not crushed under one man’s devotion: Moses is not the saviour of Israel; the LORD is.

Why it was said. Israel was about to become an organised nation under God’s law, and needed to see that its judges must be godly and honest, and that its great leader was a man who could be helped and corrected. Straight after a Gentile nation, Amalek, attacked them, they also see a Gentile who blesses their God (see the introduction).
