How the chapter makes its case. Jethro, priest of Midian, brings Moses’ wife and sons to the mountain of God (vv. 1–6). Moses tells him everything the LORD has done; Jethro rejoices, confesses that “the LORD is greater than all gods”, offers sacrifice and eats before God with Israel’s elders (vv. 7–12). The next day he watches Moses judging the people alone from morning till evening and says plainly, “What you are doing is not good” (vv. 13–18). He counsels Moses to keep his work before God and in teaching, and to appoint able, God-fearing, honest men to judge the rest (vv. 19–23). Moses listens, does it, and lets Jethro go home (vv. 24–27).

Where it leads. By promise and by the need it exposes. A Gentile priest confessing the LORD and eating at Israel’s table is an early fruit of the promise that in Abraham all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3), fulfilled when the nations come to Christ. And Moses cannot carry the people alone. Only one Mediator has ever borne his people’s whole weight, and he did it at the cross, where no one could share the load with him.

For us. Tell people what God has done for you; testimony is one of the ways he brings outsiders to worship. And if you are carrying everything yourself, hear Jethro’s words: the post of saviour is already taken, so share the load, and receive wise counsel humbly.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A foreign priest hears what God has done and comes to worship the LORD. Jethro, Moses’ Midianite father-in-law, brings Zipporah and her two sons to the camp at the mountain of God (vv. 1–6). Moses greets him and tells him the whole story, the LORD’s victory over Pharaoh and the hardships on the way (vv. 7–8). Jethro rejoices, blesses the LORD and confesses that he is greater than all gods (vv. 9–11). Then he offers sacrifice, and Aaron and the elders eat bread with him before God (v. 12). Testimony has turned an outsider into a worshipper at Israel’s table.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jethro's Worship

A foreign priest hears testimony and believes.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the Egyptians saw and would not acknowledge the LORD; a foreign priest heard and believed. Now: a testimony with the hard parts left in is more convincing, not less.

verseByVerse.quote: Jethro, the priest of Midian, Moses' father-in-law, heard of all that God had done for Moses and for Israel his people, how the LORD had brought Israel out of Egypt. Now Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, had taken Zipporah, Moses' wife, after he had sent her home, along with her two sons. The name of the one was Gershom (for he said, "I have been a sojourner in a foreign land"), and the name of the other, Eliezer (for he said, "The God of my father was my help, and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh"). Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, came with his sons and his wife to Moses in the wilderness where he was encamped at the mountain of God. And when he sent word to Moses, "I, your father-in-law Jethro, am coming to you with your wife and her two sons with her,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hearing what God has done for Israel, Jethro brings Moses’ wife and sons to him at the mountain of God.

After he had sent her home. At some point Moses had sent Zipporah and the boys back, perhaps for safety during the plagues. Now Jethro, having heard of the exodus, brings them to him.

Two sons’ names. The names of Gershom and Eliezer tell Moses’ story. Gershom sounds like the Hebrew for “a sojourner there” (2:22); Eliezer means “My God is help”, remembering his escape from Pharaoh’s sword.

Where he was encamped. The mountain of God is Horeb (Sinai). Israel only reaches Sinai in 19:1–2, and Moses later places the appointing of judges near the departure from Horeb (Deuteronomy 1:9–15), so this visit is probably told here by theme rather than strict order: straight after Amalek, a Gentile people who attacked Israel, comes a Gentile priest who blesses Israel’s God.
verseByVerse.note: Eliezer means “My God is help” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Moses went out to meet his father-in-law and bowed down and kissed him. And they asked each other of their welfare and went into the tent. Then Moses told his father-in-law all that the LORD had done to Pharaoh and to the Egyptians for Israel's sake, all the hardship that had come upon them in the way, and how the LORD had delivered them. And Jethro rejoiced for all the good that the LORD had done to Israel, in that he had delivered them out of the hand of the Egyptians. Jethro said, "Blessed be the LORD, who has delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians and out of the hand of Pharaoh and has delivered the people from under the hand of the Egyptians. Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods, because in this affair they dealt arrogantly with the people." And Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, brought a burnt offering and sacrifices to God; and Aaron came with all the elders of Israel to eat bread with Moses' father-in-law before God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses tells Jethro all that the LORD has done, and Jethro confesses the LORD, offers sacrifice and eats before God with Israel’s elders.

Moses told his father-in-law the whole story, the deliverance and the hardships along the way. He does not tell only the victories.

Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods. A pagan priest comes to know the LORD through testimony. Like Rahab, Ruth and the Magi, an outsider sees what many insiders miss.

Aaron came with all the elders of Israel. To eat bread before God is to share a covenant meal of fellowship with Israel’s leaders. A Gentile sits at Israel’s table in God’s presence, a foretaste of the nations gathered to Christ (Genesis 12:3).

What it does not mean. This does not mean all religions honour the same God: Jethro turns from other gods to confess the LORD. Tell people what God has done for you; testimony can bring others to worship.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses keeps representing the people before God, but shares the work of judging with godly men. Jethro sees Moses sitting alone from morning till evening while the people stand waiting, and Moses explains that they come to inquire of God (vv. 13–16). Jethro’s verdict is blunt: “What you are doing is not good”, for Moses and the people will wear themselves out (vv. 17–18). His counsel is to keep Moses’ unique role of bringing cases to God and teaching his statutes (vv. 19–20), and to appoint able, God-fearing, trustworthy men who hate a bribe as judges at every level (vv. 21–22). All this is offered under God’s command (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology:
Jethro's Counsel

Moses keeps representing the people before God and teaching them, and shares the judging.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the pattern returns in the seventy elders and the seven of Acts 6. Now: the work is real, the servant has limits, and the answer is sharing, not heroics.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood around Moses from morning till evening. When Moses' father-in-law saw all that he was doing for the people, he said, "What is this that you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone, and all the people stand around you from morning till evening?" And Moses said to his father-in-law, "Because the people come to me to inquire of God; when they have a dispute, they come to me and I decide between one person and another, and I make them know the statutes of God and his laws." Moses' father-in-law said to him, "What you are doing is not good. You and the people with you will certainly wear yourselves out, for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to do it alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses judges the people alone from morning to evening, and Jethro tells him it is not good: the load will wear out leader and people alike.

Moses sat to judge the people. Moses settles disputes and teaches God’s will, as the people come to inquire of God, bringing their cases for God’s decision through him.

Not good. These are the words of Genesis 2:18: being alone is not good.

Wear yourselves out is literally “wither”, like a fading leaf; both the leader and the people waiting suffer. Moses’ motives were not wrong, but sincere devotion can still be unwise. Leaders, parents and carers: doing everything yourself can harm the people you serve.

The leader who cannot stop being needed. There is a quiet idol in this scene, and it is not laziness but indispensability. Moses sits from morning till evening, and it is easy to admire him; many pastors, parents, managers and carers will recognise themselves. Being needed feels like love, and it pays in a currency the heart craves: significance. Our culture rewards it, too; we wear exhaustion like a medal. But Jethro sees what Moses cannot: “You are not able to do it alone” (v. 18), and the people are suffering for it. A saviour complex looks like self-sacrifice and is often a hunger to be the one who holds everything together. The gospel loosens its grip by reminding us that the post of saviour is taken. Moses could share the load because he was not the deliverer; the LORD was. And the one who truly carried his people’s weight, “Surely he has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows” (Isaiah 53:4), frees us to put down the burdens that were never ours. Only someone who knows he is not the Messiah can delegate in peace.

verseByVerse.quote: Now obey my voice; I will give you advice, and God be with you! You shall represent the people before God and bring their cases to God, and you shall warn them about the statutes and the laws, and make them know the way in which they must walk and what they must do. Moreover, look for able men from all the people, men who fear God, who are trustworthy and hate a bribe, and place such men over the people as chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens. And let them judge the people at all times. Every great matter they shall bring to you, but any small matter they shall decide themselves. So it will be easier for you, and they will bear the burden with you. If you do this, God will direct you, you will be able to endure, and all this people also will go to their place in peace."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses should keep his unique work before God and in teaching, and share the judging with able, God-fearing, honest men.

You shall represent the people before God. Moses keeps his unique role: to bring the people’s cases to God and to teach his statutes, the way they must walk.

Able men who fear God, trustworthy, who hate a bribe. The four qualifications are competence, godliness, honesty and integrity about money: character comes before structure. On leadership as God’s gift in every sphere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

Advice under God. “God will direct you” (v. 23) can also be rendered “and God so commands you”: Jethro offers his plan only if God approves it.

Where Christians differ: a model for church government? Some see here a pattern for elders and deacons. This commentary’s view: it shows the wisdom of shared leadership by qualified, godly people, which the New Testament also teaches (Acts 6:1–6; 1 Timothy 3), but it is not a blueprint for every church.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The man who spoke with God takes counsel from his father-in-law and puts it into practice. Moses does all that Jethro said, choosing able men from all Israel and setting them over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens (vv. 24–25). Hard cases come to Moses; the judges settle the small matters themselves (v. 26). Then Jethro goes home to his own country (v. 27). The chapter closes on a humble leader and a people better served.
verseByVerse.theology:
Moses Listens

The man who spoke with God takes counsel from an outsider.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the meekest man on earth (Num. 12:3) took correction from a newcomer. Now: not everyone who helps God's people is called to stay, and a brief contribution is not a small one.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law and did all that he had said. Moses chose able men out of all Israel and made them heads over the people, chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens. And they judged the people at all times. Any hard case they brought to Moses, but any small matter they decided themselves. Then Moses let his father-in-law depart, and he went away to his own country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses humbly takes the advice and appoints judges, and Jethro goes home.

Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law. The man who spoke with God from the bush humbly takes advice from an outsider. The hard cases came to Moses; the others were settled by the judges.

In everyday life. Not every piece of advice must be accepted; Moses tested this against God’s will (v. 23). Be willing to receive wise counsel, even from unexpected people (Proverbs 15:22).

18.theology:
The nations drawn to worship. Jethro the Gentile confesses the LORD’s supremacy, an early sign of God’s purpose to be known among all peoples.

Shared leadership and delegation. Ministry is a shared calling: wise leaders share the load with godly, qualified people rather than carrying it alone.

Character before competence. The qualifications for leadership are chiefly spiritual, as for elders in the New Testament.
18.examples:
Then: A Gentile priest worshipped the God of the exodus, then gave Moses wise counsel, and the humble leader listened.

Now: Our salvation testifies to the watching world and draws others to worship. And the work of ministry is shared: God raises up qualified, godly leaders to carry the load together.

keyVerse.quote: Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods, because in this affair they dealt arrogantly with the people.
keyVerse.note: A Midianite priest, hearing what the LORD has done, confesses him as greater than all gods. The rescue of Israel was always meant to make God known among the nations, and Jethro is its first fruit, a glimpse of the Gentiles who would one day come to worship through Christ.

18.reflection:
Jethro came to know the LORD through hearing what he had done (vv. 8–11). What has God done in your life that you could tell someone this week, and why does honest testimony include the hardships as well as the rescues?

Jethro said, “What you are doing is not good” (v. 17). Where are you carrying a load you were never meant to carry alone, and what makes it hard to share?

The judges had to be able, God-fearing, trustworthy and free from bribery (v. 21). Why does character come before skill in those who lead, and how should that shape the way we choose leaders in church?

Moses, who had spoken with God, listened to his father-in-law (v. 24). What helps you receive correction humbly, and how do you test advice against God’s word?

19.title: The Mountain That Burned with Fire
19.text: <sup>1</sup>On the third new moon after the people of Israel had gone out of the land of Egypt, on that day they came into the wilderness of Sinai.<sup>2</sup>They set out from Rephidim and came into the wilderness of Sinai, and they encamped in the wilderness. There Israel encamped before the mountain,<sup>3</sup>while Moses went up to God. The LORD called to him out of the mountain, saying, "Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob, and tell the people of Israel:<sup>4</sup>'You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself.<sup>5</sup>Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples, for all the earth is mine;<sup>6</sup>and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.' These are the words that you shall speak to the people of Israel."<sup>7</sup>So Moses came and called the elders of the people and set before them all these words that the LORD had commanded him.<sup>8</sup>All the people answered together and said, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do." And Moses reported the words of the people to the LORD.<sup>9</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, I am coming to you in a thick cloud, that the people may hear when I speak with you, and may also believe you forever." When Moses told the words of the people to the LORD,<sup>10</sup>the LORD said to Moses, "Go to the people and consecrate them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments<sup>11</sup>and be ready for the third day. For on the third day the LORD will come down on Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people.<sup>12</sup>And you shall set limits for the people all around, saying, 'Take care not to go up into the mountain or touch the edge of it. Whoever touches the mountain shall be put to death.<sup>13</sup>No hand shall touch him, but he shall be stoned or shot; whether beast or man, he shall not live.' When the trumpet sounds a long blast, they shall come up to the mountain."<sup>14</sup>So Moses went down from the mountain to the people and consecrated the people; and they washed their garments.<sup>15</sup>And he said to the people, "Be ready for the third day; do not go near a woman."<sup>16</sup>On the morning of the third day there were thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud on the mountain and a very loud trumpet blast, so that all the people in the camp trembled.<sup>17</sup>Then Moses brought the people out of the camp to meet God, and they took their stand at the foot of the mountain.<sup>18</sup>Now Mount Sinai was wrapped in smoke because the LORD had descended on it in fire. The smoke of it went up like the smoke of a kiln, and the whole mountain trembled greatly.<sup>19</sup>And as the sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder, Moses spoke, and God answered him in thunder.<sup>20</sup>The LORD came down on Mount Sinai, to the top of the mountain. And the LORD called Moses to the top of the mountain, and Moses went up.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Go down and warn the people, lest they break through to the LORD to look and many of them perish.<sup>22</sup>Also let the priests who come near to the LORD consecrate themselves, lest the LORD break out against them."<sup>23</sup>And Moses said to the LORD, "The people cannot come up to Mount Sinai, for you yourself warned us, saying, 'Set limits around the mountain and consecrate it.'"<sup>24</sup>And the LORD said to him, "Go down, and come up bringing Aaron with you. But do not let the priests and the people break through to come up to the LORD, lest he break out against them."<sup>25</sup>So Moses went down to the people and told them.
19.overview:
Where we are. About two months after leaving Egypt, Israel reaches Sinai, the mountain where God first spoke to Moses from the bush (3:12). The story of rescue (chapters 1–18) now becomes the story of covenant (chapters 19–24), and Israel will stay here nearly a year.

The message. God saves his people first and then binds them to himself. Before any command he says, “I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself”, and he offers them a calling: to be his treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. But the God who draws them near is holy, and sinners cannot approach him casually. Grace and holiness meet at Sinai.

Why it was said. Israel needed to know why they had been rescued: not only to escape Egypt but to belong to God and to show him to the nations. Every later generation, tempted either to treat God lightly or to think he must be earned, needed this mountain (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Israel camps before the mountain, and God reminds them of what he has done (vv. 1–4), then sets out the covenant and its purpose (vv. 5–6). The people promise, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do”, and God promises to come in a thick cloud (vv. 7–9). Three days of consecration follow, with washed garments and a boundary around the mountain (vv. 10–15). On the third day the LORD descends in fire, smoke, thunder and a growing trumpet blast, and the whole mountain trembles (vv. 16–20). God warns again that no one may break through to gaze (vv. 21–25).

Where it leads. By covenant and by the need it exposes. Israel was called to be a kingdom of priests, and Peter gives that calling to all who belong to Christ (1 Peter 2:9). But the boundary round Sinai shows that sinners cannot come near a holy God on their own. Hebrews sets the two mountains side by side: we have not come to a burning mountain that no one may touch, but “to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant” (Hebrews 12:18–24), whose blood opens the way.

For us. We obey God because he has already carried us to himself, not to earn his love. Come to him with confidence through Christ, and with reverence too, for he is still holy, and you are his treasured possession, set apart to make him known.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The covenant is offered to a people God has already rescued. Israel arrives at the wilderness of Sinai and camps before the mountain, and Moses goes up to God (vv. 1–3). God’s first words are a reminder of grace: he defeated Egypt and bore Israel on eagles’ wings to himself (v. 4). Only then comes the offer: if they obey his voice and keep his covenant, they will be his treasured possession among all peoples, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation (vv. 5–6). The order is the message: redemption first, then the life of the redeemed.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Kingdom of Priests

The covenant is offered to a people already carried to God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: eighteen chapters of grace come before one commandment. Now: the church too is first saved and then given its task.

verseByVerse.quote: On the third new moon after the people of Israel had gone out of the land of Egypt, on that day they came into the wilderness of Sinai. They set out from Rephidim and came into the wilderness of Sinai, and they encamped in the wilderness. There Israel encamped before the mountain, while Moses went up to God. The LORD called to him out of the mountain, saying, "Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob, and tell the people of Israel: 'You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Sinai, before he gives a single command, God reminds Israel that he has rescued them and carried them to himself.

They came into the wilderness of Sinai. Israel camps before the mountain where the bush burned, and the promise of 3:12 is fulfilled: “you shall serve God on this mountain.” Moses goes up to God.

Eagles’ wings picture strong, protective care, carrying the young (Deuteronomy 32:11). God has brought you to myself: the goal of the exodus is not only a place but God himself.

Grace before law. God reminds them of what he has done before he gives any command. The law is given to a redeemed people, not as a way to be redeemed (20:2).
verseByVerse.note: Israel reached Sinai about two months after leaving Egypt and stayed nearly a year.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples, for all the earth is mine; and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.' These are the words that you shall speak to the people of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God offers Israel his covenant: if they keep it, they will be his own treasure, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.

Obedience within grace. To obey my voice and keep my covenant is to live as God’s people. Obedience does not earn God’s choice of them, for he has already redeemed them (v. 4); it is the way to live in the covenant.

Treasured possession is Hebrew segullah, a king’s personal treasure, kept apart from the general wealth. All the earth is mine: God chooses Israel not because he owns nothing else but for a purpose among the nations.

A kingdom of priests. A priest brings God to people and people to God. Israel was to represent God to the nations as a holy nation, set apart for him and distinct in life and worship.

A royal priesthood, a holy nation. Israel often failed this calling, but Christ, the faithful Israel, fulfils it and shares it. Peter gives these titles to the church: “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession” (1 Peter 2:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7-15 — Consecration for the Holy God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sinners must be made ready before they meet the holy God. Moses sets God’s words before the elders, and the people answer as one, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do” (vv. 7–8). God promises to come in a thick cloud so that the people will hear him speak and trust Moses for ever (v. 9). Then he orders two days of consecration, washed garments and a boundary around the mountain, for whoever touches it must die (vv. 10–13). Moses carries out the instructions, adding that husbands and wives should abstain for those days (vv. 14–15).
verseByVerse.theology:
Consecration for the Holy God

Sinners must be made ready to meet him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the same promise is made twice more and broken at the golden calf. Now: sincerity in the moment of promising is not the same as power to keep it.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses came and called the elders of the people and set before them all these words that the LORD had commanded him. All the people answered together and said, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do." And Moses reported the words of the people to the LORD. And the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, I am coming to you in a thick cloud, that the people may hear when I speak with you, and may also believe you forever." When Moses told the words of the people to the LORD,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people promise to do all that the LORD says, and God promises to come in a cloud so that they will hear him and trust Moses.

All that the LORD has spoken we will do. The promise is sincere, but overconfident. They will say it again (24:3, 7) and make the golden calf within weeks (32:1–6).

That the people may hear. In a thick cloud God reveals himself while veiling his glory, and he confirms Moses as his spokesman so that the people may believe him for ever.

What their promise shows. Their promise was not hypocritical. It shows the weakness of human resolve and our need for a new heart (Jeremiah 31:31–33). Make your promises to God humbly, relying on his grace and his Spirit, not your strength.

verseByVerse.quote: the LORD said to Moses, "Go to the people and consecrate them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments and be ready for the third day. For on the third day the LORD will come down on Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people. And you shall set limits for the people all around, saying, 'Take care not to go up into the mountain or touch the edge of it. Whoever touches the mountain shall be put to death. No hand shall touch him, but he shall be stoned or shot; whether beast or man, he shall not live.' When the trumpet sounds a long blast, they shall come up to the mountain." So Moses went down from the mountain to the people and consecrated the people; and they washed their garments. And he said to the people, "Be ready for the third day; do not go near a woman."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel must spend three days getting ready to meet the holy God, and a boundary keeps everyone from touching the mountain.

Let them wash their garments. To consecrate them is to set them apart, preparing to meet the holy God. Washing their garments is outward cleanness picturing inward readiness.

You shall set limits for the people. A boundary is set around the mountain, and whoever touches it must die: God’s holiness is dangerous to sinners. Even an offender is to be stoned or shot, not seized, because anyone who laid hands on him would have to cross the boundary too.

Do not go near a woman. Husbands and wives abstain from marital relations for the three days of consecration (1 Samuel 21:4–5). This is not because sex is sinful, but because they set aside even good things to prepare to meet God (1 Corinthians 7:5).

In everyday life. Prepare your heart before you come to worship.

Uncertain wording. In v. 13 the “trumpet” is yobel, a ram’s horn (the word behind “Jubilee”). Who “they” are, and how far they may go, is unclear: the whole people coming to the foot of the mountain, or chosen representatives going higher (24:1, 9). The first is likelier, since that is what happens when the trumpet sounds (vv. 16–17).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A theophany is a visible appearing of God, and at Sinai it is terrifying. On the third day thunder, lightning, a thick cloud and a very loud trumpet make the whole camp tremble, and Moses leads the people out to meet God at the foot of the mountain (vv. 16–17). The LORD descends in fire, the mountain smokes like a kiln and quakes, and God answers Moses in thunder (vv. 18–20). Then God sends Moses down to warn the people and the priests not to break through to look, lest he break out against them (vv. 21–25). His nearness is a gift, and a danger.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Theophany

A theophany is a visible appearing of God. He comes down in majesty, and the barrier keeps the people alive.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: no one could touch the mountain and live. Now: believers have come not to Sinai but to Mount Zion and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant (Heb. 12:18-24).

verseByVerse.quote: On the morning of the third day there were thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud on the mountain and a very loud trumpet blast, so that all the people in the camp trembled. Then Moses brought the people out of the camp to meet God, and they took their stand at the foot of the mountain. Now Mount Sinai was wrapped in smoke because the LORD had descended on it in fire. The smoke of it went up like the smoke of a kiln, and the whole mountain trembled greatly. And as the sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder, Moses spoke, and God answered him in thunder. The LORD came down on Mount Sinai, to the top of the mountain. And the LORD called Moses to the top of the mountain, and Moses went up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the third day the LORD comes down on Sinai in fire, cloud and thunder, and the mountain and the people tremble before him.

The whole mountain trembled greatly. Creation shakes at God’s presence (Psalm 68:8), and the trumpet grows louder and louder, though no one is said to blow it.

God answered him in thunder, or “with a voice”: God speaks. He is not unapproachable for ever, for he has come down to make a covenant with them.

Have we made God safe? Modern spirituality prefers a God who is warm, affirming and never alarming. Sinai will not allow it. The mountain smokes, the ground shakes, and whoever touches its edge will die (v. 12). The German scholar Rudolf Otto, in The Idea of the Holy (1917), described the holy as a mystery that makes us tremble and yet draws us in. The American writer Annie Dillard put it more bluntly: given the power we claim to be addressing, we ought to wear crash helmets to church. A God who never unsettles us is usually one we have made in our own image, and such a god can soothe but never rescue. The surprise of the gospel is not that this God became tame but that he came down further than Sinai. The mountain no one could touch became a man whom lepers touched and when the earth shook and the sky went dark at Golgotha, the judgment that holiness brings fell on him, so that we could come near.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Go down and warn the people, lest they break through to the LORD to look and many of them perish. Also let the priests who come near to the LORD consecrate themselves, lest the LORD break out against them." And Moses said to the LORD, "The people cannot come up to Mount Sinai, for you yourself warned us, saying, 'Set limits around the mountain and consecrate it.'" And the LORD said to him, "Go down, and come up bringing Aaron with you. But do not let the priests and the people break through to come up to the LORD, lest he break out against them." So Moses went down to the people and told them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God warns again that no one, not even the priests, may break through to gaze at him, lest he break out against them.

Break through to the LORD to look. This is curiosity that treats holiness lightly. The priests here were perhaps the firstborn or heads of families, who served as priests before the Levites were appointed.

Break out against them. God’s holiness consumes those who approach carelessly (2 Samuel 6:6–7). Moses protests that the boundary is already set, but God sends him down again: the warning must be heard twice.

The barrier opened by his blood. The barrier that kept people out at Sinai is opened by Christ’s blood (Hebrews 12:18–24). Approach God with confidence through Christ, and with reverence and awe, “for our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29).

19.theology:
Grace before law. God redeems first, then gives the covenant. Obedience flows from salvation and never earns it.

A treasured, priestly people. God claims the redeemed as his treasured possession and a kingdom of priests, fulfilled in the church.

The holiness of God. Sinai reveals a holy God whom sinners cannot approach casually, and drives us to Christ, the Mediator.
19.examples:
Then: God established his covenant at a mountain that burned with fire, calling redeemed slaves to be his own people.

Now: We are saved by grace and then called to holy obedience. The terror of Sinai reminds us how holy God is, and how amazing it is that in Christ we now draw near to that same God with boldness and joy.

keyVerse.quote: You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself.
keyVerse.note: Before God gives a single command at Sinai, he reminds Israel of what he has already done. Grace comes before law, and the goal of rescue is not only freedom but God himself: “brought you to myself.”

19.reflection:
God reminded Israel of his rescue before he gave any commands (vv. 4–6). Why does that order matter, and what happens to our obedience when we reverse it?

Israel was called to be “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (v. 6), and Peter gives that calling to the church (1 Peter 2:9). What would it look like for your church to bring God to people and people to God where you live?

The people promised, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do” (v. 8), and soon broke their word. What does that teach us about our own resolutions, and where does real change come from?

Sinai was wrapped in fire and smoke, and no one could touch it (vv. 12, 18). How does Hebrews 12:18–24 help you hold together confidence and reverence when you come to God?

20.title: The Ten Words: Law as Gift
20.text: <sup>1</sup>And God spoke all these words, saying,<sup>2</sup>"I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.<sup>3</sup>"You shall have no other gods before me.<sup>4</sup>"You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth.<sup>5</sup>You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I the LORD your God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me,<sup>6</sup>but showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.<sup>7</sup>"You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain.<sup>8</sup>"Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.<sup>9</sup>Six days you shall labor, and do all your work,<sup>10</sup>but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, you, or your son, or your daughter, your male servant, or your female servant, or your livestock, or the sojourner who is within your gates.<sup>11</sup>For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy.<sup>12</sup>"Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.<sup>13</sup>"You shall not murder.<sup>14</sup>"You shall not commit adultery.<sup>15</sup>"You shall not steal.<sup>16</sup>"You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.<sup>17</sup>"You shall not covet your neighbor's house; you shall not covet your neighbor's wife, or his male servant, or his female servant, or his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor's."<sup>18</sup>Now when all the people saw the thunder and the flashes of lightning and the sound of the trumpet and the mountain smoking, the people were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off<sup>19</sup>and said to Moses, "You speak to us, and we will listen; but do not let God speak to us, lest we die."<sup>20</sup>Moses said to the people, "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin."<sup>21</sup>The people stood far off, while Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was.<sup>22</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Thus you shall say to the people of Israel: 'You have seen for yourselves that I have talked with you from heaven.<sup>23</sup>You shall not make gods of silver to be with me, nor shall you make for yourselves gods of gold.<sup>24</sup>An altar of earth you shall make for me and sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, your sheep and your oxen. In every place where I cause my name to be remembered I will come to you and bless you.<sup>25</sup>If you make me an altar of stone, you shall not build it of hewn stones, for if you wield your tool on it you profane it.<sup>26</sup>And you shall not go up by steps to my altar, that your nakedness be not exposed on it.'
20.overview:
Where we are. Israel stands trembling at the foot of Sinai, wrapped in smoke and fire (chapter 19). Now God himself speaks, and the words he speaks are the heart of the covenant, the Ten Commandments, which the rest of the law (chapters 21–23) will apply to daily life.

The message. The God who has already rescued his people tells them how a rescued people lives: with him alone as God, worshipped as he has revealed himself, and with love for neighbour in family, life, marriage, property, speech and heart. The commandments are not a ladder by which slaves climb to freedom but the shape of freedom for those already set free. And because no one keeps them perfectly, the chapter ends with sinners standing far off, a mediator drawing near, and an altar where sin is atoned for.

Why it was said. Israel had just left a land of many gods and of forced labour. They needed to know who their God was and what life under him would look like, so different from Pharaoh’s rule (see the introduction). Every generation after them needed the same law to show them their sin and the way of love.

How the chapter makes its case. God names himself first as Redeemer: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out” (vv. 1–2). Then come the commandments about him: no other gods, no images, no empty use of his name, and the Sabbath rest (vv. 3–11). Then the commandments about neighbour, from honour for parents to the tenth, which reaches the heart (vv. 12–17). The people, terrified, stand far off and ask Moses to speak for them, and he alone draws near to the darkness where God is (vv. 18–21). God ends with the altar, plain earth or uncut stone, the place of sacrifice (vv. 22–26).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. Jesus summed up these commandments in love for God and neighbour, and kept them perfectly in our place (Romans 5:19); the law that leaves us all guilty (Romans 3:20) drives us to him. The people who stood far off needed a mediator greater than Moses, and in Christ “you who once were far off have been brought near” (Ephesians 2:13). The plain altar points to the cross, where the offering was made entirely by God.

For us. Keep God’s commandments as one already saved, not to be saved: love comes first and obedience follows (John 14:15). Let the law search your heart and drive you to Christ, and then let it show you the shape of a life of gratitude, by the Spirit who writes it on the heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-11 — The First Table: Love for God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first table of the law is about love for God: God alone, worshipped in his own way, his name honoured, his rest received. It opens not with a command but with a sentence of history: the LORD is Israel’s God, who brought them out of slavery (vv. 1–2). Then come four commandments. No other gods may stand before him (v. 3). No image may be made to represent or worship him, for he is a jealous God whose steadfast love far outlasts his judgment (vv. 4–6). His name must not be carried emptily (v. 7). And the Sabbath must be kept holy for the whole household, because God worked six days and rested on the seventh (vv. 8–11).
verseByVerse.theology:
The First Table: Love for God

God alone, worshipped in his own way, his name honoured, his rest received.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the law was given to a people already rescued. Now: Christ’s people keep it as children already in the family, not as candidates hoping to get in.

verseByVerse.quote: And God spoke all these words, saying, "I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God introduces his commandments by naming himself as the God who has already rescued Israel: the law is for the redeemed, not a way to be redeemed.

I am the LORD your God. The commandments do not begin “obey me and I will be your God.” They begin with a God who has already acted, addressing people who are already his: the LORD your God, who brought you “out of the house of slavery”. Israel is not told how to earn deliverance but how a delivered people lives.

Why the order matters. Get that order wrong and the Decalogue (the “ten words”) becomes a way of earning. Keep it, and the commandments are how gratitude lives. “If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (John 14:15) puts the love first and the keeping second, in the same order as Sinai.

Do the Ten Commandments bind Christians? The law God gave Israel had three strands. Its ceremonial laws (sacrifices, feasts and food rules) were shadows, pictures pointing ahead, fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 10:1). Its civil laws governed Israel as a nation ruled directly under God, and ended when that nation did. Its moral law, summed up here, rests on God’s own character and still binds: Jesus and the apostles repeat these commandments (Matthew 19:18–19; Romans 13:9; Ephesians 6:2). The Christian keeps them not to be saved but as one saved, with the law written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33) by the Spirit who moves God’s people to walk in his ways (Ezekiel 36:27). The fourth, as this commentary reads it, is the one the New Testament treats as fulfilled in Christ (see on vv. 9–11, where the views are set out).
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew calls them “the ten words” (ESV note at 34:28).

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall have no other gods before me. "You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth. You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I the LORD your God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, but showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God alone is to be worshipped, and he is to be worshipped only as he has made himself known, never through images.

You shall have no other gods before me. “Before me” is literally “before my face”: not merely “ahead of me in rank” but “in my presence”, which is everywhere. There is no place where a rival may be quietly kept.

You shall not make for yourself a carved image. The second commandment is distinct, and it matters. The first forbids worshipping the wrong God; the second forbids worshipping the right God in the wrong way. Israel’s calf will not be a foreign deity: Aaron announces “a feast to the LORD” (32:5). They break the second while sincerely meaning to keep the first.

A jealous God. Jealousy is contemptible when it is possessiveness with no right behind it; it is right in a husband whose wife has broken her marriage vows. God’s jealousy is not insecurity but a husband’s response to a wife’s unfaithfulness, Scripture’s own repeated image.

To the third and fourth generation. The clause that troubles readers most needs two things said. First, the words “of those who hate me” do real work: this is not innocent descendants punished for an ancestor’s sin. Ezekiel states the principle flatly, “The soul who sins shall die” (Ezekiel 18:20), and the son does not bear his father’s guilt. What is described is idolatry spreading through a family that keeps choosing it. Second, the real point is the contrast: three or four generations against thousands. Judgment is measured in handfuls of generations; steadfast love in thousands.

The image God gave. God forbade images of himself because he would give his own. Christ “is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15): whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9).

Where Christians differ: may Jesus be pictured? The commandment plainly forbids images made to be worshipped or to represent God, since Israel saw no form at Sinai (Deuteronomy 4:15–16). Many Christians hold that since Christ took a real human body he may be pictured, especially for teaching. The Reformed confessions answer that no image can show the person who is God and man, and that an image used in worship breaks this commandment. This commentary’s view: the Reformed caution is the safer course: no image of Christ in worship or as an aid to prayer. Art in general, which God himself commanded for the tabernacle, is not forbidden.

Uncertain wording. “Before me” can also be rendered “besides me”, and “to thousands” may mean “to the thousandth generation” (v. 6). Either way the contrast stands, and the second reading only sharpens it: God’s love outlasts his judgment many times over.
verseByVerse.note: “Before me” can be rendered “besides me”; “thousands” may mean “the thousandth generation” (ESV notes). Roman Catholics and Lutherans count the commandments differently, joining “no other gods” and “no images” and dividing the tenth in two; the words themselves are the same. Deuteronomy 5 repeats them with small differences, such as a different reason for the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain. "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s name must never be carried emptily, and the Sabbath, already given with the manna, is to be remembered and kept holy.

In vain means empty, worthless, to no purpose. Casual swearing is included, but the commandment is much wider than bad language. To take up God’s name emptily is to carry it without weight: to invoke it in an oath you do not mean to keep, to claim his authority for your own preference, to be called by his name and live in a way that makes it meaningless to those watching.

The heaviest form of misuse is the one nobody notices: a person who bears the name of Christ and whose life makes that name mean nothing to the people who know them. That is why the LORD will not hold such a one guiltless. Yet the way back is open: whoever confesses finds Christ faithful to forgive and cleanse (1 John 1:9), and the name he emptied is the name that saves him.

Remember the Sabbath day. Not “institute”: Israel had kept the Sabbath since the manna (16:23), weeks before this mountain. The commandment writes into law a gift already given.

verseByVerse.quote: Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, you, or your son, or your daughter, your male servant, or your female servant, or your livestock, or the sojourner who is within your gates. For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six days are for work and the seventh for rest, for the whole household, servant, foreigner and animal included, because God made the world in six days and rested on the seventh.

You, or your son, or your daughter. The list in v. 10 is not of people who may rest but of people the head of the household is forbidden to make work: sons, daughters, servants, foreign workers, animals. No one could keep this commandment while running his farm on somebody else’s labour. The Sabbath is the first labour law in Scripture, protecting those with no power to protect themselves, given to a nation that had itself been a slave labour force weeks before. Deuteronomy makes the link: “You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 5:15).

For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth. The reason given here is larger: God’s own six days and his rest. The rhythm is not an arrangement for productivity; it is built into the world, and keeping it imitates God.

A matter of trust. This is why the manna taught the Sabbath first. To stop for a day is to act out the belief that the world is held up by someone else, and that six days of your labour with God are more than seven days of your labour alone. Refusing to rest is usually a quiet statement about who we think is keeping things going.

The New Testament and the Sabbath. The New Testament handles this commandment carefully. Jesus called himself “lord even of the Sabbath” and healed on it, insisting that “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27–28). Paul tells the Colossians not to let anyone pass judgment on them about a Sabbath, since “These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:16–17). And Hebrews says “there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God”, entered by faith (Hebrews 4:9–10).

So what does a Christian do on a Sunday? Gather gladly with God’s people to worship, rest where you can, and delight in the Lord and his gifts. The Lord’s Day is a gift, kept out of joy and wisdom, not a law with rules about work that bind the conscience. And rest finally comes not from a day but from a person: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

Where Christians differ: how long were the days of creation? The commandment’s argument depends on Israel’s six days answering to God’s six days. Faithful Christians who read the days as long ages, as a literary framework, or as God’s workdays described by analogy to ours answer that the commandment needs only a likeness of pattern, not the same length; they are brothers, and this is no test of faith. This commentary’s view: the plain sense is a week of the same kind as ours: six ordinary days, each closed with evening and morning in Genesis 1, which with Jesus’ “from the beginning of creation” (Mark 10:6) point to a young creation. The week Israel kept was patterned on the week God worked.

Where Christians differ: is the Sabbath still binding? Many godly brothers, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Sabbath is a creation ordinance moved by Christ’s resurrection to the first day, so that the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10). Their reasons deserve respect, and their strongest is this very verse, which grounds the day in creation, not in Israel’s history. Seventh-day Adventists hold that Saturday still binds. This commentary’s view: a pattern from creation can still be fulfilled. Hebrews 4 joins God’s seventh-day rest (4:4) to the rest Christ gives, so the pattern reaches its goal in him. The weight of the New Testament is that the day was a shadow now fulfilled in Christ, so that no one may bind another’s conscience about days (Romans 14:5–6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-17 — The Second Table: Love for Neighbor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second table is about love for neighbour: parents, life, marriage, property, truth and the heart are guarded. The fifth commandment, honour for father and mother, comes with a promise of long life in the land and stands as the hinge between love for God and love for neighbour (v. 12). Then four short commands protect a neighbour’s life, marriage, property and good name: no murder, no adultery, no stealing, no false witness (vv. 13–16). The tenth forbids coveting anything that belongs to a neighbour, and so carries the law from actions into desires, where no human court can reach (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Second Table: Love for Neighbor

Parents, life, marriage, property, truth and the heart are guarded.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the commandments protected the weak in Israel's courts and homes. Now: Jesus reads them at the level of the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: "Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Children are to honour their parents all their lives, and God promises that a people who do so will last in the land.

Between God and neighbour. The fifth commandment is the hinge between the commandments about God and those about neighbour. It stands at the join because the family is where a child first meets authority, and contempt learned at home rarely stays there.

Honor your father and your mother. To honour is weightier than to obey. Obedience has an expiry date; honour does not. A grown man no longer obliged to obey his father is still obliged to honour him, which in practice meant caring for parents who could no longer work, in a world without pensions. Jesus attacked the Pharisees at this point, for a device that let a man dedicate his assets to God and so avoid supporting his parents (Mark 7:9–13). On the cross he himself provided for his mother (John 19:26–27).

That your days may be long. Paul calls it “the first commandment with a promise” (Ephesians 6:2–3), and the promise is for the whole people as much as for each person: a nation whose generations hold together lasts in the land God gives.

When this commandment is hard. Some readers had fathers who were cruel and mothers who were absent. Honour is not pretending, and it does not require calling evil good or giving an abuser continued access. It is a real command with real content (respect for the office, care where care is possible, refusal to hold contempt), and it is not a command to lie about what happened. Anyone still being harmed should seek safety at once.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not murder. "You shall not commit adultery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God forbids taking human life unlawfully and breaking the marriage covenant, and Jesus shows that both commandments reach the heart.

You shall not murder. Hebrew ratsach, killing a person without the law’s authority. It covers manslaughter too, which is why the cities of refuge exist (Numbers 35:11), but never lawful judicial killing or war. The reason lies in Genesis: man is made in God’s image, so an assault on a person is an assault on the God whose image he bears (Genesis 9:6).

You shall not commit adultery. Marriage is the Bible’s picture of God’s covenant with his people, which is why unfaithfulness is treated so gravely.

Jesus goes deeper. Jesus takes both commandments inward: “everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5:22), and “everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). He is not adding stricter rules but exposing what they were always about: the heart the act comes out of.

No one innocent. Read at the level Jesus reads them, the commandments leave no one innocent, which Paul says is one of the things the law is for: “through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Romans 3:20). But the one who read the law so deeply also kept it perfectly in our place, and through his obedience the many are made righteous (Romans 5:19).

What does the commandment cover? Because it forbids unlawful killing, the same law can give the state the sword (21:12). Killing in self-defence is not murder (22:2), nor is a just war. But it covers the unborn, whom God forms in the womb (Psalm 139:13–16; compare 21:22–25), and so forbids abortion, as it forbids euthanasia and suicide. Anyone who carries grief or guilt from one of these should hear the next word too: no sin is beyond the cleansing of Christ’s blood, and the LORD is near the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18). If you are thinking of ending your life, you are not beyond help or hope: tell someone today, a friend, a pastor or your doctor, and if you are in danger call the emergency services or a crisis line now.
verseByVerse.note: Accidental killing (Numbers 35:11) was grave but not capital: the killer fled to a city of refuge.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not steal. "You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. "You shall not covet your neighbor's house; you shall not covet your neighbor's wife, or his male servant, or his female servant, or his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor's."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God protects a neighbour’s property and good name, and then forbids even the inward desire for what is his.

You shall not steal. Property is real: a person may own something, and taking it is wrong, which sounds obvious until you recall Egypt taking Israel’s labour unpaid. The commandment also protects the poor, who can least afford to lose what little they have.

False witness. Narrower than “do not lie” and sharper, it is set in a courtroom and forbids testimony that destroys a person. Where there was no police force, a false witness was a weapon that could kill, and a proven false witness received the sentence he sought for his victim (Deuteronomy 19:19). Words about people are treated as actions done to them.

You shall not covet. The tenth is unlike all the others. Every earlier commandment could be broken visibly; no court could try this one, and a man could keep the other nine in public while breaking it continually in private. Its presence shows that the commandments were always about the heart. Paul, blameless under the law by his own account, said this was the commandment that exposed him: “I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, ‘You shall not covet’” (Romans 7:7).

An economy that runs on coveting. Much of modern advertising exists to make us want what we did not want an hour ago, and our phones let us survey our neighbour’s house, holiday, marriage and body every evening in comfortable detail. We call the result aspiration. Scripture calls it coveting, and notices what it does: it turns a neighbour into a rival and a gift into a grievance, because nothing we have can be enjoyed once we are measuring it against what someone else has. The commandment cannot cure this by itself, since no one stops wanting by being told to. Only a greater fullness can displace it. That is why the New Testament grounds contentment not in having enough but in having him: “Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, ‘I will never leave you nor forsake you’” (Hebrews 13:5). The person who has Christ can afford to be glad of his neighbour’s good things.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18-21 — The Trembling People and the Mediator
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sinners need someone to stand between them and God. Seeing the thunder, lightning and smoke and hearing the trumpet, the people tremble and stand far off (v. 18). They beg Moses to speak to them instead, lest they die (v. 19). Moses tells them not to fear, for God has come to test them so that the fear of him may keep them from sin (v. 20). Then the people stay far off while Moses alone draws near to the thick darkness where God is (v. 21). The scene shows both the need for a mediator and the limits of the one they had.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Trembling People and the Mediator

Sinners need someone to stand between them and God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: one man went into the dark for the people. Now: the curtain is torn, and the far-off are brought near.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when all the people saw the thunder and the flashes of lightning and the sound of the trumpet and the mountain smoking, the people were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off and said to Moses, "You speak to us, and we will listen; but do not let God speak to us, lest we die." Moses said to the people, "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin." The people stood far off, while Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Terrified by God’s voice, the people stand far off and ask Moses to speak for them, and Moses alone draws near to the darkness where God is.

Do not let God speak to us. They had promised to do everything God said (19:8); now they back away and ask Moses to speak instead. The commandments heard in God’s holy presence have convinced them they cannot survive direct contact. That instinct is correct, and the priesthood, tabernacle and sacrifices that follow are God’s answer to the request.

Do not fear. Moses’ reply looks contradictory and is not: do not fear, so that you may fear. Two different things share one word. The terror that runs from God is to go; the reverence that keeps from sin is to remain.

Moses drew near to the thick darkness. Verse 21 is the whole chapter in a single image: the people far off, one man drawing near. That is the shape of the old covenant, and its limit: Israel’s access was only as good as their mediator, and Moses would die outside the promised land.

He bore the darkness himself. That is why the tearing of the temple curtain when Jesus died mattered. God is as holy as ever, but this mediator did not merely walk into the darkness for the people; he bore it himself. “But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ” (Ephesians 2:13). Sinai’s people sent one man in. At Calvary one man went in and brought the distant people with him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nothing of the worshipper’s workmanship may appear where atonement is made. God reminds Israel that he has spoken from heaven, so they must make no gods of silver or gold to stand beside him (vv. 22–23). He commands a simple altar of earth for burnt offerings and peace offerings, and promises to come and bless them wherever he causes his name to be remembered (v. 24). If the altar is stone, it must be uncut, for a tool would profane it, and it must have no steps, so that the worshipper’s nakedness is not exposed (vv. 25–26).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Altar of Earth

Nothing of the worshipper's workmanship may appear where atonement is made.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the law came with its own way of forgiveness. Now: at its end stands a cross to which no one can add any work of his own.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Thus you shall say to the people of Israel: 'You have seen for yourselves that I have talked with you from heaven. You shall not make gods of silver to be with me, nor shall you make for yourselves gods of gold. An altar of earth you shall make for me and sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, your sheep and your oxen. In every place where I cause my name to be remembered I will come to you and bless you. If you make me an altar of stone, you shall not build it of hewn stones, for if you wield your tool on it you profane it. And you shall not go up by steps to my altar, that your nakedness be not exposed on it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel is to worship without idols at a plain altar of earth or uncut stone, where nothing of the worshipper’s own work or body is put on display.

Not an anticlimax. After the thunder, instructions about altars can look like an anticlimax. They are not. The first law after the commandments repeats the second: no gods of silver or gold “with me”. And God promises that wherever he causes his name to be remembered, he will come and bless.

An altar of earth. Israel’s first authorised altar must be made of earth or unshaped stones. Every surrounding nation carved its holy places elaborately; Israel may not improve on the raw material at all.

You shall not go up by steps. Steps are forbidden so that nakedness is not exposed on the way up: even the approach displays nothing of the worshipper.

Ending in grace. So the chapter closes where it began, in grace: ten commandments no one in the camp will keep, and in the same breath an altar with no human contribution in it, the way to be forgiven for not keeping them. At the end of that road stands a cross on which the offering was made entirely by God.

What it does not mean. Craftsmanship is not wrong: God will fill the tabernacle with Spirit-given skill (31:1–5). The point is what an altar is for. It is where a substitute dies in the worshipper’s place, and nothing the worshipper contributes may appear on it. A tooled stone would let a man look at the place of atonement and see his own workmanship.

20.theology:
Law framed by grace. The law is a gift to the redeemed, not a price for rescue.

The two tables of love. Love for God and love for neighbour, summarised by Jesus as the whole of the law.

The law as guardian. The perfect standard exposes our sin and leads us to Christ (Gal. 3:24), who kept it for us and bore its curse.
20.examples:
Then: From a mountain of fire God spoke ten words to his redeemed people, and the terrified people begged for a mediator.

Now: The law shows us how to love God and neighbour and how far we fall short. We obey not to be saved but because we are saved, in grateful love to our Redeemer and by the Spirit he has given us.

keyVerse.quote: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
keyVerse.note: The Ten Commandments begin not with a command but with what God has already done. Everything that follows is the shape of life for a people already redeemed, which is why Christians keep God’s law out of gratitude, not to earn his favour.

20.reflection:
The commandments begin with “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out” (v. 2). How would your obedience change if you always read God’s commands in that order, grace first and then law?

The first table is about God and the second about neighbour. Which commandment do you find hardest to keep, and how does Jesus’ deeper reading of the law (Matthew 5:21–28) search your heart?

The tenth commandment forbids coveting (v. 17). Where does our culture, or your own phone, feed discontent, and how does Hebrews 13:5 offer a better way?

The people stood far off while Moses drew near (v. 21). What does it mean for you that in Christ “you who once were far off have been brought near” (Ephesians 2:13)?

21.title: The Dignity of Persons Under God's Law
21.text: <sup>1</sup>"Now these are the rules that you shall set before them.<sup>2</sup>When you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free, for nothing.<sup>3</sup>If he comes in single, he shall go out single; if he comes in married, then his wife shall go out with him.<sup>4</sup>If his master gives him a wife and she bears him sons or daughters, the wife and her children shall be her master's, and he shall go out alone.<sup>5</sup>But if the slave plainly says, 'I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free,'<sup>6</sup>then his master shall bring him to God, and he shall bring him to the door or the doorpost. And his master shall bore his ear through with an awl, and he shall be his slave forever.<sup>7</sup>"When a man sells his daughter as a slave, she shall not go out as the male slaves do.<sup>8</sup>If she does not please her master, who has designated her for himself, then he shall let her be redeemed. He shall have no right to sell her to a foreign people, since he has broken faith with her.<sup>9</sup>If he designates her for his son, he shall deal with her as with a daughter.<sup>10</sup>If he takes another wife to himself, he shall not diminish her food, her clothing, or her marital rights.<sup>11</sup>And if he does not do these three things for her, she shall go out for nothing, without payment of money.<sup>12</sup>"Whoever strikes a man so that he dies shall be put to death.<sup>13</sup>But if he did not lie in wait for him, but God let him fall into his hand, then I will appoint for you a place to which he may flee.<sup>14</sup>But if a man willfully attacks another to kill him by cunning, you shall take him from my altar, that he may die.<sup>15</sup>"Whoever strikes his father or his mother shall be put to death.<sup>16</sup>"Whoever steals a man and sells him, and anyone found in possession of him, shall be put to death.<sup>17</sup>"Whoever curses his father or his mother shall be put to death.<sup>18</sup>"When men quarrel and one strikes the other with a stone or with his fist and the man does not die but takes to his bed,<sup>19</sup>then if the man rises again and walks outdoors with his staff, he who struck him shall be clear; only he shall pay for the loss of his time, and shall have him thoroughly healed.<sup>20</sup>"When a man strikes his slave, male or female, with a rod and the slave dies under his hand, he shall be avenged.<sup>21</sup>But if the slave survives a day or two, he is not to be avenged, for the slave is his money.<sup>22</sup>"When men strive together and hit a pregnant woman, so that her children come out, but there is no harm, the one who hit her shall surely be fined, as the woman's husband shall impose on him, and he shall pay as the judges determine.<sup>23</sup>But if there is harm, then you shall pay life for life,<sup>24</sup>eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,<sup>25</sup>burn for burn, wound for wound, stripe for stripe.<sup>26</sup>"When a man strikes the eye of his slave, male or female, and destroys it, he shall let the slave go free because of his eye.<sup>27</sup>If he knocks out the tooth of his slave, male or female, he shall let the slave go free because of his tooth.<sup>28</sup>"When an ox gores a man or a woman to death, the ox shall be stoned, and its flesh shall not be eaten, but the owner of the ox shall not be liable.<sup>29</sup>But if the ox has been accustomed to gore in the past, and its owner has been warned but has not kept it in, and it kills a man or a woman, the ox shall be stoned, and its owner also shall be put to death.<sup>30</sup>If a ransom is imposed on him, then he shall give for the redemption of his life whatever is imposed on him.<sup>31</sup>If it gores a man's son or daughter, he shall be dealt with according to this same rule.<sup>32</sup>If the ox gores a slave, male or female, the owner shall give to their master thirty shekels of silver, and the ox shall be stoned.<sup>33</sup>"When a man opens a pit, or when a man digs a pit and does not cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it,<sup>34</sup>the owner of the pit shall make restoration. He shall give money to its owner, and the dead beast shall be his.<sup>35</sup>"When one man's ox butts another's, so that it dies, then they shall sell the live ox and share its price, and the dead beast also they shall share.<sup>36</sup>Or if it is known that the ox has been accustomed to gore in the past, and its owner has not kept it in, he shall repay ox for ox, and the dead beast shall be his.
21.overview:
Where we are. God has spoken the Ten Commandments from Sinai, and the terrified people have asked Moses to stand between them and God (20:18–21). Moses draws near to the thick darkness and receives “the rules” (v. 1), the first part of what 24:7 calls “the Book of the Covenant” (20:22–23:33).

The message. The God who freed Israel from slavery means his justice to reach the ordinary places of life: the household, the quarrel, the field. Every life matters to him, the servant’s, the unborn child’s, the injured neighbour’s, because people bear his image. So his law protects the weak, tells intent from accident, puts a ceiling on revenge and holds people responsible for the harm they could have prevented.

Why it was said. Israel had just come out of a land where slaves had no rights and Pharaoh drowned babies. Now they were to become a nation with courts, debts and livestock, among neighbours whose law codes often valued people by rank and property. God gave them a justice shaped by his own character and by their story (see the introduction): you were slaves, so treat the servant as a person.

How the chapter makes its case. It opens, startlingly, with servants: a Hebrew debt-servant goes free in the seventh year or may choose to stay for love, and a daughter given into service is protected (vv. 1–11). Then come the crimes that carry death: murder, though not accident, for which there is refuge; striking or cursing parents; kidnapping (vv. 12–17). Then injuries: compensation, protection for servants and for the pregnant woman, and “eye for eye” (vv. 18–27). Last, the goring ox and the open pit: owners answer for dangers they knew about (vv. 28–36).

Where it leads. Chiefly by the character of God revealed in Christ, and by pattern. The God who protects the servant, the child and the injured is the God who in Jesus touched lepers and took children in his arms. The servant who freely binds himself to his master for love points to the Son who “came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45). And the thirty shekels paid for a gored slave (v. 32) became the price set on Jesus himself (Matthew 26:15), who gave his life as the ransom for many.

For us. Holiness is not only for the mountain; it reaches how we treat employees, children, the unborn and the neighbour whose property we could damage. Christ has made us free, so we give others the dignity he gave us, refuse revenge, and own the harm we cause.
21.theology:
The dignity of the image of God. Every person, servant, child or victim, is precious because made in God's image. The law surrounds the vulnerable with protection.

Justice and its limits. The law of "eye for eye" restrains vengeance and guarantees proportion. God's justice is exacting but never cruel.

Personal responsibility before God. We answer to God for our neighbor's welfare and safety.
21.examples:
Then: God's covenant law applied his holy character to daily life, protecting servants, restraining violence, and upholding the dignity of every person in a brutal ancient world.

Now: God still cares for the vulnerable and still holds us responsible for our neighbor's welfare. None of us has kept this law fully, but Christ obeyed it perfectly in our place, his obedience is counted as ours (Rom. 5:19), and his Spirit now makes us able to love our neighbour. The Redeemer who gave his life to ransom ours is the final proof of how precious human life is to God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s law begins with the most vulnerable person in the household and sets limits on how far anyone could own another. A Hebrew who sold himself into service for debt goes free in the seventh year, for nothing, taking his wife if he came in married (vv. 1–4). If he loves the household and chooses to stay, it is done solemnly before God, with an ear bored at the doorpost (vv. 5–6). A daughter placed in a household with a view to marriage has her own protections: she cannot be sold abroad, must be treated as family, and keeps her food, clothing and marital rights, or else she goes free (vv. 7–11).
verseByVerse.theology:
Laws About Slaves

An existing institution is regulated, and pointed toward release.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the law gave the weaker person the way out. Now: those set free by Christ owe others the freedom they were given.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now these are the rules that you shall set before them. When you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free, for nothing. If he comes in single, he shall go out single; if he comes in married, then his wife shall go out with him. If his master gives him a wife and she bears him sons or daughters, the wife and her children shall be her master's, and he shall go out alone. But if the slave plainly says, 'I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free,' then his master shall bring him to God, and he shall bring him to the door or the doorpost. And his master shall bore his ear through with an awl, and he shall be his slave forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even servitude is limited: a Hebrew who sells himself into service for debt goes free in the seventh year, unless he freely chooses to stay with the household he loves.

These are the rules. Straight after the thunder of Sinai comes case law. The Ten Commandments state principles; these chapters show what they look like when two men’s oxen collide.

When you buy a Hebrew slave. The first case is slavery, startling in a book about God freeing slaves. Scripture is not endorsing the institution but regulating one that existed everywhere (see slavery in the ancient world), and radically by ancient standards. A man sold himself to clear a debt, and after six years he goes out free, for nothing: the debt could not own him for life.

Why does the wife stay with the master (v. 4)? She was a servant under her own term, given by the master, and her children were born into his house. The law does not let the man take what is not his; it lets him choose to stay with his family for life (vv. 5–6).

The pierced ear. The servant who stays has his ear bored at the doorpost, the mark that he belongs by love, not by debt. Many Christians hear in it an echo of the Son who freely took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7) and “came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45).

Uncertain wording. “Bring him to God” (v. 6) may mean to God at the sanctuary or to the judges who acted in his name (older translations have “unto the judges”). Either way the act was public and solemn, not a private bargain.
verseByVerse.note: This section (21–23) is called the Book of the Covenant (24:7). Israel’s slave laws limited service to six years and protected the servant.

verseByVerse.quote: "When a man sells his daughter as a slave, she shall not go out as the male slaves do. If she does not please her master, who has designated her for himself, then he shall let her be redeemed. He shall have no right to sell her to a foreign people, since he has broken faith with her. If he designates her for his son, he shall deal with her as with a daughter. If he takes another wife to himself, he shall not diminish her food, her clothing, or her marital rights. And if he does not do these three things for her, she shall go out for nothing, without payment of money.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A daughter placed in a household with a view to marriage is protected at every point: she cannot be sold abroad, must be treated as family, and if she is neglected she goes free.

When a man sells his daughter as a slave.
