A poor father might place his daughter in a household to become the wife of the master or his son, so she shall not go out as the male slaves do: her case is a marriage, not a fixed term. Every rule protects her. If the master does not take her, she must be redeemed, never sold to foreigners, since he has broken faith with her. Given to his son, she is a daughter. If he takes another wife, he may not reduce her food, clothing or marital rights, or she goes free without payment.

The distance we feel. It is fair to feel the distance between this and the abolition we would want, and honest to say that Scripture moves toward it rather than arriving at once. Jesus gave the reason when he spoke of divorce: some things Moses permitted and regulated “because of your hardness of heart”, though “from the beginning it was not so” (Matthew 19:8). And see where it ends: Paul asks a slave-owner to receive a runaway “no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 16), and once that sentence exists in the church the institution has no ground left to stand on.

Doesn’t the Bible endorse slavery? The objection is serious, and the honest answer has two parts. First, the word covers very different things. This chapter mainly regulates debt-service with a fixed term, release in the seventh year and freedom for a lost tooth, while the thing that built the Atlantic trade, seizing a man and selling him, is a capital crime (v. 16). Second, ask where our conviction that slavery is wrong came from. Enslaved Africans in America sang “Go Down, Moses” in the fields, and the political philosopher Michael Walzer argued in Exodus and Revolution (1985) that this story became the West’s great pattern for liberation. The book their masters quoted told of a God who hears the groaning of slaves and humbles their owners. And it goes deeper: Jesus said that “everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin” (John 8:34), and then took the form of a servant himself to set that slave free.

Uncertain wording. In v. 8 the Hebrew can also be read “so that he has not designated her”, with the same sense. In v. 10 “marital rights” renders a word found only here; most take it so, though some suggest oil or lodging.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-17 — Capital Crimes Against Life and Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some wrongs strike so deeply at life and family that the law calls for death. Deliberate murder is capital, but a killing that was not planned is distinguished from it, and God promises a place of refuge for the one who kills by accident (vv. 12–13). A man who murders by cunning finds no shelter even at God’s altar (v. 14). Striking or cursing a father or mother is capital too, showing how much rests on the fifth commandment (vv. 15, 17). So is kidnapping: stealing and selling a person, or holding one stolen, is treated as an attack on life itself (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Capital Crimes Against Life and Family

Intent distinguishes crime from accident, and stealing a person carries death.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a place of refuge stood ready for the accidental killer. Now: the guilty find their refuge in Christ (Heb. 6:18).

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever strikes a man so that he dies shall be put to death. But if he did not lie in wait for him, but God let him fall into his hand, then I will appoint for you a place to which he may flee. But if a man willfully attacks another to kill him by cunning, you shall take him from my altar, that he may die. "Whoever strikes his father or his mother shall be put to death. "Whoever steals a man and sells him, and anyone found in possession of him, shall be put to death. "Whoever curses his father or his mother shall be put to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Deliberate murder, attacking or cursing a parent, and kidnapping carry death, but the one who kills by accident is given refuge.

Whoever strikes a man so that he dies. The capital cases (those carrying death) draw careful distinctions. Where there was no lying in wait, God will appoint a place to flee, the cities of refuge (Numbers 35), a refuge Hebrews echoes for all who flee to Christ (Hebrews 6:18). Intent changes everything. But the planned murderer finds no shelter even at the altar: you shall take him from my altar (1 Kings 2:28–34).

Whoever strikes his father or his mother. Striking or cursing a parent is capital, which shows how much rested on the fifth commandment. So is kidnapping. Set that beside verse 2: voluntary debt-service with a fixed term is regulated; stealing a person is a capital crime. The slave trade that later crossed the Atlantic was, by this chapter’s standard, a capital crime at every stage.

Do these death penalties still apply? They were civil laws for Israel as a nation ruled directly under God, and they ended with that nation, though the principle that murder deserves the gravest penalty is older than Sinai (Genesis 9:6). The moral principle remains: Jesus rebukes those who dishonour father and mother (Mark 7:9–13), and kidnapping and slave-trading stand condemned (1 Timothy 1:10). The severity shows how seriously God takes the family and human freedom.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18-27 — Injury, Restitution, and the Limit of Vengeance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When people are hurt, the law demands fair repair and no more than fair punishment. A man who injures another in a quarrel pays for his lost time and his healing (vv. 18–19). A master who beats a servant to death is punished (vv. 20–21). A pregnant woman struck in a fight is protected, and so is her child, under the principle “life for life, eye for eye” (vv. 22–25), which sets a ceiling on revenge and puts the matter in the judges’ hands. A master who destroys a servant’s eye or knocks out a tooth must set the servant free (vv. 26–27).
verseByVerse.theology:
Injury, Restitution, and the Limit of Vengeance

The penalty may not exceed the harm.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the rule set the most that could be demanded, not the least. Now: Jesus forbids his disciples to insist even on the just amount (Matt. 5:38-39).

verseByVerse.quote: "When men quarrel and one strikes the other with a stone or with his fist and the man does not die but takes to his bed, then if the man rises again and walks outdoors with his staff, he who struck him shall be clear; only he shall pay for the loss of his time, and shall have him thoroughly healed. "When a man strikes his slave, male or female, with a rod and the slave dies under his hand, he shall be avenged. But if the slave survives a day or two, he is not to be avenged, for the slave is his money. "When men strive together and hit a pregnant woman, so that her children come out, but there is no harm, the one who hit her shall surely be fined, as the woman's husband shall impose on him, and he shall pay as the judges determine. But if there is harm, then you shall pay life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for wound, stripe for stripe. "When a man strikes the eye of his slave, male or female, and destroys it, he shall let the slave go free because of his eye. If he knocks out the tooth of his slave, male or female, he shall let the slave go free because of his tooth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Injury must be repaid, servants are protected even from their masters, the pregnant woman and her child are guarded, and punishment must fit the harm and go no further.

He shall pay for the loss of his time. The man who wounds another pays his lost earnings and his healing: justice here is repair.

What do verses 20–21 mean by “for the slave is his money”? They do not license beating. The master who kills his slave is to be punished, which other ancient law codes seldom required. If the slave survives a day or two, the death is not judged deliberate murder, and the master’s loss of a worker is the penalty.

Eye for eye. It sounds savage and is the opposite. In a world of blood feuds where an insult could escalate into a massacre, this is a ceiling, not a floor: the penalty may not exceed the injury. It is a rule for judges (v. 22), and its whole force is to stop revenge from growing.

Go free because of his tooth. A single tooth costs the master the servant himself, because damage to a servant’s body forfeits the right to hold him.

Jesus’ use. Jesus quotes it and does something unexpected: “But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil” (Matthew 5:38–39). He is not calling the law unjust. He moves the question from what a court may impose to what a disciple may personally demand.

Where Christians differ. In verses 22–25 the ESV’s “so that her children come out” describes a premature birth: if there is no harm, a fine; if there is harm, to mother or child, “life for life”. Others read a miscarriage, with a fine for the child’s death and the full penalty only for harm to the mother, which would make the unborn worth less.

This commentary’s view. The Hebrew words normally describe a live birth, and the law sets harm to either in the same scale. The better reading treats the unborn child as a person whose life the law protects.
verseByVerse.note: “Eye for eye” limited revenge: the penalty was to fit the crime, set by judges, not taken privately.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28-36 — The Goring Ox and the Responsible Owner
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends with the farm and the open pit, and with responsibility for known danger. An ox that kills a person is stoned, but its owner is not guilty unless he had been warned and did nothing; then he answers with his life, though a ransom may be accepted (vv. 28–30). The rule is the same whether the victim is a son or a daughter, and a slave’s death is paid for too (vv. 31–32). Whoever leaves a pit uncovered or keeps a dangerous ox must make good the loss of an animal (vv. 33–36). Love for neighbour includes care about what we could have prevented.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Goring Ox and the Responsible Owner

What the owner knew decides what he owes.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: known risk ignored became the owner's responsibility. Now: the God of the thunder claims the field and the well as well as the altar.

verseByVerse.quote: "When an ox gores a man or a woman to death, the ox shall be stoned, and its flesh shall not be eaten, but the owner of the ox shall not be liable. But if the ox has been accustomed to gore in the past, and its owner has been warned but has not kept it in, and it kills a man or a woman, the ox shall be stoned, and its owner also shall be put to death. If a ransom is imposed on him, then he shall give for the redemption of his life whatever is imposed on him. If it gores a man's son or daughter, he shall be dealt with according to this same rule. If the ox gores a slave, male or female, the owner shall give to their master thirty shekels of silver, and the ox shall be stoned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An owner who was warned that his ox was dangerous and did nothing is guilty of the death it causes, whoever the victim.

When an ox gores a man or a woman to death. The ox is stoned, for it has shed human blood (Genesis 9:5), but the owner is not responsible: no one could have foreseen it. If he was warned and did not keep it in, he must answer for the death, though since he did not intend it a ransom may redeem his life. It turns on the question a modern negligence court would ask: what did he know, and what did he do about it?

Thirty shekels of silver. Even a slave’s death is paid for: thirty shekels. It was the sum later weighed out for Jesus: “they paid him thirty pieces of silver” (Matthew 26:15). The Lord of glory was valued at the price of a gored slave, and gave his life as “a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45).
verseByVerse.note: Thirty shekels, the price of a slave, was about 12 ounces of silver (ESV note: a shekel was about 2/5 ounce). It was the sum Judas took for Jesus (Matthew 26:15), the price Zechariah had called the lordly price at which the shepherd was valued (Zechariah 11:12–13; Matthew 27:9).

verseByVerse.quote: "When a man opens a pit, or when a man digs a pit and does not cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it, the owner of the pit shall make restoration. He shall give money to its owner, and the dead beast shall be his. "When one man's ox butts another's, so that it dies, then they shall sell the live ox and share its price, and the dead beast also they shall share. Or if it is known that the ox has been accustomed to gore in the past, and its owner has not kept it in, he shall repay ox for ox, and the dead beast shall be his.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever could reasonably have prevented a loss must make it good.

When a man opens a pit. The uncovered pit and the ox known to gore are settled the same way: whoever could have prevented the loss bears it.

Why the ordinary matters. God has just appeared on a mountain in fire, and within a chapter he is legislating about livestock and open pits. That is not a come-down from the glory of Sinai; it is the point of the covenant. The God of the thunder intends to govern the field, the well and the argument between neighbours, and a holiness that does not reach the ox is not the holiness he is offering. Love for neighbour includes the dangers we know we have left uncovered.

keyVerse.quote: When you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free, for nothing.
keyVerse.note: The first law God gives his freed people protects the person with least power in the household. A people redeemed from slavery must not let anyone be owned by debt for ever, and in the seventh year freedom comes as a gift, “for nothing”.

21.reflection:
The Book of the Covenant begins with servants, not with kings or worship (vv. 1–11). What does that tell you about what God cares about, and who are the vulnerable people in your own household, workplace or church?

Read verses 12–17 alongside Genesis 9:6. Why does God draw such a sharp line between murder and accident, and between debt-service and kidnapping?

Jesus quotes “eye for eye” and then says, “Do not resist the one who is evil” (Matthew 5:38–39). What is the difference between what a court may rightly do and what you may personally demand when you are wronged?

Verses 28–36 hold people responsible for dangers they knew about. Is there a known risk or harmful habit in your life that you have left “uncovered”?

22.title: Care for the Vulnerable
22.text: <sup>1</sup>"If a man steals an ox or a sheep, and kills it or sells it, he shall repay five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep.<sup>2</sup>If a thief is found breaking in and is struck so that he dies, there shall be no bloodguilt for him,<sup>3</sup>but if the sun has risen on him, there shall be bloodguilt for him. He shall surely pay. The firstborn of your sons you shall give to me.<sup>30</sup>You shall do the same with your oxen and with your sheep: seven days it shall be with its mother; on the eighth day you shall give it to me.<sup>31</sup>"You shall be consecrated to me. Therefore you shall not eat any flesh that is torn by beasts in the field; you shall throw it to the dogs.
22.overview:
Where we are. The Book of the Covenant (20:22–23:33) continues. Chapter 21 dealt with persons, servants and injuries; now the laws turn to property, trust and the life of the community, before Moses reads the whole book to the people (24:7).

The message. God’s justice restores what was lost and protects those who cannot protect themselves. A thief must pay back more than he took, a neighbour’s goods must be guarded as one’s own, and the foreigner, the widow, the orphan and the poor are under God’s personal protection, because he hears their cry. Behind it all stands one sentence: “You shall be consecrated to me” (v. 31).

Why it was said. Israel had been the foreigner, the oppressed and the poor, crying out under Egypt’s whip until God heard (3:7). Now about to become a settled people with fields, herds and debts, they would be tempted to forget, and to treat the weak as Egypt had treated them (see the introduction). God ties their care for others to their own memory of rescue.

How the chapter makes its case. It begins with theft and restitution, the burglar by night, damage to a neighbour’s field and goods left in another’s care (vv. 1–15). Then come laws guarding purity and loyalty: the seduced young woman is protected, and sorcery, bestiality and sacrifice to other gods carry death (vv. 16–20). At its heart is mercy: the sojourner, widow and orphan must not be wronged, the poor must not be charged interest, and a pledged cloak goes back before sunset, “for I am compassionate” (vv. 21–27). It ends with reverence for God and rulers and the giving of firstfruits and firstborn (vv. 28–31).

Where it leads. Chiefly by the character of God revealed in Christ, and by pattern. The God who stops to ask where a poor man will sleep tonight is the God who in Jesus had compassion on the crowds and welcomed outsiders, and through whom we who were “strangers and aliens” are made members of his household (Ephesians 2:19). The firstborn sons given to God and bought back with a price point to the Father who “did not spare his own Son” (Romans 8:32). And when grace reached Zacchaeus, he repaid fourfold, as this chapter requires.

For us. Grace received must become grace extended. Pay back what you owe and more, keep faith with what others trust you with, and treat the stranger and the poor as God treated you when you had nothing. Our holiness is tested less on the mountain than in what we do with a neighbour’s cloak.
22.theology:
Restorative justice. Restitution, paying back, aims to make the victim whole.

God the defender of the vulnerable. The sojourner, widow, and orphan are under God's own protection.

Grace received, grace extended. Remembering our own rescue moves us to mercy toward the weak.
22.examples:
Then: God's law placed the most defenceless under his personal protection.

Now: The God who redeemed us calls us to care for the vulnerable as he cared for us, and gives his Spirit to make us merciful. He still hears the cry of the poor and warns those who oppress them. None of us has kept this law as it asks; Christ kept it perfectly in our place, and his obedience, counted as ours, is the way back for all who confess (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s justice restores what was lost, and it rests on honesty before him. A thief pays back four or five times what he slaughtered or sold, double if the animal is found alive, and if he has nothing he works it off (vv. 1–4). A burglar killed at night brings no bloodguilt, but in daylight he does (vv. 2–3). Whoever lets his animals graze another’s field or lets a fire spread pays for the damage (vv. 5–6). When goods or animals left in a neighbour’s care are lost, the matter is settled before God, by judgment or by oath, and risk falls where it fairly belongs (vv. 7–15).
verseByVerse.theology:
Laws About Restitution

The law asks first what the victim has lost.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the thief restored more than he took. Now: wrongs done to others are still to be put right where they can be, as a fruit of grace, not a price for it.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man steals an ox or a sheep, and kills it or sells it, he shall repay five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep. If a thief is found breaking in and is struck so that he dies, there shall be no bloodguilt for him, but if the sun has risen on him, there shall be bloodguilt for him. He shall surely pay. If he has nothing, then he shall be sold for his theft. If the stolen beast is found alive in his possession, whether it is an ox or a donkey or a sheep, he shall pay double. "If a man causes a field or vineyard to be grazed over, or lets his beast loose and it feeds in another man's field, he shall make restitution from the best in his own field and in his own vineyard. "If fire breaks out and catches in thorns so that the stacked grain or the standing grain or the field is consumed, he who started the fire shall make full restitution. "If a man gives to his neighbor money or goods to keep safe, and it is stolen from the man's house, then, if the thief is found, he shall pay double. If the thief is not found, the owner of the house shall come near to God to show whether or not he has put his hand to his neighbor's property.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A thief must repay more than he took, a burglar may be resisted at night, and anyone who damages a neighbour’s property must make it good.

He shall repay five oxen for an ox. The law on theft centres on restitution, paying back, rather than punishment. The thief restores more than he took, so that the victim is not left the loser. Our reflex is to ask what the offender deserves; Israel’s law asks first what the injured party has lost, and makes the offender carry it. If he cannot pay, he shall be sold for his theft: he works off the debt under the limits of 21:2, but there is no prison.

The burglar. If a burglar is killed breaking in at night, there is no bloodguilt, no guilt of murder; the same killing after sunrise brings it. The difference is visibility. In the dark you cannot know whether the intruder is armed or how many there are; in daylight you can, and lethal force stops being self-defence.

He shall make restitution from the best. Careless grazing or a spreading fire is paid for in full, from the best of one’s own field.

Fourfold in the New Testament. The principle turns up in the mouth of a man nobody expected. Zacchaeus said, “if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold” (Luke 19:8): this chapter’s rate for a stolen sheep, applied voluntarily to a career of extortion. Grace had reached him moments earlier, and the first thing it produced was restitution. Repentance still includes putting things right.

verseByVerse.quote: For every breach of trust, whether it is for an ox, for a donkey, for a sheep, for a cloak, or for any kind of lost thing, of which one says, 'This is it,' the case of both parties shall come before God. The one whom God condemns shall pay double to his neighbor. "If a man gives to his neighbor a donkey or an ox or a sheep or any beast to keep safe, and it dies or is injured or is driven away, without anyone seeing it, an oath by the LORD shall be between them both to see whether or not he has put his hand to his neighbor's property. The owner shall accept the oath, and he shall not make restitution. But if it is stolen from him, he shall make restitution to its owner. If it is torn by beasts, let him bring it as evidence. He shall not make restitution for what has been torn. "If a man borrows anything of his neighbor, and it is injured or dies, the owner not being with it, he shall make full restitution. If the owner was with it, he shall not make restitution; if it was hired, it came for its hiring fee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When goods left in someone’s care are lost, the case is settled before God, and the risk falls where it fairly belongs.

Any beast to keep safe. These cases depend on who should carry the risk. If the keeper was careless or the animal was stolen from him, he pays; if it died unseen, an oath before God settles it and the owner accepts it; if wild beasts tore it, he brings the remains as evidence (Amos 3:12); a borrower pays for loss unless the owner was there, and a hired animal’s fee covers the risk. In a world without contracts, insurance or cameras, the system rests on people telling the truth in God’s presence.

An oath by the LORD. These laws only work among people who fear God. Once the oath means nothing, the system collapses.

Uncertain wording. “Come near to God” (v. 8) and “come before God” (v. 9) may mean the sanctuary or the judges who acted for God; the verb “condemns” in v. 9 is plural in Hebrew, one reason older translations read “the judges”. Either way the dispute is settled in God’s presence, not by private force.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A people set apart for God must guard marriage and worship. A man who seduces an unbetrothed young woman must pay the bride-price and marry her, or pay it anyway if her father refuses, so that she does not bear the cost of his sin (vv. 16–17). Three practices common among the nations around Israel carry death: sorcery, sex with an animal and sacrifice to any god but the LORD (vv. 18–20). Each strikes at the covenant itself, by seeking power apart from God, by defacing the image of God, or by giving his worship to another.
verseByVerse.theology:
Purity Guarded

The man carries the whole cost, and the nation's boundaries are drawn sharply.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the woman was protected from being discarded. Now: God still cares who carries the cost of sexual sin.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man seduces a virgin who is not betrothed and lies with her, he shall give the bride-price for her and make her his wife. If her father utterly refuses to give her to him, he shall pay money equal to the bride-price for virgins. "You shall not permit a sorceress to live. "Whoever lies with an animal shall be put to death. "Whoever sacrifices to any god, other than the LORD alone, shall be devoted to destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man who seduces a young woman must bear the full cost, and sorcery, bestiality and worship of other gods carry death because they strike at the covenant.

If a man seduces a virgin. He must pay the bride-price (the groom’s payment to her family) and marry her, or, if her father refuses, pay it anyway. In that culture she had lost her marriage prospects and with them her economic future, and the law makes the man carry the full cost, with no option to walk away.

Three capital crimes. Sorcery, bestiality and sacrifice to any god but the LORD each carry death. These laws mark out a nation that is to be different, and they are severe because the nations of Canaan were known for all of them (Leviticus 18:23–24; Deuteronomy 18:9–12). Devoted to destruction means handed over wholly to God’s judgment.

Does verse 18 justify witch trials? The death penalty belonged to Israel’s civil law, and sorcery there was treason against the covenant God. The church has no such sword (John 18:36), and the witch-hunts of later centuries had no warrant from this text. What remains is the prohibition: occult practice, seeking the spirits or the dead, is forbidden to God’s people (Deuteronomy 18:10–12; Galatians 5:20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: This is the heart of the chapter and of God’s character. Israel must not wrong the sojourner, the resident foreigner, because they were sojourners in Egypt (v. 21). Whoever mistreats a widow or an orphan will find God himself as their defender, and the punishment will fit the crime (vv. 22–24). Lending to the poor must not become a way of profiting from their need (v. 25), and a cloak taken as a pledge must be returned before nightfall, because it is the poor man’s only blanket (vv. 26–27). The reason is simple and personal: “I will hear, for I am compassionate.”
verseByVerse.theology:
Mercy for the Vulnerable

Memory of Egypt becomes mercy to the weak.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: those who had been strangers were to protect strangers. Now: James catches the tone of this section: pure religion visits orphans and widows in their affliction (James 1:27).

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not wrong a sojourner or oppress him, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt. You shall not mistreat any widow or fatherless child. If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry, and my wrath will burn, and I will kill you with the sword, and your wives shall become widows and your children fatherless. "If you lend money to any of my people with you who is poor, you shall not be like a moneylender to him, and you shall not exact interest from him. If ever you take your neighbor's cloak in pledge, you shall return it to him before the sun goes down, for that is his only covering, and it is his cloak for his body; in what else shall he sleep? And if he cries to me, I will hear, for I am compassionate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is the defender of the foreigner, the widow, the orphan and the poor: he hears their cry, and he will not let his people profit from their weakness.

The sojourner is a resident foreigner, without land or family to protect him, and here Israel’s law is least like its neighbours’. The reason given is memory: “you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.” Israel is not told that foreigners have rights in the abstract; it is told to remember what it felt like, which is far harder to argue your way out of.

The widow and the fatherless. The warning has startling heat: the punishment is shaped like the crime, the oppressors’ own wives made widows and their children fatherless. God does not merely disapprove of exploiting the defenceless; he undertakes to answer it personally.

You shall not exact interest from him. The law on lending is not a ban on commerce but a ban on making money out of a neighbour’s disaster.

The cloak. Here is what kind of God stands behind this law. In the middle of a code about oxen and pits, he stops to consider whether a particular poor man will be cold tonight, and makes a law about it. What backs it is not a stated penalty but God’s own character: “I will hear, for I am compassionate.” The God of the thunder on the mountain is listening for one cold man’s complaint about a coat.

Strangers brought near. We too were strangers to God’s promises, and in Christ we are “no longer strangers and aliens” but members of his household (Ephesians 2:12, 19). Grace received becomes grace extended (Matthew 10:8).

Is lending at interest sin? The law forbids profiting from a poor neighbour in his need (Leviticus 25:35–37), and the principle stands. It did not forbid all interest: Israel could charge a foreigner in trade (Deuteronomy 23:20), and Jesus speaks of money placed with bankers to earn it (Matthew 25:27). Ordinary commercial lending and saving are not sin; exploiting the desperate is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28-31 — Reverence Toward God and Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything belongs to God first. His people must not revile him or curse their rulers (v. 28). They must not hold back the first and best of the harvest, and their firstborn sons and animals belong to him; the young animal stays seven days with its mother before it is given (vv. 29–30). The chapter closes with the reason behind every law in it, “You shall be consecrated to me”, shown even in refusing meat torn by wild beasts (v. 31). Holiness means belonging to God in every part of life.
verseByVerse.theology:
Reverence Toward God and Men

Everything belongs to God first.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul honoured verse 28 at his own trial (Acts 23:5). Now: the redeemed belong to God before they do anything for him.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler of your people. "You shall not delay to offer from the fullness of your harvest and from the outflow of your presses. The firstborn of your sons you shall give to me. You shall do the same with your oxen and with your sheep: seven days it shall be with its mother; on the eighth day you shall give it to me. "You shall be consecrated to me. Therefore you shall not eat any flesh that is torn by beasts in the field; you shall throw it to the dogs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything belongs to God first: his name, the first of the harvest, the firstborn, and his people themselves, who are set apart for him.

You shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler. Reverence for God carries over into respect for those who govern under him. Paul honoured this verse even before the high priest who had ordered him struck: “You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people” (Acts 23:5).

Everything belongs to God first. The firstfruits and firstborn are given without delay, and the newborn animal stays seven days with its mother, a small mercy tucked inside a sacrificial rule. Meat torn by wild animals is refused because its blood had not been drained and it made the eater unclean (Leviticus 17:15; 22:8): a people consecrated to God does not eat a carcass, and the dogs may have it.

The reason given. The last line supplies the reason: “You shall be consecrated to me.” Not “you shall be moral”, but set apart, belonging to someone. Every regulation in these chapters flows from that sentence, which is why Peter could write to Gentile churches, “as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct” (1 Peter 1:15).

Did God demand child sacrifice (v. 29)? No. Firstborn sons were given to God and redeemed with a payment (13:13; Numbers 18:15–16), and the law condemns child sacrifice as an abomination (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31). The firstborn of Israel lived because the firstborn of Egypt died, and every redeemed son pointed to the Son whom God did not spare (Romans 8:32).

Uncertain wording. “God” in v. 28 (elohim) was rendered “the gods” or “the judges” by some older translations. In v. 29 “fullness” and “outflow” are rare words, probably grain and the juice of grapes and olives.

keyVerse.quote: And if he cries to me, I will hear, for I am compassionate.
keyVerse.note: The chapter’s laws rest not on a penalty but on God’s own heart. The God who heard Israel in Egypt still hears the poor man shivering without his cloak, and he binds his people to be like him.

22.reflection:
Israel’s law on theft asks first what the victim has lost (vv. 1–4), and Zacchaeus applied it to himself (Luke 19:8). Is there anything you need to put right with someone, and what would restitution look like?

God grounds care for the foreigner in Israel’s memory: “you were sojourners in the land of Egypt” (v. 21). How does remembering what you were before Christ (Ephesians 2:12, 19) change the way you treat outsiders?

In verses 26–27 God stops to ask where a poor man will sleep tonight. Who are the vulnerable people near you, and how could your home group act for them this month?

“You shall be consecrated to me” (v. 31) stands behind every law in the chapter. Which part of your ordinary life (money, property, work, words about leaders) most needs to be brought under that sentence?

23.title: Sacred Time and the Guiding Angel
23.text: <sup>1</sup>"You shall not spread a false report. You shall not join hands with a wicked man to be a malicious witness.<sup>2</sup>You shall not fall in with the many to do evil, nor shall you bear witness in a lawsuit, siding with the many, so as to pervert justice,<sup>3</sup>nor shall you be partial to a poor man in his lawsuit.<sup>4</sup>"If you meet your enemy's ox or his donkey going astray, you shall bring it back to him.<sup>5</sup>If you see the donkey of one who hates you lying down under its burden, you shall refrain from leaving him with it; you shall rescue it with him.<sup>6</sup>"You shall not pervert the justice due to your poor in his lawsuit.<sup>7</sup>Keep far from a false charge, and do not kill the innocent and righteous, for I will not acquit the wicked.<sup>8</sup>And you shall take no bribe, for a bribe blinds the clear-sighted and subverts the cause of those who are in the right.<sup>9</sup>"You shall not oppress a sojourner. You know the heart of a sojourner, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.<sup>10</sup>"For six years you shall sow your land and gather in its yield,<sup>11</sup>but the seventh year you shall let it rest and lie fallow, that the poor of your people may eat; and what they leave the beasts of the field may eat. You shall do likewise with your vineyard, and with your olive orchard.<sup>12</sup>"Six days you shall do your work, but on the seventh day you shall rest; that your ox and your donkey may have rest, and the son of your servant woman, and the alien, may be refreshed.<sup>13</sup>"Pay attention to all that I have said to you, and make no mention of the names of other gods, nor let it be heard on your lips.<sup>14</sup>"Three times in the year you shall keep a feast to me.<sup>15</sup>You shall keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread. As I commanded you, you shall eat unleavened bread for seven days at the appointed time in the month of Abib, for in it you came out of Egypt. None shall appear before me empty-handed.<sup>16</sup>You shall keep the Feast of Harvest, of the firstfruits of your labor, of what you sow in the field. You shall keep the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the year, when you gather in from the field the fruit of your labor.<sup>17</sup>Three times in the year shall all your males appear before the Lord GOD.<sup>18</sup>"You shall not offer the blood of my sacrifice with anything leavened, or let the fat of my feast remain until the morning.<sup>19</sup>"The best of the firstfruits of your ground you shall bring into the house of the LORD your God. "You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk.<sup>20</sup>"Behold, I send an angel before you to guard you on the way and to bring you to the place that I have prepared.<sup>21</sup>Pay careful attention to him and obey his voice; do not rebel against him, for he will not pardon your transgression, for my name is in him.<sup>22</sup>"But if you carefully obey his voice and do all that I say, then I will be an enemy to your enemies and an adversary to your adversaries.<sup>23</sup>"When my angel goes before you and brings you to the Amorites and the Hittites and the Perizzites and the Canaanites, the Hivites and the Jebusites, and I blot them out,<sup>24</sup>you shall not bow down to their gods nor serve them, nor do as they do, but you shall utterly overthrow them and break their pillars in pieces.<sup>25</sup>You shall serve the LORD your God, and he will bless your bread and your water, and I will take sickness away from among you.<sup>26</sup>None shall miscarry or be barren in your land; I will fulfill the number of your days.<sup>27</sup>I will send my terror before you and will throw into confusion all the people against whom you shall come, and I will make all your enemies turn their backs to you.<sup>28</sup>And I will send hornets before you, which shall drive out the Hivites, the Canaanites, and the Hittites from before you.<sup>29</sup>I will not drive them out from before you in one year, lest the land become desolate and the wild beasts multiply against you.<sup>30</sup>Little by little I will drive them out from before you, until you have increased and possess the land.<sup>31</sup>And I will set your border from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines, and from the wilderness to the Euphrates, for I will give the inhabitants of the land into your hand, and you shall drive them out before you.<sup>32</sup>You shall make no covenant with them and their gods.<sup>33</sup>They shall not dwell in your land, lest they make you sin against me; for if you serve their gods, it will surely be a snare to you."
23.overview:
Where we are. This is the last chapter of the Book of the Covenant (20:22–23:33), the case laws God gave Moses on Sinai after the Ten Commandments. In the next chapter Moses will read it to the people and seal the covenant with blood (24:3–8).

The message. The God who redeemed Israel shapes their courts, their calendar and their future. His justice takes no bribes and no sides and reaches even an enemy’s straying donkey. He gives his people rest and feasts, so that their whole year is lived in thankful dependence on him. And he goes before them himself, in the angel who bears his name, to bring them into the place he has prepared.

Why it was said. Israel was about to leave Sinai for a land full of other gods, other customs and powerful enemies (see the introduction). They needed courts that could not be bought, a rhythm of life that kept them trusting God rather than grinding the poor, and the assurance that God would lead and fight for them, together with a warning that compromise would be a snare.

How the chapter makes its case. It begins in the courtroom: no false reports, no going along with the crowd, no favouritism, no bribes, and help even for an enemy’s animal (vv. 1–9). Then comes sacred time: the sabbath year that feeds the poor and the weekly rest for servants and animals (vv. 10–13), and the three pilgrim feasts that frame Israel’s year (vv. 14–19). It ends with promise and warning: God sends his angel to guard and lead them, will bless them and drive out their enemies little by little, and forbids any covenant with the gods of the land (vv. 20–33).

Where it leads. By pattern, by promise and by the need exposed. The court this chapter forbids is the court that condemned Jesus, where “many bore false witness against him” (Mark 14:56) and a governor gave way to the crowd. Two of the three feasts were fulfilled in his death, resurrection and the gift of the Spirit, and the third awaits the final harvest. And the angel in whom God’s name dwells is, as this commentary reads him, the Son himself, going before his people to bring them to “the place that I have prepared” (v. 20; John 14:2–3).

For us. Be just and honest when the crowd or your sympathies pull the other way, and do good to people who dislike you. Receive rest and worship as gifts, not burdens. And follow Christ through the land ahead, trusting him when the victory comes little by little.
23.theology:
Impartial justice and enemy-love. God’s law forbids favouritism and commands kindness even to enemies.

Sacred time. Sabbaths and feasts set time apart for rest, worship and remembrance, and point ahead to the eternal rest of God's people.

The guiding presence of God. The Angel in whom God's name dwells leads and guards his people to the prepared place, fulfilled in Christ, Immanuel, God with us.
23.examples:
Then: God sent his Angel to lead Israel to the prepared land.

Now: God still calls his people to truth, justice and love of enemies. We fail at all three; Christ did not, and his perfect obedience is counted as ours (Phil. 3:9), while his Spirit makes us able to love even those who hate us (Gal. 5:22). And he never sends us anywhere alone: in Christ, God with us, the guiding presence leads us home.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Justice in God’s people must not bend to lies, pressure, sympathy or money. No one may spread a false report, back a wicked man’s case or go along with the majority to pervert justice, and even a poor man must not be favoured in court (vv. 1–3). Kindness reaches the enemy: his straying ox must be returned and his fallen donkey helped up (vv. 4–5). The poor must not be denied justice, false charges must be kept far away, bribes refused, and the sojourner protected, because Israel knows from Egypt what it is to be a stranger (vv. 6–9).
verseByVerse.theology:
Justice for All

Truth in the witness box, and help for the enemy in the road.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the law protected the court from crowd, bribe and sympathy alike. Now: the God who loved us while we were his enemies (Rom. 5:10) asks us to lift our enemy's load.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not spread a false report. You shall not join hands with a wicked man to be a malicious witness. You shall not fall in with the many to do evil, nor shall you bear witness in a lawsuit, siding with the many, so as to pervert justice, nor shall you be partial to a poor man in his lawsuit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s people must not let lies, malice, the crowd or even sympathy for the poor bend the truth in court.

Join hands with a wicked man. To join hands is to make common cause: the witness who backs a wicked man’s case becomes his partner in it. A “malicious witness” is literally a witness of violence (Hebrew ʿed ḥamas), because false testimony could take a man’s land, liberty or life, as it took Naboth’s (1 Kings 21:10–13). The ninth commandment (20:16) is here applied to the courtroom.

The many. The commonest failure of all is crowd pressure: not bribery or malice but the ordinary instinct to go along. The number of people holding a view is not evidence for it, and a witness who shapes his testimony to suit the majority has perverted justice as surely as one who lied for money.

Partial to the poor. A startling balance: favouring a poor man in his lawsuit is forbidden (v. 3), and a few verses later so is denying him justice (v. 6). The law is fiercely protective of the poor everywhere except in the witness box, where sympathy is as corrupting as contempt. Justice is not the same thing as taking the weaker side.

The court that condemned Jesus. Every failure named here met in one trial. “Many bore false witness against him” (Mark 14:56), the crowd cried out, and Pilate, “wishing to satisfy the crowd”, handed over a man he knew to be innocent (Mark 15:15). The one perfectly just man was condemned by perverted justice, so that the guilty could be acquitted justly (Romans 3:26).

verseByVerse.quote: "If you meet your enemy's ox or his donkey going astray, you shall bring it back to him. If you see the donkey of one who hates you lying down under its burden, you shall refrain from leaving him with it; you shall rescue it with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do good even to your enemy: bring back his straying animal and help him lift his fallen donkey.

If you meet your enemy’s ox. An animal found wandering is to be taken back to its owner, even when the owner is your enemy. Deuteronomy 22:1–4 gives the same duty towards a brother’s animal and anything else he has lost. The duty to a neighbour does not depend on liking him.

Your enemy’s donkey. This small law has a long reach. It is not enough to refrain from harming your enemy: go and heave his animal upright alongside him, in the road, where you will both be sweating and neither will know what to say. It is very hard to keep hating a man you have just done that with, which is presumably the idea. Centuries later Jesus made it a principle: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44), and he loved us when we were his enemies (Romans 5:10).

Uncertain wording. Verse 5 is compressed in Hebrew and its verbs can be read more than one way, but the ESV gives the likely sense: help him, together.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not pervert the justice due to your poor in his lawsuit. Keep far from a false charge, and do not kill the innocent and righteous, for I will not acquit the wicked. And you shall take no bribe, for a bribe blinds the clear-sighted and subverts the cause of those who are in the right. "You shall not oppress a sojourner. You know the heart of a sojourner, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Justice must never be denied to the poor or bought with a bribe, and the foreigner must not be oppressed, because God himself will not acquit the wicked.

Keep far from a false charge. “Keep far” is stronger than “do not bring”: stay well away from any case built on a lie. “The innocent and righteous” are those in the right in the case; in a capital trial a false charge kills them by law. The reason is God’s own justice: “I will not acquit the wicked.” If a court lets the guilty go, God will not, and the judge who connives shares the guilt (Proverbs 17:15).

You shall take no bribe. A bribe “blinds the clear-sighted”: it works on able, honest men, not only on the corrupt, because it bends judgment before the judge notices. Deuteronomy 16:19 repeats the law, and Samuel’s defence of his whole life was that he had taken no bribe (1 Samuel 12:3). A gift that comes with an expectation of favour still does the same quiet work.

You know the heart of a sojourner. A sojourner was a foreigner living in Israel without land or kin to protect him, and so easy to wrong in court and market. The law has said this already (22:21); here the reason is personal: “you know the heart”, the inner life, of a stranger, because you were strangers in Egypt. Israel’s memory of its own suffering was to make it gentle with the outsider.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10-13 — The Sabbath Year and the Sabbath Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God builds rest and generosity into Israel’s calendar. Every seventh year the fields, vineyards and olive groves are left unharvested so that the poor and the wild animals may eat (vv. 10–11). Every seventh day work stops, so that oxen, donkeys, the servant’s son and the foreigner may be refreshed (v. 12). Then a summary warning: pay attention to all God has said, and do not even speak the names of other gods (v. 13). Rest is God’s gift to the weakest, and a sign that Israel belongs to him alone.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sabbath Year and the Sabbath Day

Rest is given to those who own nothing.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the poor and the worker were the ones the rest was for. Now: rest is a mercy the strong owe the weak.

verseByVerse.quote: "For six years you shall sow your land and gather in its yield, but the seventh year you shall let it rest and lie fallow, that the poor of your people may eat; and what they leave the beasts of the field may eat. You shall do likewise with your vineyard, and with your olive orchard. "Six days you shall do your work, but on the seventh day you shall rest; that your ox and your donkey may have rest, and the son of your servant woman, and the alien, may be refreshed. "Pay attention to all that I have said to you, and make no mention of the names of other gods, nor let it be heard on your lips.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every seventh year the land rests so that the poor can eat, and every seventh day work stops so that servants, foreigners and animals can be refreshed.

The seventh year you shall let it rest. The sabbath principle extends from the week to the calendar (see the sabbath year): every seventh year the land lies fallow. It is good agriculture, but that is not the reason given. The beneficiary named is the poor, who may glean freely from the untended fields, and the wild animals get the rest. God builds a year into Israel’s economy that hands the harvest to those with no land.

On the seventh day you shall rest. The weekly Sabbath is restated with the same emphasis: the list is of those who do not own the land they work. The rhythm that began as a gift of manna (16:29) keeps Israel from grinding down its own workforce.

Rest in Christ. The Sabbath pointed to the rest Christ gives (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9). Christians receive the Lord’s Day as a gift, and those with power still must not deny rest to those who work for them (see Worship & the Lord’s Day).

Make no mention of the names of other gods. Not even to swear by them or speak of them as real powers (Joshua 23:7). Loyalty to God reaches the tongue.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three times a year all Israel’s men are to appear before the LORD at a feast, and none may come empty-handed (vv. 14–15, 17). Unleavened Bread in spring remembers the exodus; the Feast of Harvest gives thanks for the first grain; the Feast of Ingathering closes the year at the last harvest (vv. 15–16). Short rules guard the purity of the offerings: no leaven with the blood of sacrifice, no fat left until morning, the best firstfruits brought to God’s house, and a young goat not boiled in its mother’s milk (vv. 18–19).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Three Annual Feasts

The calendar is built around harvest, gratitude and God's presence.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the nation left its fields in God’s care three times a year. Now: Christ died at Passover and the Spirit came at Pentecost; the final ingathering is still to come.

verseByVerse.quote: "Three times in the year you shall keep a feast to me. You shall keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread. As I commanded you, you shall eat unleavened bread for seven days at the appointed time in the month of Abib, for in it you came out of Egypt. None shall appear before me empty-handed. You shall keep the Feast of Harvest, of the firstfruits of your labor, of what you sow in the field. You shall keep the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the year, when you gather in from the field the fruit of your labor. Three times in the year shall all your males appear before the Lord GOD. "You shall not offer the blood of my sacrifice with anything leavened, or let the fat of my feast remain until the morning. "The best of the firstfruits of your ground you shall bring into the house of the LORD your God. "You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three times a year all Israel is to stop work and come before the LORD with thankful gifts, keeping the feasts that remember the exodus and celebrate the harvest.

Three times in the year you shall keep a feast to me. Each festival is tied to the farming year: Unleavened Bread in the spring, remembering that “in it you came out of Egypt”; Harvest at the first fruits of the grain (later called Weeks, or Pentecost); and Ingathering at the end of the year (Booths). The nation stops work and travels, a real act of trust: the fields are left, and God undertakes to guard them (34:24). None shall appear before me empty-handed: worship includes giving back from what God has given.

Fulfilled on their own festival days. These three are also the frame on which the gospel later hangs. Christ was crucified at Passover and Unleavened Bread, raised as the firstfruits (“Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep”, 1 Corinthians 15:20), and the Spirit was poured out at the Feast of Weeks, Pentecost. Two of the three were fulfilled on their own festival days, in the same city, within fifty days. The third, Ingathering, still waits for the final gathering of God’s people.

Why not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk (v. 19)? Nobody knows for certain. Older scholars thought it a Canaanite ritual, though the ancient text once cited for this is now read differently; many think it simply forbade turning what was meant to nourish a young animal into the means of cooking it. The later Jewish rule of separating all meat and dairy grew from this verse. Christians are not bound by it, since the food laws are fulfilled in Christ (Mark 7:19).
verseByVerse.note: The three pilgrim feasts: Unleavened Bread (with Passover), Harvest (later called Weeks or Pentecost), and Ingathering (Booths).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20-33 — The Angel and the Promise of Conquest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God promises to go before his people and warns them not to compromise. He sends an angel to guard them and bring them to the place he has prepared, an angel who bears God’s own name and must be obeyed (vv. 20–22). He will bring them into the land, and they must destroy its idols and serve the LORD, who will bless their food, health and families (vv. 23–26). He will send terror and hornets ahead of them and drive out their enemies little by little (vv. 27–30). He sets wide borders, and forbids any covenant with the nations or their gods, which would be a snare (vv. 31–33).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Angel and the Promise of Conquest

God goes ahead of his people, at a pace they can manage.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the land was taken at the pace it could be held. Now: compromise with what God has judged is still a snare.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I send an angel before you to guard you on the way and to bring you to the place that I have prepared. Pay careful attention to him and obey his voice; do not rebel against him, for he will not pardon your transgression, for my name is in him. "But if you carefully obey his voice and do all that I say, then I will be an enemy to your enemies and an adversary to your adversaries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends before Israel an angel who bears his own name, to guard them and bring them home, and to obey him is to obey God.

I send an angel before you. Israel is to obey this angel as they would obey God, for my name is in him, and he can withhold pardon (v. 21), as only God can. He is the figure who appeared in the bush and spoke as God in the first person (3:2–6).

An enemy to your enemies. Obedience to his voice is the condition, and the promise is God’s own alliance: whoever fights Israel will find God fighting them, as he promised Abraham (Genesis 12:3).

The place that I have prepared. The angel goes ahead to bring God’s people to a prepared place. Jesus used the same words of himself: “I go to prepare a place for you” and “I will come again and will take you to myself” (John 14:2–3).

Where Christians differ. Some read this angel as a created angel who speaks for God, as an ambassador carries his king’s authority.

This commentary’s view. He is not a created angel but the LORD present with his people, best read as the Son appearing before his incarnation. God’s name is in him and he can pardon or refuse to pardon. Paul says that the Rock that followed Israel “was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).

verseByVerse.quote: "When my angel goes before you and brings you to the Amorites and the Hittites and the Perizzites and the Canaanites, the Hivites and the Jebusites, and I blot them out, you shall not bow down to their gods nor serve them, nor do as they do, but you shall utterly overthrow them and break their pillars in pieces. You shall serve the LORD your God, and he will bless your bread and your water, and I will take sickness away from among you. None shall miscarry or be barren in your land; I will fulfill the number of your days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God brings Israel into the land, they must destroy its idols and serve the LORD alone, and he promises to bless their food, health and families.

Break their pillars in pieces. The “pillars” were standing stones set up for Canaanite gods. Israel is not only to refuse their worship but to destroy its equipment, and not to “do as they do”: the danger was never the stones but the way of life that went with them.

He will bless your bread and your water. Serving the LORD brings daily food, health, children and a full span of life. These were covenant promises to Israel in the land (Deuteronomy 7:12–15). Christians are not promised freedom from sickness or childlessness, but they have the Father who knows what they need and gives it to those who seek his kingdom first (Matthew 6:31–33). Childlessness and miscarriage are never in themselves signs of God’s displeasure.

Was it just for God to command the Canaanites destroyed (vv. 23–24)? The question should be felt at full strength, for whole communities fell. It was his judgment on peoples whose sin had reached its full measure (Genesis 15:16), which included child sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31), and Israel was warned that it would be judged in the same way if it did the same (Leviticus 18:24–28). It was a unique command, carried out by Israel under God, and it gives no warrant for any later war in God’s name. Christ’s kingdom is “not of this world”, and his servants do not fight for it with the sword (John 18:36).

verseByVerse.quote: I will send my terror before you and will throw into confusion all the people against whom you shall come, and I will make all your enemies turn their backs to you. And I will send hornets before you, which shall drive out the Hivites, the Canaanites, and the Hittites from before you. I will not drive them out from before you in one year, lest the land become desolate and the wild beasts multiply against you. Little by little I will drive them out from before you, until you have increased and possess the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself will rout Israel’s enemies, but he will drive them out little by little, at the pace his people can hold the land.

My terror … hornets. God himself goes ahead: panic in the enemy, as at the sea (14:24), and hornets. Joshua 24:12 looks back on it: the hornet drove out the Amorite kings, “it was not by your sword or by your bow.” Either way the victory is God’s.

Little by little. God explains his own slowness: he could clear Canaan in a season, but a small nation in an emptied country would be overrun by wild animals before it could fill the space. So progress is deliberately gradual, matched to what Israel can occupy and hold.

In the Christian life. The same pattern governs the Christian life. Sanctification, growth in holiness, is almost never one sweeping victory; it is ground taken slowly, and the slowness is not God’s reluctance but his knowledge of the ground. “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6): the completion is certain and the timetable is his.

Uncertain wording. “Hornets” renders a word found only here and in Deuteronomy 7:20 and Joshua 24:12: literal hornets, or a picture of the terror that routs the enemy.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will set your border from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines, and from the wilderness to the Euphrates, for I will give the inhabitants of the land into your hand, and you shall drive them out before you. You shall make no covenant with them and their gods. They shall not dwell in your land, lest they make you sin against me; for if you serve their gods, it will surely be a snare to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises Israel wide borders and victory, and forbids any treaty with the nations or their gods, because their gods would be a snare.

From the Red Sea to the Euphrates. The promised borders are wide: from the Red Sea (here probably the Gulf of Aqaba) to the Mediterranean, “the Sea of the Philistines”, and from the southern wilderness to the Euphrates, the land promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18). Israel held something like them only under David and Solomon (1 Kings 4:21), and only for a time.

No covenant with them. The final warning is about compromise: their gods will be a snare. Israel will ignore it, and the book of Judges tells what followed (Judges 2:1–3). The snare for us is rarely a carved idol; it is the quiet treaty with whatever rivals Christ for our trust.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, I send an angel before you to guard you on the way and to bring you to the place that I have prepared.
keyVerse.note: The laws of the covenant end not with a demand but with a promise: God himself goes ahead of his people, in the angel who bears his name, to guard them and bring them home. Jesus speaks the same language of a prepared place (John 14:2–3).

23.reflection:
Verses 1–3 forbid going along with “the many” and even favouring the poor in court. Where do you feel pressure to shade the truth to suit the crowd, or to suit your sympathies?

God commands Israel to help an enemy lift his fallen donkey (v. 5). Who is the person you find hardest to love, and what practical help could you give them this week?

The sabbath year and the weekly rest protected the poor, servants and animals (vv. 10–12). How do you receive rest as God’s gift, and how might your choices give or deny rest to others?

God drives out Israel’s enemies “little by little” (v. 30). How does that encourage you in a slow fight against a particular sin, and how does Philippians 1:6 give you hope?

24.title: The Blood of the Covenant
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Then he said to Moses, "Come up to the LORD, you and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel, and worship from afar.<sup>2</sup>Moses alone shall come near to the LORD, but the others shall not come near, and the people shall not come up with him."<sup>3</sup>Moses came and told the people all the words of the LORD and all the rules. And all the people answered with one voice and said, "All the words that the LORD has spoken we will do."<sup>4</sup>And Moses wrote down all the words of the LORD. He rose early in the morning and built an altar at the foot of the mountain, and twelve pillars, according to the twelve tribes of Israel.<sup>5</sup>And he sent young men of the people of Israel, who offered burnt offerings and sacrificed peace offerings of oxen to the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And Moses took half of the blood and put it in basins, and half of the blood he threw against the altar.<sup>7</sup>Then he took the Book of the Covenant and read it in the hearing of the people. And they said, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient."<sup>8</sup>And Moses took the blood and threw it on the people and said, "Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words."<sup>9</sup>Then Moses and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel went up,<sup>10</sup>and they saw the God of Israel. There was under his feet as it were a pavement of sapphire stone, like the very heaven for clearness.<sup>11</sup>And he did not lay his hand on the chief men of the people of Israel; they beheld God, and ate and drank.<sup>12</sup>The LORD said to Moses, "Come up to me on the mountain and wait there, that I may give you the tablets of stone, with the law and the commandment, which I have written for their instruction."<sup>13</sup>So Moses rose with his assistant Joshua, and Moses went up into the mountain of God.<sup>14</sup>And he said to the elders, "Wait here for us until we return to you. And behold, Aaron and Hur are with you. Whoever has a dispute, let him go to them."<sup>15</sup>Then Moses went up on the mountain, and the cloud covered the mountain.<sup>16</sup>The glory of the LORD dwelt on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days. And on the seventh day he called to Moses out of the midst of the cloud.<sup>17</sup>Now the appearance of the glory of the LORD was like a devouring fire on the top of the mountain in the sight of the people of Israel.<sup>18</sup>Moses entered the cloud and went up on the mountain. And Moses was on the mountain forty days and forty nights.
24.overview:
Where we are. God has spoken the Ten Commandments (chapter 20) and given Moses the case laws of the Book of the Covenant (20:22–23:33). Now the covenant offered at the foot of Sinai (19:5–6) is formally sealed, and this chapter closes the second movement of the book; from chapter 25 God speaks of the tabernacle where he will live among them.

The message. God binds a sinful people to himself, and the bond is sealed in blood. Sacrifices are offered, the covenant is read, the people promise obedience, and the blood is thrown on the altar and on them. Then their leaders go up, see the God of Israel, and eat and drink in his presence without being destroyed. Sinners may have fellowship with the holy God, but only through blood and only on his terms.

Why it was said. Israel needed to know that they belonged to the LORD by a covenant he had made and sealed, not by a vague agreement they could drop when it suited them (see the introduction). Every later generation, renewing the covenant or breaking it, looked back to this day, and the prophets would promise a new covenant because this one was so soon broken (Jeremiah 31:31–32).

How the chapter makes its case. God summons Moses and the leaders, and Moses tells the people all his words; they answer, “All the words that the LORD has spoken we will do” (vv. 1–3). Moses writes the words down, builds an altar with twelve pillars, offers sacrifices, reads the Book of the Covenant, and throws the blood on altar and people (vv. 4–8). Then seventy-four men see the God of Israel and eat and drink before him (vv. 9–11). Finally Moses goes up into the cloud of fire to receive the tablets and stays forty days (vv. 12–18).

Where it leads. By covenant, and by the need it exposes. Jesus took Moses’ words at the Last Supper and made them his own: “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many” (Mark 14:24). The meal on the mountain points to the Lord’s Supper and to “the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9). And the people’s eager promise, soon broken, shows why we need a covenant in which Christ has already given the obedience and shed the blood.

For us. We come to God only through the blood of Christ, and through it we may come with joy and sit at his table. Our promises to God are as fragile as Israel’s, so we rest on his promise and his Son’s faithfulness, and we keep trusting when he seems slow to come down the mountain.
24.theology:
The covenant sealed in blood. A holy God and sinful people can be bound only through sacrificial blood, fulfilled in Christ's blood of the new covenant (Matt. 26:28).

Communion with God as the goal. The elders see God and eat and drink in his presence.

The mediator who ascends. Moses enters God’s glory for the people, pointing ahead to Christ, who entered heaven itself on our behalf (Heb. 9:24).
24.examples:
Then: The covenant was ratified in blood thrown on altar and people, and the elders ate and drank in God's presence.

Now: By the blood of Christ, poured out for the forgiveness of sins, we are brought into communion with God, and feast at the Lord's table until we eat with him face to face.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-8 — The Blood of the Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The covenant between God and Israel is sealed in blood. God calls Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu and seventy elders to worship from a distance, while Moses alone draws near (vv. 1–2). Moses tells the people all God’s words, and they promise as one to do them (v. 3). He writes the words down, builds an altar with twelve pillars for the tribes, and has young men offer sacrifices (vv. 4–5). Half the blood is thrown on the altar; then the Book of the Covenant is read, the people promise again, and the rest of the blood is thrown on them: “Behold the blood of the covenant” (vv. 6–8).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Blood of the Covenant

The same blood is put on God’s altar and on the people: one death binds both.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the people promised a third time, and meant it. Now: the new covenant rests on God’s promises, which are better than ours (Heb. 8:6).

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to Moses, "Come up to the LORD, you and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel, and worship from afar. Moses alone shall come near to the LORD, but the others shall not come near, and the people shall not come up with him." Moses came and told the people all the words of the LORD and all the rules. And all the people answered with one voice and said, "All the words that the LORD has spoken we will do." And Moses wrote down all the words of the LORD. He rose early in the morning and built an altar at the foot of the mountain, and twelve pillars, according to the twelve tribes of Israel. And he sent young men of the people of Israel, who offered burnt offerings and sacrificed peace offerings of oxen to the LORD. And Moses took half of the blood and put it in basins, and half of the blood he threw against the altar. Then he took the Book of the Covenant and read it in the hearing of the people. And they said, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient." And Moses took the blood and threw it on the people and said, "Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The covenant is sealed: the people hear God’s words and promise obedience, and the blood of sacrifice is thrown on God’s altar and on them.

Worship from afar. God calls the leaders up, but even they must keep their distance; Moses alone may come near. The boundaries of chapter 19 still stand.

Twelve pillars, according to the twelve tribes of Israel. Moses writes the words down, builds an altar, and sets up twelve pillars, one for each tribe. Young men offer burnt offerings and peace offerings because Israel has no priests yet; Aaron and his sons are ordained only later (chapters 28–29).

Blood on both sides. Half goes on the altar, God’s side, and half on the people, theirs, and between the two the Book of the Covenant is read and the people promise yet again (19:8; 24:3, 7). The same death now stands over both parties. That is what a covenant is: not a contract between equals but a bond sealed in death, with both sides inside it.

Behold the blood of the covenant. Hebrews takes this scene as its proof that “without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins”, quoting Moses’ words almost exactly: “This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you” (Hebrews 9:18–22).

This is my blood of the covenant. Those words were to be spoken again, more famously. On the night he was betrayed, at Passover, Jesus took a cup and said, “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many” (Mark 14:24). His disciples would have known where the words came from: Moses, a basin and a mountain. He took them and made it my blood. He was not inventing a metaphor but announcing that the ceremony at Sinai had reached the reality it pointed to: the blood thrown over a crowd was always a rehearsal for blood poured out for many.

We will be obedient. That matters because of what the people had just promised. They meant it, standing under blood, and within forty days they would be dancing round a calf. The blood of Exodus 24 sealed a covenant Israel broke almost at once. The blood of the new covenant seals a covenant in which the obedience required has already been given by Christ, whose blood it is. Make your promises to God, but rest your hope on his.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9-11 — They Beheld God and Ate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Once the blood has been shed, the leaders of a sinful people are welcomed into God’s presence. Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu and seventy elders go up the mountain and see the God of Israel (vv. 9–10). The text describes only what was under his feet, a pavement like sapphire, clear as the sky, and it records twice that they saw him. God does not strike them down; instead they eat and drink before him (v. 11). The covenant meal shows what the covenant is for: fellowship between God and his people, made possible by sacrifice.
verseByVerse.theology:
They Beheld God and Ate

Sinners under the blood sit at God's table and live.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the elders saw only what was under his feet, and it was enough. Now: the Lord's table is a meal in the presence of the same God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel went up, and they saw the God of Israel. There was under his feet as it were a pavement of sapphire stone, like the very heaven for clearness. And he did not lay his hand on the chief men of the people of Israel; they beheld God, and ate and drank.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the blood, Israel’s leaders go up, see the God of Israel and eat and drink in his presence, and he does not destroy them.

They saw the God of Israel. These three verses are so unexpected that readers often pass over them. Seventy-four men climbed a mountain and saw God. The text says it twice, plainly, and goes out of its way to record that nobody died, which tells you what everyone in the story expected to happen.

Under his feet. The description is careful about its limits: a pavement like the sky for clearness. The narrator will describe the floor and will not describe the person standing on it.

Ate and drank. This is the point. On the mountain fenced with a death penalty five chapters ago, seventy-four men sat down in the presence of God and ate a meal. It is a rare and astonishing moment when human beings eat in God’s company and live, and it happens straight after blood has been thrown over them.

Blood first, then a meal. That order is the logic of the Bible. It is why the church’s central act is a table, where we eat and drink with the one whose blood sealed the covenant. And it is where all of it is going: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9).

What it does not mean. No one can see God and live (33:20), and “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18). What the elders saw was a revealed form, and the text describes only what was under his feet. They saw what God chose to show, and lived to eat in his presence. Nor does such a privilege make anyone safe from treating God lightly: Nadab and Abihu, who ate on this mountain, later died for offering fire he had not commanded (Leviticus 10:1–2).

Uncertain wording. “Sapphire” is probably lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone; ancient sapphire was not the modern gem. “Chief men” (v. 11) renders a rare word, perhaps meaning the leading men or nobles.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-18 — Into the Cloud of Glory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses goes up alone into the glory of God. God calls him to receive the stone tablets he has written (v. 12). Moses takes his assistant Joshua, leaves Aaron and Hur to settle disputes, and climbs while the cloud covers the mountain (vv. 13–15). For six days the glory of the LORD rests on Sinai, and on the seventh God calls Moses into the cloud (v. 16). To the people below the glory looks like a devouring fire, and Moses walks into it and stays forty days and nights (vv. 17–18). The scene is set both for the tabernacle and for the people’s failure.
verseByVerse.theology:
Into the Cloud of Glory

The mediator disappears into the fire, and the people must wait.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the people at the foot watched a fire with their leader inside it. Now: waiting for God is part of trusting him.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Come up to me on the mountain and wait there, that I may give you the tablets of stone, with the law and the commandment, which I have written for their instruction." So Moses rose with his assistant Joshua, and Moses went up into the mountain of God. And he said to the elders, "Wait here for us until we return to you. And behold, Aaron and Hur are with you. Whoever has a dispute, let him go to them." Then Moses went up on the mountain, and the cloud covered the mountain. The glory of the LORD dwelt on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days. And on the seventh day he called to Moses out of the midst of the cloud. Now the appearance of the glory of the LORD was like a devouring fire on the top of the mountain in the sight of the people of Israel. Moses entered the cloud and went up on the mountain. And Moses was on the mountain forty days and forty nights.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses goes up alone into the cloud of God’s glory, which blazes like a devouring fire, to receive the tablets, and he stays forty days.

Come up to me on the mountain. Moses is called higher, for the tablets God himself has written. He takes Joshua part of the way and leaves Aaron and Hur (17:10–12) in charge, which will turn out badly. The cloud covers the mountain for six days, and on the seventh God calls him into it.

A devouring fire. The people at the bottom watch a blaze on a summit and know their leader has walked into it. Hebrews uses the phrase of God at the end of its argument about the two mountains, Sinai and Zion: “our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29).

Moses entered the cloud. Moses goes where no one else may go and comes back with God’s word. He is a mediator, but only a shadow of the greater one: Christ has entered “into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf” (Hebrews 9:24), and he does not leave his people without a word.

Forty days. A long time to watch a fire on a mountain with no word from the man inside it. The narrator drops the detail without comment, and the reader can already hear the talk starting at the bottom of the hill: “as for this Moses … we do not know what has become of him” (32:1). The golden calf is not built by people who have forgotten God. It is built by people who got tired of waiting for him, nearly six weeks after promising to do everything he said, with the fire still burning in plain sight. Waiting is where faith is most often tested.
