keyVerse.quote: Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words.
keyVerse.note: This sentence seals the covenant at Sinai and gives it its meaning: God binds himself to a sinful people through the death of a sacrifice. Jesus took these words at the Last Supper and made them his own (Mark 14:24).

24.reflection:
The blood was thrown on both the altar and the people (vv. 6–8). Why does a covenant between a holy God and sinners need blood, and how does Hebrews 9:18–22 help you understand the cross?

Israel promised twice, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do” (vv. 3, 7), and broke the covenant within weeks. How should that shape the way we make promises to God, and where is our confidence to rest?

The elders “beheld God, and ate and drank” (v. 11). How does this meal help you see what happens at the Lord’s Supper, and what the marriage supper of the Lamb will be?

The people grew tired of waiting while Moses was on the mountain for forty days (v. 18; 32:1). Where are you tempted to make your own “golden calf” because God seems slow?

25.title: That I May Dwell in Their Midst
25.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Moses,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, that they take for me a contribution. From every man whose heart moves him you shall receive the contribution for me.<sup>3</sup>And this is the contribution that you shall receive from them: gold, silver, and bronze,<sup>4</sup>blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen, goats' hair,<sup>5</sup>tanned rams' skins, goatskins, acacia wood,<sup>6</sup>oil for the lamps, spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense,<sup>7</sup>onyx stones, and stones for setting, for the ephod and for the breastpiece.<sup>8</sup>And let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst.<sup>9</sup>Exactly as I show you concerning the pattern of the tabernacle, and of all its furniture, so you shall make it.<sup>10</sup>"They shall make an ark of acacia wood. Two cubits and a half shall be its length, a cubit and a half its breadth, and a cubit and a half its height.<sup>11</sup>You shall overlay it with pure gold, inside and outside shall you overlay it, and you shall make on it a molding of gold around it.<sup>12</sup>You shall cast four rings of gold for it and put them on its four feet, two rings on the one side of it, and two rings on the other side of it.<sup>13</sup>You shall make poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold.<sup>14</sup>And you shall put the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark to carry the ark by them.<sup>15</sup>The poles shall remain in the rings of the ark; they shall not be taken from it.<sup>16</sup>And you shall put into the ark the testimony that I shall give you.<sup>17</sup>"You shall make a mercy seat of pure gold. Two cubits and a half shall be its length, and a cubit and a half its breadth.<sup>18</sup>And you shall make two cherubim of gold; of hammered work shall you make them, on the two ends of the mercy seat.<sup>19</sup>Make one cherub on the one end, and one cherub on the other end. Of one piece with the mercy seat shall you make the cherubim on its two ends.<sup>20</sup>The cherubim shall spread out their wings above, overshadowing the mercy seat with their wings, their faces one to another; toward the mercy seat shall the faces of the cherubim be.<sup>21</sup>And you shall put the mercy seat on the top of the ark, and in the ark you shall put the testimony that I shall give you.<sup>22</sup>There I will meet with you, and from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim that are on the ark of the testimony, I will speak with you about all that I will give you in commandment for the people of Israel.<sup>23</sup>"You shall make a table of acacia wood. Two cubits shall be its length, a cubit its breadth, and a cubit and a half its height.<sup>24</sup>You shall overlay it with pure gold and make a molding of gold around it.<sup>25</sup>And you shall make a rim around it a handbreadth wide, and a molding of gold around the rim.<sup>26</sup>And you shall make for it four rings of gold, and fasten the rings to the four corners at its four legs.<sup>27</sup>Close to the frame the rings shall lie, as holders for the poles to carry the table.<sup>28</sup>You shall make the poles of acacia wood, and overlay them with gold, and the table shall be carried with these.<sup>29</sup>And you shall make its plates and dishes for incense, and its flagons and bowls with which to pour drink offerings; you shall make them of pure gold.<sup>30</sup>And you shall set the bread of the Presence on the table before me regularly.<sup>31</sup>"You shall make a lampstand of pure gold. The lampstand shall be made of hammered work: its base, its stem, its cups, its calyxes, and its flowers shall be of one piece with it.<sup>32</sup>And there shall be six branches going out of its sides, three branches of the lampstand out of one side of it and three branches of the lampstand out of the other side of it;<sup>33</sup>three cups made like almond blossoms, each with calyx and flower, on one branch, and three cups made like almond blossoms, each with calyx and flower, on the other branch—so for the six branches going out of the lampstand.<sup>34</sup>And on the lampstand itself there shall be four cups made like almond blossoms, with their calyxes and flowers,<sup>35</sup>and a calyx of one piece with it under each pair of the six branches going out from the lampstand.<sup>36</sup>Their calyxes and their branches shall be of one piece with it, the whole of it a single piece of hammered work of pure gold.<sup>37</sup>You shall make seven lamps for it. And the lamps shall be set up so as to give light on the space in front of it.<sup>38</sup>Its tongs and their trays shall be of pure gold.<sup>39</sup>It shall be made, with all these utensils, out of a talent of pure gold.<sup>40</sup>And see that you make them after the pattern for them, which is being shown you on the mountain.
25.overview:
Where we are. The covenant has been sealed in blood and Israel’s leaders have eaten in God’s presence (24:1–11). Moses has gone up into the cloud for forty days (24:18), and the first thing God tells him there is not another law but a building plan. Here begins the third movement of Exodus, the presence of God (chapters 25–40; see the introduction).

The message. The God who came down to rescue his people now means to stay with them: “let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst” (v. 8). Redemption was never only about getting out of Egypt; its goal is God living among the people he has saved. And because he is holy, he dwells among them on his terms, at a place of atonement, after a pattern he himself gives.

Why it was said. Israel was a nation of freed slaves camped in a desert, about to travel for years. Their neighbours had temples full of images; Israel was forbidden images (20:4). They needed to know whether the God of Sinai would stay at Sinai or go with them, and how sinners could live next door to him without being destroyed.

How the chapter makes its case. God asks for a freewill offering of the materials, states the purpose, and insists on the pattern shown on the mountain (vv. 1–9). Then he begins at the centre, the holiest place, and works outwards: the ark holding the law, with the golden mercy seat and cherubim above it, where he promises to meet and speak with Moses (vv. 10–22); the table with the bread of the Presence (vv. 23–30); and the golden lampstand shaped like a flowering tree (vv. 31–40).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by promise. The tent is “a copy and shadow of the heavenly things” (Hebrews 8:5), and its meaning arrives in a person: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), literally pitched his tent among us. The mercy seat, where blood covered the broken law, is the word Paul uses of Christ, “put forward as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25). The bread and the light point to the one who said, “I am the bread of life” and “I am the light of the world” (John 6:35; 8:12). The Bible ends where this chapter points: “the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3).

For us. God does not merely tolerate his people; he wants to live with them, and in Christ he has come to do it. We come near not on our own terms but at the place of atonement he provides, and we give to his work, as Israel did, from hearts moved by what he has done for us.
25.theology:
God's desire to dwell with his people. The goal of redemption is not only escape from Egypt but God's presence, a purpose fulfilled in Christ and completed in the New Jerusalem.

The mercy seat and atonement. God meets sinners only where blood covers the broken law. There justice and mercy meet, and Paul names Christ as that meeting place (Rom. 3:25).

Worship after the heavenly pattern. Because the tent copies a heavenly reality, nothing in it is left to human invention; God himself says how he is to be approached.
25.examples:
Then: willing hearts built a sanctuary after a heavenly pattern, with a blood-sprinkled lid as the place where God would meet his redeemed people.

Now: God still means to dwell with his people. He has come among us in Christ, and we meet him at the cross, where mercy and justice embrace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-9 — The Freewill Offering and the Pattern
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God wants to live among his people, and his dwelling is to be built from willing gifts and exactly to his design. He asks for a contribution only from those whose hearts move them (v. 2), and lists what is needed: metals, coloured yarns, linen, skins, wood, oil, spices and stones (vv. 3–7). Then comes the reason for it all, the centre of the second half of Exodus: “let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst” (v. 8). Last, nothing is left to human imagination: everything must follow the pattern God shows Moses on the mountain (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Freewill Offering and the Pattern

God's house is built from what willing hearts bring, and built exactly after his pattern.
verseByVerse.examples: The plunder of Egypt became the furniture of worship. The earthly sanctuary was only "a copy and shadow of the heavenly things" (Heb. 8:5), but God's aim in it is the one he still has: to live among his people.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Speak to the people of Israel, that they take for me a contribution. From every man whose heart moves him you shall receive the contribution for me. And this is the contribution that you shall receive from them: gold, silver, and bronze, blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen, goats' hair, tanned rams' skins, goatskins, acacia wood, oil for the lamps, spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense, onyx stones, and stones for setting, for the ephod and for the breastpiece. And let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst. Exactly as I show you concerning the pattern of the tabernacle, and of all its furniture, so you shall make it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God asks his rescued people for willing gifts to build him a sanctuary, because he means to live among them, on the pattern he shows Moses.

Whose heart moves him. The tabernacle begins with giving, not architecture. No tax, no quota: the materials come only from people who want to give them, and by chapter 36 Moses has to tell everyone to stop (36:5–7). The giving flows from rescue.

Where does a nation of escaped slaves get gold, yarns, linen and onyx? From Egypt: the silver and gold the Egyptians handed over (12:35–36), as God had promised Abraham (Genesis 15:14). The plunder of the oppressor becomes the furniture of worship.

That I may dwell in their midst. The whole second half of Exodus serves this sentence. God has been after it since 3:8: not merely a rescued people, but a people he lives among. The book began with God saying “I have come down”; it will end with him moving in (40:34).

Exactly as I show you. Nothing here is Moses’ design. The earthly sanctuary is “a copy and shadow of the heavenly things”, which is why Moses had to make everything “according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain” (Hebrews 8:5). The tent is a scale model of something real, and its reality came when the Word “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).
verseByVerse.note: The tabernacle was a portable tent-sanctuary, made to be taken down and carried as Israel travelled.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10-22 — The Ark and the Mercy Seat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the heart of God’s dwelling is a place where he meets sinners over a covered law. The ark is a gold-covered chest of acacia wood, with poles that never leave their rings, so that it is always ready to travel (vv. 10–15). Into it goes “the testimony”, the tablets of the law (v. 16). On top sits the mercy seat, a slab of pure gold with two cherubim beaten from the same piece, wings spread and faces turned down toward it (vv. 17–21). There, above the mercy seat and between the cherubim, God promises to meet Moses and speak all his commands (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ark and the Mercy Seat

The holiest object in Israel is a gold-covered chest holding the tablets of the law, with a lid of pure gold between two cherubim. The place where God chooses to meet his people is the place where atonement is made.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: between the holy God and the broken law lay a lid sprinkled with blood. Now: that meeting place is a person, Christ, whom God put forward to turn away his wrath by his blood.

verseByVerse.quote: "They shall make an ark of acacia wood. Two cubits and a half shall be its length, a cubit and a half its breadth, and a cubit and a half its height. You shall overlay it with pure gold, inside and outside shall you overlay it, and you shall make on it a molding of gold around it. You shall cast four rings of gold for it and put them on its four feet, two rings on the one side of it, and two rings on the other side of it. You shall make poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold. And you shall put the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark to carry the ark by them. The poles shall remain in the rings of the ark; they shall not be taken from it. And you shall put into the ark the testimony that I shall give you. "You shall make a mercy seat of pure gold. Two cubits and a half shall be its length, and a cubit and a half its breadth. And you shall make two cherubim of gold; of hammered work shall you make them, on the two ends of the mercy seat. Make one cherub on the one end, and one cherub on the other end. Of one piece with the mercy seat shall you make the cherubim on its two ends. The cherubim shall spread out their wings above, overshadowing the mercy seat with their wings, their faces one to another; toward the mercy seat shall the faces of the cherubim be. And you shall put the mercy seat on the top of the ark, and in the ark you shall put the testimony that I shall give you. There I will meet with you, and from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim that are on the ark of the testimony, I will speak with you about all that I will give you in commandment for the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the centre of God’s dwelling is a chest holding his law, and above it a golden lid where blood covers the broken law and God meets with his people.

An ark of acacia wood. The ark comes first because it is the centre. Its poles stay in the rings permanently, so it is always ready to move: Israel’s God travels with a walking people. Inside goes “the testimony”, the tablets of the law (v. 16).

A mercy seat of pure gold. Everything turns on the lid. Inside the box is the law Israel will break; above it God’s presence rests and speaks (v. 22). Between a holy God and a broken commandment lies a slab of gold, and once a year, on the Day of Atonement, blood is sprinkled on it (Leviticus 16:14–15).

Two cherubim of gold. Cherubim, heavenly attendants of God’s throne, last appeared at the gate of Eden with a flaming sword, keeping people out (Genesis 3:24). Here they are again, in gold, bowed over the place of atonement, looking at blood. The guards at the door have become witnesses at the mercy seat.

A propitiation by his blood. The Greek translators rendered the lid hilastērion, “place of atonement”, and Paul uses exactly that word: God put forward Christ Jesus “as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25). A propitiation is a sacrifice that turns away God’s just anger, and Paul may well be picturing the mercy seat itself. The place where blood covers a broken law, and where God speaks to his people without destroying them, is in the end a person: Christ.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew name of the lid, kapporet, is related to the verb for making atonement, but scholars debate whether it meant simply “cover” or “place of atonement”. Its role on the Day of Atonement shows what it was for.
verseByVerse.note: The ark was about 45 by 27 by 27 inches (a cubit was about 18 inches, ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23-30 — The Table of the Presence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God keeps his people continually before his face, and sets a meal in his own house. The table is acacia wood overlaid with gold, with a rim and moulding, rings and poles for carrying (vv. 23–28). Its golden plates, dishes, flagons and bowls are for incense and drink offerings (v. 29). On it the bread of the Presence is to lie “before me regularly” (v. 30): twelve loaves, renewed each Sabbath, for the twelve tribes (Leviticus 24:5–9). The whole people lies before God’s face, week after week.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Table of the Presence

A gold-overlaid table, with its plates and dishes, keeps bread always set before the LORD.
verseByVerse.examples: God kept a place at his table for every tribe, week after week; in Christ he still sets bread before the hungry (Luke 6:3-4).

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall make a table of acacia wood. Two cubits shall be its length, a cubit its breadth, and a cubit and a half its height. You shall overlay it with pure gold and make a molding of gold around it. And you shall make a rim around it a handbreadth wide, and a molding of gold around the rim. And you shall make for it four rings of gold, and fasten the rings to the four corners at its four legs. Close to the frame the rings shall lie, as holders for the poles to carry the table. You shall make the poles of acacia wood, and overlay them with gold, and the table shall be carried with these. And you shall make its plates and dishes for incense, and its flagons and bowls with which to pour drink offerings; you shall make them of pure gold. And you shall set the bread of the Presence on the table before me regularly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sets twelve loaves on a golden table before his face: his whole people are continually remembered in his presence.

The bread of the Presence. Twelve loaves, one per tribe, set out fresh every Sabbath and eaten by the priests (Leviticus 24:5–9): a standing meal in God’s house. The Hebrew is literally “bread of the face”, set before God’s face continually. Every tribe is on that table, week after week, whether or not it is behaving.

Jesus and the loaves. Jesus once appealed to these loaves, reminding the Pharisees how David and his men ate “the bread of the Presence, which is not lawful for any but the priests to eat” (Luke 6:4); in Matthew’s account he adds that mercy matters more than ritual (Matthew 12:7). Later he said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). The bread before God’s face pointed to him, and he offers himself to anyone who is hungry.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s house is to be filled with his light, and it comes from a golden tree in blossom. The lampstand is hammered from a single talent of pure gold, base, stem and branches all one piece (vv. 31, 36). Six branches spring from the central stem, each with cups shaped like almond blossoms, with calyx and flower (vv. 32–35). Its seven lamps throw light on the space in front of it, and even its tongs and trays are pure gold (vv. 37–39). The section closes with the chapter’s refrain: make it after the pattern shown on the mountain (v. 40).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Golden Lampstand

The light of the holy place comes from a golden tree in blossom, made, like everything else, after the pattern shown on the mountain.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a golden tree in blossom lit the one room no window reached. Now: the lampstands are the churches, with the Son of Man walking among them (Rev. 1:12-20).

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall make a lampstand of pure gold. The lampstand shall be made of hammered work: its base, its stem, its cups, its calyxes, and its flowers shall be of one piece with it. And there shall be six branches going out of its sides, three branches of the lampstand out of one side of it and three branches of the lampstand out of the other side of it; three cups made like almond blossoms, each with calyx and flower, on one branch, and three cups made like almond blossoms, each with calyx and flower, on the other branch—so for the six branches going out of the lampstand. And on the lampstand itself there shall be four cups made like almond blossoms, with their calyxes and flowers, and a calyx of one piece with it under each pair of the six branches going out from the lampstand. Their calyxes and their branches shall be of one piece with it, the whole of it a single piece of hammered work of pure gold. You shall make seven lamps for it. And the lamps shall be set up so as to give light on the space in front of it. Its tongs and their trays shall be of pure gold. It shall be made, with all these utensils, out of a talent of pure gold. And see that you make them after the pattern for them, which is being shown you on the mountain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s house is lit by a golden tree in blossom, beaten from one piece: his light shines among his people and is tended so that it never fails.

A lampstand of pure gold. It is described in more loving detail than anything else in the chapter, and it is not assembled from parts but beaten from one talent of gold, so stem and branches are a single object. And it is a tree: inside a desert tent, God’s light comes from a golden tree in permanent blossom, its lamps burning every night (27:20–21).

Back to the garden. There was once a garden with a tree in the middle and God walking in it, and the way back was shut. Many have seen in this blossoming tree a memory of Eden, burning in the dark where God lives among his people again.

He walks among the lampstands. John sees seven golden lampstands, the churches, with “one like a son of man” among them (Revelation 1:12–13, 20). The light in the holy place was tended daily so it would not fail; the light in the world now is the church, and it does not go out, because Christ “walks among the seven golden lampstands” (Revelation 2:1).
verseByVerse.note: A talent of gold was about 75 pounds (ESV note), all of it beaten into one lampstand.

keyVerse.quote: And let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst.
keyVerse.note: This is the purpose of the whole tabernacle and of the last sixteen chapters of Exodus: God rescued his people in order to live among them. It looks forward to the Word who “dwelt among us” (John 1:14) and to the day when “the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3).

25.reflection:
The materials came only from those “whose heart moves him” (v. 2), and the people gave so much they had to be told to stop (36:5–7). What moves your giving, and how does remembering what God has rescued you from change it?

God says the whole tabernacle exists “that I may dwell in their midst” (v. 8). How does it change your view of salvation to see that its goal is not only forgiveness but God living with his people?

Inside the ark lay the law Israel would break; above it was the mercy seat, where blood was sprinkled and God spoke (vv. 16–22). How does Romans 3:25 help you see Christ in this picture, and what does it mean for how you approach God?

The bread lay before God’s face “regularly” (v. 30) and the lamps burned every night. What do these quiet, constant things tell you about God’s care for his people, and about your place in the church as a lampstand (Revelation 1:20)?

26.title: The Way into the Presence
26.text: <sup>1</sup>"Moreover, you shall make the tabernacle with ten curtains of fine twined linen and blue and purple and scarlet yarns; you shall make them with cherubim skillfully worked into them.<sup>2</sup>The length of each curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits, and the breadth of each curtain four cubits; all the curtains shall be the same size.<sup>3</sup>Five curtains shall be coupled to one another, and the other five curtains shall be coupled to one another.<sup>4</sup>And you shall make loops of blue on the edge of the outermost curtain in the first set. Likewise you shall make loops on the edge of the outermost curtain in the second set.<sup>5</sup>Fifty loops you shall make on the one curtain, and fifty loops you shall make on the edge of the curtain that is in the second set; the loops shall be opposite one another.<sup>6</sup>And you shall make fifty clasps of gold, and couple the curtains one to the other with the clasps, so that the tabernacle may be a single whole.<sup>7</sup>"You shall also make curtains of goats' hair for a tent over the tabernacle; eleven curtains shall you make.<sup>8</sup>The length of each curtain shall be thirty cubits, and the breadth of each curtain four cubits. The eleven curtains shall be the same size.<sup>9</sup>You shall couple five curtains by themselves, and six curtains by themselves, and the sixth curtain you shall double over at the front of the tent.<sup>10</sup>You shall make fifty loops on the edge of the curtain that is outermost in one set, and fifty loops on the edge of the curtain that is outermost in the second set.<sup>11</sup>"You shall make fifty clasps of bronze, and put the clasps into the loops, and couple the tent together that it may be a single whole.<sup>12</sup>And the part that remains of the curtains of the tent, the half curtain that remains, shall hang over the back of the tabernacle.<sup>13</sup>And the extra that remains in the length of the curtains, the cubit on the one side, and the cubit on the other side, shall hang over the sides of the tabernacle, on this side and that side, to cover it.<sup>14</sup>And you shall make for the tent a covering of tanned rams' skins and a covering of goatskins on top.<sup>15</sup>"You shall make upright frames for the tabernacle of acacia wood.<sup>16</sup>Ten cubits shall be the length of a frame, and a cubit and a half the breadth of each frame.<sup>17</sup>There shall be two tenons in each frame, for fitting together. So shall you do for all the frames of the tabernacle.<sup>18</sup>You shall make the frames for the tabernacle: twenty frames for the south side;<sup>19</sup>and forty bases of silver you shall make under the twenty frames, two bases under one frame for its two tenons, and two bases under the next frame for its two tenons;<sup>20</sup>and for the second side of the tabernacle, on the north side twenty frames,<sup>21</sup>and their forty bases of silver, two bases under one frame, and two bases under the next frame.<sup>22</sup>And for the rear of the tabernacle westward you shall make six frames.<sup>23</sup>And you shall make two frames for corners of the tabernacle in the rear;<sup>24</sup>they shall be separate beneath, but joined at the top, at the first ring. Thus shall it be with both of them; they shall form the two corners.<sup>25</sup>And there shall be eight frames, with their bases of silver, sixteen bases; two bases under one frame, and two bases under another frame.<sup>26</sup>"You shall make bars of acacia wood, five for the frames of the one side of the tabernacle,<sup>27</sup>and five bars for the frames of the other side of the tabernacle, and five bars for the frames of the side of the tabernacle at the rear westward.<sup>28</sup>The middle bar, halfway up the frames, shall run from end to end.<sup>29</sup>You shall overlay the frames with gold and shall make their rings of gold for holders for the bars, and you shall overlay the bars with gold.<sup>30</sup>Then you shall erect the tabernacle according to the plan for it that you were shown on the mountain.<sup>31</sup>"And you shall make a veil of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen. It shall be made with cherubim skillfully worked into it.<sup>32</sup>And you shall hang it on four pillars of acacia overlaid with gold, with hooks of gold, on four bases of silver.<sup>33</sup>And you shall hang the veil from the clasps, and bring the ark of the testimony in there within the veil. And the veil shall separate for you the Holy Place from the Most Holy.<sup>34</sup>You shall put the mercy seat on the ark of the testimony in the Most Holy Place.<sup>35</sup>And you shall set the table outside the veil, and the lampstand on the south side of the tabernacle opposite the table, and you shall put the table on the north side.<sup>36</sup>"You shall make a screen for the entrance of the tent, of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen, embroidered with needlework.<sup>37</sup>And you shall make for the screen five pillars of acacia, and overlay them with gold. Their hooks shall be of gold, and you shall cast five bases of bronze for them.
26.overview:
Where we are. God has described the furniture at the heart of his dwelling: the ark and mercy seat, the table and the lampstand (chapter 25). Now he describes the house that will hold them, the tent itself, still on the mountain with Moses during the forty days (24:18).

The message. God truly comes to live among his people, and yet a holy God cannot simply be walked in on by sinners. The tent is one dwelling, beautiful within, plain without, but at its heart hangs a veil that keeps everyone out of the room where God is enthroned. The chapter shows both the wonder of God’s nearness and the barrier that sin still puts between him and us.

Why it was said. Israel had seen at Sinai that to touch the mountain was death (19:12–13). Now God was moving into the middle of their camp (see the introduction). They needed a dwelling that let him be near and kept them safe, and a picture they could see every day of how holy he is and how carefully sinners must approach him.

How the chapter makes its case. The tent is built from the inside out: ten linen curtains worked with cherubim, then goats’ hair curtains, then two coverings of skins, all clasped together “so that the tabernacle may be a single whole” (vv. 1–14). It stands on gold-covered frames set in silver bases and held by bars, after the plan shown on the mountain (vv. 15–30). Inside, a veil embroidered with cherubim divides the Holy Place from the Most Holy, where the ark stands; outside it are the table and lampstand, and a screen closes the entrance (vv. 31–37).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. The tent is where God dwelt among his people, and “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), his glory hidden under an ordinary human life. The veil exposes the need: “the way into the holy places is not yet opened as long as the first section is still standing” (Hebrews 9:8). When Jesus died, “the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51), and now we enter “by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh” (Hebrews 10:20).

For us. No one should treat the presence of God lightly; the veil was real, and so is his holiness. But no believer should stand outside either. Christ has opened the way, so we come to God with confidence, not to a curtain but to a Father.
26.theology:
The holiness of God and the barrier of sin. The layout and the veil declare that sinners cannot casually approach the holy God.

Christ the torn veil. The barrier was removed from God's side, and we now enter by the new and living way Christ opened by his death (Heb. 10:20).

Worship after the pattern. The tabernacle is built exactly as God commanded, because worship is governed by what God has revealed, not by human invention.
26.examples:
Then: a tent of hidden glory, ordered exactly to God's pattern, whose veil kept everyone but the high priest out.

Now: those who once stood outside draw near with confidence, because Christ has opened the way.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s dwelling is one whole tent, glorious within and plain without. The innermost layer is ten curtains of fine linen in blue, purple and scarlet, with cherubim worked into them, joined in two sets by blue loops and gold clasps “so that the tabernacle may be a single whole” (vv. 1–6). Over them goes a tent of eleven goats’ hair curtains, joined with bronze clasps and hanging over the back and sides (vv. 7–13). On top come two coverings, of tanned rams’ skins and of goatskins (v. 14). Only the priests inside would ever see the beauty; the camp saw weatherproof skins.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Curtains and Coverings

Many curtains are fastened into one dwelling, plain on the outside and glorious within.
verseByVerse.examples: The glory was on the inside of a plain tent, and the New Testament describes the church in the same terms, built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit (Eph. 2:21-22).

verseByVerse.quote: "Moreover, you shall make the tabernacle with ten curtains of fine twined linen and blue and purple and scarlet yarns; you shall make them with cherubim skillfully worked into them. The length of each curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits, and the breadth of each curtain four cubits; all the curtains shall be the same size. Five curtains shall be coupled to one another, and the other five curtains shall be coupled to one another. And you shall make loops of blue on the edge of the outermost curtain in the first set. Likewise you shall make loops on the edge of the outermost curtain in the second set. Fifty loops you shall make on the one curtain, and fifty loops you shall make on the edge of the curtain that is in the second set; the loops shall be opposite one another. And you shall make fifty clasps of gold, and couple the curtains one to the other with the clasps, so that the tabernacle may be a single whole. "You shall also make curtains of goats' hair for a tent over the tabernacle; eleven curtains shall you make. The length of each curtain shall be thirty cubits, and the breadth of each curtain four cubits. The eleven curtains shall be the same size. You shall couple five curtains by themselves, and six curtains by themselves, and the sixth curtain you shall double over at the front of the tent. You shall make fifty loops on the edge of the curtain that is outermost in one set, and fifty loops on the edge of the curtain that is outermost in the second set. "You shall make fifty clasps of bronze, and put the clasps into the loops, and couple the tent together that it may be a single whole. And the part that remains of the curtains of the tent, the half curtain that remains, shall hang over the back of the tabernacle. And the extra that remains in the length of the curtains, the cubit on the one side, and the cubit on the other side, shall hang over the sides of the tabernacle, on this side and that side, to cover it. And you shall make for the tent a covering of tanned rams' skins and a covering of goatskins on top.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s dwelling is one tent made of many pieces, glorious within and plain without.

From the inside out. The layers are listed from the inside out. Outside, all anyone sees is plain skins; beneath are goats’ hair curtains, the stuff of every desert tent. Only inside, seen by the priests alone, is linen in blue, purple and scarlet with cherubim worked into it.

Glory on the inside. A passer-by would see a drab tent and never guess its interior was embroidered with cherubim. Many see the same pattern in Isaiah’s Servant, who “had no form or majesty that we should look at him” (Isaiah 53:2). What God dwells in is rarely impressive from outside.

So that the tabernacle may be a single whole. Many pieces become one, as the New Testament says of the church, “joined together” and “being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit” (Ephesians 2:21–22).

Uncertain wording. The outer covering of “goatskins” (v. 14) renders a rare Hebrew word, tahash. The KJV has “badgers’ skins”; others suggest fine leather or the hide of a sea creature such as the dugong. Clearly it was a tough, weatherproof outer layer.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s house is to stand firm, on a foundation he provides and to a plan he gives. Upright frames of acacia wood, each ten cubits high, are fitted with tenons into silver bases, two under each frame: twenty frames on the south, twenty on the north, and six with two corner frames at the west (vv. 15–25). Bars of acacia, five on each side with a middle bar running the full length, hold them together (vv. 26–28). Frames and bars are overlaid with gold (v. 29), and the whole is to be raised “according to the plan for it that you were shown on the mountain” (v. 30).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Frames and Bases

God's house stands on silver bases and rises according to the plan shown on the mountain.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the silver under every board was ransom money paid for Israel's lives. Now: God’s house, the church, still stands on a ransom: the blood of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall make upright frames for the tabernacle of acacia wood. Ten cubits shall be the length of a frame, and a cubit and a half the breadth of each frame. There shall be two tenons in each frame, for fitting together. So shall you do for all the frames of the tabernacle. You shall make the frames for the tabernacle: twenty frames for the south side; and forty bases of silver you shall make under the twenty frames, two bases under one frame for its two tenons, and two bases under the next frame for its two tenons; and for the second side of the tabernacle, on the north side twenty frames, and their forty bases of silver, two bases under one frame, and two bases under the next frame. And for the rear of the tabernacle westward you shall make six frames. And you shall make two frames for corners of the tabernacle in the rear; they shall be separate beneath, but joined at the top, at the first ring. Thus shall it be with both of them; they shall form the two corners. And there shall be eight frames, with their bases of silver, sixteen bases; two bases under one frame, and two bases under another frame. "You shall make bars of acacia wood, five for the frames of the one side of the tabernacle, and five bars for the frames of the other side of the tabernacle, and five bars for the frames of the side of the tabernacle at the rear westward. The middle bar, halfway up the frames, shall run from end to end. You shall overlay the frames with gold and shall make their rings of gold for holders for the bars, and you shall overlay the bars with gold. Then you shall erect the tabernacle according to the plan for it that you were shown on the mountain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s house stands on silver paid as the ransom for lives, and is built of desert wood made fit for him by the gold laid over it.

Where did the silver of the bases come from? From the census money (38:25–27), the half-shekel “ransom for his life” paid by every man counted in Israel (30:12). Every frame in God’s house stands on redemption money.

Upright frames of acacia wood. Acacia is a gnarled, thorny desert tree. Each frame grew in a wilderness and is then shaped, overlaid with gold and stood in silver. Ordinary wilderness wood is made fit for God’s house by what is laid over it and what it stands on.

According to the plan. For the third time (25:9, 40), everything must follow the plan shown on the mountain.

Uncertain wording. The word rendered “frames” was traditionally translated “boards” (KJV). Solid boards that size would be very heavy to carry, so many think they were open frames. How the corner frames joined (vv. 23–24) is also unclear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31-37 — The Veil and the Screen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Inside God’s dwelling a veil bars the way to his presence. It is woven of blue, purple and scarlet yarns and fine linen with cherubim worked into it, and hung on four gold-covered pillars (vv. 31–32). Behind it goes the ark with the mercy seat, in the Most Holy Place (vv. 33–34). In front of it, in the Holy Place, stand the table on the north and the lampstand on the south (v. 35). At the entrance of the tent hangs a second, embroidered screen on five pillars set in bronze bases (vv. 36–37). The veil marks the line no one may cross.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Veil and the Screen

The veil divides the room of daily service, with its table and lampstand, from the room of the ark and mercy seat, which one man may enter once a year.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the tabernacle said both “God is here” and “you may not come in.” Now: the curtain has been torn from top to bottom (Matt. 27:51), and believers are invited in.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you shall make a veil of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen. It shall be made with cherubim skillfully worked into it. And you shall hang it on four pillars of acacia overlaid with gold, with hooks of gold, on four bases of silver. And you shall hang the veil from the clasps, and bring the ark of the testimony in there within the veil. And the veil shall separate for you the Holy Place from the Most Holy. You shall put the mercy seat on the ark of the testimony in the Most Holy Place. And you shall set the table outside the veil, and the lampstand on the south side of the tabernacle opposite the table, and you shall put the table on the north side. "You shall make a screen for the entrance of the tent, of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen, embroidered with needlework. And you shall make for the screen five pillars of acacia, and overlay them with gold. Their hooks shall be of gold, and you shall cast five bases of bronze for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A veil embroidered with cherubim shuts the Most Holy Place, where God is enthroned: he is near, yet sinners may not walk in.

A veil of blue and purple and scarlet yarns. The difference between the two hangings is the point of the chapter. The outer screen carries no figures; the inner veil has cherubim, like the guards at Eden’s gate (Genesis 3:24). It divides the room where priests work daily from the room one man may enter once a year, on the Day of Atonement, with blood (Leviticus 16).

The limit of the old covenant. The veil shows in fabric the great limit of the old covenant: God has come down to dwell among his people, and still almost nobody may go past the curtain.

From top to bottom. That is why three Gospels record the tearing of a cloth. At the moment Jesus died, “the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51). No one reached up and cut it: the barrier was removed from God’s side, when the true sacrifice was complete.

Now open to us. So we have “confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh” (Hebrews 10:19–20). The room nobody could enter is now open to every believer.
verseByVerse.note: The outer “goatskins” (v. 14) render an uncertain Hebrew word: the KJV has “badgers’ skins”, and others suggest dugong or porpoise leather.

keyVerse.quote: And the veil shall separate for you the Holy Place from the Most Holy.
keyVerse.note: The veil is the heart of the chapter: God lives among his people, yet his holiness keeps sinners out of his presence. Its tearing “from top to bottom” at Jesus’ death (Matthew 27:51) is the clearest sign that Christ has opened the way.

26.reflection:
From outside the tabernacle looked like a plain tent of skins; its beauty was all inside (vv. 1–14). How does this help you understand Isaiah 53:2 and John 1:14, and how might it change what you look for in a church or in a Christian?

The frames stood on silver paid as a “ransom” for lives (30:12; 38:25–27). What does it mean that God’s house is built on redemption, and how does that apply to the church today?

The veil kept everyone but the high priest out of the Most Holy Place (vv. 31–33). Why was it needed, and what does it teach about the holiness of God?

Hebrews 10:19–22 says we may now enter God’s presence with confidence. What keeps you from coming to God boldly in prayer, and how does the torn curtain answer it?

27.title: The Altar Where Blood Is Shed
27.text: <sup>1</sup>"You shall make the altar of acacia wood, five cubits long and five cubits broad. The altar shall be square, and its height shall be three cubits.<sup>2</sup>And you shall make horns for it on its four corners; its horns shall be of one piece with it, and you shall overlay it with bronze.<sup>3</sup>You shall make pots for it to receive its ashes, and shovels and basins and forks and fire pans. You shall make all its utensils of bronze.<sup>4</sup>You shall also make for it a grating, a network of bronze, and on the net you shall make four bronze rings at its four corners.<sup>5</sup>And you shall set it under the ledge of the altar so that the net extends halfway down the altar.<sup>6</sup>And you shall make poles for the altar, poles of acacia wood, and overlay them with bronze.<sup>7</sup>And the poles shall be put through the rings, so that the poles are on the two sides of the altar when it is carried.<sup>8</sup>You shall make it hollow, with boards. As it has been shown you on the mountain, so shall it be made.<sup>9</sup>"You shall make the court of the tabernacle. On the south side the court shall have hangings of fine twined linen a hundred cubits long for one side.<sup>10</sup>Its twenty pillars and their twenty bases shall be of bronze, but the hooks of the pillars and their fillets shall be of silver.<sup>11</sup>And likewise for its length on the north side there shall be hangings a hundred cubits long, its pillars twenty and their bases twenty, of bronze, but the hooks of the pillars and their fillets shall be of silver.<sup>12</sup>And for the breadth of the court on the west side there shall be hangings for fifty cubits, with ten pillars and ten bases.<sup>13</sup>The breadth of the court on the front to the east shall be fifty cubits.<sup>14</sup>The hangings for the one side of the gate shall be fifteen cubits, with their three pillars and three bases.<sup>15</sup>On the other side the hangings shall be fifteen cubits, with their three pillars and three bases.<sup>16</sup>For the gate of the court there shall be a screen twenty cubits long, of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen, embroidered with needlework. It shall have four pillars and with them four bases.<sup>17</sup>All the pillars around the court shall be filleted with silver. Their hooks shall be of silver, and their bases of bronze.<sup>18</sup>The length of the court shall be a hundred cubits, the breadth fifty, and the height five cubits, with hangings of fine twined linen and bases of bronze.<sup>19</sup>All the utensils of the tabernacle for every use, and all its pegs and all the pegs of the court, shall be of bronze.<sup>20</sup>"You shall command the people of Israel that they bring to you pure beaten olive oil for the light, that a lamp may regularly be set up to burn.<sup>21</sup>In the tent of meeting, outside the veil that is before the testimony, Aaron and his sons shall tend it from evening to morning before the LORD. It shall be a statute forever to be observed throughout their generations by the people of Israel.
27.overview:
Where we are. God has described the furniture of the inner rooms (chapter 25) and the tent that houses them (chapter 26). Now he moves outside, into the courtyard: the altar, the linen wall with its single gate, and the oil that keeps the lamp burning inside. Next he will turn to the priests who serve there (chapters 28–29).

The message. No one comes near the holy God except by sacrifice. The first thing a worshipper met inside the gate was the great bronze altar, where animals died in the place of sinners day after day. The way into God’s presence begins where blood is shed, through the one gate he provides, and inside, his light is kept burning for his people all night long.

Why it was said. Israel had just been told that God would live among them (25:8), behind a veil no one could pass (26:33). They needed to know how ordinary sinners could come near at all. The answer stood in bronze at the entrance of the court, and every Israelite who brought an offering walked past it (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. First the bronze altar: square, with horns at its corners, a bronze grating, bronze utensils and poles for carrying, made as shown on the mountain (vv. 1–8). Then the court: a hundred cubits by fifty, walled with linen on bronze pillars, with a single embroidered gate twenty cubits wide on the east (vv. 9–19). Last, the people are to bring pure beaten olive oil so that Aaron and his sons can keep the lamp burning “from evening to morning before the LORD” (vv. 20–21).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. The endless sacrifices on this altar could never finally take away sin; every priest “stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices” (Hebrews 10:11). They pointed to the one who “offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins” and then sat down (Hebrews 10:12). The single gate points to the one who said, “I am the door” (John 10:9), and the priests trimming the lamp all night point to the High Priest who “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

For us. There is no way to God that bypasses the cross, and there is no need to look for one: the way is wide open to anyone who comes through Christ. And the quiet, unseen faithfulness of keeping a lamp burning is still the shape of much of the Christian life.
27.theology:
No approach to God without sacrifice. The altar at the gate declares that the way to God begins at the place of shed blood, a way finally opened by Christ's once-for-all sacrifice.

One appointed way. The single gate points forward to Christ, the one door and the one way to the Father (John 14:6).

The unceasing presence of God. The lamp that never goes out speaks of God's constant presence among his people and of worship that does not stop.
27.examples:
Then: no one approached the holy God except past the altar, through the one appointed gate.

Now: the cross stands at the entrance of our salvation, and we come to God through Christ alone.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No one comes near God except past the altar, where a substitute dies. The altar is acacia wood overlaid with bronze, five cubits square and three high, with horns of one piece with it at the four corners (vv. 1–2). Its pots, shovels, basins, forks and fire pans are all bronze (v. 3), and a bronze grating with rings is set under its ledge (vv. 4–5). Poles overlaid with bronze carry it, and it is hollow, made of boards, so that it can travel (vv. 6–8). Like everything else, it must be made as God showed Moses on the mountain (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Bronze Altar

The place of fire and blood stands first, before every other approach to God.
verseByVerse.examples: No one reached the tent except past the altar, and there is still no approach to God except through the sacrifice of Christ, offered once and never repeated (Heb. 10:11-12).

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall make the altar of acacia wood, five cubits long and five cubits broad. The altar shall be square, and its height shall be three cubits. And you shall make horns for it on its four corners; its horns shall be of one piece with it, and you shall overlay it with bronze. You shall make pots for it to receive its ashes, and shovels and basins and forks and fire pans. You shall make all its utensils of bronze. You shall also make for it a grating, a network of bronze, and on the net you shall make four bronze rings at its four corners. And you shall set it under the ledge of the altar so that the net extends halfway down the altar. And you shall make poles for the altar, poles of acacia wood, and overlay them with bronze. And the poles shall be put through the rings, so that the poles are on the two sides of the altar when it is carried. You shall make it hollow, with boards. As it has been shown you on the mountain, so shall it be made.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Inside the gate stands the bronze altar: no one comes near God except where a substitute dies.

The altar of acacia wood. Standing just inside the gate, it is the largest object in the complex, about seven and a half feet square, and is overlaid with bronze rather than gold. Gold is for the inner rooms; bronze is for the place where fire burns all day and blood runs down. And it is hollow, light enough to carry: even the altar travels.

Horns for it on its four corners. Blood of sin offerings was daubed on the horns (29:12), and fugitives clung to them for mercy (1 Kings 1:50).

No way in but past the altar. The order of the furniture preaches. You cannot reach the lampstand, the bread or the mercy seat except past the altar. Every route to God begins where something dies in your place. Its fires pointed to Christ, who “offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins” (Hebrews 10:12).

Uncertain wording. “Ledge” (v. 5) renders a rare word; exactly where the grating sat is unknown.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9-19 — The Court of the Tabernacle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s dwelling is closed on every side but one, and that one entrance is wide. The court measures a hundred cubits on the north and south and fifty on the east and west, walled with hangings of fine linen on bronze pillars and bases, with silver hooks and fillets (vv. 9–13). On the east, hangings of fifteen cubits flank a gate twenty cubits wide, its screen embroidered in blue, purple and scarlet like the tent (vv. 14–16). The wall is five cubits high, and all the pegs and utensils of the court are bronze (vv. 17–19).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Court of the Tabernacle

A linen wall marks out holy ground, and one embroidered gate, twenty cubits wide, lets the worshipper in.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: there was one way in, and a wide one. Now: Christ is that door: the only way in, and open to all who come.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall make the court of the tabernacle. On the south side the court shall have hangings of fine twined linen a hundred cubits long for one side. Its twenty pillars and their twenty bases shall be of bronze, but the hooks of the pillars and their fillets shall be of silver. And likewise for its length on the north side there shall be hangings a hundred cubits long, its pillars twenty and their bases twenty, of bronze, but the hooks of the pillars and their fillets shall be of silver. And for the breadth of the court on the west side there shall be hangings for fifty cubits, with ten pillars and ten bases. The breadth of the court on the front to the east shall be fifty cubits. The hangings for the one side of the gate shall be fifteen cubits, with their three pillars and three bases. On the other side the hangings shall be fifteen cubits, with their three pillars and three bases. For the gate of the court there shall be a screen twenty cubits long, of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen, embroidered with needlework. It shall have four pillars and with them four bases. All the pillars around the court shall be filleted with silver. Their hooks shall be of silver, and their bases of bronze. The length of the court shall be a hundred cubits, the breadth fifty, and the height five cubits, with hangings of fine twined linen and bases of bronze. All the utensils of the tabernacle for every use, and all its pegs and all the pegs of the court, shall be of bronze.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s court has one gate: the way to him is single, and it is open to all who come by it.

The gate of the court. The linen wall, higher than a man, is unbroken except for one screen on the east, thirty feet wide. An Israelite could walk the whole circuit and find no other way in.

I am the door. The court is shaped like Jesus’ claim: “I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved” (John 10:9). The gate says two things. It is exclusive: there is no other way in. And it is generous: the widest opening in the whole structure, open to every Israelite who came with an offering.

Bronze and gold. Bronze in the court, gold in the tent: the metal grows more precious the nearer you come to God, and every worshipper could see how far in he stood.
verseByVerse.note: The courtyard was about 150 by 75 feet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s light among his people is kept burning through every night by daily, faithful service. The people are to bring pure beaten olive oil for the lamp so that it burns regularly (v. 20); the light in God’s house depends on the gifts of the whole people. Inside the tent of meeting, in front of the veil, Aaron and his sons are to tend it “from evening to morning before the LORD” (v. 21). It is “a statute forever”, a duty for every generation of Israel (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology:
Oil for the Lamp

The people supply the oil; the priests keep the light burning through the night.
verseByVerse.examples: The finest oil went into a lamp most of the nation never saw. The light in God’s house is still kept burning by faithfulness that nobody watches, in the dark.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall command the people of Israel that they bring to you pure beaten olive oil for the light, that a lamp may regularly be set up to burn. In the tent of meeting, outside the veil that is before the testimony, Aaron and his sons shall tend it from evening to morning before the LORD. It shall be a statute forever to be observed throughout their generations by the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people supply the purest oil and the priests tend the lamp all night, so that God’s house is never dark.

Pure beaten olive oil for the light. “Beaten” oil was probably the first, hand-crushed oil from the olive, the purest and costliest grade.

From evening to morning. Israel sleeps; the priests do not. All night, by the lampstand in the holy place, Aaron and his sons trim wicks and top up oil so that at dawn there is still light in God’s house.

Unwatched faithfulness. A small duty, yet “a statute forever”: the light is kept burning not by one dramatic act but by somebody getting up in the dark, regularly, to do a job everyone would notice only if it stopped. Behind those priests stands a greater one, who “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25), whose care never sleeps.

keyVerse.quote: You shall make the altar of acacia wood, five cubits long and five cubits broad. The altar shall be square, and its height shall be three cubits.
keyVerse.note: The altar was the first and largest thing a worshipper met inside the gate: no one came near God except past the place of sacrifice. Its endless offerings pointed to the one sacrifice of Christ, “offered for all time” (Hebrews 10:12).

27.reflection:
Every worshipper had to pass the bronze altar before going any further (vv. 1–8). Why must the way to God begin with sacrifice, and how does Hebrews 10:11–14 show what the altar could not do?

The court had one gate, and it was the widest opening in the whole structure (vv. 9–16). How does Jesus’ claim “I am the door” (John 10:9) speak both to people who think every road leads to God and to people who fear they are not welcome?

The metals grow more precious from the court to the Most Holy Place. What does the layout of the tabernacle teach about the holiness of God, and about the privilege of drawing near to him through Christ?

The lamp was tended every night by priests no one saw (vv. 20–21). What unseen, regular acts of faithfulness has God given you, and how does Christ’s unsleeping intercession encourage you in them?

28.title: Israel on the High Priest's Heart
28.text: <sup>1</sup>"Then bring near to you Aaron your brother, and his sons with him, from among the people of Israel, to serve me as priests—Aaron and Aaron's sons, Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar.<sup>2</sup>And you shall make holy garments for Aaron your brother, for glory and for beauty.<sup>3</sup>You shall speak to all the skillful, whom I have filled with a spirit of skill, that they make Aaron's garments to consecrate him for my priesthood.<sup>4</sup>These are the garments that they shall make: a breastpiece, an ephod, a robe, a coat of checker work, a turban, and a sash. They shall make holy garments for Aaron your brother and his sons to serve me as priests.<sup>5</sup>They shall receive gold, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and fine twined linen.<sup>6</sup>"And they shall make the ephod of gold, of blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and of fine twined linen, skillfully worked.<sup>7</sup>It shall have two shoulder pieces attached to its two edges, so that it may be joined together.<sup>8</sup>And the skillfully woven band on it shall be made like it and be of one piece with it, of gold, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and fine twined linen.<sup>9</sup>You shall take two onyx stones, and engrave on them the names of the sons of Israel,<sup>10</sup>six of their names on the one stone, and the names of the remaining six on the other stone, in the order of their birth.<sup>11</sup>As a jeweler engraves signets, so shall you engrave the two stones with the names of the sons of Israel. You shall enclose them in settings of gold filigree.<sup>12</sup>And you shall set the two stones on the shoulder pieces of the ephod, as stones of remembrance for the sons of Israel. And Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD on his two shoulders for remembrance.<sup>13</sup>You shall make settings of gold filigree,<sup>14</sup>and two chains of pure gold, twisted like cords; and you shall attach the corded chains to the settings.<sup>15</sup>"You shall make a breastpiece of judgment, in skilled work. In the style of the ephod you shall make it—of gold, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and fine twined linen shall you make it.<sup>16</sup>It shall be square and doubled, a span its length and a span its breadth.<sup>17</sup>You shall set in it four rows of stones. A row of sardius, topaz, and carbuncle shall be the first row;<sup>18</sup>and the second row an emerald, a sapphire, and a diamond;<sup>19</sup>and the third row a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst;<sup>20</sup>and the fourth row a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper. They shall be set in gold filigree.<sup>21</sup>There shall be twelve stones with their names according to the names of the sons of Israel. They shall be like signets, each engraved with its name, for the twelve tribes.<sup>22</sup>You shall make for the breastpiece twisted chains like cords, of pure gold.<sup>23</sup>And you shall make for the breastpiece two rings of gold, and put the two rings on the two edges of the breastpiece.<sup>24</sup>And you shall put the two cords of gold in the two rings at the edges of the breastpiece.<sup>25</sup>The two ends of the two cords you shall attach to the two settings of filigree, and so attach it in front to the shoulder pieces of the ephod.<sup>26</sup>You shall make two rings of gold, and put them at the two ends of the breastpiece, on its inside edge next to the ephod.<sup>27</sup>And you shall make two rings of gold, and attach them in front to the lower part of the two shoulder pieces of the ephod, at its seam above the skillfully woven band of the ephod.<sup>28</sup>And they shall bind the breastpiece by its rings to the rings of the ephod with a lace of blue, so that it may lie on the skillfully woven band of the ephod, so that the breastpiece shall not come loose from the ephod.<sup>29</sup>So Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel in the breastpiece of judgment on his heart, when he goes into the Holy Place, to bring them to regular remembrance before the LORD.<sup>30</sup>And in the breastpiece of judgment you shall put the Urim and the Thummim, and they shall be on Aaron's heart, when he goes in before the LORD. Thus Aaron shall bear the judgment of the people of Israel on his heart before the LORD regularly.<sup>31</sup>"You shall make the robe of the ephod all of blue.<sup>32</sup>It shall have an opening for the head in the middle of it, with a woven binding around the opening, like the opening in a garment, so that it may not tear.<sup>33</sup>On its hem you shall make pomegranates of blue and purple and scarlet yarns, around its hem, with bells of gold between them,<sup>34</sup>a golden bell and a pomegranate, a golden bell and a pomegranate, around the hem of the robe.<sup>35</sup>And it shall be on Aaron when he ministers, and its sound shall be heard when he goes into the Holy Place before the LORD, and when he comes out, so that he does not die.<sup>36</sup>"You shall make a plate of pure gold and engrave on it, like the engraving of a signet, 'Holy to the LORD.'<sup>37</sup>And you shall fasten it on the turban by a cord of blue. It shall be on the front of the turban.<sup>38</sup>It shall be on Aaron's forehead, and Aaron shall bear any guilt from the holy things that the people of Israel consecrate as their holy gifts. It shall regularly be on his forehead, that they may be accepted before the LORD.<sup>39</sup>"You shall weave the coat in checker work of fine linen, and you shall make a turban of fine linen, and you shall make a sash embroidered with needlework.<sup>40</sup>"For Aaron's sons you shall make coats and sashes and caps. You shall make them for glory and beauty.<sup>41</sup>And you shall put them on Aaron your brother, and on his sons with him, and shall anoint them and ordain them and consecrate them, that they may serve me as priests.<sup>42</sup>You shall make for them linen undergarments to cover their naked flesh. They shall reach from the hips to the thighs;<sup>43</sup>and they shall be on Aaron and on his sons when they go into the tent of meeting or when they come near the altar to minister in the Holy Place, lest they bear guilt and die. This shall be a statute forever for him and for his offspring after him.
28.overview:
Where we are. God has described his dwelling from the ark outwards to the courtyard and the lamp (chapters 25–27). Now he turns from the place to the people who will serve in it: Aaron and his sons, and the garments they must wear. Chapter 29 will describe their ordination.

The message. Sinners need someone to stand for them before a holy God, and God himself provides and clothes him. The high priest carries the names of all twelve tribes on his shoulders and over his heart whenever he goes in before the LORD, and wears on his forehead “Holy to the LORD” so that the people’s gifts may be accepted. He is beautiful not for his own sake but for theirs: God looks at the priest and sees his people, named, carried and covered.

Why it was said. Israel had just learned that God would live among them behind a veil (26:33), and that no one could come near except by sacrifice (27:1–8). They needed a mediator. The nation that trembled at Sinai and begged Moses to speak for them (20:19) is now given a whole order of priests to go between them and God (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. God sets apart Aaron and his sons and orders holy garments “for glory and for beauty” (vv. 1–5). The ephod carries two onyx stones engraved with the tribes’ names on its shoulders (vv. 6–14). The breastpiece of judgment carries twelve stones engraved with the names over Aaron’s heart, and holds the Urim and Thummim (vv. 15–30). Then the blue robe with its bells, the gold plate engraved “Holy to the LORD”, the coat, turban and sash, the garments of Aaron’s sons and the linen undergarments (vv. 31–43).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. Aaron was a sinner who would make the golden calf, and his priesthood had to be renewed generation after generation. But “we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God” (Hebrews 4:14), “holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners” (Hebrews 7:26). He has entered “into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf” (Hebrews 9:24), and he “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25). Aaron carried names on stones; Christ carries his people in his heart and in his wounded body.

For us. No believer comes to God alone or on the strength of his own worship. Christ carries us in, by name, and covers even our best gifts with his holiness. And because we are in him, we too are “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9), called to carry others to God in prayer.
28.theology:
The necessity of a mediator. The priesthood exists because sinners cannot approach God directly and need a go-between, and it is fulfilled in Christ, our great High Priest.

Borne on the heart of the priest. Israel's names on the shoulders and heart picture Christ, who carries his people before the Father with strength and with love.

Holiness and the bearing of guilt. The plate reading "Holy to the LORD" and the bearing of the people's guilt point to Christ, who is holy and bore our guilt so that we might be accepted.
28.examples:
Then: the high priest carried the people into God's presence and bore the guilt even of their gifts, so that they might be accepted.

Now: Jesus carries us before God, on his shoulders like the shepherd and on his heart like the bridegroom, and we are accepted in him forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-5 — Garments for Glory and for Beauty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God chooses and clothes the priests who will stand between him and his people. Moses is to bring near Aaron and his four sons, Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar, from among the people of Israel to serve as priests (v. 1). They are to have holy garments “for glory and for beauty” (v. 2), made by skilled workers whom God has filled with a spirit of skill (v. 3). The list follows: breastpiece, ephod, robe, coat, turban and sash, all of gold, coloured yarns and fine linen (vv. 4–5). Every garment serves a man who stands for others.
verseByVerse.theology:
Garments for Glory and for Beauty

The best skill in Israel is spent on clothing one man, because he will stand before God on behalf of everyone else.
verseByVerse.examples: God appointed the man who would make the golden calf, knowing that he would. The priesthood rested on his choice, not on their record, and the priest is the one brought near so that others can be.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then bring near to you Aaron your brother, and his sons with him, from among the people of Israel, to serve me as priests—Aaron and Aaron's sons, Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. And you shall make holy garments for Aaron your brother, for glory and for beauty. You shall speak to all the skillful, whom I have filled with a spirit of skill, that they make Aaron's garments to consecrate him for my priesthood. These are the garments that they shall make: a breastpiece, an ephod, a robe, a coat of checker work, a turban, and a sash. They shall make holy garments for Aaron your brother and his sons to serve me as priests. They shall receive gold, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and fine twined linen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God brings Aaron and his sons near to serve him for the people, and clothes them for glory and beauty.

Bring near to you Aaron your brother. “Bring near” is the language of approach: the priest is the man brought near so that others can be (see Priests and Levites).

For glory and for beauty. It is the only reason given for so much gold and precious stone.

Appointed before the sin. Aaron will make the golden calf four chapters from now. God appoints him knowing it, and keeps him. Nadab and Abihu will die offering unauthorised fire (Leviticus 10:1–2). The family’s weakness shows why a better priest was needed, one with no sin of his own to offer for (Hebrews 7:27).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6-14 — The Ephod: Israel on the Shoulders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The high priest carries the whole people into God’s presence on his shoulders. The ephod is woven of gold, blue, purple and scarlet yarns and fine linen, with two shoulder pieces and a woven band of one piece with it (vv. 6–8). On the shoulders are set two onyx stones, engraved like a seal with the names of the sons of Israel, six on each, in the order of their birth (vv. 9–11). Aaron is to bear their names “before the LORD on his two shoulders for remembrance” (v. 12). Gold settings and chains hold them in place (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ephod: Israel on the Shoulders

Six names are engraved on each shoulder stone, so that the whole people is borne before the LORD for remembrance.
verseByVerse.examples: Every tribe was carried in, every time, and Christ carries his people as the shepherd carries home the lost sheep.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they shall make the ephod of gold, of blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and of fine twined linen, skillfully worked. It shall have two shoulder pieces attached to its two edges, so that it may be joined together. And the skillfully woven band on it shall be made like it and be of one piece with it, of gold, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and fine twined linen. You shall take two onyx stones, and engrave on them the names of the sons of Israel, six of their names on the one stone, and the names of the remaining six on the other stone, in the order of their birth. As a jeweler engraves signets, so shall you engrave the two stones with the names of the sons of Israel. You shall enclose them in settings of gold filigree. And you shall set the two stones on the shoulder pieces of the ephod, as stones of remembrance for the sons of Israel. And Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD on his two shoulders for remembrance. You shall make settings of gold filigree, and two chains of pure gold, twisted like cords; and you shall attach the corded chains to the settings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On his shoulders the high priest carries the names of all twelve tribes into God’s presence.

On his two shoulders for remembrance. Two onyx stones sit on the ephod’s shoulders, six names on each, and the shoulder is where weight is carried. The high priest came into the sanctuary bearing the whole nation, not merely in his intentions but on his body, in stone. Nobody was left out because they were unimportant or in disgrace that year. All twelve, every time. The same names stand on the gates of the city of God (Revelation 21:12).

Uncertain wording. The exact shape of the ephod is unknown: probably a vest or apron with shoulder straps and a woven waistband.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15-30 — The Breastpiece: Israel over the Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The high priest carries the whole people over his heart whenever he goes in before God. The breastpiece of judgment is a square pouch of the same rich material, a span each way (vv. 15–16). On it are set four rows of three precious stones, each engraved with the name of a tribe (vv. 17–21). Gold chains, rings and a blue lace bind it to the ephod so that it cannot come loose (vv. 22–28). So Aaron bears the names “on his heart” in the Holy Place “to bring them to regular remembrance before the LORD” (v. 29), and in the breastpiece go the Urim and Thummim (v. 30).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Breastpiece: Israel over the Heart

The tribes' names are fastened over Aaron's heart whenever he goes in.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the people were carried in by strength and by love. Now: Christ bears his people in his own body and always lives to pray for them.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall make a breastpiece of judgment, in skilled work. In the style of the ephod you shall make it—of gold, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and fine twined linen shall you make it. It shall be square and doubled, a span its length and a span its breadth. You shall set in it four rows of stones. A row of sardius, topaz, and carbuncle shall be the first row; and the second row an emerald, a sapphire, and a diamond; and the third row a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst; and the fourth row a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper. They shall be set in gold filigree. There shall be twelve stones with their names according to the names of the sons of Israel. They shall be like signets, each engraved with its name, for the twelve tribes. You shall make for the breastpiece twisted chains like cords, of pure gold. And you shall make for the breastpiece two rings of gold, and put the two rings on the two edges of the breastpiece. And you shall put the two cords of gold in the two rings at the edges of the breastpiece. The two ends of the two cords you shall attach to the two settings of filigree, and so attach it in front to the shoulder pieces of the ephod. You shall make two rings of gold, and put them at the two ends of the breastpiece, on its inside edge next to the ephod. And you shall make two rings of gold, and attach them in front to the lower part of the two shoulder pieces of the ephod, at its seam above the skillfully woven band of the ephod. And they shall bind the breastpiece by its rings to the rings of the ephod with a lace of blue, so that it may lie on the skillfully woven band of the ephod, so that the breastpiece shall not come loose from the ephod. So Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel in the breastpiece of judgment on his heart, when he goes into the Holy Place, to bring them to regular remembrance before the LORD. And in the breastpiece of judgment you shall put the Urim and the Thummim, and they shall be on Aaron's heart, when he goes in before the LORD. Thus Aaron shall bear the judgment of the people of Israel on his heart before the LORD regularly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Over his heart the high priest carries the names of God’s people, with the means of receiving God’s decisions.

A breastpiece of judgment. This is the heart of the chapter, chained in place so it cannot come loose (v. 28). Names on the shoulders and on the heart: carried by strength and by love, both at once, every time he went in (v. 29).

They shall be on Aaron’s heart. The Urim and Thummim went in the breastpiece: the means of knowing God’s will was kept with the names of his people, over the priest’s heart (v. 30).

Always lives to make intercession. Here we think of the one who “always lives to make intercession for them” (Hebrews 7:25). He needs no engraved stones to remember his people’s names: he bears them in his body, with the marks of the nails still in it.

Do Christians have anything like the Urim and Thummim? No. God now guides through his completed word, prayer, wisdom and godly counsel (Psalm 119:105; James 1:5); the apostles last cast lots before Pentecost (Acts 1:26).

Uncertain wording. No one knows exactly what the Urim and Thummim were; most likely objects used to receive a yes or no from God (Numbers 27:21; 1 Samuel 28:6), hence “breastpiece of judgment”. Several of the stones are also uncertain (ESV note): ancient gem names do not match modern ones.
verseByVerse.note: The identity of some of the stones is uncertain (ESV note).
