verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31-43 — The Robe, the Golden Plate, and the Holy Vestments
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Every part of the priest’s dress says that sinful people can come to God only covered by holiness that God provides. The robe of the ephod is all blue, with pomegranates and golden bells around the hem, whose sound is heard when Aaron goes in and comes out, “so that he does not die” (vv. 31–35). A gold plate engraved “Holy to the LORD” is fastened to his turban so that he may bear the guilt of the people’s holy gifts and they may be accepted (vv. 36–38). Coat, turban and sash complete his dress (v. 39). His sons receive coats, sashes and caps, all are to be anointed and ordained, and linen undergarments cover their nakedness when they serve (vv. 40–43).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Robe, the Golden Plate, and the Holy Vestments

The priest bears the guilt even of Israel's holy gifts, and he comes in entirely covered by what he has been given.
verseByVerse.examples: Even Israel's best gifts needed covering. God still removes his people's filthy garments and clothes them in what they did not make.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall make the robe of the ephod all of blue. It shall have an opening for the head in the middle of it, with a woven binding around the opening, like the opening in a garment, so that it may not tear. On its hem you shall make pomegranates of blue and purple and scarlet yarns, around its hem, with bells of gold between them, a golden bell and a pomegranate, a golden bell and a pomegranate, around the hem of the robe. And it shall be on Aaron when he ministers, and its sound shall be heard when he goes into the Holy Place before the LORD, and when he comes out, so that he does not die. "You shall make a plate of pure gold and engrave on it, like the engraving of a signet, 'Holy to the LORD.' And you shall fasten it on the turban by a cord of blue. It shall be on the front of the turban. It shall be on Aaron's forehead, and Aaron shall bear any guilt from the holy things that the people of Israel consecrate as their holy gifts. It shall regularly be on his forehead, that they may be accepted before the LORD. "You shall weave the coat in checker work of fine linen, and you shall make a turban of fine linen, and you shall make a sash embroidered with needlework. "For Aaron's sons you shall make coats and sashes and caps. You shall make them for glory and beauty. And you shall put them on Aaron your brother, and on his sons with him, and shall anoint them and ordain them and consecrate them, that they may serve me as priests. You shall make for them linen undergarments to cover their naked flesh. They shall reach from the hips to the thighs; and they shall be on Aaron and on his sons when they go into the tent of meeting or when they come near the altar to minister in the Holy Place, lest they bear guilt and die. This shall be a statute forever for him and for his offspring after him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Robe, plate and linen say that the priest and his people come to God only covered by a holiness God provides.

Bells of gold. They sounded as Aaron went in and out, “so that he does not die” (v. 35); the text does not say more. Perhaps the people listened for them outside.

Holy to the LORD. The gold plate is startling: even Israel’s gifts carry guilt. Offerings brought in devotion need covering, and the priest wears “Holy to the LORD” on his forehead so that God can accept worship that is not clean (v. 38). Nothing anybody brings is good enough on its own, including their best.

Linen undergarments. As with the altar without steps (20:26), nothing of the priest’s own flesh is exposed: he comes in covered, wearing what he was given.

The whole outfit. The garments describe a man who is nothing in himself: he carries names that are not his, wears a plate that makes other people’s gifts acceptable, and his bells are heard by people he cannot see. Zechariah saw the high priest Joshua in filthy garments while Satan accused him, and the angel said, “Remove the filthy garments from him … Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments” (Zechariah 3:4). That is what the gospel does with everyone it saves. Our High Priest alone needs no covering: he is “holy, innocent, unstained” (Hebrews 7:26).

keyVerse.quote: So Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel in the breastpiece of judgment on his heart, when he goes into the Holy Place, to bring them to regular remembrance before the LORD.
keyVerse.note: This verse holds the meaning of the priest’s whole dress: he goes in before God carrying God’s people by name, over his heart. It points to Christ, who has entered God’s presence “on our behalf” (Hebrews 9:24) and always lives to intercede for us.

28.reflection:
God chose Aaron knowing that he would make the golden calf (vv. 1–3; 32:1–6). What does this tell you about God’s grace, and why did Israel still need a better priest (Hebrews 5:1–5; 7:26–27)?

Aaron carried the tribes’ names on his shoulders and over his heart (vv. 12, 29). How does it comfort you that Christ carries his people by name into God’s presence, especially when you feel unimportant or in disgrace?

The gold plate “Holy to the LORD” was needed so that even the people’s holy gifts could be accepted (v. 38). What does that teach about your best efforts in worship and service, and how do you rest in Christ’s holiness instead of your own?

Believers are now “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9). Whose names will you carry to God in prayer this week?

29.title: Consecrated by Blood and Sacrifice
29.text: <sup>1</sup>"Now this is what you shall do to them to consecrate them, that they may serve me as priests. Take one bull of the herd and two rams without blemish,<sup>2</sup>and unleavened bread, unleavened cakes mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers smeared with oil. You shall make them of fine wheat flour.<sup>3</sup>You shall put them in one basket and bring them in the basket, and bring the bull and the two rams.<sup>4</sup>You shall bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the tent of meeting and wash them with water.<sup>5</sup>Then you shall take the garments, and put on Aaron the coat and the robe of the ephod, and the ephod, and the breastpiece, and gird him with the skillfully woven band of the ephod.<sup>6</sup>And you shall set the turban on his head and put the holy crown on the turban.<sup>7</sup>You shall take the anointing oil and pour it on his head and anoint him.<sup>8</sup>Then you shall bring his sons and put coats on them,<sup>9</sup>and you shall gird Aaron and his sons with sashes and bind caps on them. And the priesthood shall be theirs by a statute forever. Thus you shall ordain Aaron and his sons.<sup>10</sup>"Then you shall bring the bull before the tent of meeting. It is a burnt offering to the LORD. He and his garments shall be holy, and his sons and his sons' garments with him.<sup>22</sup>"You shall also take the fat from the ram and the fat tail and the fat that covers the entrails, and the long lobe of the liver and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them, and the right thigh (for it is a ram of ordination),<sup>23</sup>and one loaf of bread and one cake of bread made with oil, and one wafer out of the basket of unleavened bread that is before the LORD.<sup>24</sup>You shall put all these on the palms of Aaron and on the palms of his sons, and wave them for a wave offering before the LORD.<sup>25</sup>Then you shall take them from their hands and burn them on the altar on top of the burnt offering, as a pleasing aroma before the LORD. It shall not be eaten, because it is holy.<sup>35</sup>"Thus you shall do to Aaron and to his sons, according to all that I have commanded you. Through seven days shall you ordain them,<sup>36</sup>and every day you shall offer a bull as a sin offering for atonement. Also you shall purify the altar, when you make atonement for it, and shall anoint it to consecrate it.<sup>37</sup>Seven days you shall make atonement for the altar and consecrate it, and the altar shall be most holy. Whatever touches the altar shall become holy.<sup>38</sup>"Now this is what you shall offer on the altar: two lambs a year old day by day regularly.<sup>39</sup>One lamb you shall offer in the morning, and the other lamb you shall offer at twilight.<sup>40</sup>And with the first lamb a tenth measure of fine flour mingled with a fourth of a hin of beaten oil, and a fourth of a hin of wine for a drink offering.<sup>41</sup>The other lamb you shall offer at twilight, and shall offer with it a grain offering and its drink offering, as in the morning, for a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.<sup>42</sup>It shall be a regular burnt offering throughout your generations at the entrance of the tent of meeting before the LORD, where I will meet with you, to speak to you there.<sup>43</sup>There I will meet with the people of Israel, and it shall be sanctified by my glory.<sup>44</sup>I will consecrate the tent of meeting and the altar. Aaron also and his sons I will consecrate to serve me as priests.<sup>45</sup>I will dwell among the people of Israel and will be their God.<sup>46</sup>And they shall know that I am the LORD their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt that I might dwell among them. I am the LORD their God.
29.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 25–28 gave the pattern of the tabernacle and the clothes of the priests. Now God tells Moses how to set Aaron and his sons apart to serve in it, the ceremony carried out in Leviticus 8.

The message. No one may come near the holy God on his own terms, not even the man chosen to stand between God and Israel. The priests must be washed, clothed, anointed and covered by blood before they serve, and even the altar must be atoned for. Yet the point of all the blood is not distance but fellowship: “I will dwell among the people of Israel and will be their God” (v. 45).

Why it was said. Israel had just seen the fire on Sinai and been told that whoever touched the mountain would die (19:12). They needed to learn how a holy God could live among an unholy people, and that the way in was his gift, not their achievement (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Aaron and his sons are washed, dressed and anointed (vv. 1–9). A bull is offered as a sin offering and a ram as a burnt offering, with hands laid on each (vv. 10–18). A second ram, the ram of ordination, marks ear, thumb and toe with blood, and its portions are put in the priests’ hands and waved before the LORD (vv. 19–28). The rite lasts seven days, with a sin offering every day, and the altar too is atoned for (vv. 29–37). Then come the daily lambs, morning and evening, and the promise that gives the whole system its purpose: God will meet with his people and dwell among them (vv. 38–46).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. Hebrews reads this chapter closely: priests who had to offer first for their own sins, sacrifices repeated day after day, and a priesthood handed from father to son because death kept interrupting it (Hebrews 7:23–27; 10:11). Jesus needs no cleansing for himself, offered himself once for all, and “holds his priesthood permanently” (Hebrews 7:24). In him the promise of verse 45 comes true: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

For us. You cannot make yourself fit for God, and in Christ you do not need to: he washes, clothes and anoints his people, and his blood covers what we hear, what we do and where we go. Believers are now “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2:9), so serve gladly, knowing that the goal of it all is God himself living with his people.
29.theology:
Even mediators need atonement. The priests must be washed and atoned for by blood before they serve. No one is fit by nature to approach God.

The costliness of atonement. The repeated sacrifices preach the seriousness of sin and point to Christ's one final sacrifice (Heb. 10:12).

The goal of sacrifice is communion. All the blood serves one end: that the holy God might dwell with his people.
29.examples:
Then: priests were consecrated with washing, anointing and blood, and a lamb died every morning and evening, so that God might dwell among his people.

Now: the one Lamb of God, slain once, cleanses us, sets us apart for God and brings us near.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Priests are made, not self-made. Moses gathers the bull, the two rams and the unleavened bread (vv. 1–3), brings Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the tent and washes them (v. 4), dresses Aaron in the high priest’s garments of chapter 28 (vv. 5–6) and pours the anointing oil on his head (v. 7). The sons are then clothed in coats, sashes and caps (vv. 8–9). Every verb is done to them: they are washed, dressed and anointed. The priesthood is theirs “by a statute forever” (v. 9), a calling received, not earned.
verseByVerse.theology:
Consecration: Washed, Clothed, Anointed

Everything is done to the priests before they do anything themselves.
verseByVerse.examples: Christians are made fit for God's service the same way: washed, clothed and given the Spirit by another, before they lift a finger.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now this is what you shall do to them to consecrate them, that they may serve me as priests. Take one bull of the herd and two rams without blemish, and unleavened bread, unleavened cakes mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers smeared with oil. You shall make them of fine wheat flour. You shall put them in one basket and bring them in the basket, and bring the bull and the two rams. You shall bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the tent of meeting and wash them with water. Then you shall take the garments, and put on Aaron the coat and the robe of the ephod, and the ephod, and the breastpiece, and gird him with the skillfully woven band of the ephod. And you shall set the turban on his head and put the holy crown on the turban. You shall take the anointing oil and pour it on his head and anoint him. Then you shall bring his sons and put coats on them, and you shall gird Aaron and his sons with sashes and bind caps on them. And the priesthood shall be theirs by a statute forever. Thus you shall ordain Aaron and his sons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sets Aaron and his sons apart in a fixed order: washed, then clothed, then anointed, and only then fit to serve.

To consecrate them. To consecrate is to set apart for God’s use. The order never varies, here and in Leviticus 8: washed before dressed, dressed before anointed, anointed before serving. Nothing in it is achieved by the men themselves. A priest in Israel did not qualify for office; everything was done to him, and Aaron brings only himself.

Clothed by God. The pattern reaches its climax in Zechariah’s vision of Joshua the high priest, in filthy garments: “Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments” (Zechariah 3:4). That is the gospel in priestly dress: in Christ we are washed and clothed in his righteousness, and only so do we serve.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10-18 — Sin Offering and Burnt Offering
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before the priests can offer for others, sacrifice must be offered for them. Aaron and his sons lay their hands on a bull, which is killed; its blood is put on the horns of the altar and poured at its base, its fat is burned on the altar, and its flesh, skin and dung are burned outside the camp as a sin offering (vv. 10–14). Then they lay their hands on a ram, which is burned whole as a burnt offering, “a pleasing aroma” to the LORD (vv. 15–18). Sin is dealt with first; then the whole life is given to God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sin Offering and Burnt Offering

First the sin is dealt with; then the whole life is offered up as a pleasing aroma.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: laying hands on the animal identified the worshipper with his substitute. Now: Christ took the substitute’s place, and was put outside the camp to do it (Heb. 13:12).

verseByVerse.quote: "Then you shall bring the bull before the tent of meeting. Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on the head of the bull. Then you shall kill the bull before the LORD at the entrance of the tent of meeting, and shall take part of the blood of the bull and put it on the horns of the altar with your finger, and the rest of the blood you shall pour out at the base of the altar. And you shall take all the fat that covers the entrails, and the long lobe of the liver, and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them, and burn them on the altar. But the flesh of the bull and its skin and its dung you shall burn with fire outside the camp; it is a sin offering. "Then you shall take one of the rams, and Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on the head of the ram, and you shall kill the ram and shall take its blood and throw it against the sides of the altar. Then you shall cut the ram into pieces, and wash its entrails and its legs, and put them with its pieces and its head, and burn the whole ram on the altar. It is a burnt offering to the LORD. It is a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the priests can offer for Israel, their own sin must be dealt with, and then their whole lives given to God.

Lay their hands on the head of the bull. The laying on of hands is the visual centre of the sacrificial system. It is not a blessing but identification: what happens next happens to the animal instead of to the worshipper. On the Day of Atonement the same gesture openly lays the people’s sins on the goat (Leviticus 16:21).

The horns of the altar. The blood goes on the horns, the altar’s highest points. A fugitive who took hold of the horns of the altar was claiming sanctuary (1 Kings 1:50). Blood is applied precisely where people grabbed when they had nowhere else to go.

Outside the camp. The bull’s carcass is burned outside the camp, and Hebrews takes up the detail with great force: “the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Hebrews 13:11–12). The place of disgrace, where the refuse went, is where he died.

Does God need food, or enjoy the smell of burning meat? No: “If I were hungry, I would not tell you” (Psalm 50:12). “A pleasing aroma” means the offering is accepted. The same words are used of Christ, who “gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (Ephesians 5:2).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ram of ordination marks the priests as wholly God’s. Its blood is put on the right ear, thumb and great toe of Aaron and his sons, and blood from the altar is sprinkled with the anointing oil on them and their garments (vv. 19–21). The richest parts of the ram, with bread from the basket, are placed in their hands and waved before the LORD, then burned (vv. 22–25). The breast and thigh become the priests’ portion, a lasting share from Israel’s peace offerings (vv. 26–28). God fills their hands, and then he feeds them from his altar.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ram of Ordination

Blood and then oil mark the whole man for service.
verseByVerse.examples: What a priest heard, what he did and where he walked were marked with blood before he served. Christians are cleansed by Christ's blood before the Spirit equips them, and every gift for service comes in that order.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall take the other ram, and Aaron and his sons shall lay their hands on the head of the ram, and you shall kill the ram and take part of its blood and put it on the tip of the right ear of Aaron and on the tips of the right ears of his sons, and on the thumbs of their right hands and on the great toes of their right feet, and throw the rest of the blood against the sides of the altar. Then you shall take part of the blood that is on the altar, and of the anointing oil, and sprinkle it on Aaron and his garments, and on his sons and his sons' garments with him. He and his garments shall be holy, and his sons and his sons' garments with him. "You shall also take the fat from the ram and the fat tail and the fat that covers the entrails, and the long lobe of the liver and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them, and the right thigh (for it is a ram of ordination), and one loaf of bread and one cake of bread made with oil, and one wafer out of the basket of unleavened bread that is before the LORD. You shall put all these on the palms of Aaron and on the palms of his sons, and wave them for a wave offering before the LORD. Then you shall take them from their hands and burn them on the altar on top of the burnt offering, as a pleasing aroma before the LORD. It is a food offering to the LORD. "You shall take the breast of the ram of Aaron's ordination and wave it for a wave offering before the LORD, and it shall be your portion. And you shall consecrate the breast of the wave offering that is waved and the thigh of the priests' portion that is contributed from the ram of ordination, from what was Aaron's and his sons'. It shall be for Aaron and his sons as a perpetual due from the people of Israel, for it is a contribution. It shall be a contribution from the people of Israel from their peace offerings, their contribution to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ram of ordination marks the whole of the priest’s life with blood and fills his hands with what God gives.

Ear, thumb and toe. The blood goes on what the priest hears, what he does and where he goes: his whole life is marked before he may serve. The same marking is used for a cleansed leper (Leviticus 14:14): the priest and the outcast are made clean in the same way.

Blood first, then oil. Blood and anointing oil are sprinkled together, blood first. That is the pattern of the gospel: atonement before anointing. The Spirit is given to people who have been cleansed, never instead of cleansing, and the power to serve comes as a gift.

Put all these on the palms of Aaron. The Hebrew for ordaining a priest is to “fill the hand” (v. 9), and here it happens literally (vv. 24–25): the priest brings nothing to the office; the office puts something into his hands.

Uncertain wording. The “wave offering” (Hebrew tenuphah) was presented before the LORD, but the movement is uncertain: moved to and fro, or lifted up (hence “elevation offering” in some translations). Either way it was given to God and received back from him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29-37 — Seven Days, and an Atoned Altar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ordination takes a whole week, and even the altar must be cleansed. The holy garments will pass from Aaron to the son who succeeds him (vv. 29–30). The priests eat the flesh of the ram and the bread at the entrance of the tent, food no outsider may eat, and whatever is left till morning is burned (vv. 31–34). For seven days a bull is offered every day as a sin offering, and the altar is atoned for and anointed until it is “most holy” (vv. 35–37). The repetition shows how much it takes for sinners to draw near to God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Seven Days, and an Atoned Altar

Even the altar must be atoned for before it becomes most holy.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: even the instrument of atonement needed atoning for. Now: one offering has done what seven days of bulls could not.

verseByVerse.quote: "The holy garments of Aaron shall be for his sons after him; they shall be anointed in them and ordained in them. The son who succeeds him as priest, who comes into the tent of meeting to minister in the Holy Place, shall wear them seven days. "You shall take the ram of ordination and boil its flesh in a holy place. And Aaron and his sons shall eat the flesh of the ram and the bread that is in the basket in the entrance of the tent of meeting. They shall eat those things with which atonement was made at their ordination and consecration, but an outsider shall not eat of them, because they are holy. And if any of the flesh for the ordination or of the bread remain until the morning, then you shall burn the remainder with fire. It shall not be eaten, because it is holy. "Thus you shall do to Aaron and to his sons, according to all that I have commanded you. Through seven days shall you ordain them, and every day you shall offer a bull as a sin offering for atonement. Also you shall purify the altar, when you make atonement for it, and shall anoint it to consecrate it. Seven days you shall make atonement for the altar and consecrate it, and the altar shall be most holy. Whatever touches the altar shall become holy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven days of daily sin offerings are needed to ordain the priests and cleanse the altar, a repetition that shows both the cost of drawing near and how little these sacrifices could settle.

For his sons after him. The holy garments pass to Aaron’s successor (vv. 29–30): Israel’s priests “were prevented by death from continuing in office” (Hebrews 7:23), and the robes outlived every man who wore them. The ordination meal is for the priests alone; an outsider here means anyone not of the priestly family (vv. 31–34).

Through seven days shall you ordain them. It takes a week of sacrifice, with a sin offering every day, to consecrate one family for one task, and the altar itself must be atoned for, built as it was by sinful hands. Everything here needs cleansing, even the instruments of cleansing. Hebrews builds on exactly this: every priest stands daily, “offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins”, and the repetition is itself the proof (Hebrews 10:11).

One offering for all time. Set against that: “by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14). Seven days of bulls and rams to make one man fit to stand in a tent, against one afternoon at the cross that finished the matter for ever.

Uncertain wording. “Whatever touches the altar shall become holy” (v. 37) could also be “whoever”, and the verb can mean “will become holy” or “must be holy”. It may mean that what touches the altar is claimed for God, or that only the holy may touch it. Holiness does not spread like a contagion (Haggai 2:12), so the likely sense is that whatever touches the altar comes under its claim and belongs to God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 38-46 — The Daily Lamb, and God Dwelling Among Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends with the daily rhythm of worship and the reason for everything. Two year-old lambs are offered every day, one in the morning and one at twilight, with flour, oil and wine (vv. 38–41), a regular burnt offering at the entrance of the tent where God will meet his people (v. 42). Then God speaks of what he himself will do: meet with Israel, sanctify the tent by his glory, consecrate the priests, and dwell among them as their God (vv. 43–45). He brought them out of Egypt for this: “that I might dwell among them” (v. 46).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Daily Lamb, and God Dwelling Among Them

At the place of continual sacrifice God meets his people, consecrates his house and dwells with them as their God.
verseByVerse.examples: God brought Israel out of Egypt "that I might dwell among them," and every page after this reaches toward the same goal.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now this is what you shall offer on the altar: two lambs a year old day by day regularly. One lamb you shall offer in the morning, and the other lamb you shall offer at twilight. And with the first lamb a tenth measure of fine flour mingled with a fourth of a hin of beaten oil, and a fourth of a hin of wine for a drink offering. The other lamb you shall offer at twilight, and shall offer with it a grain offering and its drink offering, as in the morning, for a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD. It shall be a regular burnt offering throughout your generations at the entrance of the tent of meeting before the LORD, where I will meet with you, to speak to you there. There I will meet with the people of Israel, and it shall be sanctified by my glory. I will consecrate the tent of meeting and the altar. Aaron also and his sons I will consecrate to serve me as priests. I will dwell among the people of Israel and will be their God. And they shall know that I am the LORD their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt that I might dwell among them. I am the LORD their God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every day begins and ends with a lamb on the altar, and God gives the reason for all of it: he brought Israel out of Egypt in order to live among them.

Two lambs a year old day by day regularly. One lamb in the morning and one at twilight, every day, with flour, oil and a quarter of a hin of wine. Whatever else happened in Israel, harvest, war, plague or coronation, a lamb died at dawn and a lamb died at dusk, and the nation’s day began and ended with sacrifice.

That I might dwell among them. At the end of all these instructions it is God who says “I will consecrate” (v. 44), and then he says why. The goal of the exodus is not land, nor even freedom, but “that I might dwell among them” (v. 46). The plagues, the sea, the manna and the mountain were all so that God could live in the middle of his people.

God dwelling with us. The rest of the Bible keeps reaching for that sentence. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14) uses the word for pitching a tent. “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16). And at the end: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people” (Revelation 21:3). These chapters of sacrifices serve one purpose, from Egypt to the new creation: that God should live with us, not at a distance.
verseByVerse.note: A hin was about 4 quarts (ESV note).

keyVerse.quote: I will dwell among the people of Israel and will be their God.
keyVerse.note: After all the washing, robing, anointing and blood, God names the purpose behind it: not distance but fellowship. The verse gathers up the whole exodus (v. 46), and its promise runs on to the Word who “dwelt among us” and the new creation where God dwells with his people for ever.

29.reflection:
Aaron and his sons were washed, dressed and anointed; they did nothing to qualify themselves (vv. 4–9). How does that help someone who feels they must make themselves good enough before coming to God?

The blood of the ram was put on the ear, thumb and toe (v. 20). What would it mean for what you hear, what you do and where you go to be wholly given to God?

Seven days of sacrifices could not finally take away sin (Hebrews 10:11–14). How does the once-for-all offering of Christ change the way you deal with guilt?

God says he brought Israel out of Egypt “that I might dwell among them” (v. 46). If God’s goal in saving you is to live with you, how should that shape your prayer and your hope?

30.title: Every Detail of Worship Ordained by God
30.text: <sup>1</sup>"You shall make an altar on which to burn incense; you shall make it of acacia wood.<sup>2</sup>A cubit shall be its length, and a cubit its breadth. It shall be square, and two cubits shall be its height. Its horns shall be of one piece with it.<sup>3</sup>You shall overlay it with pure gold, its top and around its sides and its horns. And you shall make a molding of gold around it.<sup>4</sup>And you shall make two golden rings for it. Under its molding on two opposite sides of it you shall make them, and they shall be holders for poles with which to carry it.<sup>5</sup>You shall make the poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold.<sup>6</sup>And you shall put it in front of the veil that is above the ark of the testimony, in front of the mercy seat that is above the testimony, where I will meet with you.<sup>7</sup>And Aaron shall burn fragrant incense on it. Every morning when he dresses the lamps he shall burn it,<sup>8</sup>and when Aaron sets up the lamps at twilight, he shall burn it, a regular incense offering before the LORD throughout your generations.<sup>9</sup>You shall not offer unauthorized incense on it, or a burnt offering, or a grain offering, and you shall not pour a drink offering on it.<sup>10</sup>Aaron shall make atonement on its horns once a year. With the blood of the sin offering of atonement he shall make atonement for it once in the year throughout your generations. It is most holy to the LORD."<sup>11</sup>The LORD said to Moses,<sup>12</sup>"When you take the census of the people of Israel, then each shall give a ransom for his life to the LORD when you number them, that there be no plague among them when you number them.<sup>13</sup>Each one who is numbered in the census shall give this: half a shekel according to the shekel of the sanctuary (the shekel is twenty gerahs), half a shekel as an offering to the LORD.<sup>14</sup>Everyone who is numbered in the census, from twenty years old and upward, shall give the LORD's offering.<sup>15</sup>The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less, than the half shekel, when you give the LORD's offering to make atonement for your lives.<sup>16</sup>You shall take the atonement money from the people of Israel and shall give it for the service of the tent of meeting, that it may bring the people of Israel to remembrance before the LORD, so as to make atonement for your lives."<sup>17</sup>The LORD said to Moses,<sup>18</sup>"You shall also make a basin of bronze, with its stand of bronze, for washing. You shall put it between the tent of meeting and the altar, and you shall put water in it,<sup>19</sup>with which Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet.<sup>20</sup>When they go into the tent of meeting, or when they come near the altar to minister, to burn a food offering to the LORD, they shall wash with water, so that they may not die.<sup>21</sup>They shall wash their hands and their feet, so that they may not die. It shall be a statute forever to them, even to him and to his offspring throughout their generations."<sup>22</sup>The LORD said to Moses,<sup>23</sup>"Take the finest spices: of liquid myrrh 500 shekels, and of sweet-smelling cinnamon half as much, that is, 250, and 250 of aromatic cane,<sup>24</sup>and 500 of cassia, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, and a hin of olive oil.<sup>25</sup>And you shall make of these a sacred anointing oil blended as by the perfumer; it shall be a holy anointing oil.<sup>26</sup>With it you shall anoint the tent of meeting and the ark of the testimony,<sup>27</sup>and the table and all its utensils, and the lampstand and its utensils, and the altar of incense,<sup>28</sup>and the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils and the basin and its stand.<sup>29</sup>You shall consecrate them, that they may be most holy. Whatever touches them will become holy.<sup>30</sup>You shall anoint Aaron and his sons, and consecrate them, that they may serve me as priests.<sup>31</sup>And you shall say to the people of Israel, 'This shall be my holy anointing oil throughout your generations.<sup>32</sup>It shall not be poured on the body of an ordinary person, and you shall make no other like it in composition. It is holy, and it shall be holy to you.<sup>33</sup>Whoever compounds any like it or whoever puts any of it on an outsider shall be cut off from his people.'"<sup>34</sup>The LORD said to Moses, "Take sweet spices, stacte, and onycha, and galbanum, sweet spices with pure frankincense (of each shall there be an equal part),<sup>35</sup>and make an incense blended as by the perfumer, seasoned with salt, pure and holy.<sup>36</sup>You shall beat some of it very small, and put part of it before the testimony in the tent of meeting where I shall meet with you. It shall be most holy for you.<sup>37</sup>And the incense that you shall make according to its composition, you shall not make for yourselves. It shall be for you holy to the LORD.<sup>38</sup>Whoever makes any like it to use as perfume shall be cut off from his people."
30.overview:
Where we are. The instructions for the tabernacle are drawing to a close. Chapter 29 ordained the priests and set the daily lambs; now God adds the furnishings and rules that belong to their daily ministry: the incense altar, the ransom money, the basin, the anointing oil and the incense.

The message. God alone decides how sinners may come near him, and every part of his provision says the same thing: we come by ransom and cleansing, and what is holy must stay holy. Prayer rises before him, but even the altar of prayer needs blood; every life in Israel is redeemed at the same price; the priests must wash or die.

Why it was said. A people fresh from Egypt’s many gods needed to learn that worship is received, not invented, and that the LORD cannot be handled like a household idol (see the introduction). Chapter 32 is about to show what happens when people invent their own way to worship.

How the chapter makes its case. A golden altar of incense stands before the veil, burning morning and evening, its horns cleansed with blood once a year (vv. 1–10). At every census each man pays the same half shekel as a ransom for his life, and the silver serves the tent (vv. 11–16). A bronze basin stands between altar and tent for the priests to wash (vv. 17–21). A holy anointing oil consecrates the tent, its furniture and the priests, and must never be copied (vv. 22–33). A holy incense, likewise, is for God alone (vv. 34–38).

Where it leads. By pattern. The incense pictures prayer heard because of the blood, and Christ “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25). The ransom points to “the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:19), the same price for every one of his people. The basin points to the washing he gives (John 13:10), and the anointing oil to the one whose very title, Messiah or Christ, means “anointed”.

For us. We do not design our own approach to God; we come by the way he has opened in Christ. That is a relief, not a restriction: our prayers are accepted for his sake, no one is worth more or less in his ransom, and those washed once in him may come back every day to be cleansed.
30.theology:
Worship ordained by God. We approach God on his terms, not our own. Reformed churches have drawn from the second commandment what is called the regulative principle: worship should include only what God has commanded. Many faithful Christians hold instead that worship may include what Scripture does not forbid; both sides agree that God, not our taste, sets its terms.

Prayer as incense. The altar of incense pictures the prayers of the saints rising before God, made acceptable because Christ intercedes for us (Ps. 141:2; Rev. 5:8).

Ransom and cleansing. The atonement money and the basin point to the ransom of Christ's blood (1 Pet. 1:18-19) and the washing of new birth (Titus 3:5).
30.examples:
Then: God prescribed every detail of worship, teaching Israel that all worship needs atonement and cleansing.

Now: our prayers are made acceptable by Christ our Intercessor, we are ransomed by his blood and washed by his Spirit, and we worship God on his terms, in spirit and truth.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Prayer rises before God, but even the place of prayer must be atoned for. Israel is to make a small square altar of acacia wood overlaid with gold, with horns, rings and poles (vv. 1–5). It stands before the veil, in front of the mercy seat where God meets with Moses (v. 6). Aaron burns fragrant incense on it every morning and evening as he tends the lamps (vv. 7–8). Nothing else may be offered on it, no unauthorized incense and no sacrifice (v. 9), and once a year its horns receive the blood of the sin offering, for it is “most holy to the LORD” (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology:
Sacrifice Outside, Prayer Inside

Prayer rises nearest the ark, and even its altar must be atoned for.
verseByVerse.examples: The smoke rose at the hours the lambs died. Christian prayer still rises on the strength of a sacrifice, not on its own merit.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall make an altar on which to burn incense; you shall make it of acacia wood. A cubit shall be its length, and a cubit its breadth. It shall be square, and two cubits shall be its height. Its horns shall be of one piece with it. You shall overlay it with pure gold, its top and around its sides and its horns. And you shall make a molding of gold around it. And you shall make two golden rings for it. Under its molding on two opposite sides of it you shall make them, and they shall be holders for poles with which to carry it. You shall make the poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold. And you shall put it in front of the veil that is above the ark of the testimony, in front of the mercy seat that is above the testimony, where I will meet with you. And Aaron shall burn fragrant incense on it. Every morning when he dresses the lamps he shall burn it, and when Aaron sets up the lamps at twilight, he shall burn it, a regular incense offering before the LORD throughout your generations. You shall not offer unauthorized incense on it, or a burnt offering, or a grain offering, and you shall not pour a drink offering on it. Aaron shall make atonement on its horns once a year. With the blood of the sin offering of atonement he shall make atonement for it once in the year throughout your generations. It is most holy to the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The altar of incense pictures prayer rising to God, and even this altar needs blood: prayers are heard because of atonement, not their own worth.

An altar on which to burn incense. It stands as close to the ark as anything can without being behind the curtain. Twice a day, at the hours the lambs were offered in the courtyard (29:38–42), smoke rose just before the veil: sacrifice outside, prayer inside, at the same moment.

Incense and prayer. Scripture says plainly that the smoke stands for prayer. “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you” (Psalm 141:2), and in Revelation the elders hold “golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints” (Revelation 5:8). Luke opens his Gospel at this altar, with Zechariah burning incense while “the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense” (Luke 1:10).

You shall not offer unauthorized incense. Only God’s incense, on God’s terms (v. 9). Aaron’s sons Nadab and Abihu died when they offered “unauthorized fire” (Leviticus 10:1).

Atonement on its horns once a year. Even the place where prayer ascends must be atoned for (v. 10): our prayers are not clean either, and are heard because of the blood, and because they reach God through a priest who “always lives to make intercession” for us (Hebrews 7:25). Hebrews 9:4 links this golden altar with the Most Holy Place, probably because its work belonged to the inner room it stood before (compare 1 Kings 6:22).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No one in Israel may be counted without being ransomed. Whenever the people are numbered, every man from twenty years old pays half a shekel as “a ransom for his life”, so that no plague falls on them (vv. 11–14). The rich may not give more, nor the poor less: every life is redeemed at the same price (v. 15). The silver goes to the service of the tent of meeting, a standing reminder before the LORD that his people live by atonement (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology:
A Flat Price

Every counted life is ransomed at the same small price, and the silver is given to the service of the tent.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: rich and poor paid one price for their lives. Now: every believer is ransomed by the same infinitely costly payment, and none adds anything to it.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "When you take the census of the people of Israel, then each shall give a ransom for his life to the LORD when you number them, that there be no plague among them when you number them. Each one who is numbered in the census shall give this: half a shekel according to the shekel of the sanctuary (the shekel is twenty gerahs), half a shekel as an offering to the LORD. Everyone who is numbered in the census, from twenty years old and upward, shall give the LORD's offering. The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less, than the half shekel, when you give the LORD's offering to make atonement for your lives. You shall take the atonement money from the people of Israel and shall give it for the service of the tent of meeting, that it may bring the people of Israel to remembrance before the LORD, so as to make atonement for your lives."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone counted in Israel pays the same small ransom for his life: every life belongs to the LORD who redeemed it, and no one can buy a higher place.

A ransom for his life. The reason given for the census tax is unexpected: to be counted in Israel, a man had to pay a ransom for his own life. The sum is half a shekel by the sanctuary’s standard weight (“twenty gerahs”), a small amount.

The rich shall not give more. Everybody pays the same. The point is not revenue but a statement no Israelite could miss: a human life is not graded by wealth, and no one can pay more to be worth more.

For the service of the tent of meeting. This silver became the bases of the tabernacle (38:25–27). The whole house of God stood on ransom money.

The same price for everyone. Peter shows what it pointed to: “you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). Everyone paid the same half shekel because the real price would be the same for everyone: one payment of infinite worth, to which no one adds anything. In Jesus’ day the half shekel had become a yearly temple tax, and he, the Son of the house, owed nothing, yet paid it for himself and Peter (Matthew 17:24–27).

Why would counting the people bring a plague? Each life belonged to the LORD who had redeemed it, and the ransom acknowledged that. A census without it treated the people as the leader’s own strength, as David found (2 Samuel 24).
verseByVerse.note: Half a shekel was about 1/5 ounce of silver (ESV note: a shekel was about 2/5 ounce).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Those already consecrated must keep being washed. A bronze basin on a bronze stand is set between the tent and the altar and filled with water (v. 18). Aaron and his sons must wash their hands and feet every time they enter the tent or approach the altar, “so that they may not die” (vv. 19–20). The command is repeated for emphasis and made “a statute forever” (v. 21). The priests were washed once at their ordination; now they return to the basin every time they serve.
verseByVerse.theology:
One Bath, Many Washings

The priests wash hands and feet every time they come near to minister.
verseByVerse.examples: Nobody walked from the altar into God's house without stopping at the basin. A Christian, once washed, still comes back daily for cleansing.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "You shall also make a basin of bronze, with its stand of bronze, for washing. You shall put it between the tent of meeting and the altar, and you shall put water in it, with which Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet. When they go into the tent of meeting, or when they come near the altar to minister, to burn a food offering to the LORD, they shall wash with water, so that they may not die. They shall wash their hands and their feet, so that they may not die. It shall be a statute forever to them, even to him and to his offspring throughout their generations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests, washed once at their ordination, must wash hands and feet every time they serve: those made clean still need daily cleansing.

A basin of bronze. The priests were washed once when they were ordained (29:4), and that was never repeated. But hands get dirty doing the work and feet get dirty walking the courtyard, so they wash at the basin every time they approach, “so that they may not die”.

One bath, many washings. It is the distinction Jesus made when Peter asked to be washed all over: “The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean” (John 13:10). A believer is not converted afresh every time he sins. He is washed once, counted clean in Christ, and keeps coming back to have his feet washed: daily confession, and the forgiveness God has promised (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Anointing sets things apart for God, and its sign must not be cheapened. God gives the recipe: myrrh, cinnamon, aromatic cane and cassia, blended into a hin of olive oil (vv. 22–25). With it Moses is to anoint the tent, the ark, every piece of furniture and the priests, so that they become most holy (vv. 26–30). The oil must never be poured on an ordinary person or copied for private use, on pain of being cut off from the people (vv. 31–33). What belongs to God carries his mark alone.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Anointed One

The oil consecrates; whoever copies it or puts it to common use is cut off.
verseByVerse.examples: The scent was to mean one thing only, and every drop of this oil looked ahead to the one whose title is simply the Anointed.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Take the finest spices: of liquid myrrh 500 shekels, and of sweet-smelling cinnamon half as much, that is, 250, and 250 of aromatic cane, and 500 of cassia, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, and a hin of olive oil. And you shall make of these a sacred anointing oil blended as by the perfumer; it shall be a holy anointing oil. With it you shall anoint the tent of meeting and the ark of the testimony, and the table and all its utensils, and the lampstand and its utensils, and the altar of incense, and the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils and the basin and its stand. You shall consecrate them, that they may be most holy. Whatever touches them will become holy. You shall anoint Aaron and his sons, and consecrate them, that they may serve me as priests. And you shall say to the people of Israel, 'This shall be my holy anointing oil throughout your generations. It shall not be poured on the body of an ordinary person, and you shall make no other like it in composition. It is holy, and it shall be holy to you. Whoever compounds any like it or whoever puts any of it on an outsider shall be cut off from his people.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives a holy oil to anoint the tent and the priests and forbids any copy, so that its fragrance says one thing: this belongs to God.

A holy anointing oil. Everything in the tent is anointed with this oil, and so are Aaron and his sons (vv. 26–30). The prohibition is severe: it must not be poured on an ordinary person, copied, or put on an outsider.

You shall make no other like it. The recipe was not secret; the smell was to mean one thing only. Anyone in Israel who caught that scent knew what it belonged to. Used as everyday perfume, it would soon have meant nothing. In Scripture, holy things are kept apart from ordinary ones.

Anointed for his death. Messiah is Hebrew for “anointed one”; Christ is the same word in Greek. Every object and priest in this tent is anointed in anticipation of a person whose title would simply be “the Anointed”. When a woman poured costly ointment over Jesus and the room complained of waste, he said, “she has done it to prepare me for burial” (Matthew 26:12). The Anointed One was anointed for his death. And the anointing once kept for priests is now given, through him, to all his people: “you have been anointed by the Holy One” (1 John 2:20).

Uncertain wording. “Aromatic cane” and “cassia” are likely but not certain identifications (perhaps a fragrant reed, and a bark related to cinnamon). The point is clear: the finest spices, blended with skill.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The incense, too, belongs to God alone. Moses is to blend equal parts of stacte, onycha, galbanum and pure frankincense, seasoned with salt, “pure and holy” (vv. 34–35). Some is beaten fine and placed before the testimony where God meets with him (v. 36). No one may make it for himself or use it as perfume (vv. 37–38). The chapter ends where it began, with the fragrance of worship, guarded so that it means one thing only.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Restricted Thing, Given Away

The incense is holy to the LORD and may not be made for private use.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: no Israelite could wear it. Now: the church itself is called the aroma of Christ to God (2 Cor. 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Take sweet spices, stacte, and onycha, and galbanum, sweet spices with pure frankincense (of each shall there be an equal part), and make an incense blended as by the perfumer, seasoned with salt, pure and holy. You shall beat some of it very small, and put part of it before the testimony in the tent of meeting where I shall meet with you. It shall be most holy for you. And the incense that you shall make according to its composition, you shall not make for yourselves. It shall be for you holy to the LORD. Whoever makes any like it to use as perfume shall be cut off from his people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The holy incense is for God alone and must never be copied as perfume, so that its fragrance keeps its meaning.

You shall not make for yourselves. Take the two recipes together and the chapter has a shape. Israel is given a fragrance for prayer and a fragrance for anointing, and forbidden to use either for itself. Not because God is stingy with pleasant things, but because a sign used for everything stops meaning anything.

The aroma of Christ. Paul uses the language of fragrance in a new way: God “through us spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere”, for “we are the aroma of Christ to God” (2 Corinthians 2:14–15). This is an echo rather than a fulfilment of the incense law, but a lovely one: what was kept for God alone now describes a people who carry Christ.

Uncertain wording. Frankincense and galbanum (a pungent resin) are known. “Stacte” (literally “drops”) was probably a tree resin, and “onycha” may have come from a sea creature’s shell or from a plant; no one now knows for sure. The blend cannot be recovered, which is fitting: it was never meant to be copied.

keyVerse.quote: The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less, than the half shekel, when you give the LORD’s offering to make atonement for your lives.
keyVerse.note: In a chapter about drawing near to God, this verse puts every Israelite on the same level. No one could buy a better place, and no one was too poor to be ransomed; the same price for all points to the one ransom of Christ’s blood.

30.reflection:
The incense altar stood before the veil, and its smoke pictured prayer, yet even it needed blood once a year (vv. 1–10). How does knowing that your prayers are heard because of Christ, not because of their quality, encourage you to pray?

Rich and poor paid the same half shekel (v. 15). Where do you or your church quietly treat some people as worth more than others, and how does the gospel answer that?

The priests, washed once, kept returning to the basin (vv. 17–21; John 13:10). What does daily confession look like for a believer who is already clean in Christ?

The oil and incense were not to be copied for ordinary use (vv. 32, 37). What helps keep worship and holy things from becoming ordinary to us?

31.title: The Spirit Equips for God's Work
31.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Moses,<sup>2</sup>"See, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah,<sup>3</sup>and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship,<sup>4</sup>to devise artistic designs, to work in gold, silver, and bronze,<sup>5</sup>in cutting stones for setting, and in carving wood, to work in every craft.<sup>6</sup>And behold, I have appointed with him Oholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan. And I have given to all able men ability, that they may make all that I have commanded you:<sup>7</sup>the tent of meeting, and the ark of the testimony, and the mercy seat that is on it, and all the furnishings of the tent,<sup>8</sup>the table and its utensils, and the pure lampstand with all its utensils, and the altar of incense,<sup>9</sup>and the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils, and the basin and its stand,<sup>10</sup>and the finely worked garments, the holy garments for Aaron the priest and the garments of his sons, for their service as priests,<sup>11</sup>and the anointing oil and the fragrant incense for the Holy Place. According to all that I have commanded you, they shall do."<sup>12</sup>And the LORD said to Moses,<sup>13</sup>"You are to speak to the people of Israel and say, 'Above all you shall keep my Sabbaths, for this is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, that you may know that I, the LORD, sanctify you.<sup>14</sup>You shall keep the Sabbath, because it is holy for you. Everyone who profanes it shall be put to death. Whoever does any work on it, that soul shall be cut off from among his people.<sup>15</sup>Six days shall work be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of solemn rest, holy to the LORD. Whoever does any work on the Sabbath day shall be put to death.<sup>16</sup>Therefore the people of Israel shall keep the Sabbath, observing the Sabbath throughout their generations, as a covenant forever.<sup>17</sup>It is a sign forever between me and the people of Israel that in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, and on the seventh day he rested and was refreshed.'"<sup>18</sup>And he gave to Moses, when he had finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, the two tablets of the testimony, tablets of stone, written with the finger of God.
31.overview:
Where we are. This is the last of the speeches in which God gives Moses the pattern of the tabernacle (chapters 25–31). Moses has been on the mountain forty days (24:18), and when God finishes speaking he hands him the two tablets. Below, the people are already growing restless (32:1).

The message. God not only commands his house; he provides the people to build it, filling Bezalel with his Spirit for skilled work and giving ability to every craftsman. Then he sets the Sabbath over the whole project as the sign of his covenant: it is the LORD who makes his people holy, not their labour, not even labour on his own house.

Why it was said. Former slaves who had known only forced labour needed to learn that God gives the skill for his work and also commands rest from it. Their identity as his people rested on what he does for them (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. God names Bezalel of Judah, filled with the Spirit for every craft, and appoints Oholiab of Dan beside him, with ability given to all the skilled workers (vv. 1–6). He lists everything they will make (vv. 7–11). Then he commands the Sabbath “above all”, as a sign that he sanctifies Israel, with death for anyone who profanes it (vv. 12–15), a covenant sign rooted in creation (vv. 16–17). Finally he gives Moses the two tablets written with the finger of God (v. 18).

Where it leads. By pattern and by promise. The Spirit who filled a craftsman to build God’s tent is now given by the ascended Christ to all his people, to build the church, the house where God now lives (Ephesians 2:21–22; 4:11–12). And the Sabbath rest that marked Israel as God’s finds its substance in Christ, who says, “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28; compare Hebrews 4:9–10).

For us. Every gift you have, practical ones included, comes from the Spirit and can serve God’s house. And your holiness rests on what God does, not on how hard you work: resting in Christ is the deepest sign that you belong to him.
31.theology:
The Spirit equips for God's work. God gifts those he calls, and every ability used in his work is grace.

The dignity of skilled labour. Skill is not less spiritual than speech; artistry and excellence offered for God's glory are gifts of the Spirit.

The Sabbath as sign of grace. God, not our labour, makes us holy, and the sign points to our rest in Christ's finished work.
31.examples:
Then: God filled Bezalel with his Spirit to build the tabernacle, and gave the Sabbath as a sign that the LORD sanctifies his people.

Now: God still equips by his Spirit those he calls, and every skill used for his glory is his gift. And Christ gives the soul the rest the Sabbath pictured.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-11 — Bezalel and Oholiab, Filled with the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God provides the builders for his house and fills them with his Spirit. He has called Bezalel by name, of the tribe of Judah, and filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability, intelligence and knowledge for every craft: design, metalwork, stone-cutting and carving (vv. 1–5). He appoints Oholiab of the tribe of Dan to work with him, and gives ability to all the skilled workers (v. 6). Then he lists all they will make, from the tent and the ark to the priests’ garments, the oil and the incense (vv. 7–11). The work is God’s from design to craftsmanship.
verseByVerse.theology:
The First Man Filled With the Spirit Is a Craftsman

The Spirit's filling is described entirely in terms of skill.
verseByVerse.examples: The whole workforce's competence was credited to God. A Christian whose gifts are practical rather than public need not think them second-class.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "See, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship, to devise artistic designs, to work in gold, silver, and bronze, in cutting stones for setting, and in carving wood, to work in every craft. And behold, I have appointed with him Oholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan. And I have given to all able men ability, that they may make all that I have commanded you: the tent of meeting, and the ark of the testimony, and the mercy seat that is on it, and all the furnishings of the tent, the table and its utensils, and the pure lampstand with all its utensils, and the altar of incense, and the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils, and the basin and its stand, and the finely worked garments, the holy garments for Aaron the priest and the garments of his sons, for their service as priests, and the anointing oil and the fragrant incense for the Holy Place. According to all that I have commanded you, they shall do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself chooses and equips the builders of his house, filling Bezalel with his Spirit for skilled craftsmanship and giving ability to every worker.

I have called by name Bezalel. After six chapters of instructions, God names the builder. The first person in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit of God is not a prophet, priest or king but a craftsman, and the filling is described entirely as skill: ability, intelligence, knowledge, the capacity to design beautiful things and make them in metal, stone and wood. His grandfather Hur may be the Hur who held up Moses’ hands at the battle with Amalek (17:12).

Spiritual gifts and daily work. That deserves saying plainly, because much Christian thinking quietly assumes that spiritual gifts are the ones used in front of a congregation. God lists this man’s gifts as trades. He does not divide work into sacred and secular: the craftsman working with gold and wood is filled with the same Spirit who would later fill prophets and apostles.

I have given to all able men ability. Every skilled worker in the camp is included. The tabernacle was built not by two geniuses but by a workforce whose competence is credited to God. The pattern runs on: the ascended Christ gives gifts to his people “for building up the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:8–12), the house in which God now lives, and it is still the Spirit who makes the work possible.

Where did these men learn their trade? Very likely as slaves in Egypt, a land of extraordinary metalwork and joinery. Skills learned in captivity, under compulsion, now build God’s house. What was learned in years that felt wasted, God can still use.

Uncertain wording. The “finely worked garments” (v. 10) translate a rare phrase. It may mean garments of fine or plaited weaving, or “garments for service”; the exact sense is unknown. Either way, they belong with the priests’ holy clothing.
verseByVerse.note: Bezalel was from the tribe of Judah and Oholiab from the tribe of Dan, so the work was not left to one tribe.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-18 — The Sabbath, a Sign Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before Moses comes down, God sets the Sabbath over the whole work as the sign of the covenant. “Above all” Israel must keep it, as a sign that the LORD sanctifies them (v. 13). Whoever profanes it by working must be put to death (vv. 14–15). It is “a covenant forever”, a sign rooted in creation, for in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth and rested on the seventh (vv. 16–17). Then God gives Moses the two tablets of stone, written with the finger of God (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology:
Not Even Work Commanded by God

The last word before the tablets is rest, the sign of whose people Israel is.
verseByVerse.examples: The tabernacle could wait a day a week. Our holiness is something God does in us, not something we achieve, and the Lord's Day is a weekly gift that says so.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "You are to speak to the people of Israel and say, 'Above all you shall keep my Sabbaths, for this is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, that you may know that I, the LORD, sanctify you. You shall keep the Sabbath, because it is holy for you. Everyone who profanes it shall be put to death. Whoever does any work on it, that soul shall be cut off from among his people. Six days shall work be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of solemn rest, holy to the LORD. Whoever does any work on the Sabbath day shall be put to death. Therefore the people of Israel shall keep the Sabbath, observing the Sabbath throughout their generations, as a covenant forever. It is a sign forever between me and the people of Israel that in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, and on the seventh day he rested and was refreshed.'" And he gave to Moses, when he had finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, the two tablets of the testimony, tablets of stone, written with the finger of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Over all the work God sets the Sabbath, a weekly sign that he, not their labour, makes Israel holy; then he gives Moses the tablets written by his own finger.

Above all you shall keep my Sabbaths. Straight after the building instructions God returns to the Sabbath, and the placement is the point. Israel has just been handed the most important construction project in its history, and the last word before Moses comes down is “Above all”, keep the Sabbath. Not even work commanded by God was a reason to skip Israel’s rest; the tabernacle could wait a day a week.

This is a sign between me and you. The Sabbath is a weekly marker that this people belongs to God, “that you may know that I, the LORD, sanctify you” (v. 13): their holiness is something he does, not something they achieve. A nation that downs tools every seventh day says, publicly and repeatedly, that the world is not held up by its effort.

In six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth. The sign rests on creation. As in 20:11, Israel’s week copies God’s week, and this commentary takes the six days of Genesis 1 as ordinary days (see on Genesis 1:5), while honouring faithful Christians who read them as long ages or as a framework. “Refreshed” does not mean God was tired (Isaiah 40:28); it pictures him taking delight in finished work.

Written with the finger of God. The “finger of God” is the phrase Egypt’s magicians used when they failed (8:19), and the phrase Jesus used of his own authority over demons (Luke 11:20). The same finger that brought gnats out of dust and set people free in Galilee wrote the commandments into rock. Moses now holds a covenant Israel has three times sworn to keep (19:8; 24:3, 7), and at the bottom of the mountain, at this very moment, they are dancing round a golden calf.

Was Sabbath-breaking really punished by death? It was, and once the penalty was carried out (Numbers 15:32–36). Under the covenant at Sinai the Sabbath was the sign of the covenant itself, so to defy it openly was to reject the covenant. That civil penalty ended with Israel’s theocracy (God’s direct rule of the nation), and the “forever” of verse 16 lasts as long as the covenant it belongs to.

Where Christians differ. Many godly Christians, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 Baptist Confession, keep Sunday as the Christian Sabbath; Seventh-day Adventists keep Saturday.

This commentary’s view. The Sabbath’s substance is now Christ, who gives the true rest (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). Sunday, the Lord’s Day, is a gift gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest, but no day binds the Christian conscience (Colossians 2:16–17).

keyVerse.quote: Above all you shall keep my Sabbaths, for this is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, that you may know that I, the LORD, sanctify you.
keyVerse.note: God’s last word before Moses comes down is not about building but about rest. The Sabbath marked Israel as his and taught them that their holiness was his work, not theirs, a truth fulfilled in the rest Christ gives.

31.reflection:
Bezalel was filled with the Spirit for craftsmanship (vv. 3–5). How does that change the way you think about your own work and skills, whether in an office, a kitchen or a workshop?

Skills learned in slavery in Egypt went into building God’s house. What experiences in your life that felt wasted might God be able to use?

God set the Sabbath “above all”, even over work on his own tent (v. 13). What does your pattern of work and rest say about where you think your worth and security come from?

The Sabbath was a sign “that I, the LORD, sanctify you” (v. 13). How does Christ’s promise of rest (Matthew 11:28) free you from trying to make yourself holy by effort?

32.title: The Golden Calf and the Intercessor
32.text: <sup>1</sup>When the people saw that Moses delayed to come down from the mountain, the people gathered themselves together to Aaron and said to him, "Up, make us gods who shall go before us. As for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him."<sup>2</sup>So Aaron said to them, "Take off the rings of gold that are in the ears of your wives, your sons, and your daughters, and bring them to me."<sup>3</sup>So all the people took off the rings of gold that were in their ears and brought them to Aaron.<sup>4</sup>And he received the gold from their hand and fashioned it with a graving tool and made a golden calf. And they said, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!"<sup>5</sup>When Aaron saw this, he built an altar before it. And Aaron made a proclamation and said, "Tomorrow shall be a feast to the LORD."<sup>6</sup>And they rose up early the next day and offered burnt offerings and brought peace offerings. And the people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.<sup>7</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Go down, for your people, whom you brought up out of the land of Egypt, have corrupted themselves.<sup>8</sup>They have turned aside quickly out of the way that I commanded them. They have made for themselves a golden calf and have worshiped it and sacrificed to it and said, 'These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!'"<sup>9</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "I have seen this people, and behold, it is a stiff-necked people.<sup>10</sup>Now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may burn hot against them and I may consume them, in order that I may make a great nation of you."<sup>11</sup>But Moses implored the LORD his God and said, "O LORD, why does your wrath burn hot against your people, whom you have brought out of the land of Egypt with great power and with a mighty hand?<sup>12</sup>Why should the Egyptians say, 'With evil intent did he bring them out, to kill them in the mountains and to consume them from the face of the earth'? Turn from your burning anger and relent from this disaster against your people.<sup>13</sup>Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants, to whom you swore by your own self, and said to them, 'I will multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven, and all this land that I have promised I will give to your offspring, and they shall inherit it forever.'"<sup>14</sup>And the LORD relented from the disaster that he had spoken of bringing on his people.<sup>15</sup>Then Moses turned and went down from the mountain with the two tablets of the testimony in his hand, tablets that were written on both sides; on the front and on the back they were written.<sup>16</sup>The tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, engraved on the tablets.<sup>17</sup>When Joshua heard the noise of the people as they shouted, he said to Moses, "There is a noise of war in the camp."<sup>18</sup>But he said, "It is not the sound of shouting for victory, or the sound of the cry of defeat, but the sound of singing that I hear."<sup>19</sup>And as soon as he came near the camp and saw the calf and the dancing, Moses' anger burned hot, and he threw the tablets out of his hands and broke them at the foot of the mountain.<sup>20</sup>He took the calf that they had made and burned it with fire and ground it to powder and scattered it on the water and made the people of Israel drink it.<sup>21</sup>And Moses said to Aaron, "What did this people do to you that you have brought such a great sin upon them?"<sup>22</sup>And Aaron said, "Let not the anger of my lord burn hot. You know the people, that they are set on evil.<sup>23</sup>For they said to me, 'Make us gods who shall go before us. As for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.'<sup>24</sup>So I said to them, 'Let any who have gold take it off.' So they gave it to me, and I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf."<sup>25</sup>And when Moses saw that the people had broken loose (for Aaron had let them break loose, to the derision of their enemies),<sup>26</sup>then Moses stood in the gate of the camp and said, "Who is on the LORD's side? Come to me." And all the sons of Levi gathered around him.<sup>27</sup>And he said to them, "Thus says the LORD God of Israel, 'Put your sword on your side each of you, and go to and fro from gate to gate throughout the camp, and each of you kill his brother and his companion and his neighbor.'"<sup>28</sup>And the sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses. And that day about three thousand men of the people fell.<sup>29</sup>And Moses said, "Today you have been ordained for the service of the LORD, each one at the cost of his son and of his brother, so that he might bestow a blessing upon you this day."<sup>30</sup>The next day Moses said to the people, "You have sinned a great sin. And now I will go up to the LORD; perhaps I can make atonement for your sin."<sup>31</sup>So Moses returned to the LORD and said, "Alas, this people has sinned a great sin. They have made for themselves gods of gold.<sup>32</sup>But now, if you will forgive their sin—but if not, please blot me out of your book that you have written."<sup>33</sup>But the LORD said to Moses, "Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot out of my book.<sup>34</sup>But now go, lead the people to the place about which I have spoken to you; behold, my angel shall go before you. Nevertheless, in the day when I visit, I will visit their sin upon them."<sup>35</sup>Then the LORD sent a plague on the people, because they made the calf, the one that Aaron made.
32.overview:
Where we are. While Moses is on the mountain receiving the plans for God’s dwelling (chapters 25–31), the people below grow tired of waiting. About forty days after promising, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do” (24:7), they break the covenant at its heart.

The message. Left to ourselves we will turn even the true God into something we can see and manage, and that sin deserves to be consumed. What stands between a guilty people and God’s wrath is not their repentance or their merit but a mediator who pleads God’s own promises and offers himself in their place.

Why it was said. Israel needed to know that the covenant almost ended before the tabernacle was even built, and that they lived only by God’s mercy through a mediator. Later generations needed the warning too: when Jeroboam set up golden calves, he used Aaron’s very words, “Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt” (1 Kings 12:28; see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Impatient at Moses’ delay, the people demand gods, and Aaron makes the calf and proclaims a feast to the LORD (vv. 1–6). God tells Moses and offers to destroy them and make a nation from him instead; Moses pleads God’s people, God’s name and God’s oath, and the LORD relents (vv. 7–14). Moses comes down, breaks the tablets, destroys the calf and confronts Aaron, who blames the people and the fire (vv. 15–24). The Levites answer Moses’ call, and about three thousand fall (vv. 25–29). The next day Moses goes back to plead, offering to be blotted out of God’s book; God refuses, sends him on with an angel, and sends a plague (vv. 30–35).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. Moses stands in the breach and offers his life for the people, but he cannot pay a debt that is also his own. Christ, the greater Moses, did what Moses could only offer: he bore the curse, crying, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34), and he “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25). The calf shows the depth of our sin; the mediator shows the height of God’s mercy.

For us. Idolatry is rarely announced; it grows out of impatience and often speaks the language of faith. When we are tempted to make God manageable, or crushed by having done so, the answer is not a better excuse than Aaron’s but the Mediator whose plea never fails.
32.theology:
The idolatry of the human heart. As Calvin observed, the human heart is a perpetual factory of idols. A calf made within weeks of Sinai shows that we need not only rescue but a new heart.

The wrath of God against sin. Sin against the holy God is no small thing; justice cannot simply ignore rebellion.

The mediator who stands in the breach. Moses offers his own life, a shadow of Christ, who actually became a curse for us (Gal. 3:13) and was forsaken that we might be forgiven.
32.examples:
Then: the people broke the covenant almost before it was given, and Moses stood in the breach, offering to be blotted out for them.

Now: our hearts still make idols. But we have a greater Mediator, forsaken on the cross in our place, so that those who confess their sin and trust him will never be blotted out of the book of life.
