verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Impatience turns into idolatry dressed up as worship. Moses has been gone so long that the people gather around Aaron and demand gods to go before them (v. 1). Aaron collects their gold earrings and fashions a calf, and the people hail it as the gods who brought them out of Egypt (vv. 2–4). Aaron builds an altar and proclaims “a feast to the LORD”, and the next day they offer sacrifices, eat, drink and rise up to play (vv. 5–6). They have not stopped worshipping; they have made a god of their own shape.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Second Commandment Broken While the First Is Intended

Aaron uses the covenant name, the LORD, over a metal animal.
verseByVerse.examples: The trigger was nothing more than a delay. Waiting on God is still where many of our substitutes for him are made.

verseByVerse.quote: When the people saw that Moses delayed to come down from the mountain, the people gathered themselves together to Aaron and said to him, "Up, make us gods who shall go before us. As for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him." So Aaron said to them, "Take off the rings of gold that are in the ears of your wives, your sons, and your daughters, and bring them to me." So all the people took off the rings of gold that were in their ears and brought them to Aaron. And he received the gold from their hand and fashioned it with a graving tool and made a golden calf. And they said, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!" When Aaron saw this, he built an altar before it. And Aaron made a proclamation and said, "Tomorrow shall be a feast to the LORD." And they rose up early the next day and offered burnt offerings and brought peace offerings. And the people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tired of waiting for Moses, the people demand a god they can see, and Aaron makes a golden calf and calls its worship a feast to the LORD.

Moses delayed to come down. The trigger is a delay. Not persecution, famine or a rival prophet: Moses is late. Forty days of waiting with the fire still visible on the summit (24:17–18), and the nation decides he is gone and that they need something they can see.

As for this Moses. Their phrasing gives them away: Moses is “the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt.” They have already begun crediting the exodus to a man rather than to God, so replacing him seems a simple practical matter.

Made a golden calf. And Aaron does it. He does not refuse or stall or remind them of the voice they all heard from the mountain. The gold came from Egypt, the back wages God gave them (12:35–36), meant for the tabernacle and melted down for this. Whatever is not given to God gets given to something.

Tomorrow shall be a feast to the LORD. That detail makes the chapter frightening rather than merely disappointing. They are not turning to a foreign god. Aaron uses the covenant name, holding a service for the LORD in front of a statue they watched being made. The feast ends with the people rising up “to play”, unrestrained revelry, and Paul quotes the verse to warn Christians tempted to share in idol feasts (1 Corinthians 10:7).

The second commandment broken. The first commandment forbids other gods; the second forbids worshipping God by images. Israel breaks the second while meaning to keep the first, which is why the two were given separately. The calf may well have been meant as a pedestal for the invisible God rather than a rival to him. A young bull was a common ancient symbol of divine strength and fertility, familiar from Egypt’s sacred Apis bull, and gods in the region were often pictured standing on one. The danger is rarely that we worship something else, but that we worship the true God in a shape we have chosen, and find the shape easier to love than the God.

The god who is never late. What broke Israel was not suffering but waiting. We understand that well: we expect answers within seconds, and a God who works in forty-day silences feels almost intolerable. A god you make is always available, always on time and always visible, because it never actually does anything. That is the hidden attraction of every idol, from a career plan to a bank balance (see the note on Isaiah 44:9–20): it is something we can manage, and it never asks us to wait in the dark. The true God will not be hurried or shrunk. Yet in his own time he did give his people a face to look at, not one cast in a morning but the Son, “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15). He too seemed to delay, staying two days longer while Lazarus died (John 11:6). He was not late. He was about to do something no calf ever could.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew elohim can mean “God” or “gods”. Here the verbs are plural, so the ESV has “gods”, though the people may have meant the calf to stand for the LORD (v. 5); Nehemiah 9:18 renders their cry, “This is your God”. “Play” (v. 6) can mean laughing, sport or revelry, and sometimes sexual play (as in Genesis 26:8); here it at least means a feast that had lost all restraint (v. 25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7-14 — Moses Stands in the Breach
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sin deserves destruction, but a mediator’s prayer turns it aside. God tells Moses to go down, for “your people” have corrupted themselves and worshipped the calf (vv. 7–8). He calls them stiff-necked and tells Moses to let him alone, so that he may consume them and make a great nation of Moses instead (vv. 9–10). Moses pleads that they are God’s own people whom he brought out, that the Egyptians will say he meant them harm, and that God swore by himself to Abraham, Isaac and Israel (vv. 11–13). The LORD relents from the disaster (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Art of Intercession

Moses pleads three things: that they are God's people, that God's name is at stake, and that God has sworn an oath.
verseByVerse.examples: Moses found nothing good to say about Israel, so he appealed to what was true about God. Christians pray for others, and for themselves, on the same ground.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Go down, for your people, whom you brought up out of the land of Egypt, have corrupted themselves. They have turned aside quickly out of the way that I commanded them. They have made for themselves a golden calf and have worshiped it and sacrificed to it and said, 'These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!'" And the LORD said to Moses, "I have seen this people, and behold, it is a stiff-necked people. Now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may burn hot against them and I may consume them, in order that I may make a great nation of you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Moses what the people have done, disowns them as “your people”, and offers to destroy them and begin again with Moses.

Have corrupted themselves. The language is cold: “your people, whom you brought up.” Yesterday they were God’s people; today he calls them Moses’.

They have turned aside quickly. Quickly indeed: about forty days after they heard God’s voice and promised, “All that the LORD has spoken we will do” (24:3, 7). God quotes their own words back, “These are your gods, O Israel”: the credit for the exodus has been handed to a lump of gold. “Stiff-necked” pictures an ox that will not bend its neck to the yoke.

Let me alone. A strange thing for God to say, as if Moses could hold him back. Many have seen in it an invitation in disguise: by naming the one thing standing between Israel and his wrath, God shows Moses where to stand. The psalm says Israel was spared because “Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him” (Psalm 106:23).

That I may make a great nation of you. Then Moses is offered what Abraham was promised (Genesis 12:2): to be the father of a new nation once the ungrateful one is gone.

verseByVerse.quote: But Moses implored the LORD his God and said, "O LORD, why does your wrath burn hot against your people, whom you have brought out of the land of Egypt with great power and with a mighty hand? Why should the Egyptians say, 'With evil intent did he bring them out, to kill them in the mountains and to consume them from the face of the earth'? Turn from your burning anger and relent from this disaster against your people. Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants, to whom you swore by your own self, and said to them, 'I will multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven, and all this land that I have promised I will give to your offspring, and they shall inherit it forever.'" And the LORD relented from the disaster that he had spoken of bringing on his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses refuses the offer and pleads for Israel, not on their merit but on God’s own people, name and promise, and the LORD relents.

Moses implored the LORD his God. His prayer is a model of intercession. He argues three things, and not one is that Israel deserves rescuing. First, whose people they are: he hands them straight back, “your people, whom you have brought out”. Second, God’s reputation among the Egyptians. Third, and decisively, God’s oath to Abraham, Isaac and Israel. Intercession does not consist in finding something good to say about the guilty, but in appealing to something true about God.

He always lives to make intercession. Israel survived that day because a mediator refused to step aside and held God to his promises. It is a picture of the one who “always lives to make intercession” (Hebrews 7:25), whose plea is better than Moses’ because it rests not only on God’s promise but on his own finished work.

Did Moses change God’s mind? “God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind” (Numbers 23:19). Scripture says God “relented” to show his real response to prayer and repentance; the threat of judgment was real, and the outcome was what God had always purposed, through the prayer he himself invited (compare Jeremiah 18:7–10). God is not moved like a man, but he is moved by the prayers of his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15-24 — The Tablets Broken and the Calf Destroyed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Seeing the sin close up, Moses acts out the breaking of the covenant and confronts the leader who allowed it. He comes down with the tablets, God’s own work and writing (vv. 15–16). Joshua hears the noise as war; Moses knows it is singing (vv. 17–18). Seeing the calf and the dancing, Moses smashes the tablets at the foot of the mountain, burns the calf, grinds it to powder and makes the people drink it (vv. 19–20). Asked to account for himself, Aaron blames the people’s evil and says the calf simply came out of the fire (vv. 21–24).
verseByVerse.theology:
Breaking the Tablets Is a Legal Act

The covenant document is smashed at the foot of the mountain, because the covenant has already been broken.
verseByVerse.examples: Aaron's excuse is worth recognising in ourselves. Honest confession names what I did; it does not say that something happened.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses turned and went down from the mountain with the two tablets of the testimony in his hand, tablets that were written on both sides; on the front and on the back they were written. The tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, engraved on the tablets. When Joshua heard the noise of the people as they shouted, he said to Moses, "There is a noise of war in the camp." But he said, "It is not the sound of shouting for victory, or the sound of the cry of defeat, but the sound of singing that I hear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses comes down carrying the tablets God himself wrote, and hears from the camp not the noise of battle but of singing.

The work of God. The text lingers on the tablets as God’s own work and writing, written on both sides, so that we feel what is about to be smashed.

Joshua heard the noise. Joshua had gone part of the way up the mountain with Moses (24:13) and had not seen the camp, so he hears the noise as a soldier would. Moses has already been told what is happening (vv. 7–8), and now hears it for himself: not victory, not defeat, but a festival for the calf (v. 6).

Uncertain wording. Verse 18 plays on one Hebrew verb three times: the sound of victory, the sound of defeat, and a third sound that the ESV renders “singing”. The exact sense of the last is uncertain (perhaps chanting or wild revelry), but the point is clear: this is the noise of a feast, not a battle.

verseByVerse.quote: And as soon as he came near the camp and saw the calf and the dancing, Moses' anger burned hot, and he threw the tablets out of his hands and broke them at the foot of the mountain. He took the calf that they had made and burned it with fire and ground it to powder and scattered it on the water and made the people of Israel drink it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing the sin with his own eyes, Moses breaks the tablets to show that the covenant has been broken, and destroys the calf so completely that the people drink it.

Moses’ anger burned hot. These are the words God used on the mountain (v. 10). Moses had pleaded with God to turn from his burning anger; now, seeing the calf and the dancing, he burns with it himself. It is not inconsistency. Hearing about sin and seeing it are different things.

He threw the tablets out of his hands. It is easy to read this as a loss of temper, and it is more. The tablets were a covenant document, and Israel had already broken the covenant; smashing them at the foot of the mountain declares the agreement void. He is showing Israel what they have done.

Ground it to powder. He burns the calf, grinds it to powder and makes them drink it: every person in the camp swallows their god and finds it goes down like grit. The god that was to go before them ends up in the dust and the water.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses said to Aaron, "What did this people do to you that you have brought such a great sin upon them?" And Aaron said, "Let not the anger of my lord burn hot. You know the people, that they are set on evil. For they said to me, 'Make us gods who shall go before us. As for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.' So I said to them, 'Let any who have gold take it off.' So they gave it to me, and I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Called to account, Aaron blames the people and the fire, and will not say, “I did it.”

What did this people do to you? Moses assumes the people pressed Aaron, and asks what could justify giving in: a leader answers for what he allows. Aaron begins by calling Moses “my lord” and blaming the people, who are “set on evil”. Deuteronomy 9:20 adds that the LORD was angry enough with Aaron to destroy him, and that Moses prayed for Aaron too.

Out came this calf. Then Aaron’s explanation, one of the most human sentences in the Bible, as if he had been standing nearby when it happened. Verse 4 says he fashioned it with a graving tool. Aaron is weak rather than wicked, and under pressure he blames the people, the fire and the metal. It is the oldest reflex there is, running back to Adam’s “The woman whom you gave to be with me” (Genesis 3:12), and it survives in every apology that says “it happened” instead of “I did it”.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25-29 — The Levites Take Their Stand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Open rebellion must be stopped, and the call goes out to choose sides. The people have broken loose, to the derision of their enemies (v. 25). Moses stands in the gate of the camp and calls, “Who is on the LORD’s side? Come to me”, and the Levites gather to him (v. 26). At his command they go through the camp with the sword, sparing not even their own kin, and about three thousand fall (vv. 27–28). Moses tells them they have been ordained that day for the LORD’s service, at great cost (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology:
Not to Be Softened, and Not to Be Filed Away

Judgment falls only after a public call to come over to the LORD's side.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: an invitation came first, and anyone could have crossed the line. Now: God takes the corruption of his people seriously in both Testaments (Acts 5:1-11).

verseByVerse.quote: And when Moses saw that the people had broken loose (for Aaron had let them break loose, to the derision of their enemies), then Moses stood in the gate of the camp and said, "Who is on the LORD's side? Come to me." And all the sons of Levi gathered around him. And he said to them, "Thus says the LORD God of Israel, 'Put your sword on your side each of you, and go to and fro from gate to gate throughout the camp, and each of you kill his brother and his companion and his neighbor.'" And the sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses. And that day about three thousand men of the people fell. And Moses said, "Today you have been ordained for the service of the LORD, each one at the cost of his son and of his brother, so that he might bestow a blessing upon you this day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the people will not stop, Moses calls for those on the LORD’s side, and the Levites carry out a terrible judgment that marks the start of their service.

A hard passage. This should not be softened or hurried past, though a few things should be noted. The judgment falls on those who carried on after a public call to stop: Moses issues an invitation first, and anyone could have crossed to his side and lived. The number is a fraction of a nation of hundreds of thousands, so the great majority were spared. And the alternative an hour earlier had been the destruction of everybody (v. 10).

Today you have been ordained. Literally, “fill your hand”, the phrase used of the priests’ ordination (29:9). This is where the Levites’ calling to serve God’s house begins, and what marked them out is not comfortable: they put loyalty to the LORD above their own relatives when the covenant was at stake. Many preachers have set beside this day another, at Pentecost, when about three thousand were added to the church (Acts 2:41), for Paul says “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6).

What it does not mean. It must not be filed away as the God of the Old Testament being harsher than the God of the New. It was Jesus who spoke most often about hell, and the New Testament records Ananias and Sapphira dead on the floor of the first church (Acts 5:1–11). God takes the corruption of his people with a seriousness we find shocking, and the shock measures how lightly we take it. Nor is it a pattern for Christians: the church bears no sword, and its discipline is spiritual (Matthew 18:15–17).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “derision” (v. 25) occurs only here in the Old Testament. It probably means a whisper of scorn: the nations who heard would mock Israel and its God. “Broken loose” pictures people throwing off all restraint.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A sinner cannot make atonement, however willing. Moses tells the people they have sinned a great sin and goes up, hoping to make atonement for them (v. 30). He confesses their sin and asks God to forgive them, or else to blot him out of his book (vv. 31–32). God refuses: it is the one who has sinned whom he will blot out (v. 33). He sends Moses on to lead the people with his angel going ahead, warns that he will visit their sin, and sends a plague (vv. 34–35). The need for a greater mediator stands open.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sentence That Breaks Off

Moses offers himself as a substitute, and God refuses.
verseByVerse.examples: The offer was magnificent, and it was refused because the substitute needed a mediator himself. Only one who had no sin of his own could take the place Moses offered to take.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day Moses said to the people, "You have sinned a great sin. And now I will go up to the LORD; perhaps I can make atonement for your sin." So Moses returned to the LORD and said, "Alas, this people has sinned a great sin. They have made for themselves gods of gold. But now, if you will forgive their sin—but if not, please blot me out of your book that you have written." But the LORD said to Moses, "Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot out of my book. But now go, lead the people to the place about which I have spoken to you; behold, my angel shall go before you. Nevertheless, in the day when I visit, I will visit their sin upon them." Then the LORD sent a plague on the people, because they made the calf, the one that Aaron made.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses offers to be blotted out of God’s book in the people’s place, and God refuses, because a sinner cannot bear the penalty for others.

Perhaps I can make atonement. What Moses prays the next day is the high point of his life. The sentence breaks off in the middle. He starts “if you will forgive their sin” and cannot finish it, because there is nothing to put after it: no merit, no mitigating circumstance, nothing Israel can offer.

Please blot me out of your book. So he offers himself, and asks to be erased in their place. It is an offer to bear their penalty, from a man with no power to do it, and God refuses: “Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot out of my book” (v. 33). Moses is a sinner himself; a man in debt cannot pay the debt of others. The people will go on, with God’s angel before them, but their sin is not yet dealt with (vv. 34–35).

Paul’s echo. Paul echoed this prayer for his own people: “I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers” (Romans 9:3). He too could not do it. Neither could anyone else.

The same offer, not refused. About fifteen centuries later someone made the same offer and was not refused. He was forsaken and made a curse, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34), and his people’s names stayed in the book. What Moses proposed and could not do, Christ did at Calvary, because the only one who could be cut off in place of sinners was the one man who had never deserved it himself.

What is the book? It is God’s register of his people, “the book of the living” (Psalm 69:28), which the New Testament calls the book of life (Philippians 4:3; Revelation 20:15). Here it includes all Israel, the living members of the covenant people, and those blotted out are those who rebelled.

Where Christians differ. Some take verse 33 to mean that a true believer can lose salvation and be erased from the book of life.

This commentary’s view. Those God has truly saved are kept by his power and will never finally perish. Christ promises his own, “I will never blot his name out of the book of life” (Revelation 3:5), and those written there “before the foundation of the world” (Revelation 13:8) are kept.

keyVerse.quote: And the LORD relented from the disaster that he had spoken of bringing on his people.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on this verse. Israel deserved to be consumed, and nothing in them had changed; what turned the judgment aside was a mediator pleading God’s own promises, a picture of the greater Mediator through whom God’s people are spared for ever.

32.reflection:
The calf was made not in a time of suffering but of waiting (v. 1). Where are you most tempted to reach for something you can see and control while God seems silent?

Aaron called the calf’s feast “a feast to the LORD” (v. 5). In what ways can we keep using the right words about God while worshipping him on our own terms?

Moses pleaded not Israel’s goodness but God’s people, God’s name and God’s promise (vv. 11–13). How could that shape the way you pray for others, and for yourself when you have failed?

Moses offered to be blotted out and could not be accepted; Christ was forsaken in our place (v. 32; Mark 15:34). How does that change the way you face your own guilt, and the way you see Jesus?

33.title: If Your Presence Will Not Go
33.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Moses, "Depart; go up from here, you and the people whom you have brought up out of the land of Egypt, to the land of which I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying, 'To your offspring I will give it.'<sup>2</sup>I will send an angel before you, and I will drive out the Canaanites, the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.<sup>3</sup>Go up to a land flowing with milk and honey; but I will not go up among you, lest I consume you on the way, for you are a stiff-necked people."<sup>4</sup>When the people heard this disastrous word, they mourned, and no one put on his ornaments.<sup>5</sup>For the LORD had said to Moses, "Say to the people of Israel, 'You are a stiff-necked people; if for a single moment I should go up among you, I would consume you. So now take off your ornaments, that I may know what to do with you.'"<sup>6</sup>Therefore the people of Israel stripped themselves of their ornaments, from Mount Horeb onward.<sup>7</sup>Now Moses used to take the tent and pitch it outside the camp, far off from the camp, and he called it the tent of meeting. And everyone who sought the LORD would go out to the tent of meeting, which was outside the camp.<sup>8</sup>Whenever Moses went out to the tent, all the people would rise up, and each would stand at his tent door, and watch Moses until he had gone into the tent.<sup>9</sup>When Moses entered the tent, the pillar of cloud would descend and stand at the entrance of the tent, and the LORD would speak with Moses.<sup>10</sup>And when all the people saw the pillar of cloud standing at the entrance of the tent, all the people would rise up and worship, each at his tent door.<sup>11</sup>Thus the LORD used to speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. When Moses turned again into the camp, his assistant Joshua the son of Nun, a young man, would not depart from the tent.<sup>12</sup>Moses said to the LORD, "See, you say to me, 'Bring up this people,' but you have not let me know whom you will send with me. Yet you have said, 'I know you by name, and you have also found favor in my sight.'<sup>13</sup>Now therefore, if I have found favor in your sight, please show me now your ways, that I may know you in order to find favor in your sight. Consider too that this nation is your people."<sup>14</sup>And he said, "My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest."<sup>15</sup>And he said to him, "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here.<sup>16</sup>For how shall it be known that I have found favor in your sight, I and your people? Is it not in your going with us, so that we are distinct, I and your people, from every other people on the face of the earth?"<sup>17</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "This very thing that you have spoken I will do, for you have found favor in my sight, and I know you by name."<sup>18</sup>Moses said, "Please show me your glory."<sup>19</sup>And he said, "I will make all my goodness pass before you and will proclaim before you my name 'The LORD.' And I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy.<sup>20</sup>But," he said, "you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live."<sup>21</sup>And the LORD said, "Behold, there is a place by me where you shall stand on the rock,<sup>22</sup>and while my glory passes by I will put you in a cleft of the rock, and I will cover you with my hand until I have passed by.<sup>23</sup>Then I will take away my hand, and you shall see my back, but my face shall not be seen."
33.overview:
Where we are. The golden calf has been destroyed and the guilty judged, but the covenant lies broken (chapter 32). God has told Moses to lead the people on, with an angel going before them (32:34). The question now is whether God himself will go.

The message. The greatest blessing is not God’s gifts but God himself, and a people given the land without his presence would have lost the one thing that made them his. Moses would rather stay in the wilderness with God than enter the land without him, and God, answering his mediator’s plea, promises to go. Yet even God’s friend may see only his goodness passing by, for no one can see his face and live.

Why it was said. Israel would live for centuries in a land full of blessings and be constantly tempted to want the gifts without the Giver (see the introduction). This chapter taught them what made them distinct among the nations: not their territory, nor even their law, but the LORD living among them.

How the chapter makes its case. God offers the land and an angel, but not his own presence, and the people mourn and strip off their ornaments (vv. 1–6). Meanwhile Moses meets God in a tent outside the camp, where the LORD speaks with him as a friend (vv. 7–11). Moses pleads to know God and refuses to go on without him, and God promises, “My presence will go with you” (vv. 12–17). Then Moses asks to see God’s glory, and God shelters him in the rock while his goodness passes by (vv. 18–23).

Where it leads. By promise, and by the character of God revealed in Christ. The presence Moses begged for came to stay when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). The face Moses could not see now shines “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). Moses could plead for God’s presence; Christ is God’s presence with his people, and he has promised, “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

For us. It is possible to want heaven without wanting God, and this chapter exposes that wish. In Christ we have seen more of God’s glory than Moses did, so ask not only for his help but for him, and come to him knowing that you are fully known and still welcome.
33.theology:
The supreme value of God's presence. The presence of God is what sets his people apart, and true faith wants him more than anything he gives.

The problem of a holy God dwelling with sinners. God's presence among an unholy people would consume them, a crisis resolved only in Christ, who deals with our sin so that God can dwell with us.

The unseeable glory revealed in Christ. No one can see God's face and live, yet in Christ we behold "the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor. 4:6).
33.examples:
Then: God threatened to send Israel on without his presence, and Moses refused to go without it and asked to see his glory.

Now: the glory Moses could not fully see has drawn near in Christ, and in him God's presence is ours forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-6 — 'I Will Not Go Up Among You'
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God offers Israel everything except himself, and the people rightly grieve. He tells Moses to lead them on to the land he swore to the patriarchs, with an angel going ahead to drive out the nations (vv. 1–2). But he will not go up among them, for a holy God in the midst of a stiff-necked people would consume them (v. 3). The people hear it as a disastrous word and mourn (v. 4). Told to take off their ornaments while God decides what to do with them, they strip them off from Mount Horeb onward (vv. 5–6). For the first time, the thought of losing God grieves them more than the thought of losing anything else.
verseByVerse.theology:
Everything Except Him

Every gift remains on offer; only the Giver withdraws.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel's repentance came not from the threat of punishment but from the threat of God's absence. Grief at the thought of losing him is itself a sign that he is at work.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Depart; go up from here, you and the people whom you have brought up out of the land of Egypt, to the land of which I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying, 'To your offspring I will give it.' I will send an angel before you, and I will drive out the Canaanites, the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites. Go up to a land flowing with milk and honey; but I will not go up among you, lest I consume you on the way, for you are a stiff-necked people." When the people heard this disastrous word, they mourned, and no one put on his ornaments. For the LORD had said to Moses, "Say to the people of Israel, 'You are a stiff-necked people; if for a single moment I should go up among you, I would consume you. So now take off your ornaments, that I may know what to do with you.'" Therefore the people of Israel stripped themselves of their ornaments, from Mount Horeb onward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promises Israel everything except himself, and the people, hearing that he will not go among them, mourn and strip off their ornaments.

I will not go up among you. This is the most chilling offer in the book. Everything is still on the table: the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, an angel to drive out the nations, milk and honey. Only God himself is withdrawn. Earlier he had promised an angel in whom his own name dwelt (23:20–21); now an angel is offered instead of God going up “among you” (v. 3): a guide without the presence. It is presented as mercy, and partly is: a holy God travelling in the middle of a stiff-necked people would consume them.

No one put on his ornaments. The people understand at once. They had given their gold to make a calf; now they take off the rest. This is the first genuine repentance in the story, produced not by the threat of punishment but by the threat of absence.

Would the land without God be enough? Since the sea Israel had complained about food, water and leadership, and never once grieved at the thought of losing God’s company. Now everything they had asked for, minus him, registers as a “disastrous word”. Something in them has grown up. The question still searches us: would heaven be enough if God were not there? The gospel offers not the gifts without the Giver but God with us: “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

Uncertain wording. “From Mount Horeb onward” (v. 6) may mean that from that place on they never wore their ornaments again, or simply that they took them off there, at Horeb, another name for Sinai.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7-11 — The Tent of Meeting, and a Friend of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even while God’s presence hangs in the balance, he can still be found by those who seek him. Moses pitches a tent far outside the camp and calls it the tent of meeting, and anyone who seeks the LORD goes out to it (v. 7). When Moses goes in, the people stand and watch, and the pillar of cloud descends at the entrance while the LORD speaks with him (vv. 8–9). The people worship, each at his own tent door (v. 10). The LORD speaks with Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend, and young Joshua stays on in the tent when Moses returns to the camp (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology:
Face to Face

God speaks with Moses directly, the way friends talk.
verseByVerse.examples: The young man stayed where God speaks. Leaders are often formed in places nobody ordered them to stay.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Moses used to take the tent and pitch it outside the camp, far off from the camp, and he called it the tent of meeting. And everyone who sought the LORD would go out to the tent of meeting, which was outside the camp. Whenever Moses went out to the tent, all the people would rise up, and each would stand at his tent door, and watch Moses until he had gone into the tent. When Moses entered the tent, the pillar of cloud would descend and stand at the entrance of the tent, and the LORD would speak with Moses. And when all the people saw the pillar of cloud standing at the entrance of the tent, all the people would rise up and worship, each at his tent door. Thus the LORD used to speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. When Moses turned again into the camp, his assistant Joshua the son of Nun, a young man, would not depart from the tent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While God’s presence hangs in the balance, Moses meets him in a tent outside the camp, where the LORD speaks with him as a friend.

Pitch it outside the camp. This is not the tabernacle, which is not yet built, but a tent Moses used to pitch “far off from the camp”, probably acting out what God had just said: after the calf, he would not go up among his people (v. 3). Anyone who sought the LORD went out to it, and when the pillar of cloud stood at its door the people rose and worshipped at their own tent doors.

Face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. A few verses later God says no one may see his face and live (v. 20). The two are not in conflict: face to face is an idiom for direct conversation with no go-between (compare Numbers 12:8), not a claim about physical sight. But the phrase is not diminished by that. God spoke to this man the way friends talk.

Friends of God. What Moses had alone, Jesus opens to all who are his: “I have called you friends” (John 15:15). And Hebrews turns the tent outside the camp round: Jesus “suffered outside the gate”, so “let us go to him outside the camp” (Hebrews 13:12–13).

Would not depart from the tent. A quiet detail at the end: the older man goes back to work; the young Joshua stays behind in the place where God speaks. He is being prepared to lead, forty years on, in a tent nobody ordered him to remain in.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-17 — 'If Your Presence Will Not Go'
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses refuses to go on without God, and God grants his plea. Moses presses God on his own words: he has been told to lead the people but not who will go with him, yet God has said he knows him by name (v. 12). He asks to know God’s ways, that he may know God himself, and reminds him that this nation is his people (v. 13). God promises his presence and rest (v. 14). Moses answers that without that presence they should not go at all, for only God’s going with them makes them distinct from every other people (vv. 15–16). God agrees, because Moses has found favour and is known by name (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Presence Is the Distinctive

God's going with them is what makes Israel different from every other nation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the land was never what made Israel special. Now: a church's life depends on the same presence, which God has promised to those who ask.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses said to the LORD, "See, you say to me, 'Bring up this people,' but you have not let me know whom you will send with me. Yet you have said, 'I know you by name, and you have also found favor in my sight.' Now therefore, if I have found favor in your sight, please show me now your ways, that I may know you in order to find favor in your sight. Consider too that this nation is your people." And he said, "My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest." And he said to him, "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here. For how shall it be known that I have found favor in your sight, I and your people? Is it not in your going with us, so that we are distinct, I and your people, from every other people on the face of the earth?" And the LORD said to Moses, "This very thing that you have spoken I will do, for you have found favor in my sight, and I know you by name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses pleads to know God and refuses to go on without his presence, and God, who knows him by name, promises to go with his people.

That I may know you. Now the conversation the chapter exists for. Moses argues like a man with nothing left to lose. He presses God on his own words, “I know you by name”, asks not for the route but “that I may know you”, and will not let go of God’s claim on the people: “Consider too that this nation is your people.”

If your presence will not go with me. God grants it: “My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest.” Moses’ reply ought to be carved over the whole chapter. He would rather stay in the desert with God than enter the land without him, and his reason is not sentiment. God’s presence is the only thing that makes Israel distinct “from every other people on the face of the earth” (v. 16). Strip that out and they are one more nation with a territory and a flag.

What it means to know God. We usually mean by knowing having information. When Moses prays “that I may know you” (v. 13), he means a personal, trusting closeness that changes the one who has it. Yet God has already said, twice, “I know you by name” (vv. 12, 17): Moses is answering a God who knew him first. Most of us work hard at managing what others know about us, suspecting that being fully known would end being loved. Timothy Keller put it memorably in The Meaning of Marriage: “To be loved but not known is comforting but superficial. To be known and not loved is our greatest fear. But to be fully known and truly loved is, well, a lot like being loved by God.” Moses was fully known, the killing in Egypt and the excuses at the bush included, and still heard, “you have found favor in my sight.” In Christ that is your standing too: “I know my own and my own know me” (John 10:14). So you need not perform for him.

The presence that came to stay. God answered Moses’ prayer more fully than Moses could have imagined. The presence came to live among us in a body, Immanuel, “God with us” (Matthew 1:23), and the rest promised in verse 14 is the rest Jesus gives (Matthew 11:28).

The test for a church. Moses’ test still works, on a church or a life. Take away everything explained by history, culture, effort or good management: what remains that only God’s presence can account for? If the honest answer is nothing much, the offer of verse 1 has quietly been accepted: all the blessings and none of him. The remedy is Moses’ own: not more effort but asking, on the ground of God’s promise, “please show me now your ways, that I may know you.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses asks for the greatest thing of all, and God gives as much of himself as a sinner can bear. Moses prays, “Please show me your glory” (v. 18). God promises to make all his goodness pass before him and to proclaim his name, the LORD, adding that he will be gracious and merciful as he freely chooses (v. 19). But no one can see his face and live (v. 20). So God places Moses in a cleft of the rock, covers him with his hand while his glory passes, and lets him see only his back (vv. 21–23). God’s glory is his goodness, and even in showing it he shelters the one who sees.
verseByVerse.theology:
What God Says His Glory Consists Of

God defines his glory as his goodness and his name, and Moses sees it only from behind.
verseByVerse.examples: Moses was given a glimpse of God's back. The church has been shown his face, in Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses said, "Please show me your glory." And he said, "I will make all my goodness pass before you and will proclaim before you my name 'The LORD.' And I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy. But," he said, "you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live." And the LORD said, "Behold, there is a place by me where you shall stand on the rock, and while my glory passes by I will put you in a cleft of the rock, and I will cover you with my hand until I have passed by. Then I will take away my hand, and you shall see my back, but my face shall not be seen."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses asks to see God’s glory, and God shows him his goodness and his name, but hides him in the rock, for no one can see God’s face and live.

Please show me your glory. Emboldened, Moses asks for the thing he has wanted all his life. He has seen a bush burn, a sea open and a mountain smoke, and it has not been enough. Knowing God makes a person want more of him, not less.

I will make all my goodness pass before you. God’s answer grants and refuses in one breath. What he calls his glory is his goodness and his name, which he proclaims in the next chapter (34:6–7). Moses, hidden in a cleft of the rock and covered by God’s own hand, may see only his back. That is the most the old covenant could give, even to God’s friend, and the refusal is itself mercy: the hand that hides Moses from a holiness he could not survive is the hand that shelters him.

The face we have been shown. That makes John’s sentence extraordinary: “No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18). God has shone “in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6), and the face Moses was refused is the face the church has been shown. Ordinary people in Galilee looked at it across a supper table and did not know what they were seeing. Moses was given his answer at last: on another mountain he talked with Jesus while that face “shone like the sun” (Matthew 17:2–3). And what God said his glory consisted of, goodness and a name, proved exactly right: when the glory stood still long enough to be seen, it was a man doing good and bearing the name Jesus, given because “he will save his people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21).

I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious. Paul cites verse 19 to show that God’s mercy “depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy” (Romans 9:15–16). The objection is that this makes God arbitrary. But it is said as part of his goodness passing by, to a people who deserved nothing after the calf. Mercy that could be earned would not be mercy.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “back” (v. 23) normally means the back or hinder part, and some take it here as “what comes after”, the trace God leaves as he passes. God is spirit (John 4:24), so this is a picture of a partial, after-the-event sight: Moses saw where God had been, not God as he is.

keyVerse.quote: If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here.
keyVerse.note: Moses would rather stay in the wilderness with God than enter the promised land without him. The verse gathers up the chapter’s question, whether God’s gifts are enough without God, and gives the answer every true believer gives, an answer finally met in Christ, God with us.

33.reflection:
Israel mourned when God offered the land without himself (v. 4). If God gave you everything you want but withdrew his presence, would you notice? What does your honest answer show?

Moses prayed, “that I may know you” (v. 13). What is the difference between knowing about God and knowing him, and what has helped you grow in the second?

What marks your church, or your own life, as distinct in a way only God’s presence can explain (v. 16)?

Moses saw only God’s back; we have been shown “the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6). How might that change the way you read the Gospels this week?

34.title: The LORD, the LORD, a God Merciful and Gracious
34.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Moses, "Cut for yourself two tablets of stone like the first, and I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke.<sup>2</sup>Be ready by the morning, and come up in the morning to Mount Sinai, and present yourself there to me on the top of the mountain.<sup>3</sup>No one shall come up with you, and let no one be seen throughout all the mountain. Let no flocks or herds graze opposite that mountain."<sup>4</sup>So Moses cut two tablets of stone like the first. And he rose early in the morning and went up on Mount Sinai, as the LORD had commanded him, and took in his hand two tablets of stone.<sup>5</sup>The LORD descended in the cloud and stood with him there, and proclaimed the name of the LORD.<sup>6</sup>The LORD passed before him and proclaimed, "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness,<sup>7</sup>keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children and the children's children, to the third and the fourth generation."<sup>8</sup>And Moses quickly bowed his head toward the earth and worshiped.<sup>9</sup>And he said, "If now I have found favor in your sight, O Lord, please let the Lord go in the midst of us, for it is a stiff-necked people, and pardon our iniquity and our sin, and take us for your inheritance."<sup>10</sup>And he said, "Behold, I am making a covenant. Before all your people I will do marvels, such as have not been created in all the earth or in any nation. And all the people among whom you are shall see the work of the LORD, for it is an awesome thing that I will do with you.<sup>11</sup>"Observe what I command you this day. Behold, I will drive out before you the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.<sup>12</sup>Take care, lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land to which you go, lest it become a snare in your midst.<sup>13</sup>You shall tear down their altars and break their pillars and cut down their Asherim<sup>14</sup>(for you shall worship no other god, for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God),<sup>15</sup>lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land, and when they whore after their gods and sacrifice to their gods and you are invited, you eat of his sacrifice,<sup>16</sup>and you take of their daughters for your sons, and their daughters whore after their gods and make your sons whore after their gods.<sup>17</sup>"You shall not make for yourself any gods of cast metal.<sup>18</sup>"You shall keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the time appointed in the month Abib, for in the month Abib you came out from Egypt.<sup>19</sup>All that open the womb are mine, all your male livestock, the firstborn of cow and sheep.<sup>20</sup>The firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb, or if you will not redeem it you shall break its neck. All the firstborn of your sons you shall redeem. And none shall appear before me empty-handed.<sup>21</sup>"Six days you shall work, but on the seventh day you shall rest. In plowing time and in harvest you shall rest.<sup>22</sup>You shall observe the Feast of Weeks, the firstfruits of wheat harvest, and the Feast of Ingathering at the year's end.<sup>23</sup>Three times in the year shall all your males appear before the Lord GOD, the God of Israel.<sup>24</sup>For I will cast out nations before you and enlarge your borders; no one shall covet your land, when you go up to appear before the LORD your God three times in the year.<sup>25</sup>"You shall not offer the blood of my sacrifice with anything leavened, or let the sacrifice of the Feast of the Passover remain until the morning.<sup>26</sup>The best of the firstfruits of your ground you shall bring to the house of the LORD your God. You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk."<sup>27</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Write these words, for in accordance with these words I have made a covenant with you and with Israel."<sup>28</sup>So he was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights. He neither ate bread nor drank water. And he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the Ten Commandments.<sup>29</sup>When Moses came down from Mount Sinai, with the two tablets of the testimony in his hand as he came down from the mountain, Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God.<sup>30</sup>Aaron and all the people of Israel saw Moses, and behold, the skin of his face shone, and they were afraid to come near him.<sup>31</sup>But Moses called to them, and Aaron and all the leaders of the congregation returned to him, and Moses talked with them.<sup>32</sup>Afterward all the people of Israel came near, and he commanded them all that the LORD had spoken with him on Mount Sinai.<sup>33</sup>And when Moses had finished speaking with them, he put a veil over his face.<sup>34</sup>Whenever Moses went in before the LORD to speak with him, he would remove the veil, until he came out. And when he came out and told the people of Israel what he was commanded,<sup>35</sup>the people of Israel would see the face of Moses, that the skin of Moses' face was shining. And Moses would put the veil over his face again, until he went in to speak with him.
34.overview:
Where we are. After the golden calf, Moses has pleaded for God’s presence and asked to see his glory, and God has promised to pass by and proclaim his name (33:12–23). Now he does so, and the broken covenant is renewed.

The message. God’s glory is above all the glory of his grace. He is “merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness”, forgiving the very people who have just betrayed him, and yet he “will by no means clear the guilty.” He renews his covenant on the same terms as before, and the man who has been speaking with him comes down shining.

Why it was said. Israel needed to know, the morning after their great sin, what kind of God they were bound to. These words became the creed Israel returned to in every later crisis (Numbers 14:18; Psalm 103:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2), and the warnings against Canaan’s gods answered the temptations waiting for them in the land (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. Moses cuts new tablets, and the LORD descends and proclaims his name; Moses worships and pleads for God to go with them and pardon them (vv. 1–9). God makes the covenant again, forbidding treaties, intermarriage and the gods of the land (vv. 10–17), and restating the feasts, the firstborn and the Sabbath (vv. 18–26). Moses spends another forty days on the mountain, and the Ten Commandments are written again (vv. 27–28). He comes down with his face shining, and veils it (vv. 29–35).

Where it leads. By the character of God revealed in Christ, and by pattern. The Word made flesh was “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14), the steadfast love and faithfulness of verse 6 in human form. The question the name leaves open, how God can forgive iniquity and yet not clear the guilty, is answered at the cross, where God shows himself “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). And Moses’ fading glory gives way to a glory that does not fade, as believers “with unveiled face” behold the Lord and are changed (2 Corinthians 3:18).

For us. When we have failed God, we are tempted to keep away until we feel we deserve to come back. This chapter tells us who he is on our worst day: slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, because in Christ the guilt has gone somewhere. Come back to him, keep looking at him, and you will be changed, often without knowing it.
34.theology:
The glory of God is the glory of his grace. God reveals his glory by proclaiming his name, and these verses become among the most-quoted in the rest of the Old Testament.

Mercy and justice held together. God forgives, yet "will by no means clear the guilty." The tension is resolved only at the cross, where God is "just and the justifier" (Rom. 3:26).

Transforming glory. Moses' shining face is surpassed by the glory of the gospel; beholding Christ, we are transformed from one degree of glory to another.
34.examples:
Then: God answered Moses' plea by proclaiming his name, renewing the covenant after the calf and sending Moses down with a shining face.

Now: this is the God we worship: merciful and gracious, yet perfectly just. Beholding his glory in the face of Christ, we are being changed by his Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-9 — The LORD Proclaims His Name
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God proclaims his own name, and its heart is mercy. He tells Moses to cut two new tablets like the first and to come up the mountain alone in the morning (vv. 1–3), and Moses does so (v. 4). The LORD descends in the cloud and passes before him, proclaiming himself merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, forgiving iniquity, yet by no means clearing the guilty (vv. 5–7). Moses bows at once in worship and builds his prayer on what he has heard: since God is like this, let him go in the midst of a stiff-necked people, pardon their sin and take them as his inheritance (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Proportions of the Name

God gives six words of mercy and only one clause of judgment.
verseByVerse.examples: This time Moses cut the stone and God wrote on it. Restored sinners often carry some of the cost of what they broke, and they are restored all the same.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Cut for yourself two tablets of stone like the first, and I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke. Be ready by the morning, and come up in the morning to Mount Sinai, and present yourself there to me on the top of the mountain. No one shall come up with you, and let no one be seen throughout all the mountain. Let no flocks or herds graze opposite that mountain." So Moses cut two tablets of stone like the first. And he rose early in the morning and went up on Mount Sinai, as the LORD had commanded him, and took in his hand two tablets of stone. The LORD descended in the cloud and stood with him there, and proclaimed the name of the LORD. The LORD passed before him and proclaimed, "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children and the children's children, to the third and the fourth generation." And Moses quickly bowed his head toward the earth and worshiped. And he said, "If now I have found favor in your sight, O Lord, please let the Lord go in the midst of us, for it is a stiff-necked people, and pardon our iniquity and our sin, and take us for your inheritance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God proclaims his own name: abundant mercy that forgives sin, joined to a justice that will not clear the guilty.

Cut for yourself two tablets of stone. The covenant is remade, with one difference. The first tablets were God’s work throughout (32:16); this time Moses cuts the stone and God writes on it. Grace does not always restore a thing exactly as it was; sometimes the man who broke it has to cut the new stone and carry it up the hill.

Proclaimed the name of the LORD. Answering Moses’ prayer (33:18), God proclaims his own name, the fullest self-description he ever gives. Look at the proportions. Asked to show his glory, God announces mercy, grace, patience, steadfast love, faithfulness and forgiveness, and then one clause of judgment. The judgment is real, but it is not what he most wants to be known by.

Abounding in steadfast love. Twice God names what he has most of. The Hebrew word, hesed, has no single English equivalent. It is not a feeling that comes and goes, but love that has bound itself by a promise and keeps that promise when the other party has given it every reason to stop. That is why it is announced here, weeks after the calf, to a people who broke the covenant almost as soon as they had sworn to keep it. See also Steadfast love in the Theological Dictionary.

Who will by no means clear the guilty. The judgment clause stands right after the offer of forgiveness, and raises a question this chapter cannot answer: how does a God who forgives iniquity also refuse to clear the guilty? Both cannot be true unless the guilt goes somewhere. The answer comes at a cross, where God proved himself “just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26): iniquity truly forgiven and the guilty truly not cleared, because the guilt was borne by someone else. Many think John had this verse in mind when he called the Word made flesh “full of grace and truth” (John 1:14), the old pair “steadfast love and faithfulness” in new words.

Moses quickly bowed his head. Moses answers with worship and then with prayer, and the prayer is built on the name. God had said he could not go among them because they were stiff-necked (33:3); Moses now asks him to go “for it is a stiff-necked people”. Only a God like this could travel with people like them, and Moses appeals to nothing but his mercy.

Echoed through Scripture. Israel’s settled understanding of God’s character came from this sentence, spoken to one man on a mountain in the aftermath of a national catastrophe. The psalms return to it again and again (Psalm 86:15; 103:8; 145:8), the prophets plead it (Joel 2:13), and Jonah is furious about it, because he knew it by heart and knew what it meant for Nineveh (Jonah 4:2).

On your worst day. We love on a sliding scale, warmly when people deserve it and coolly when they let us down, and we assume God does too, so we keep away from him on our worst days. Hesed says the opposite. So the morning after you have failed him, do not wait to earn your way back: “The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end” (Lamentations 3:22).

What about the angry God of the Old Testament? Richard Dawkins opened a famous paragraph in The God Delusion (2006) by calling him “arguably the most unpleasant character in all fiction”, and many who would never put it so harshly half agree: the God of Sinai and the plagues seems a different being from the God of Jesus. This verse is the best place to test that, because here God describes himself at the moment his people have given him most reason for fury, and he calls himself “slow to anger”. The anger is real, and we should be glad of it: a God who felt nothing when Pharaoh drowned Hebrew baby boys, or when a poor man’s cloak was taken, would not be kind; he would be a bystander. But anger is what he is slow to, and steadfast love is what he abounds in. Nor is the God of Jesus milder; no one in Scripture speaks of judgment more than Jesus. The difference is not between two Gods. Sinai shows how seriously he takes evil; Calvary shows how far his steadfast love will go to deal with it without destroying us.

Does verse 7 teach generational curses? No guilt is inherited: “The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father” (Ezekiel 18:20). The second commandment adds “of those who hate me” (20:5): children who repeat their parents’ sin share their judgment, and the effects of sin run through families. But in Christ no curse remains (Galatians 3:13), and the contrast is the point: judgment to the third and fourth generation, steadfast love for thousands.

Uncertain wording. The word introducing Moses’ reason in verse 9 can mean “for” (ESV) or “although”; either way, the people’s stubbornness is why they need God’s pardon.
verseByVerse.note: “Thousands” may mean “the thousandth generation” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God renews the covenant, and its first concern is the sin that broke it. He promises marvels never seen in any nation and undertakes to drive out the peoples of Canaan (vv. 10–11). Israel in turn must make no covenant with them, but tear down their altars, pillars and Asherim, for the LORD’s name is Jealous (vv. 12–14). Treaties would lead to shared sacrifices, and intermarriage to sons drawn after other gods (vv. 15–16). And there must be no gods of cast metal: no more golden calves (v. 17). A forgiven people must guard the faithfulness they so quickly lost.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jealous Is a Name

The renewed terms guard Israel's worship at exactly the point where it failed.
verseByVerse.examples: God's jealousy is not an insecure rival's but a husband's, and it comes from the God who has just forgiven his bride.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Behold, I am making a covenant. Before all your people I will do marvels, such as have not been created in all the earth or in any nation. And all the people among whom you are shall see the work of the LORD, for it is an awesome thing that I will do with you. "Observe what I command you this day. Behold, I will drive out before you the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites. Take care, lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land to which you go, lest it become a snare in your midst. You shall tear down their altars and break their pillars and cut down their Asherim (for you shall worship no other god, for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God), lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land, and when they whore after their gods and sacrifice to their gods and you are invited, you eat of his sacrifice, and you take of their daughters for your sons, and their daughters whore after their gods and make your sons whore after their gods. "You shall not make for yourself any gods of cast metal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God renews his covenant and warns Israel against any alliance with Canaan’s peoples or gods, for the LORD’s name is Jealous.

Whose name is Jealous. The covenant terms are restated, and the emphasis falls where the failure was: other gods, and gods “of cast metal” (v. 17), which is exactly what the calf was. Jealousy is given as a name rather than described as a mood, and the commands around it are about the company Israel keeps. God’s jealousy is not insecurity; it is a husband’s response to the one thing a marriage cannot survive, unfaithfulness. Paul felt this jealousy for the church, betrothed “to one husband” (2 Corinthians 11:2), for the Bridegroom who gave himself for his bride will not share her.

Was the ban on intermarriage racial? No. It was religious: such wives would “make your sons whore after their gods” (v. 16). Rahab of Jericho and Ruth the Moabite joined Israel by faith and were ancestors of Christ. The principle carries over: a Christian should marry “only in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:39; 2 Corinthians 6:14). The command to drive out the nations belonged to the conquest and is not a pattern for today.

Uncertain wording. The Asherim (v. 13) were cult objects linked with the Canaanite goddess Asherah, probably wooden poles or stylised trees set up beside altars. Exactly what they looked like is not known.
verseByVerse.note: Asherah poles were wooden cult objects of the Canaanite goddess Asherah.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The renewed covenant repeats the rhythm of Israel’s year, because the basics are what a forgiven people needs. Israel must keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread in memory of the exodus (v. 18), give God every firstborn and redeem the firstborn of donkeys and of sons (vv. 19–20), and rest every seventh day, even in ploughing and harvest (v. 21). Three times a year the men must appear before the LORD, at Unleavened Bread, Weeks and Ingathering, trusting him to guard their land while they are away (vv. 22–24). Rules for the Passover sacrifice and the firstfruits close the list (vv. 25–26).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Remedy for Failing at the Basics Is the Basics

After the calf, God gives the same rhythms of worship and rest again, unchanged.
verseByVerse.examples: The command to rest names the seasons when it is hardest to obey, and God's rest is still a gift most needed when we feel we cannot stop.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the time appointed in the month Abib, for in the month Abib you came out from Egypt. All that open the womb are mine, all your male livestock, the firstborn of cow and sheep. The firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb, or if you will not redeem it you shall break its neck. All the firstborn of your sons you shall redeem. And none shall appear before me empty-handed. "Six days you shall work, but on the seventh day you shall rest. In plowing time and in harvest you shall rest. You shall observe the Feast of Weeks, the firstfruits of wheat harvest, and the Feast of Ingathering at the year's end. Three times in the year shall all your males appear before the Lord GOD, the God of Israel. For I will cast out nations before you and enlarge your borders; no one shall covet your land, when you go up to appear before the LORD your God three times in the year. "You shall not offer the blood of my sacrifice with anything leavened, or let the sacrifice of the Feast of the Passover remain until the morning. The best of the firstfruits of your ground you shall bring to the house of the LORD your God. You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The renewed covenant repeats the rhythm of Israel’s year, because a forgiven people needs the basics said again.

The same covenant repeated. The repetition is the point (compare 23:14–19). Israel has just broken this covenant spectacularly, and God’s response is to say the same things over: no stricter version, no extra clauses to prevent a recurrence. The remedy for a forgiven people who failed at the basics is the basics, said again.

In plowing time and in harvest. The Sabbath command names ploughing and harvest (v. 21), the two seasons when stopping costs most, and so when resting most plainly trusts God.

Three times in the year. The three pilgrim feasts took every man away from his fields, and God promises that meanwhile “no one shall covet your land” (v. 24): the God they went to meet would guard what they left behind.

Why redeem a donkey with a lamb (v. 20)? The firstborn belonged to God because he spared Israel’s firstborn at the Passover (13:11–15). A donkey could not be sacrificed, so a lamb died in its place, or the donkey died. Every firstborn son was bought back the same way: life for life, a picture of the substitute who redeems us, “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). On the young goat in its mother’s milk (v. 26), see the note on 23:19.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27-28 — Forty Days, the Ten Words
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The covenant is written down again, through the same mediator. God tells Moses to write these words, because in accordance with them he has made a covenant with Moses and with Israel (v. 27). Moses stays on the mountain forty days and forty nights, eating no bread and drinking no water, and the Ten Commandments are written on the new tablets (v. 28). The second forty days mirror the first (24:18), as if the weeks that ended in the calf were being lived again and completed. What Israel broke, God has restored, on the same terms and by his own initiative.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Fasts of the Same Length

The words of the covenant are written again, after a second forty days.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Moses fasted forty days on this mountain, twice. Now: Christ fasted forty days and kept the covenant Israel broke.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Write these words, for in accordance with these words I have made a covenant with you and with Israel." So he was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights. He neither ate bread nor drank water. And he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the Ten Commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses writes down the covenant words and spends another forty days with God, and the Ten Commandments are written again on the new tablets.

Forty days and forty nights. Two forty-day fasts on this mountain, either side of the nation’s great sin. One other man fasted forty days and nights in a wilderness, and when the tempter came he answered out of the book Moses was writing: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4). Jesus, the greater Moses, quoted the first Moses from a fast of the same length, and did not break: he kept, in our place, the covenant Israel had broken.

Uncertain wording. “He wrote” (v. 28) does not name the writer. It is most naturally the LORD, as verse 1 promised and Deuteronomy 10:2–4 confirms; Moses wrote the wider words of the covenant (v. 27).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29-35 — The Shining Face of Moses
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The man who has been with God comes down shining. Moses descends with the tablets, not knowing that the skin of his face shines because he has been talking with God (v. 29). Aaron and the people are afraid to come near, but Moses calls them back and gives them all that the LORD has commanded (vv. 30–32). Then he veils his face. From then on he removes the veil whenever he goes in before the LORD and while he passes on God’s words, and veils it again afterwards (vv. 33–35). God’s glory, reflected on a human face, both draws and frightens a sinful people.
verseByVerse.theology:
What the Veil Was Hiding

Moses covers his shining face between his meetings with God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the glory on Moses' face was fading (2 Cor. 3:13). Now: the glory the Spirit works in believers keeps increasing.

verseByVerse.quote: When Moses came down from Mount Sinai, with the two tablets of the testimony in his hand as he came down from the mountain, Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God. Aaron and all the people of Israel saw Moses, and behold, the skin of his face shone, and they were afraid to come near him. But Moses called to them, and Aaron and all the leaders of the congregation returned to him, and Moses talked with them. Afterward all the people of Israel came near, and he commanded them all that the LORD had spoken with him on Mount Sinai. And when Moses had finished speaking with them, he put a veil over his face. Whenever Moses went in before the LORD to speak with him, he would remove the veil, until he came out. And when he came out and told the people of Israel what he was commanded, the people of Israel would see the face of Moses, that the skin of Moses' face was shining. And Moses would put the veil over his face again, until he went in to speak with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses comes down from God’s presence with his face shining and veils it between his times of speaking for God: a reflected, fading glory that Paul says is surpassed in Christ.

The skin of his face shone. Moses did not know his face shone. A man can spend forty days in God’s presence and be the only person in the camp unaware of what it has done to him, which is generally how it works. The people, who had feared to hear God’s voice (20:19), now fear even his glory reflected on a man’s face (v. 30).

He put a veil over his face. Paul read this closely and saw something the Old Testament never says outright: the veil was “so that the Israelites might not gaze at the outcome of what was being brought to an end” (2 Corinthians 3:13). The glory on Moses’ face was fading, and the veil hid that. From it Paul draws his comparison: if the ministry carved in letters on stone came with such glory, “will not the ministry of the Spirit have even more glory?” (2 Corinthians 3:8). The old glory was real and temporary; the new does not fade.

With unveiled face. Then comes the sentence this chapter has been moving toward: “And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Moses shone and faded and had to go back up for more. What Paul describes is a transformation that keeps increasing, worked by the Spirit in people looking at Christ, and it happens, as with Moses, without the person concerned being aware of it.

Uncertain wording. The verb for “shone” is rare and comes from the word for “horn”, probably picturing rays of light. The Latin Bible translated it “horned”, which is why medieval artists, Michelangelo among them, gave Moses horns. The ESV’s “shone” is almost certainly right.

keyVerse.quote: The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty
keyVerse.note: Asked to show his glory, God proclaims his name, and these words became Israel’s creed about who God is, echoed through the psalms and prophets. They hold mercy and justice together in a way only the cross explains, where sin is forgiven because the guilt was borne by Christ.

34.reflection:
God proclaimed his mercy to a people who had just betrayed him (vv. 6–7). When you have failed God, what do you tend to believe about how he sees you, and how does this passage answer it?

How can God forgive iniquity and yet “by no means clear the guilty” (v. 7)? How does the cross hold the two together?

Moses’ face shone and he did not know it (v. 29). Who have you seen changed by time with God, and what helps you keep “beholding the glory of the Lord” (2 Corinthians 3:18)?

God’s name is Jealous (v. 14). What rivals for your heart would he want you to tear down, and why is his jealousy good news?

35.title: The Willing Heart
35.text: <sup>1</sup>Moses assembled all the congregation of the people of Israel and said to them, "These are the things that the LORD has commanded you to do.<sup>2</sup>Six days work shall be done, but on the seventh day you shall have a Sabbath of solemn rest, holy to the LORD. Whoever does any work on it shall be put to death.<sup>3</sup>You shall kindle no fire in all your dwelling places on the Sabbath day."<sup>4</sup>Moses said to all the congregation of the people of Israel, "This is the thing that the LORD has commanded.<sup>5</sup>Take from among you a contribution to the LORD. Whoever is of a generous heart, let him bring the LORD's contribution: gold, silver, and bronze;<sup>6</sup>blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen; goats' hair,<sup>7</sup>tanned rams' skins, and goatskins; acacia wood,<sup>8</sup>oil for the light, spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense,<sup>9</sup>and onyx stones and stones for setting, for the ephod and for the breastpiece.<sup>10</sup>"Let every skillful craftsman among you come and make all that the LORD has commanded:<sup>11</sup>the tabernacle, its tent and its covering, its hooks and its frames, its bars, its pillars, and its bases;<sup>12</sup>the ark with its poles, the mercy seat, and the veil of the screen;<sup>13</sup>the table with its poles and all its utensils, and the bread of the Presence;<sup>14</sup>the lampstand also for the light, with its utensils and its lamps, and the oil for the light;<sup>15</sup>and the altar of incense, with its poles, and the anointing oil and the fragrant incense, and the screen for the door, at the door of the tabernacle;<sup>16</sup>the altar of burnt offering, with its grating of bronze, its poles, and all its utensils, the basin and its stand;<sup>17</sup>the hangings of the court, its pillars and its bases, and the screen for the gate of the court;<sup>18</sup>the pegs of the tabernacle and the pegs of the court, and their cords;<sup>19</sup>the finely worked garments for ministering in the Holy Place, the holy garments for Aaron the priest, and the garments of his sons, for their service as priests."<sup>20</sup>Then all the congregation of the people of Israel departed from the presence of Moses.<sup>21</sup>And they came, everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him, and brought the LORD's contribution to be used for the tent of meeting, and for all its service, and for the holy garments.<sup>22</sup>So they came, both men and women. All who were of a willing heart brought brooches and earrings and signet rings and armlets, all sorts of gold objects, every man dedicating an offering of gold to the LORD.<sup>23</sup>And every one who possessed blue or purple or scarlet yarns or fine linen or goats' hair or tanned rams' skins or goatskins brought them.<sup>24</sup>Everyone who could make a contribution of silver or bronze brought it as the LORD's contribution.
