And every one who possessed acacia wood of any use in the work brought it.<sup>25</sup>And every skillful woman spun with her hands, and they all brought what they had spun in blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen.<sup>26</sup>All the women whose hearts stirred them to use their skill spun the goats' hair.<sup>27</sup>And the leaders brought onyx stones and stones to be set, for the ephod and for the breastpiece,<sup>28</sup>and spices and oil for the light, and for the anointing oil, and for the fragrant incense.<sup>29</sup>All the men and women, the people of Israel, whose heart moved them to bring anything for the work that the LORD had commanded by Moses to be done brought it as a freewill offering to the LORD.<sup>30</sup>Then Moses said to the people of Israel, "See, the LORD has called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah;<sup>31</sup>and he has filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, with intelligence, with knowledge, and with all craftsmanship,<sup>32</sup>to devise artistic designs, to work in gold and silver and bronze,<sup>33</sup>in cutting stones for setting, and in carving wood, for work in every skilled craft.<sup>34</sup>And he has inspired him to teach, both him and Oholiab the son of Ahisamach of the tribe of Dan.<sup>35</sup>He has filled them with skill to do every sort of work done by an engraver or by a designer or by an embroiderer in blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen, or by a weaver—by any sort of workman or skilled designer.
35.overview:
Where we are. The covenant broken at the golden calf has been renewed, and God has promised to go with his people (chapters 32–34). Now, for the first time since the instructions of chapters 25–31, work on God’s dwelling begins.

The message. A people forgiven and promised God’s presence respond by giving freely and working gladly. Everything God’s house needs comes from willing hearts that he himself has stirred, and from craftsmen he has filled with his Spirit. The same gold that made the calf now builds the place where God will live.

Why it was said. Israel had just shown what their hearts and their gold could do when left to themselves. They needed to see that grace does not only forgive but redirects, and that God’s house is built by gifts he first puts into his people’s hearts and hands (see the introduction on the tabernacle chapters).

How the chapter makes its case. Before any work begins, Moses repeats the Sabbath (vv. 1–3). He calls for a contribution from everyone with a generous heart and for every skilled craftsman to come, and he lists everything to be made (vv. 4–19). The people go away and come back with gifts, men and women together, the women spinning and the leaders bringing jewels and spices, all moved in heart (vv. 20–29). Moses presents Bezalel and Oholiab, filled with God’s Spirit and gifted to teach (vv. 30–35).

Where it leads. By pattern. The willing giving of a redeemed people answers the giving of God, and Paul grounds Christian generosity in Christ: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). And as the Spirit filled Bezalel to build God’s dwelling, so the ascended Christ gives his Spirit and his gifts to build the church, which “grows into a holy temple in the Lord” (Ephesians 2:21).

For us. God still does not want reluctant gifts, for “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). The answer to a closed hand is not pressure but a fresh look at what Christ has given. And every skill we have, at a workbench, a desk or a kitchen table, can be offered to build what he is building.
35.theology:
Worship from a willing heart. The tabernacle is built by freewill offerings from hearts God has stirred, not by compulsion. "God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Cor. 9:7).

Redemption redirects what idolatry corrupted. The gold that made the calf now builds God's dwelling.

The Spirit-gifted community. Men and women, leaders and craftsmen all contribute; the Spirit equips, and the gifted teach others (Eph. 4:11-12).
35.examples:
Then: the wealth once given to an idol was freely given to build God's house.

Now: generosity is not squeezed out by pressure; it flows from hearts the Spirit has stirred with the grace already shown us, and the church is built when the whole community gives and serves together.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The work on God’s house begins with a command to stop. Moses gathers the whole congregation and gives them, first of all, what the LORD has commanded about the Sabbath (v. 1). Six days are for work, but the seventh is a Sabbath of solemn rest, holy to the LORD, and whoever works on it is to be put to death (v. 2). Not even a fire is to be kindled in their homes on that day (v. 3). The most important building project in Israel’s history must fit inside the rhythm of rest God has set, because the people who build his house are made holy by him, not by their labour.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Order Is Deliberate

Rest is commanded before any work is begun.
verseByVerse.examples: Even sacred work rests on what God does, not on our ceaseless effort. A Christian who cannot stop, even for good work, has something to learn from this order.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses assembled all the congregation of the people of Israel and said to them, "These are the things that the LORD has commanded you to do. Six days work shall be done, but on the seventh day you shall have a Sabbath of solemn rest, holy to the LORD. Whoever does any work on it shall be put to death. You shall kindle no fire in all your dwelling places on the Sabbath day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before any work on God’s house begins, the Sabbath is repeated: even the holiest project stops on the seventh day.

Six days work shall be done. The building begins with a command to stop. Before a single curtain is cut, Moses repeats the Sabbath, in the same order God used on the mountain (31:12–17). The most important project in Israel’s history does not run seven days a week. The one example given, “You shall kindle no fire”, probably has the coming work in view, since the craftsmen’s smelting and metalwork needed fires.

Whoever does any work on it. On the death penalty for Sabbath work, see the note on 31:12–18: it belonged to Israel’s theocracy (God’s direct rule of the nation), where the Sabbath was the sign of the covenant, and it ended with that covenant. In Christ the Sabbath is fulfilled, for he gives the true rest (Hebrews 4:9–10); no day binds the Christian conscience, though rest and gathering with God’s people on the Lord’s Day are good gifts.

Work for God is no exception. Those busiest in God’s service are often slowest to rest, as if the work depended on them; the builders of God’s own house are told to stop.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4-19 — The Call for Freewill Offerings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses calls for two things, gifts and skilled hands, and asks for both from willing hearts. Whoever has a generous heart is to bring the LORD’s contribution: metals, yarns and linen, goats’ hair and skins, acacia wood, oil, spices and precious stones (vv. 4–9). Every skilled craftsman is to come and make everything the LORD has commanded (v. 10). Then Moses lists it all: the tabernacle and its tent, the ark and mercy seat, the table, the lampstand and the altar of incense, the altar of burnt offering and the basin, the court, and the priests’ garments (vv. 11–19). The people hear the whole plan before anything is asked of them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Nobody Is Assessed

The gifts come from the willing and the work from the skilled.
verseByVerse.examples: The people were told the whole plan before they were asked for anything, and God's house was built from what they wanted to give.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses said to all the congregation of the people of Israel, "This is the thing that the LORD has commanded. Take from among you a contribution to the LORD. Whoever is of a generous heart, let him bring the LORD's contribution: gold, silver, and bronze; blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen; goats' hair, tanned rams' skins, and goatskins; acacia wood, oil for the light, spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense, and onyx stones and stones for setting, for the ephod and for the breastpiece. "Let every skillful craftsman among you come and make all that the LORD has commanded: the tabernacle, its tent and its covering, its hooks and its frames, its bars, its pillars, and its bases; the ark with its poles, the mercy seat, and the veil of the screen; the table with its poles and all its utensils, and the bread of the Presence; the lampstand also for the light, with its utensils and its lamps, and the oil for the light; and the altar of incense, with its poles, and the anointing oil and the fragrant incense, and the screen for the door, at the door of the tabernacle; the altar of burnt offering, with its grating of bronze, its poles, and all its utensils, the basin and its stand; the hangings of the court, its pillars and its bases, and the screen for the gate of the court; the pegs of the tabernacle and the pegs of the court, and their cords; the finely worked garments for ministering in the Holy Place, the holy garments for Aaron the priest, and the garments of his sons, for their service as priests."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses calls for gifts from every generous heart and for every skilled craftsman to come, and he reads out the whole plan before asking for anything.

Whoever is of a generous heart. Nobody is told how much to give. The contribution is “to the LORD” (v. 5), and the only condition is the heart (compare 2 Corinthians 9:7).

All that the LORD has commanded. The list that follows summarises chapters 25 to 31: everything specified on the mountain is now read out to the people who will make it, and they hear the whole plan before being asked for anything. They are invited into God’s purpose, not simply asked for funds.

Uncertain wording. The “finely worked garments” (v. 19) translate a rare phrase whose exact sense is unknown (see the note on 31:10).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people respond with glad, abundant, heartfelt giving. They leave Moses and come back, everyone whose heart stirred him and whose spirit moved him (vv. 20–21). Men and women alike bring brooches, earrings, rings and armlets of gold (v. 22). Those who have yarn, linen, skins, silver, bronze or acacia wood bring them (vv. 23–24). Skilled women spin the yarn and the goats’ hair (vv. 25–26), and the leaders bring precious stones, spices and oil (vv. 27–28). All of it is a freewill offering from people whose hearts moved them (v. 29). The gold that once made a calf now builds God’s house.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Material Was Never the Problem

The gold is the same gold that made the calf; what has changed is the heart.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the gold that made a calf now built a tabernacle. Now: money, time and skill serve God or an idol depending on the heart that gives them.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the congregation of the people of Israel departed from the presence of Moses. And they came, everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him, and brought the LORD's contribution to be used for the tent of meeting, and for all its service, and for the holy garments. So they came, both men and women. All who were of a willing heart brought brooches and earrings and signet rings and armlets, all sorts of gold objects, every man dedicating an offering of gold to the LORD. And every one who possessed blue or purple or scarlet yarns or fine linen or goats' hair or tanned rams' skins or goatskins brought them. Everyone who could make a contribution of silver or bronze brought it as the LORD's contribution. And every one who possessed acacia wood of any use in the work brought it. And every skillful woman spun with her hands, and they all brought what they had spun in blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen. All the women whose hearts stirred them to use their skill spun the goats' hair. And the leaders brought onyx stones and stones to be set, for the ephod and for the breastpiece, and spices and oil for the light, and for the anointing oil, and for the fragrant incense. All the men and women, the people of Israel, whose heart moved them to bring anything for the work that the LORD had commanded by Moses to be done brought it as a freewill offering to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moved in heart, men and women alike bring their gold, cloth, skill and treasures as a freewill offering, the same people who had just made the calf.

Both men and women. The text is generous about who gave: men and women together, the women bringing their own jewellery and spinning the goats’ hair, the leaders bringing onyx and spices. And the motive is named again and again (vv. 21, 22, 26, 29): hearts stirred, spirits moved. They gave because God had moved them to want to.

The same gold. Set that against chapter 32. The same gold, from the same Egyptian back wages (12:35–36), from the same people. Not long ago they took off their earrings to make a calf; now they take them off to build a tabernacle. The material was never the problem, and it never is. What changed was the heart, and what changed the heart was being forgiven.

Why Christians give. Paul roots Christian giving in the same place: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). The cure for a closed hand is not pressure but a fresh look at what Christ has given.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God provides not only the materials but the makers. Moses tells the people that the LORD has called Bezalel of the tribe of Judah by name and filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, intelligence, knowledge and all craftsmanship (vv. 30–31), to design and to work in metal, stone and wood (vv. 32–33). God has also enabled him and Oholiab of the tribe of Dan to teach others (v. 34), and filled them with skill for every kind of engraving, design, embroidery and weaving (v. 35). The gifts are God’s, and they are given so that the whole people’s work may go forward.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gift Includes Handing It On

The Spirit-filled craftsmen are also teachers.
verseByVerse.examples: Two men were filled so that they could train others. Gifts in the church are given to be passed on, not kept.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses said to the people of Israel, "See, the LORD has called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah; and he has filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, with intelligence, with knowledge, and with all craftsmanship, to devise artistic designs, to work in gold and silver and bronze, in cutting stones for setting, and in carving wood, for work in every skilled craft. And he has inspired him to teach, both him and Oholiab the son of Ahisamach of the tribe of Dan. He has filled them with skill to do every sort of work done by an engraver or by a designer or by an embroiderer in blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen, or by a weaver—by any sort of workman or skilled designer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has called Bezalel by name and filled him with his Spirit for skilled work, and he has enabled him and Oholiab to teach others.

Filled him with the Spirit of God. The Spirit-filling of 31:1–5 is repeated, with something new: “he has inspired him to teach”. God does not fill two craftsmen and leave the camp watching; he fills two men who can train the others, which is why the next chapter has a workforce rather than a pair of artisans.

Gifts for building God’s house. The pattern runs on into the church: the ascended Christ gives gifts to his people “for building up the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4:12; see the note on 31:1–11). A skill passed on to others serves God twice.

keyVerse.quote: And they came, everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him, and brought the LORD’s contribution to be used for the tent of meeting, and for all its service, and for the holy garments.
keyVerse.note: The whole chapter turns on the stirred heart. The people who gave their gold for a calf now give it freely for God’s dwelling, because forgiveness has changed what they want, and that is still the spring of all true Christian giving.

35.reflection:
The work on God’s house began with a command to rest (vv. 1–3). Why might people busy in God’s service find rest hardest, and what does that show about whom we are trusting?

No one was told how much to give, only to give with a willing heart (v. 5). What helps your giving come from gratitude rather than guilt or pressure?

The same gold that made the calf now built the tabernacle (v. 22). What in your life, once used for yourself or for idols, could be turned to God’s service?

Bezalel and Oholiab were gifted to teach others (v. 34). What skill or gift do you have that you could pass on to someone else in your church?

36.title: More Than Enough
36.text: <sup>1</sup>"Bezalel and Oholiab and every craftsman in whom the LORD has put skill and intelligence to know how to do any work in the construction of the sanctuary shall work in accordance with all that the LORD has commanded."<sup>2</sup>And Moses called Bezalel and Oholiab and every craftsman in whose mind the LORD had put skill, everyone whose heart stirred him up to come to do the work.<sup>3</sup>And they received from Moses all the contribution that the people of Israel had brought for doing the work on the sanctuary. They still kept bringing him freewill offerings every morning,<sup>4</sup>so that all the craftsmen who were doing every sort of task on the sanctuary came, each from the task that he was doing,<sup>5</sup>and said to Moses, "The people bring much more than enough for doing the work that the LORD has commanded us to do."<sup>6</sup>So Moses gave command, and word was proclaimed throughout the camp, "Let no man or woman do anything more for the contribution for the sanctuary." So the people were restrained from bringing,<sup>7</sup>for the material they had was sufficient to do all the work, and more.<sup>8</sup>And all the craftsmen among the workmen made the tabernacle with ten curtains. They were made of fine twined linen and blue and purple and scarlet yarns, with cherubim skillfully worked.<sup>9</sup>The length of each curtain was twenty-eight cubits, and the breadth of each curtain four cubits. All the curtains were the same size.<sup>10</sup>He coupled five curtains to one another, and the other five curtains he coupled to one another.<sup>11</sup>He made loops of blue on the edge of the outermost curtain of the first set. Likewise he made them on the edge of the outermost curtain of the second set.<sup>12</sup>He made fifty loops on the one curtain, and he made fifty loops on the edge of the curtain that was in the second set. The loops were opposite one another.<sup>13</sup>And he made fifty clasps of gold, and coupled the curtains one to the other with clasps. So the tabernacle was a single whole.<sup>14</sup>He also made curtains of goats' hair for a tent over the tabernacle. He made eleven curtains.<sup>15</sup>The length of each curtain was thirty cubits, and the breadth of each curtain four cubits. The eleven curtains were the same size.<sup>16</sup>He coupled five curtains by themselves, and six curtains by themselves.<sup>17</sup>And he made fifty loops on the edge of the outermost curtain of the one set, and fifty loops on the edge of the other connecting curtain.<sup>18</sup>And he made fifty clasps of bronze to couple the tent together that it might be a single whole.<sup>19</sup>And he made for the tent a covering of tanned rams' skins and goatskins.<sup>20</sup>Then he made the upright frames for the tabernacle of acacia wood.<sup>21</sup>Ten cubits was the length of a frame, and a cubit and a half the breadth of each frame.<sup>22</sup>Each frame had two tenons for fitting together. He did this for all the frames of the tabernacle.<sup>23</sup>The frames for the tabernacle he made thus: twenty frames for the south side.<sup>24</sup>And he made forty bases of silver under the twenty frames, two bases under one frame for its two tenons, and two bases under the next frame for its two tenons.<sup>25</sup>For the second side of the tabernacle, on the north side, he made twenty frames<sup>26</sup>and their forty bases of silver, two bases under one frame and two bases under the next frame.<sup>27</sup>For the rear of the tabernacle westward he made six frames.<sup>28</sup>He made two frames for corners of the tabernacle in the rear.<sup>29</sup>And they were separate beneath but joined at the top, at the first ring. He made two of them this way for the two corners.<sup>30</sup>There were eight frames with their bases of silver: sixteen bases, under every frame two bases.<sup>31</sup>He made bars of acacia wood, five for the frames of the one side of the tabernacle,<sup>32</sup>and five bars for the frames of the other side of the tabernacle, and five bars for the frames of the tabernacle at the rear westward.<sup>33</sup>And he made the middle bar to run from end to end halfway up the frames.<sup>34</sup>And he overlaid the frames with gold, and made their rings of gold for holders for the bars, and overlaid the bars with gold.<sup>35</sup>He made the veil of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen; with cherubim skillfully worked into it he made it.<sup>36</sup>And for it he made four pillars of acacia and overlaid them with gold. Their hooks were of gold, and he cast for them four bases of silver.<sup>37</sup>He also made a screen for the entrance of the tent, of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen, embroidered with needlework,<sup>38</sup>and its five pillars with their hooks. He overlaid their capitals, and their fillets were of gold, but their five bases were of bronze.
36.overview:
Where we are. Moses has asked for gifts from willing hearts, the people have responded in a flood, and Bezalel and Oholiab have been presented as the Spirit-filled master craftsmen (chapter 35). Now the work itself begins.

The message. When God’s grace moves his people, they give more than enough, and the work is done exactly as God said. The gifts overflow until the people have to be told to stop, and the craftsmen build the tent of God’s dwelling to his pattern, curtain by curtain and frame by frame.

Why it was said. Israel had just made a god in their own way (chapter 32). The careful report of the building, matching the instructions of chapter 26 almost word for word, showed them and every later generation that the same people, forgiven, could now do what God commanded (see the introduction on the tabernacle chapters).

How the chapter makes its case. The craftsmen receive the offerings, but the people keep bringing more every morning, until the workers tell Moses there is far more than enough and a proclamation stops the giving (vv. 1–7). Then the tent itself is made: the inner curtains of linen worked with cherubim and joined into a single whole, the outer tent of goats’ hair and the coverings of skins (vv. 8–19), and the gold-covered frames and bars on silver bases, the veil and the entrance screen (vv. 20–38).

Where it leads. By pattern. This tent was where God would live among his people, and John says the Word “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), using a verb that means he pitched his tent. The veil that barred the way into the Most Holy Place had its successor in the temple, and that curtain was torn in two when Jesus died (Matthew 27:51); now we enter “through the curtain, that is, through his flesh” (Hebrews 10:20). And the people’s overflowing gifts reflect a God who is able to do “far more abundantly than all that we ask or think” (Ephesians 3:20).

For us. A people moved by grace does not need to be coaxed into giving, and work done carefully and without fanfare, exactly as God asks, is precious to him. Above all, the way into God’s presence that this tent both opened and guarded now stands open to all who come through Christ.
36.theology:
Generosity that must be restrained. The people give more than enough, the fruit of hearts captivated by grace, the grace seen fully in Christ: "Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich" (2 Cor. 8:9).

Skill as a gift of grace. God "put skill" in the workers; even our abilities are his gifts, which leaves no room for pride in service.

Worship ordered by God's pattern. Every element is made exactly as God commanded.
36.examples:
Then: the people gave until they had to be stopped, while Spirit-gifted craftsmen built everything to God's pattern.

Now: when we grasp the riches we have in Christ, giving overflows, and our gifts and skills are offered back to God with joyful care.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Grace produces generosity so great that it has to be stopped. Bezalel, Oholiab and every skilled worker are to build the sanctuary exactly as the LORD has commanded (v. 1). Moses calls them, everyone whose heart stirred him to come (v. 2), and hands them the offerings, but every morning the people keep bringing more (v. 3). The craftsmen leave their work to tell Moses that the people are bringing much more than enough (vv. 4–5). So Moses has it proclaimed through the camp that no one is to bring anything further, and the people are restrained, for there is enough and more (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Only Time Generosity Had to Be Stopped

This building project ends up with a surplus.
verseByVerse.examples: The surplus came from hearts that had recently been at their worst and had been forgiven. Forgiveness, not pressure, is still what opens hands.

verseByVerse.quote: "Bezalel and Oholiab and every craftsman in whom the LORD has put skill and intelligence to know how to do any work in the construction of the sanctuary shall work in accordance with all that the LORD has commanded." And Moses called Bezalel and Oholiab and every craftsman in whose mind the LORD had put skill, everyone whose heart stirred him up to come to do the work. And they received from Moses all the contribution that the people of Israel had brought for doing the work on the sanctuary. They still kept bringing him freewill offerings every morning, so that all the craftsmen who were doing every sort of task on the sanctuary came, each from the task that he was doing, and said to Moses, "The people bring much more than enough for doing the work that the LORD has commanded us to do." So Moses gave command, and word was proclaimed throughout the camp, "Let no man or woman do anything more for the contribution for the sanctuary." So the people were restrained from bringing, for the material they had was sufficient to do all the work, and more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people give so freely that the craftsmen report more than enough, and Moses has to tell them to stop.

Much more than enough. The work begins, and within seven verses it hits a problem building projects almost never have. The people keep bringing freewill offerings “every morning” (v. 3), until the craftsmen leave their tasks to report that there is far more than the work needs. So a proclamation goes through the camp telling every man and woman to stop, and the people are “restrained from bringing” (v. 6).

Generosity restrained. This is the only recorded occasion in Scripture where giving has to be halted, and it comes from the people who complained about food, water, leadership and the route, and who built a calf. Nothing had changed about them except that they had been forgiven, and had been given something worth building. When was a congregation last told to stop giving?

The God of more than enough. Their overflowing gifts reflect the God who gave first, who “is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think” (Ephesians 3:20). Generosity like Israel’s is not squeezed out of people. It overflows from those who know how much they have been given.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tent of God’s dwelling is made exactly as God designed it. The craftsmen make ten curtains of fine linen and coloured yarns, with cherubim skilfully worked, all the same size (vv. 8–9). They join them in two sets of five, with loops of blue and fifty clasps of gold, so that the tabernacle is a single whole (vv. 10–13). Over it goes a tent of eleven curtains of goats’ hair, joined with clasps of bronze (vv. 14–18), and over that a covering of rams’ skins and goatskins (v. 19). Every detail matches the instructions of chapter 26: what God said, Israel did.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Repetition Is the Report

Each phrase answers an instruction God had already given.
verseByVerse.examples: What God said and what Israel did matched, line for line. After the calf, that match is good news: a forgiven people can obey.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the craftsmen among the workmen made the tabernacle with ten curtains. They were made of fine twined linen and blue and purple and scarlet yarns, with cherubim skillfully worked. The length of each curtain was twenty-eight cubits, and the breadth of each curtain four cubits. All the curtains were the same size. He coupled five curtains to one another, and the other five curtains he coupled to one another. He made loops of blue on the edge of the outermost curtain of the first set. Likewise he made them on the edge of the outermost curtain of the second set. He made fifty loops on the one curtain, and he made fifty loops on the edge of the curtain that was in the second set. The loops were opposite one another. And he made fifty clasps of gold, and coupled the curtains one to the other with clasps. So the tabernacle was a single whole. He also made curtains of goats' hair for a tent over the tabernacle. He made eleven curtains. The length of each curtain was thirty cubits, and the breadth of each curtain four cubits. The eleven curtains were the same size. He coupled five curtains by themselves, and six curtains by themselves. And he made fifty loops on the edge of the outermost curtain of the one set, and fifty loops on the edge of the other connecting curtain. And he made fifty clasps of bronze to couple the tent together that it might be a single whole. And he made for the tent a covering of tanned rams' skins and goatskins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The craftsmen make the curtains and coverings of the tabernacle exactly as God commanded in chapter 26, joined so that the dwelling is a single whole.

Made the tabernacle with ten curtains. The curtains are made as chapter 26 specified: ten of fine twined linen with cherubim, each twenty-eight cubits long, eleven of goats’ hair, the clasps and loops, the coverings of rams’ skins and goatskins. The account is deliberately repetitive, and the repetition is the report. Every phrase matches an instruction in chapter 26, so a reader comparing the two can see that what God said and what Israel did are the same thing. After the golden calf, that matters.

A tent for God. This was a tent, not a palace: God chose to live among a travelling people in a dwelling like theirs. John reaches for the same picture when he says the Word “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14); the verb means he pitched his tent among us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20-38 — The Frames, the Veil, the Screen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The framework, the veil and the entrance complete the tent. Frames of acacia wood, ten cubits high, stand on silver bases: twenty on the south side, twenty on the north and eight at the rear, including the corner frames (vv. 20–30). Bars of acacia hold them together, with a middle bar running from end to end, and frames and bars alike are overlaid with gold (vv. 31–34). The veil, worked with cherubim, hangs on four gold-covered pillars to screen off the Most Holy Place (vv. 35–36), and an embroidered screen on five pillars closes the entrance (vv. 37–38). The chapter ends without comment, for faithful obedience needs none.
verseByVerse.theology:
Obedience Without Commentary

The structure goes up exactly as commanded.
verseByVerse.examples: Nothing was improvised or embellished. Much faithful service looks like this: plain work, done as God said, without remark.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he made the upright frames for the tabernacle of acacia wood. Ten cubits was the length of a frame, and a cubit and a half the breadth of each frame. Each frame had two tenons for fitting together. He did this for all the frames of the tabernacle. The frames for the tabernacle he made thus: twenty frames for the south side. And he made forty bases of silver under the twenty frames, two bases under one frame for its two tenons, and two bases under the next frame for its two tenons. For the second side of the tabernacle, on the north side, he made twenty frames and their forty bases of silver, two bases under one frame and two bases under the next frame. For the rear of the tabernacle westward he made six frames. He made two frames for corners of the tabernacle in the rear. And they were separate beneath but joined at the top, at the first ring. He made two of them this way for the two corners. There were eight frames with their bases of silver: sixteen bases, under every frame two bases. He made bars of acacia wood, five for the frames of the one side of the tabernacle, and five bars for the frames of the other side of the tabernacle, and five bars for the frames of the tabernacle at the rear westward. And he made the middle bar to run from end to end halfway up the frames. And he overlaid the frames with gold, and made their rings of gold for holders for the bars, and overlaid the bars with gold. He made the veil of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen; with cherubim skillfully worked into it he made it. And for it he made four pillars of acacia and overlaid them with gold. Their hooks were of gold, and he cast for them four bases of silver. He also made a screen for the entrance of the tent, of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen, embroidered with needlework, and its five pillars with their hooks. He overlaid their capitals, and their fillets were of gold, but their five bases were of bronze.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The frames, bars, veil and entrance screen are made to God’s design, and the chapter ends without comment, letting faithful work speak for itself.

The upright frames for the tabernacle. The frames, bars, veil and screen follow in the language of chapter 26: forty-eight frames of acacia overlaid with gold, the silver bases, the veil with cherubim worked into it, the screen on its five pillars. The chapter closes without a summary or a reflection. The frames are stood up, the veil is hung, and the account moves on to the furniture. It reads like a builder’s log because that is what it is, and the plainness says something: obedience does not need comment.

He made the veil. The veil, worked with cherubim like those that guarded the way back into Eden (Genesis 3:24), screened off the Most Holy Place where God was enthroned: a sign that the way into his presence was not yet open (Hebrews 9:8). When Jesus died, the curtain of the temple, its successor, “was torn in two, from top to bottom” (Matthew 27:51), and believers now enter “through the curtain, that is, through his flesh” (Hebrews 10:20).

Uncertain wording. How the corner frames were built (vv. 28–29, “separate beneath but joined at the top, at the first ring”) is not clear, and reconstructions differ; they probably strengthened the rear corners. The “fillets” (v. 38) were probably bands or connecting rods on the pillars, but the word’s exact meaning is uncertain.

keyVerse.quote: The people bring much more than enough for doing the work that the LORD has commanded us to do.
keyVerse.note: The craftsmen’s report sums up what grace had done. The people who built a calf now give so freely that they must be told to stop, an overflow that reflects the God who gives far more than we ask, and gave his own Son.

36.reflection:
The people had to be restrained from giving (vv. 5–7). What would it take for your church, or for you, to give like that?

Israel’s generosity came from people who had just been forgiven. How does remembering what Christ has given you change the way you give?

The building account simply records that the work was done as God commanded, without comment (vv. 8–38). What ordinary, unseen faithfulness is God asking of you this week?

The veil shut the way into God’s presence, and it was torn when Jesus died. How should that open way shape the way you pray?

37.title: Obedience in Every Detail
37.text: <sup>1</sup>Bezalel made the ark of acacia wood. Two cubits and a half was its length, a cubit and a half its breadth, and a cubit and a half its height.<sup>2</sup>And he overlaid it with pure gold inside and outside, and made a molding of gold around it.<sup>3</sup>And he cast for it four rings of gold for its four feet, two rings on its one side and two rings on its other side.<sup>4</sup>And he made poles of acacia wood and overlaid them with gold<sup>5</sup>and put the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark to carry the ark.<sup>6</sup>And he made a mercy seat of pure gold. Two cubits and a half was its length, and a cubit and a half its breadth.<sup>7</sup>And he made two cherubim of gold. He made them of hammered work on the two ends of the mercy seat,<sup>8</sup>one cherub on the one end, and one cherub on the other end. Of one piece with the mercy seat he made the cherubim on its two ends.<sup>9</sup>The cherubim spread out their wings above, overshadowing the mercy seat with their wings, with their faces one to another; toward the mercy seat were the faces of the cherubim.<sup>10</sup>He also made the table of acacia wood. Two cubits was its length, a cubit its breadth, and a cubit and a half its height.<sup>11</sup>And he overlaid it with pure gold, and made a molding of gold around it.<sup>12</sup>And he made a rim around it a handbreadth wide, and made a molding of gold around the rim.<sup>13</sup>He cast for it four rings of gold and fastened the rings to the four corners at its four legs.<sup>14</sup>Close to the frame were the rings, as holders for the poles to carry the table.<sup>15</sup>He made the poles of acacia wood to carry the table, and overlaid them with gold.<sup>16</sup>And he made the vessels of pure gold that were to be on the table, its plates and dishes for incense, and its bowls and flagons with which to pour drink offerings.<sup>17</sup>He also made the lampstand of pure gold. He made the lampstand of hammered work. Its base, its stem, its cups, its calyxes, and its flowers were of one piece with it.<sup>18</sup>And there were six branches going out of its sides, three branches of the lampstand out of one side of it and three branches of the lampstand out of the other side of it;<sup>19</sup>three cups made like almond blossoms, each with calyx and flower, on one branch, and three cups made like almond blossoms, each with calyx and flower, on the other branch—so for the six branches going out of the lampstand.<sup>20</sup>And on the lampstand itself were four cups made like almond blossoms, with their calyxes and flowers,<sup>21</sup>and a calyx of one piece with it under each pair of the six branches going out of it.<sup>22</sup>Their calyxes and their branches were of one piece with it. The whole of it was a single piece of hammered work of pure gold.<sup>23</sup>And he made its seven lamps and its tongs and its trays of pure gold.<sup>24</sup>He made it and all its utensils out of a talent of pure gold.<sup>25</sup>He made the altar of incense of acacia wood. Its length was a cubit, and its breadth was a cubit. It was square, and two cubits was its height. Its horns were of one piece with it.<sup>26</sup>He overlaid it with pure gold, its top and around its sides and its horns. And he made a molding of gold around it,<sup>27</sup>and made two rings of gold on it under its molding, on two opposite sides of it, as holders for the poles with which to carry it.<sup>28</sup>And he made the poles of acacia wood and overlaid them with gold.<sup>29</sup>He made the holy anointing oil also, and the pure fragrant incense, blended as by the perfumer.
37.overview:
Where we are. The calf has been judged and the covenant renewed (chapters 32–34). The people have brought more than enough for the work (36:5–7), and Bezalel’s team has built the tent itself (chapter 36). Now he makes the furnishings that stand inside it.

The message. What God designed on the mountain is now made on the ground, item by item, in almost the same words. A forgiven people approaches God exactly as he said, because the way into his presence is his to set, not theirs to improve. And at the very centre of that way stands a mercy seat, the place where sin is covered.

Why it was said. Israel had just tried to worship the LORD in a way of their own devising, with a golden calf (32:4–5). These careful repetitions show the same people, forgiven, learning to come to God on his terms (see the introduction on the tabernacle chapters).

How the chapter makes its case. It works from the inside outward, in the order of holiness. First the ark, the mercy seat and the cherubim, the throne of the unseen God (vv. 1–9); then the table for the bread of the Presence (vv. 10–16); then the lampstand, beaten from a single talent of gold (vv. 17–24); and last the golden altar of incense, with the anointing oil and the incense (vv. 25–29). Each item is made as commanded in chapters 25 and 30; nothing is added and nothing is left out.

Where it leads. By pattern. These objects were made after “the pattern that was shown you on the mountain”, and Hebrews says they “serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things” (Hebrews 8:5). The mercy seat finds its meaning in Christ, “whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25), using the Greek word for the mercy seat. Jesus took up the bread and the lamp himself: “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35), “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). And the incense rising before the veil pictures the prayer that now rises through the one who “always lives to make intercession” for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

For us. We do not come to God by designs of our own, however sincere; we come by the way he has given, and that way turns out to be a person. Bezalel’s care also says something about our work: skill, patience and craftsmanship offered to God are worship, not a distraction from it.
37.theology:
Obedience in every detail. Bezalel makes each furnishing exactly as God commanded, because true worship is governed by God's word. Faithfulness in small things is itself worship.

The furnishings point to Christ. The mercy seat pictures the propitiation he made, the sacrifice that turned away God’s anger (Rom. 3:25). The bread and the lamp picture the one who is the bread of life (John 6) and the light of the world, and the incense the prayers of the saints (Rev. 5:8) rising through him.

Excellence offered to God. The craftsmanship reflects the worth of the God whose house this is.
37.examples:
Then: Bezalel made each sacred object exactly as God commanded, his Spirit-given skill submitted to God's design.

Now: the furnishings still preach Christ, our mercy seat, our bread, our light and our Intercessor.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the heart of the camp stands a throne for the unseen God. Bezalel makes the ark of acacia wood overlaid with gold, with rings and poles to carry it (vv. 1–5). Then he makes its lid, the mercy seat of pure gold, where atoning blood would be sprinkled (v. 6), and beats out two golden cherubim of one piece with it, wings spread over it and faces turned toward it (vv. 7–9). There is no image of God between them: the LORD is enthroned there unseen, above the tablets of his covenant, over a place of mercy.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Object Before the Explanation

The place of atonement is made by a named man's hands.
verseByVerse.examples: The place of atonement existed long before anyone understood it. God's purposes often run ahead of his people's grasp of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Bezalel made the ark of acacia wood. Two cubits and a half was its length, a cubit and a half its breadth, and a cubit and a half its height. And he overlaid it with pure gold inside and outside, and made a molding of gold around it. And he cast for it four rings of gold for its four feet, two rings on its one side and two rings on its other side. And he made poles of acacia wood and overlaid them with gold and put the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark to carry the ark. And he made a mercy seat of pure gold. Two cubits and a half was its length, and a cubit and a half its breadth. And he made two cherubim of gold. He made them of hammered work on the two ends of the mercy seat, one cherub on the one end, and one cherub on the other end. Of one piece with the mercy seat he made the cherubim on its two ends. The cherubim spread out their wings above, overshadowing the mercy seat with their wings, with their faces one to another; toward the mercy seat were the faces of the cherubim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bezalel makes the ark and its mercy seat as God designed them: a throne for the unseen God, over a place where sin is covered.

Bezalel made the ark of acacia wood. The most important object in Israel is credited to a named man working with his hands (31:2–5), and the text does not hurry past his name.

He made a mercy seat of pure gold. On this lid blood was sprinkled once a year for the people’s sin (Leviticus 16:14–15). The place of atonement existed before anyone understood what it pictured, and Paul uses its word for Christ, “whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood” (Romans 3:25).

Did the cherubim break the second commandment? No. God himself commanded them; they represented the angels round his throne, not God, and they were never worshipped. Between them was empty space: the LORD was “enthroned upon the cherubim” (Psalm 80:1), unseen.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The table is made to hold the bread of the Presence, the standing meal in God’s house. It is acacia wood overlaid with gold, with a rim and moulding (vv. 10–12), rings and poles for carrying (vv. 13–15), and vessels of pure gold for the bread and the drink offerings (v. 16). Twelve loaves, one for each tribe, would lie on it before the LORD continually: a sign that his people were always in his sight and always fed from his hand.
verseByVerse.theology:
Vessels for a Standing Meal

Even the tableware for God's house is built to be carried.
verseByVerse.examples: The bread stood before God continually, and the one who calls himself the bread of life still feeds his people.

verseByVerse.quote: He also made the table of acacia wood. Two cubits was its length, a cubit its breadth, and a cubit and a half its height. And he overlaid it with pure gold, and made a molding of gold around it. And he made a rim around it a handbreadth wide, and made a molding of gold around the rim. He cast for it four rings of gold and fastened the rings to the four corners at its four legs. Close to the frame were the rings, as holders for the poles to carry the table. He made the poles of acacia wood to carry the table, and overlaid them with gold. And he made the vessels of pure gold that were to be on the table, its plates and dishes for incense, and its bowls and flagons with which to pour drink offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The table held the bread that lay before God continually: his people always in his sight, and always fed by him.

The table of acacia wood. With its rings, poles and vessels of pure gold, the table is equipped for a standing meal in God’s house: twelve loaves, one for each tribe, renewed every Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5–8). Jesus says, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lampstand is beaten from one talent of pure gold into the shape of a flowering almond tree. Its base, stem, cups and blossoms are of one piece (vv. 17–18); six branches go out from its sides, each with three almond cups (vv. 19–21); and the whole is a single piece of hammered work (v. 22). With its seven lamps and gold tongs and trays (vv. 23–24), it gives the only light in the Holy Place, God’s light among his people.
verseByVerse.theology:
Of One Piece

The light in God's house is not bolted together from parts.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: one golden lamp lit the Holy Place. Now: Christ is the light of the world (John 8:12), and his churches carry that light.

verseByVerse.quote: He also made the lampstand of pure gold. He made the lampstand of hammered work. Its base, its stem, its cups, its calyxes, and its flowers were of one piece with it. And there were six branches going out of its sides, three branches of the lampstand out of one side of it and three branches of the lampstand out of the other side of it; three cups made like almond blossoms, each with calyx and flower, on one branch, and three cups made like almond blossoms, each with calyx and flower, on the other branch—so for the six branches going out of the lampstand. And on the lampstand itself were four cups made like almond blossoms, with their calyxes and flowers, and a calyx of one piece with it under each pair of the six branches going out of it. Their calyxes and their branches were of one piece with it. The whole of it was a single piece of hammered work of pure gold. And he made its seven lamps and its tongs and its trays of pure gold. He made it and all its utensils out of a talent of pure gold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beaten from one talent of gold into a flowering almond tree, the lampstand gave the only light in the Holy Place.

Of one piece with it. Like the cherubim (v. 7), the lampstand was not assembled from parts but beaten out of a single talent of gold, about 75 pounds (34 kg). Its light was God’s light among his people. Jesus says, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), and in Revelation the churches are lampstands, carrying his light (Revelation 1:20).

Uncertain wording. The words translated “calyxes” and “flowers” are craft terms whose exact shapes are unknown (the first is used of a pillar’s capital in Amos 9:1). The picture of a flowering almond branch is clear; the details of each ornament are not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25-29 — The Incense Altar, Oil, and Incense
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Last comes the altar of incense, which stood just before the veil. It is square, with horns of one piece with it, overlaid with gold and fitted with rings and poles (vv. 25–28). Then the holy anointing oil and the fragrant incense are made, “blended as by the perfumer” (v. 29). The place of prayer and the means of consecration are prepared with the same care as everything else, by people skilled enough to do it properly.
verseByVerse.theology:
Skill Credited

A perfumer's competence is recorded as service to God.
verseByVerse.examples: Ordinary skill, done well and offered to God, is noticed and honoured by him.

verseByVerse.quote: He made the altar of incense of acacia wood. Its length was a cubit, and its breadth was a cubit. It was square, and two cubits was its height. Its horns were of one piece with it. He overlaid it with pure gold, its top and around its sides and its horns. And he made a molding of gold around it, and made two rings of gold on it under its molding, on two opposite sides of it, as holders for the poles with which to carry it. And he made the poles of acacia wood and overlaid them with gold. He made the holy anointing oil also, and the pure fragrant incense, blended as by the perfumer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The altar of incense, the anointing oil and the incense are made with a craftsman’s care, ready for prayer and consecration.

Blended as by the perfumer. The golden altar stood just before the veil, its smoke picturing prayer rising to God (Psalm 141:2; Revelation 8:3–4). The narrator also pays a small tribute: the oil and incense were compounded to God’s formula by someone who knew how to do it properly. Skill offered to God is not a side issue in this book; it is named, credited and Spirit-given.

keyVerse.quote: And he made a mercy seat of pure gold. Two cubits and a half was its length, and a cubit and a half its breadth.
keyVerse.note: Everything else in the tent surrounds this lid. It is the place where blood covered sin and the unseen God met his people, the picture Paul uses for what Christ did on the cross (Romans 3:25).

37.reflection:
Israel had just worshipped God in a way they invented (32:4–5). Why does it matter that we come to God in the way he has given rather than one we prefer?

The mercy seat stood at the very centre of the camp. What does it tell you about God that the heart of his house was a place where sin is covered?

Jesus calls himself the bread of life and the light of the world. Which of these pictures speaks most to where you are this week, and why?

The narrator credits the perfumer’s skill (v. 29). What skill or ordinary work of yours could you offer to God with the same care?

38.title: The Altar, the Court, and the Reckoning
38.text: <sup>1</sup>He made the altar of burnt offering of acacia wood. Five cubits was its length, and five cubits its breadth. It was square, and three cubits was its height.<sup>2</sup>He made horns for it on its four corners. Its horns were of one piece with it, and he overlaid it with bronze.<sup>3</sup>And he made all the utensils of the altar, the pots, the shovels, the basins, the forks, and the fire pans. He made all its utensils of bronze.<sup>4</sup>And he made for the altar a grating, a network of bronze, under its ledge, extending halfway down.<sup>5</sup>He cast four rings on the four corners of the bronze grating as holders for the poles.<sup>6</sup>He made the poles of acacia wood and overlaid them with bronze.<sup>7</sup>And he put the poles through the rings on the sides of the altar to carry it with them. He made it hollow, with boards.<sup>8</sup>He made the basin of bronze and its stand of bronze, from the mirrors of the ministering women who ministered in the entrance of the tent of meeting.<sup>9</sup>And he made the court. For the south side the hangings of the court were of fine twined linen, a hundred cubits;<sup>10</sup>their twenty pillars and their twenty bases were of bronze, but the hooks of the pillars and their fillets were of silver.<sup>11</sup>And for the north side there were hangings of a hundred cubits; their twenty pillars and their twenty bases were of bronze, but the hooks of the pillars and their fillets were of silver.<sup>12</sup>And for the west side were hangings of fifty cubits, their ten pillars, and their ten bases; the hooks of the pillars and their fillets were of silver.<sup>13</sup>And for the front to the east, fifty cubits.<sup>14</sup>The hangings for one side of the gate were fifteen cubits, with their three pillars and three bases.<sup>15</sup>And so for the other side. On both sides of the gate of the court were hangings of fifteen cubits, with their three pillars and their three bases.<sup>16</sup>All the hangings around the court were of fine twined linen.<sup>17</sup>And the bases for the pillars were of bronze, but the hooks of the pillars and their fillets were of silver. The overlaying of their capitals was also of silver, and all the pillars of the court were filleted with silver.<sup>18</sup>And the screen for the gate of the court was embroidered with needlework in blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen. It was twenty cubits long and five cubits high in its breadth, corresponding to the hangings of the court.<sup>19</sup>And their pillars were four in number. Their four bases were of bronze, their hooks of silver, and the overlaying of their capitals and their fillets of silver.<sup>20</sup>And all the pegs for the tabernacle and for the court all around were of bronze.<sup>21</sup>These are the records of the tabernacle, the tabernacle of the testimony, as they were recorded at the commandment of Moses, the responsibility of the Levites under the direction of Ithamar the son of Aaron the priest.<sup>22</sup>Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, made all that the LORD commanded Moses;<sup>23</sup>and with him was Oholiab the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, an engraver and designer and embroiderer in blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen.<sup>24</sup>All the gold that was used for the work, in all the construction of the sanctuary, the gold from the offering, was twenty-nine talents and 730 shekels, by the shekel of the sanctuary.<sup>25</sup>The silver from those of the congregation who were recorded was a hundred talents and 1,775 shekels, by the shekel of the sanctuary:<sup>26</sup>a beka a head (that is, half a shekel, by the shekel of the sanctuary), for everyone who was listed in the records, from twenty years old and upward, for 603,550 men.<sup>27</sup>The hundred talents of silver were for casting the bases of the sanctuary and the bases of the veil; a hundred bases for the hundred talents, a talent a base.<sup>28</sup>And of the 1,775 shekels he made hooks for the pillars and overlaid their capitals and made fillets for them.<sup>29</sup>The bronze that was offered was seventy talents and 2,400 shekels;<sup>30</sup>with it he made the bases for the entrance of the tent of meeting, the bronze altar and the bronze grating for it and all the utensils of the altar,<sup>31</sup>the bases around the court, and the bases of the gate of the court, all the pegs of the tabernacle, and all the pegs around the court.
38.overview:
Where we are. Inside the tent the holy furnishings are finished (chapter 37). Now Bezalel moves outward to the things that stood in the open air: the bronze altar, the basin and the linen court. The chapter closes with the accounts for the whole project.

The message. The way to God is open, but it is ordered. There is one gate, and inside it everyone meets first an altar of sacrifice and then a basin for washing: no one comes near a holy God except through atonement and cleansing. And the gifts given for his house, from the women’s mirrors to the silver of the ransom money, are received, used and accounted for with care.

Why it was said. A people who had broken the covenant within weeks of making it (chapter 32) needed to see that the God who forgave them was still holy, and that his forgiveness came by a way he provided (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. First the bronze altar of burnt offering, with all its utensils, and the bronze basin, made from mirrors given by women who served at the entrance (vv. 1–8). Then the court: linen hangings on sixty pillars, a wall broken by a single embroidered gate (vv. 9–20). Last, a public reckoning under Ithamar of every talent of gold, silver and bronze, with the silver traced to the half-shekel paid by each of 603,550 men as a ransom for his life (vv. 21–31).

Where it leads. By pattern and by the need it exposes. The altar at the gate says that sinners come to God only through a death in their place, a need finally met when Christ offered himself once for all. The basin points to the cleansing he gives, “our bodies washed with pure water” (Hebrews 10:22). The single gate anticipates the one who said, “I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved” (John 10:9). And the silver bases, cast from ransom money, rest the whole sanctuary on redemption, the price Peter says was paid for us “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19).

For us. There is still one way into God’s presence, and it is wide open to anyone who comes through Christ. Those who come find that he notices the quiet, costly gifts nobody asked for, and that his work is to be done honestly, in the open.
38.theology:
The order of approach to God. Altar and basin at the entrance declare that we come to God through sacrifice and cleansing, both fulfilled in Christ.

Consecration transforms what we treasure. When people give themselves to God, the things they prize become tools for his service.

Integrity in God's work. Every ounce is accounted for, openly, as Paul later accounted for the gifts he carried.
38.examples:
Then: the altar, the basin made from surrendered mirrors, the court with its one gate, and a transparent reckoning of every gift.

Now: we approach God only through Christ's sacrifice and cleansing. Grace reorders our treasures, and God's work is still to be done with integrity.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-8 — The Bronze Altar and the Basin of Mirrors
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the entrance to God’s house stand an altar and a basin: sacrifice first, then washing. Bezalel makes the altar of burnt offering of acacia wood overlaid with bronze, square, with horns at its corners (vv. 1–2), all its bronze utensils (v. 3), a bronze grating, and rings and poles for carrying it (vv. 4–7). Then he makes the bronze basin and its stand from the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance of the tent (v. 8), a gift no instruction asked for and the narrator does not forget.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Detail in No Instruction

A gift God never asked for is recorded all the same.
verseByVerse.examples: Gifts nobody commanded are noticed by God. Quiet sacrifices made in his service are not forgotten.

verseByVerse.quote: He made the altar of burnt offering of acacia wood. Five cubits was its length, and five cubits its breadth. It was square, and three cubits was its height. He made horns for it on its four corners. Its horns were of one piece with it, and he overlaid it with bronze. And he made all the utensils of the altar, the pots, the shovels, the basins, the forks, and the fire pans. He made all its utensils of bronze. And he made for the altar a grating, a network of bronze, under its ledge, extending halfway down. He cast four rings on the four corners of the bronze grating as holders for the poles. He made the poles of acacia wood and overlaid them with bronze. And he put the poles through the rings on the sides of the altar to carry it with them. He made it hollow, with boards. He made the basin of bronze and its stand of bronze, from the mirrors of the ministering women who ministered in the entrance of the tent of meeting.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone who drew near came past the altar and the basin, by sacrifice and by washing; and the basin was cast from mirrors that serving women gave up.

The altar of burnt offering. The largest object in the sanctuary stood just inside the gate, so that nobody reached the tent without passing it. The way to God began with a death in the worshipper’s place.

The mirrors of the ministering women. Bronze mirrors were costly, polished metal and one of the few ways to see your own face. Women serving at the entrance gave theirs up, and they were melted into the basin where the priests washed before entering God’s presence. Nobody commanded it; it is recorded because it happened. The basin washed hands and feet; the cleansing it pointed to is Christ’s, with “our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water” (Hebrews 10:22).

Uncertain wording. The verb behind “ministered” is used of military service and of the Levites’ duties at the tent (Numbers 4:23). These women appear again in 1 Samuel 2:22, but Scripture never says what their work was, only that it was a recognised, regular duty.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The court gives God’s house a boundary and a single way in. Linen hangings on bronze-based pillars with silver hooks enclose a rectangle a hundred cubits by fifty: twenty pillars on each long side and ten at the west (vv. 9–12). The east end has fifteen cubits of hangings either side of the gate (vv. 13–17), and the gate itself is a screen twenty cubits wide, embroidered in blue, purple and scarlet (vv. 18–19). Even the pegs are listed (v. 20). There is one gate in an otherwise unbroken wall.
verseByVerse.theology:
One Gate, As Specified

The court rises in bronze outside, silver on the hooks and gold within, with a single way in.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: one gate in an unbroken wall. Now: Christ is the one door (John 10:9).

verseByVerse.quote: And he made the court. For the south side the hangings of the court were of fine twined linen, a hundred cubits; their twenty pillars and their twenty bases were of bronze, but the hooks of the pillars and their fillets were of silver. And for the north side there were hangings of a hundred cubits; their twenty pillars and their twenty bases were of bronze, but the hooks of the pillars and their fillets were of silver. And for the west side were hangings of fifty cubits, their ten pillars, and their ten bases; the hooks of the pillars and their fillets were of silver. And for the front to the east, fifty cubits. The hangings for one side of the gate were fifteen cubits, with their three pillars and three bases. And so for the other side. On both sides of the gate of the court were hangings of fifteen cubits, with their three pillars and their three bases. All the hangings around the court were of fine twined linen. And the bases for the pillars were of bronze, but the hooks of the pillars and their fillets were of silver. The overlaying of their capitals was also of silver, and all the pillars of the court were filleted with silver. And the screen for the gate of the court was embroidered with needlework in blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen. It was twenty cubits long and five cubits high in its breadth, corresponding to the hangings of the court. And their pillars were four in number. Their four bases were of bronze, their hooks of silver, and the overlaying of their capitals and their fillets of silver. And all the pegs for the tabernacle and for the court all around were of bronze.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The linen court encloses God’s house with a single gate: it can be approached, but only by the way he gives.

He made the court. Linen hangings on sixty pillars enclose a space a hundred cubits by fifty (about 45 by 23 metres), with one embroidered gate, exactly as specified (27:9–19). An unbroken wall with one entrance said that God’s house was not open on any terms, and yet that there was a way in. Jesus says, “I am the door. If anyone enters by me, he will be saved” (John 10:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21-31 — The Reckoning of the Metals
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The building ends with a public audit. The records were kept by the Levites under Ithamar, Aaron’s son (v. 21), and Bezalel and Oholiab are named as the makers (vv. 22–23). Then come the figures: twenty-nine talents of gold (v. 24); over a hundred talents of silver from the half-shekel paid by 603,550 men, cast into the hundred bases and the hooks (vv. 25–28); and seventy talents of bronze for the altar, bases and pegs (vv. 29–31). Gifts for God’s house are counted, recorded and used for what they were given for.
verseByVerse.theology:
Money Given to God Is Handled in Public

Every talent is counted and its use recorded.
verseByVerse.examples: The sums were written down where anyone could check them. Churches and ministries that handle gifts openly are following this pattern.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the records of the tabernacle, the tabernacle of the testimony, as they were recorded at the commandment of Moses, the responsibility of the Levites under the direction of Ithamar the son of Aaron the priest. Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, made all that the LORD commanded Moses; and with him was Oholiab the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, an engraver and designer and embroiderer in blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen. All the gold that was used for the work, in all the construction of the sanctuary, the gold from the offering, was twenty-nine talents and 730 shekels, by the shekel of the sanctuary. The silver from those of the congregation who were recorded was a hundred talents and 1,775 shekels, by the shekel of the sanctuary: a beka a head (that is, half a shekel, by the shekel of the sanctuary), for everyone who was listed in the records, from twenty years old and upward, for 603,550 men. The hundred talents of silver were for casting the bases of the sanctuary and the bases of the veil; a hundred bases for the hundred talents, a talent a base. And of the 1,775 shekels he made hooks for the pillars and overlaid their capitals and made fillets for them. The bronze that was offered was seventy talents and 2,400 shekels; with it he made the bases for the entrance of the tent of meeting, the bronze altar and the bronze grating for it and all the utensils of the altar, the bases around the court, and the bases of the gate of the court, all the pegs of the tabernacle, and all the pegs around the court.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The building closes with a public audit of every talent of gold, silver and bronze, because gifts given to God are handled honestly and in the open.

A beka a head. Ithamar son of Aaron keeps the accounts, and every talent is itemised. The silver came from the half-shekel (a beka) each man paid, which God called “a ransom for his life” (30:12), and it was cast into the bases the sanctuary stood on. The whole house rested on ransom money. Christians were ransomed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19).

Accounts made public. A book about God dwelling with his people stops for a page of arithmetic, because the gifts were enormous and the figures were published, with the priest’s own son responsible. Paul handled his collection the same way, “for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man” (2 Corinthians 8:21).

Were there really 603,550 men (v. 26)? The silver adds up exactly: a hundred talents and 1,775 shekels is 301,775 shekels, half a shekel a man, and Numbers 1:46 gives the same total. Reading “thousand” as a clan or unit to shrink the number cannot fit an exact sum of silver. This commentary takes the numbers as written.
verseByVerse.note: A talent was about 75 pounds and a beka (half shekel) about 1/5 ounce (ESV notes): over a ton of gold went into the work.

keyVerse.quote: He made the basin of bronze and its stand of bronze, from the mirrors of the ministering women who ministered in the entrance of the tent of meeting.
keyVerse.note: Sacrifice and washing stood at the entrance to God’s house, and this verse adds a gift no one commanded. It shows both the way to God, through cleansing, and the God who sees and records the quiet devotion of people the story never names.

38.reflection:
Everyone entering the court met the altar first and then the basin (vv. 1–8). What do these teach about how a sinner can come near a holy God, and how does Christ fulfil both?

The women gave up their mirrors, which nobody had asked for (v. 8). What does it mean for you to give God something you value that no one would ever require of you?

The court had only one gate (vv. 18–19). How would you explain to a friend why Christians say Jesus is the only way to God, without sounding arrogant?

Every talent was counted and published (vv. 21–31). What would honest, open handling of money look like in your church, your giving or your home?

39.title: As the LORD Had Commanded Moses

They made the holy garments for Aaron, as the LORD had commanded Moses.<sup>2</sup>He made the ephod of gold, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and fine twined linen.<sup>3</sup>And they hammered out gold leaf, and he cut it into threads to work into the blue and purple and the scarlet yarns, and into the fine twined linen, in skilled design.<sup>4</sup>They made for the ephod attaching shoulder pieces, joined to it at its two edges.<sup>5</sup>And the skillfully woven band on it was of one piece with it and made like it, of gold, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and fine twined linen, as the LORD had commanded Moses.<sup>6</sup>They made the onyx stones, enclosed in settings of gold filigree, and engraved like the engravings of a signet, according to the names of the sons of Israel.<sup>7</sup>And he set them on the shoulder pieces of the ephod to be stones of remembrance for the sons of Israel, as the LORD had commanded Moses.<sup>8</sup>He made the breastpiece, in skilled work, in the style of the ephod, of gold, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and fine twined linen.<sup>9</sup>It was square. They made the breastpiece doubled, a span its length and a span its breadth when doubled.<sup>10</sup>And they set in it four rows of stones. A row of sardius, topaz, and carbuncle was the first row;<sup>11</sup>and the second row, an emerald, a sapphire, and a diamond;<sup>12</sup>and the third row, a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst;<sup>13</sup>and the fourth row, a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper. They were enclosed in settings of gold filigree.<sup>14</sup>There were twelve stones with their names according to the names of the sons of Israel. They were like signets, each engraved with its name, for the twelve tribes.<sup>15</sup>And they made on the breastpiece twisted chains like cords, of pure gold.<sup>16</sup>And they made two settings of gold filigree and two gold rings, and put the two rings on the two edges of the breastpiece.<sup>17</sup>And they put the two cords of gold in the two rings at the edges of the breastpiece.<sup>18</sup>They attached the two ends of the two cords to the two settings of filigree. Thus they attached it in front to the shoulder pieces of the ephod.<sup>19</sup>Then they made two rings of gold, and put them at the two ends of the breastpiece, on its inside edge next to the and all its utensils; the basin and its stand;<sup>40</sup>the hangings of the court, its pillars, and its bases, and the screen for the gate of the court, its cords, and its pegs; and all the
