of his sons for their service as priests.<sup>42</sup>According to all that the LORD had commanded Moses, so the people of Israel had done all the work.<sup>43</sup>And Moses saw all the work, and behold, they had done it; as the LORD had commanded, so had they done it. Then Moses blessed them.
39.overview:
Where we are. The tent, its furnishings and its court are finished (chapters 36–38). What remains are the clothes of the priests who will serve in it, and then the handing over of the completed work to Moses.

The message. The people who did what they wanted at the calf now do exactly what God commanded, gladly and completely. Seven times in the making of the garments, and again at the end, the refrain sounds: “as the LORD had commanded Moses.” Forgiven people have become obedient people, and when Moses sees the finished work he blesses them, in words that echo God finishing creation.

Why it was said. Israel’s covenant had nearly ended at the foot of the mountain (32:10). This chapter shows the fruit of God’s mercy: not a people anxiously earning their way back, but a forgiven people serving him with skill and care (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The ephod is made of gold thread and coloured yarn, with two onyx stones on the shoulders engraved with the names of Israel’s sons, and the breastpiece set with twelve engraved stones, one for each tribe (vv. 1–21). Then come the blue robe with its bells and pomegranates, the linen tunics, turban, caps and sash, and the gold plate engraved “Holy to the LORD” (vv. 22–31). Finally every part of the tabernacle is brought to Moses, he inspects it all, finds it done as commanded, and blesses the people (vv. 32–43).

Where it leads. By pattern, and by the need it exposes. The high priest carried his people’s names on his shoulders and over his heart, and wore on his forehead a holiness that was true of his office but not of the man who had made the calf. Christ is the high priest these garments were waiting for, “holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners” (Hebrews 7:26), who carries his people before God. And the refrain of complete obedience, which Israel kept here but would not keep for long, was finally kept without a gap by the Son who could say to his Father, “having accomplished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4).

For us. Obedience is not how we earn God’s favour but how forgiven people answer it. If past failure weighs on you, notice who built God’s house: the calf-makers, forgiven and given work. And when you see how far your obedience falls short of this refrain, look to the one whose obedience was complete, and who wears your name before God.
39.theology:
Complete, joyful obedience. The refrain "as the LORD had commanded Moses" shows the redeemed delighting to do God's will, in contrast to the self-will of the calf.

Worship by God's design. The garments and the structure are made exactly as commanded; the way to God through a priest is appointed by God and fulfilled in Christ.

A finished work, inspected and blessed. The completion echoes creation, and many Christians have heard in it an anticipation of Christ's "It is finished."
39.examples:
Then: the garments and tabernacle were completed as commanded, and Moses saw the work and blessed the people.

Now: grace produces glad obedience, by the Spirit God gives his people. Yet ours is never as complete as this refrain; Christ's was, to the last detail, so that we are counted obedient in him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priestly garments are made exactly as God commanded, and the refrain “as the LORD had commanded Moses” closes paragraph after paragraph, seven times in all. The ephod is woven with threads of beaten gold, and its shoulder pieces carry two onyx stones engraved with the names of Israel’s sons (vv. 1–7). The breastpiece holds twelve engraved stones in four rows, one for each tribe, bound to the ephod so it cannot come loose (vv. 8–21). Then come the blue robe with its golden bells and pomegranates, the linen garments for Aaron and his sons, and the gold plate on the turban engraved “Holy to the LORD” (vv. 22–31).
verseByVerse.theology:
A Phrase Like a Drumbeat

Each paragraph closes with a note of obedience.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the priest wore his people's names in stone and holiness on his forehead. Now: Christ wears both truly, for us.

verseByVerse.quote: From the blue and purple and scarlet yarns they made finely woven garments, for ministering in the Holy Place. They made the holy garments for Aaron, as the LORD had commanded Moses. He made the ephod of gold, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and fine twined linen. And they hammered out gold leaf, and he cut it into threads to work into the blue and purple and the scarlet yarns, and into the fine twined linen, in skilled design. They made for the ephod attaching shoulder pieces, joined to it at its two edges. And the skillfully woven band on it was of one piece with it and made like it, of gold, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and fine twined linen, as the LORD had commanded Moses. They made the onyx stones, enclosed in settings of gold filigree, and engraved like the engravings of a signet, according to the names of the sons of Israel. And he set them on the shoulder pieces of the ephod to be stones of remembrance for the sons of Israel, as the LORD had commanded Moses. He made the breastpiece, in skilled work, in the style of the ephod, of gold, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, and fine twined linen. It was square. They made the breastpiece doubled, a span its length and a span its breadth when doubled. And they set in it four rows of stones. A row of sardius, topaz, and carbuncle was the first row; and the second row, an emerald, a sapphire, and a diamond; and the third row, a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst; and the fourth row, a beryl, an onyx, and a jasper. They were enclosed in settings of gold filigree. There were twelve stones with their names according to the names of the sons of Israel. They were like signets, each engraved with its name, for the twelve tribes. And they made on the breastpiece twisted chains like cords, of pure gold. And they made two settings of gold filigree and two gold rings, and put the two rings on the two edges of the breastpiece. And they put the two cords of gold in the two rings at the edges of the breastpiece. They attached the two ends of the two cords to the two settings of filigree. Thus they attached it in front to the shoulder pieces of the ephod. Then they made two rings of gold, and put them at the two ends of the breastpiece, on its inside edge next to the ephod. And they made two rings of gold, and attached them in front to the lower part of the two shoulder pieces of the ephod, at its seam above the skillfully woven band of the ephod. And they bound the breastpiece by its rings to the rings of the ephod with a lace of blue, so that it should lie on the skillfully woven band of the ephod, and that the breastpiece should not come loose from the ephod, as the LORD had commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ephod and breastpiece are made as commanded, so that Israel’s high priest carries all twelve tribes on his shoulders and over his heart before God.

As the LORD had commanded Moses. One phrase recurs like a drumbeat through the making of the garments, seven times in all (vv. 1–31). After the golden calf, the repetition is the point: this time they obeyed.

They hammered out gold leaf. Gold beaten thin and cut into threads was woven in, so that the priest wore the glory of God in thread and Israel’s names in stone, on his shoulders “for remembrance” (28:12) and in the breastpiece over his heart (28:29). Christ is that kind of high priest: “we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses” (Hebrews 4:15).

Uncertain wording. Several of the twelve stones cannot be identified with confidence, since ancient gem names do not match modern ones; the “diamond”, which had to be engraved, was probably another hard stone. Each was precious, and each carried a tribe’s name.

verseByVerse.quote: He also made the robe of the ephod woven all of blue, and the opening of the robe in it was like the opening in a garment, with a binding around the opening, so that it might not tear. On the hem of the robe they made pomegranates of blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen. They also made bells of pure gold, and put the bells between the pomegranates all around the hem of the robe, between the pomegranates— a bell and a pomegranate, a bell and a pomegranate around the hem of the robe for ministering, as the LORD had commanded Moses. They also made the coats, woven of fine linen, for Aaron and his sons, and the turban of fine linen, and the caps of fine linen, and the linen undergarments of fine twined linen, and the sash of fine twined linen and of blue and purple and scarlet yarns, embroidered with needlework, as the LORD had commanded Moses. They made the plate of the holy crown of pure gold, and wrote on it an inscription, like the engraving of a signet, "Holy to the LORD." And they tied to it a cord of blue to fasten it on the turban above, as the LORD had commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The words on Aaron’s forehead declare a holiness his office required and only Christ fully possesses.

The robe of the ephod woven all of blue. Its hem carried golden bells and pomegranates, so that the priest’s movements could be heard in the Holy Place (28:35). The linen garments follow, and the refrain closes almost every paragraph.

Holy to the LORD. The words on Aaron’s forehead were true of his office, not of the man; he had made the calf. They are fully true of the high priest Hebrews describes: “holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners” (Hebrews 7:26). Zechariah foresaw a day when the same words would be “inscribed on the bells of the horses” (Zechariah 14:20), holiness reaching into ordinary life.

Uncertain wording. The rare word behind “garment” (v. 23) may mean a leather or linen corselet; the sense is a reinforced neckline that would not tear.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32-43 — The Work Finished, and Moses Blessed Them
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole work is finished and handed over. The people bring Moses everything they have made, and the narrator lists it all, from the tent and its clasps to the ark, the table, the lampstand, the altars, the court and the priests’ garments (vv. 32–41). The people have done all the work “according to all that the LORD had commanded Moses” (v. 42). Moses inspects it, sees that it is done as commanded, and blesses them (v. 43), in words that echo God seeing, finishing and blessing his creation.
verseByVerse.theology:
Written to Echo Genesis 1

The work is finished, seen, found to be as commanded, and blessed.
verseByVerse.examples: The calf-makers, forgiven and given work, did it right. Past failure does not disqualify a forgiven person from faithful service.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus all the work of the tabernacle of the tent of meeting was finished, and the people of Israel did according to all that the LORD had commanded Moses; so they did. Then they brought the tabernacle to Moses, the tent and all its utensils, its hooks, its frames, its bars, its pillars, and its bases; the covering of tanned rams' skins and goatskins, and the veil of the screen; the ark of the testimony with its poles and the mercy seat; the table with all its utensils, and the bread of the Presence; the lampstand of pure gold and its lamps with the lamps set and all its utensils, and the oil for the light; the golden altar, the anointing oil and the fragrant incense, and the screen for the entrance of the tent; the bronze altar, and its grating of bronze, its poles, and all its utensils; the basin and its stand; the hangings of the court, its pillars, and its bases, and the screen for the gate of the court, its cords, and its pegs; and all the utensils for the service of the tabernacle, for the tent of meeting; the finely worked garments for ministering in the Holy Place, the holy garments for Aaron the priest, and the garments of his sons for their service as priests. According to all that the LORD had commanded Moses, so the people of Israel had done all the work. And Moses saw all the work, and behold, they had done it; as the LORD had commanded, so had they done it. Then Moses blessed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses sees that the finished work has been done just as the LORD commanded and blesses the people, in words that echo God finishing and blessing creation.

Then Moses blessed them. Every item is carried to Moses for inspection. Read the verdict against Genesis 1–2. There the heavens and the earth “were finished” (Genesis 2:1), God saw what he had made, “and behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31), and he blessed. Here the work “was finished” (v. 32), Moses saw it, and behold, it was done as commanded, and he blessed. The tabernacle is a small world in which God dwells with people and everything is as it should be.

Forgiven people obeying. This is the nation that made the calf, and the chapter does not need to say so. Past failure does not disqualify forgiven people from faithful service. Nor did their obedience earn God’s presence: they built because they had already been forgiven (34:6–9). Their obedience would not last; Christ’s was complete, “having accomplished the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4).

keyVerse.quote: And Moses saw all the work, and behold, they had done it; as the LORD had commanded, so had they done it. Then Moses blessed them.
keyVerse.note: The verse gathers up the chapter’s refrain and echoes God seeing and blessing his finished creation. The people who made the calf, now forgiven, have done everything God said, and the last word before the glory comes is a blessing.

39.reflection:
The refrain “as the LORD had commanded Moses” sounds again and again. How is obedience that flows from being forgiven different from obedience that tries to earn forgiveness?

Aaron wore the names of the tribes on his shoulders and over his heart. What does it mean to you that Christ carries your name before God?

“Holy to the LORD” was true of Aaron’s office but not of Aaron. Where do you most feel the gap between what you are called to be and what you are, and how does Hebrews 7:26 speak into it?

The calf-makers built God’s house. Is there a past failure that makes you feel disqualified from serving God, and what does this chapter say to it?

40.title: The Glory of the LORD Filled the Tabernacle
40.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,<sup>2</sup>"On the first day of the first month you shall erect the tabernacle of the tent of meeting.<sup>3</sup>And you shall put in it the ark of the testimony, and you shall screen the ark with the veil.<sup>4</sup>And you shall bring in the table and arrange it, and you shall bring in the lampstand and set up its lamps.<sup>5</sup>And you shall put the golden altar for incense before the ark of the testimony, and set up the screen for the door of the tabernacle.<sup>6</sup>You shall set the altar of burnt offering before the door of the tabernacle of the tent of meeting,<sup>7</sup>and place the basin between the tent of meeting and the altar, and put water in it.<sup>8</sup>And you shall set up the court all around, and hang up the screen for the gate of the court.<sup>9</sup>"Then you shall take the anointing oil and anoint the tabernacle and all that is in it, and consecrate it and all its furniture, so that it may become holy.<sup>10</sup>You shall also anoint the altar of burnt offering and all its utensils, and consecrate the altar, so that the altar may become most holy.<sup>11</sup>You shall also anoint the basin and its stand, and consecrate it.<sup>12</sup>Then you shall bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the tent of meeting and shall wash them with water<sup>13</sup>and put on Aaron the holy garments. And you shall anoint him and consecrate him, that he may serve me as priest.<sup>14</sup>You shall bring his sons also and put coats on them,<sup>15</sup>and anoint them, as you anointed their father, that they may serve me as priests. And their anointing shall admit them to a perpetual priesthood throughout their generations."<sup>16</sup>This Moses did; according to all that the LORD commanded him, so he did.<sup>17</sup>In the first month in the second year, on the first day of the month, the tabernacle was erected.<sup>18</sup>Moses erected the tabernacle. He laid its bases, and set up its frames, and put in its poles, and raised up its pillars.<sup>19</sup>And he spread the tent over the tabernacle and put the covering of the tent over it, as the LORD had commanded Moses.<sup>20</sup>He took the testimony and put it into the ark, and put the poles on the ark and set the mercy seat above on the ark.<sup>21</sup>And he brought the ark into the tabernacle and set up the veil of the screen, and screened the ark of the testimony, as the LORD had commanded Moses.<sup>22</sup>He put the table in the tent of meeting, on the north side of the tabernacle, outside the veil,<sup>23</sup>and arranged the bread on it before the LORD, as the LORD had commanded Moses.<sup>24</sup>He put the lampstand in the tent of meeting, opposite the table on the south side of the tabernacle,<sup>25</sup>and set up the lamps before the LORD, as the LORD had commanded Moses.<sup>26</sup>He put the golden altar in the tent of meeting before the veil,<sup>27</sup>and burned fragrant incense on it, as the LORD had commanded Moses.<sup>28</sup>He put in place the screen for the door of the tabernacle.<sup>29</sup>And he set the altar of burnt offering at the entrance of the tabernacle of the tent of meeting, and offered on it the burnt offering and the grain offering, as the LORD had commanded Moses.<sup>30</sup>He set the basin between the tent of meeting and the altar, and put water in it for washing,<sup>31</sup>with which Moses and Aaron and his sons washed their hands and their feet.<sup>32</sup>When they went into the tent of meeting, and when they approached the altar, they washed, as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>33</sup>And he erected the court around the tabernacle and the altar, and set up the screen of the gate of the court. So Moses finished the work.<sup>34</sup>Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle.<sup>35</sup>And Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting because the cloud settled on it, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle.<sup>36</sup>Throughout all their journeys, whenever the cloud was taken up from over the tabernacle, the people of Israel would set out.<sup>37</sup>But if the cloud was not taken up, then they did not set out till the day that it was taken up.<sup>38</sup>For the cloud of the LORD was on the tabernacle by day, and fire was in it by night, in the sight of all the house of Israel throughout all their journeys.
40.overview:
Where we are. Every part of the tabernacle has been made and inspected, and Moses has blessed the people (chapter 39). Almost a year after the first Passover, the book reaches its last scene.

The message. The God who came down to rescue his people now comes down to live among them. When the tent is set up exactly as he commanded, his glory fills it, so fully that not even Moses can go in. From then on Israel’s whole life is ordered by his presence: they move when the cloud moves and stay when it stays. Redemption has reached its goal, God dwelling with his people.

Why it was said. The book opened with slaves building store cities for Pharaoh (1:11) and nearly broke apart at the calf, when God threatened not to go up among them (33:3). This ending answers both: the people are free, forgiven, and the LORD himself is in the middle of their camp (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. God commands Moses to set up the tabernacle on the first day of the first month, to anoint it and its furnishings, and to wash, clothe and anoint Aaron and his sons (vv. 1–15); Moses does it all (v. 16). Then Moses raises the tent piece by piece, the refrain “as the LORD had commanded Moses” sounding seven times, until “Moses finished the work” (vv. 17–33). And the glory of the LORD fills the tabernacle, and the cloud leads Israel on all their journeys (vv. 34–38).

Where it leads. By promise and by pattern, and by a need left open. God had said he brought Israel out “that I might dwell among them” (29:46), and here he does. Yet Moses stands outside: God has come near, but the way in is not yet open. The next book begins with God calling to Moses from the tent and giving the sacrifices (Leviticus 1:1). In Christ the promise is kept in person: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). By his blood “we have confidence to enter the holy places” (Hebrews 10:19), and at the end a loud voice says, “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man” (Revelation 21:3).

For us. The point of salvation is not only to get us out but to bring us home to God. A Christian’s life, like Israel’s in the desert, is shaped by his presence: following where Christ leads, waiting when he says wait, and living in the sight of a glory that will one day fill everything.
40.theology:
God dwells with his people. The glory filling the tabernacle is the climax of Exodus: "I will dwell among them" is fulfilled.

A finished work and a new creation. "Moses finished the work" echoes creation and points to Christ's finished work, which opens the way into God's presence.

The trajectory of glory. The tabernacle glory points to Christ, who tabernacled among us (John 1:14), to Pentecost, and to the New Jerusalem, where God dwells with man forever.
40.examples:
Then: the glory of the LORD filled the finished tabernacle, and the God who redeemed his people dwelt in their midst.

Now: he brought us out that he might bring us in, to dwell in his presence forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-16 — Command to Raise the Tabernacle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s new year begins with God’s house. The LORD tells Moses to set up the tabernacle on the first day of the first month (vv. 1–2) and lays out the order of assembly, from the ark and veil inward to the court outside (vv. 3–8). Then everything is to be anointed and made holy, the altar most holy (vv. 9–11), and Aaron and his sons washed, clothed and anointed to a perpetual priesthood (vv. 12–15). The section closes on obedience: Moses did all that the LORD commanded him (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Date

Israel's new year begins with God's house set up.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel's first year of freedom ended with God moving in. A redeemed life is ordered around his presence.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, "On the first day of the first month you shall erect the tabernacle of the tent of meeting. And you shall put in it the ark of the testimony, and you shall screen the ark with the veil. And you shall bring in the table and arrange it, and you shall bring in the lampstand and set up its lamps. And you shall put the golden altar for incense before the ark of the testimony, and set up the screen for the door of the tabernacle. You shall set the altar of burnt offering before the door of the tabernacle of the tent of meeting, and place the basin between the tent of meeting and the altar, and put water in it. And you shall set up the court all around, and hang up the screen for the gate of the court. "Then you shall take the anointing oil and anoint the tabernacle and all that is in it, and consecrate it and all its furniture, so that it may become holy. You shall also anoint the altar of burnt offering and all its utensils, and consecrate the altar, so that the altar may become most holy. You shall also anoint the basin and its stand, and consecrate it. Then you shall bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the tent of meeting and shall wash them with water and put on Aaron the holy garments. And you shall anoint him and consecrate him, that he may serve me as priest. You shall bring his sons also and put coats on them, and anoint them, as you anointed their father, that they may serve me as priests. And their anointing shall admit them to a perpetual priesthood throughout their generations." This Moses did; according to all that the LORD commanded him, so he did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Moses to set up and anoint the tabernacle on New Year’s Day and to consecrate its priests, so that Israel’s second year of freedom begins with God’s house in the middle of the camp.

On the first day of the first month. This is the first day of the second year (v. 17), almost a year since the first Passover, in the calendar God reset in 12:2 (see The Jewish calendar and months). Israel’s first year as a free people ends with God moving in.

This Moses did. The order of assembly runs from the ark and veil outward to the court; everything is anointed, and Aaron and his sons are washed, clothed and consecrated. The section closes with a sentence that will be repeated seven more times before the chapter ends: Moses did all that the LORD commanded him.

A perpetual priesthood? Aaron’s line was to serve “throughout their generations” (v. 15), and it did, for as long as the covenant at Sinai lasted. Hebrews explains that this priesthood was a shadow, replaced by Christ, who holds his priesthood permanently because he continues forever (Hebrews 7:23–24).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses sets up the tabernacle exactly as commanded, and the narrator marks each step. The frames and coverings go up (vv. 17–19); the testimony is placed in the ark and the veil hung (vv. 20–21); the table, lampstand and golden altar are set in place and put to use (vv. 22–27); then the entrance screen, the altar of burnt offering, the basin and the court (vv. 28–33). Seven times the refrain sounds, “as the LORD had commanded Moses,” and then, as at the end of creation, “Moses finished the work” (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology:
Creation Language

Seven acts of obedience lead to a finished work.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Moses finished the work, as God once finished his. Now: Christ finished the work that brings God and his people together for good.

verseByVerse.quote: In the first month in the second year, on the first day of the month, the tabernacle was erected. Moses erected the tabernacle. He laid its bases, and set up its frames, and put in its poles, and raised up its pillars. And he spread the tent over the tabernacle and put the covering of the tent over it, as the LORD had commanded Moses. He took the testimony and put it into the ark, and put the poles on the ark and set the mercy seat above on the ark. And he brought the ark into the tabernacle and set up the veil of the screen, and screened the ark of the testimony, as the LORD had commanded Moses. He put the table in the tent of meeting, on the north side of the tabernacle, outside the veil, and arranged the bread on it before the LORD, as the LORD had commanded Moses. He put the lampstand in the tent of meeting, opposite the table on the south side of the tabernacle, and set up the lamps before the LORD, as the LORD had commanded Moses. He put the golden altar in the tent of meeting before the veil, and burned fragrant incense on it, as the LORD had commanded Moses. He put in place the screen for the door of the tabernacle. And he set the altar of burnt offering at the entrance of the tabernacle of the tent of meeting, and offered on it the burnt offering and the grain offering, as the LORD had commanded Moses. He set the basin between the tent of meeting and the altar, and put water in it for washing, with which Moses and Aaron and his sons washed their hands and their feet. When they went into the tent of meeting, and when they approached the altar, they washed, as the LORD commanded Moses. And he erected the court around the tabernacle and the altar, and set up the screen of the gate of the court. So Moses finished the work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses sets up every part exactly as commanded, seven times over, and then finishes the work, as God once finished the work of creation.

Moses erected the tabernacle. The narrator walks through the tent item by item: frames, coverings, the testimony placed in the ark, the veil, the table set with bread, the lamps lit, the incense burned, the burnt offering made, the basin filled, the court raised round it all. Seven times he stops to say as the LORD had commanded Moses, a sevenfold rhythm like the seven days of Genesis 1.

So Moses finished the work. The words echo Genesis 2:2, where “God finished his work that he had done” and rested. The book that began with slaves making bricks for a tyrant ends with a free people finishing a house for their God, told in creation language.
verseByVerse.note: Israel had arrived at Sinai in the third month (19:1), so Israel spent most of a year at the mountain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 34-38 — The Glory Fills the Tabernacle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The glory of the LORD fills the finished tabernacle. The cloud covers the tent of meeting and the glory fills it, so that even Moses cannot enter (vv. 34–35). From then on the cloud governs Israel’s journeys: when it lifts they set out, and when it stays they stay (vv. 36–37), with the cloud by day and fire by night in the sight of all Israel (v. 38). The book that began in slavery ends with God living among his people and leading them.
verseByVerse.theology:
What the Whole Book Was Travelling Toward

God takes up residence in the middle of the camp.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel's only plan was the presence of God. A Christian's life, too, is shaped by following where he leads.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. And Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting because the cloud settled on it, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. Throughout all their journeys, whenever the cloud was taken up from over the tabernacle, the people of Israel would set out. But if the cloud was not taken up, then they did not set out till the day that it was taken up. For the cloud of the LORD was on the tabernacle by day, and fire was in it by night, in the sight of all the house of Israel throughout all their journeys.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The glory of the LORD fills the finished tabernacle so fully that even Moses cannot enter, and from then on God’s presence leads his people on every stage of their journey.

The glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. This is what the whole book has been travelling toward: not the sea, not the mountain, not the law, but this. At the bush God said, “I have come down to deliver them” (3:8); he brought them out “that I might dwell among them” (29:46); and here he arrives and takes up residence in the middle of the camp.

Moses was not able to enter. The man who spoke with God face to face stands outside his own tent. The glory is not tame: God has come near without becoming any less holy. The same happened when Solomon’s temple was dedicated, when the priests “could not stand to minister because of the cloud” (1 Kings 8:11).

What the glory of the LORD is. We use “glory” for fame or a fine view, so the phrase can sound vague. The Hebrew word, kabod, comes from a root meaning “heavy”. God’s glory is his weight: the sheer reality and worth of who he is, made visible, here as a cloud so full of him that there was no room left for Moses. Beside it everything else is light, which is why the things we make heaviest in our lives, a reputation, a bank balance, someone’s approval, crush us when we load them with a weight only God can bear. This glory has a face: the Son “is the radiance of the glory of God” (Hebrews 1:3), and through him even our troubles are “preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison” (2 Corinthians 4:17). When something other than God starts to feel like the heaviest thing in your week, take it as a call to look at him again. See also Glory in the Theological Dictionary.

Throughout all their journeys. The last verses describe every day that followed, and the book ends without arriving anywhere. Israel is camped in a desert round a tent, watching a cloud, and their whole travel plan is to move when it moves and stay when it stays: a people whose only plan is the presence of God.

And dwelt among us. Centuries later John wrote of someone he had eaten and travelled with, and reached for this scene: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father (John 1:14). The verb means to pitch a tent. The glory that kept Moses outside walked out of Nazareth as a man and let people sit beside him.

The end of the story. The last page of Scripture finishes the sentence. There is no temple in the city, because God himself is there (Revelation 21:22), and a loud voice says, Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God (Revelation 21:3). That is Exodus 40:34 with the tent removed, the veil gone and nobody standing outside.

keyVerse.quote: Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle.
keyVerse.note: This is the goal of the whole book. The God who came down to deliver his people now comes down to dwell with them, a promise fulfilled in Christ, who “dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and completed when God dwells with his people forever (Revelation 21:3).

40.reflection:
Exodus ends not with Israel in the promised land but with God living among them. Why do you think the book makes God’s presence, rather than freedom or the land, its climax?

Even Moses could not enter the tent when the glory filled it (v. 35). How does that help you appreciate what Christ has opened for us (Hebrews 10:19)?

God’s glory is his “weight”. What in your life is starting to feel heavier than God, and what would it look like to look at him again?

Israel moved when the cloud moved and stayed when it stayed. Where are you finding it hardest to wait for God’s leading, or to follow it, right now?
